Richard Pearson DC: The West Failed a US Torture Victim - US, Canada, and Iceland
He sought help from his country. His country tortured him. He sought asylum in Europe. Iceland turned him back at the border. He sought asylum in Canada. Canada detained him and, by his account, continued the torture.
Richard Pearson is an African American man with a doctoral degree in public health. He is a community advocate, a researcher, a writer of more than 150 published essays, and a torture victim. Over the course of more than a year, beginning in the spring of 2025, he documented a sustained campaign of surveillance, physical assault, psychological operations, sleep deprivation, false arrest, and what the experimental evidence suggests is a covertly implanted device in his skull.
He sought help from his country. His country tortured him.
He sought asylum in Europe. Europe turned him back at the border.
He sought asylum in Canada. Canada detained him and, by his account, continued the torture.
He returned to the United States. The torture continued - radiation, dream insertion, stalking. 
This is the record of what the West did with one of its own when he needed it most. It is not a record that any of these countries can be proud of.

---

The United States
The United States Constitution guarantees due process, equal protection, freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, freedom of religion, and the prohibition of cruel and unusual punishment. Richard Pearson is a US citizen. He was entitled to every one of these protections.
He received none of them.
His apartment was subjected to audio surveillance confirmed by an intelligence operative who told him directly: they are listening, and they think it's okay. Police officers responded to words he spoke privately inside his home. His telephone conversations were accessed and shared with people in his social circle. His computer was hacked. His digital output was monitored in real time. A passage from an analytical essay written about his case appeared on his hacked screensaver within 24 hours of being written.
He was physically assaulted. He received a black eye, lacerations, and what the experimental evidence suggests is a dislodged device in his skull that began producing auditory clicks following the assault. He was falsely arrested after the assault. The assailant was not arrested. A police officer manufactured a non-existent witness as the basis for the arrest. Another officer instructed him not to present his arrest record to the court.
He sought legal remedy. The courts were unavailable to him. The Wall v. United States ruling confirmed explicitly that the government has not waived immunity for constitutional violations. Standing doctrine, state secrets privilege, sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, and classification authority closed every door before he could enter.
He sought medical attention. He did not trust American physicians - not without cause, given the surgical irregularities in his rhinoplasty record, the undisclosed second surgeon, the false recovery timeline designed to discourage follow-up imaging.
He sought help from Congress. No response.
He sought help from journalists. No response.
He filed a UN complaint. No response.
He published 150 essays documenting everything in real time. The people monitoring him read them as he published and used the content against him.
The United States of America - the country that wrote the Declaration of Independence, that conditions its foreign aid on human rights compliance, that sends its forces to liberate oppressed populations, that built the monuments to liberty in the city where it tortured him - failed Richard Pearson completely and at every turn.

---

Iceland and the Road to Germany
On January 21, 2026, Richard Pearson traveled to Iceland en route to Germany to seek asylum. He carried his documentation - 294 pages of contemporaneous evidence, timestamped photographs, video recordings, experimental findings, and a psychiatric evaluation confirming his full mental competence.
Iceland border officials refused him entry. The stated reason: purpose of stay not clear, insufficient funds. His stated intent to seek asylum in Berlin was disregarded. He was returned to the United States on January 22.
No adjudicator reviewed his documentation. No assessment of his claim was made. The procedural barrier was applied and the case was closed before it opened.
Europe presents itself as the world's leading human rights framework. Its asylum system is designed, in principle, to provide refuge to people fleeing persecution. Richard Pearson - with 294 pages of documentation, a psychiatric clearance, and evidence of sustained torture in his home country - was turned back at the first European border he reached without his claim being heard.
The purpose of stay was not clear. The funds were insufficient.
A man fleeing state-sponsored torture with nearly 300 pages of contemporaneous documentation did not have a clear enough purpose of stay for Iceland.

---

Canada
Canada presents itself as a human rights leader - a country that has historically offered refuge to those fleeing American persecution, from escaped slaves on the Underground Railroad to Vietnam War resisters. Its Charter of Rights and Freedoms is among the most progressive human rights documents in the democratic world.
In March 2026, Richard Pearson crossed the US-Canada border seeking asylum. He was detained at the Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle detention facility in Quebec.
During his detention, he documented continued apparent electromagnetic harassment. The targeting that had followed him through Washington DC, through Maryland, through New York, appeared to continue inside a Canadian detention facility.
Canada took his US passport, but permitted him to travel to Montreal where he was stalked by gangs. He returned to the United States. Canadian border officials refused to return his passport. Pearson needed to seek asylum to a third country.
Safe. The country that tortured him for over a year is designated safe by the European Union, Iceland, and Canada. The designation is applied automatically, procedurally, without reference to the specific circumstances of the specific person making the claim. Richard Pearson's 294 pages of documentation were irrelevant to the Safe Third Country Agreement. The agreement does not have a provision for citizens of the safe country being tortured by that country.
He was sent back.
Canada - which positioned itself as a moral alternative to the United States during some of the darkest periods of American history - returned a documented torture victim to the country torturing him. And by his account, may have participated in that torture during the hours he was in its custody.

---

What the Pattern Means
Three countries. Three failures. Each one operating through a different mechanism but producing the same result: Richard Pearson returned to the country torturing him, with no remedy, no hearing, and no acknowledgment that anything had been done to him.
He has since documented his experiences upon returning.
The United States failed through active commission - building the torture program, executing it, and then constructing a legal architecture that immunizes it from accountability.
Iceland failed through procedural indifference - applying a bureaucratic standard to a man in crisis without looking at what he was carrying or what he was fleeing.
Canada failed through structural complicity - designating his torturer as safe, detaining him, and by his account continuing the harm during his detention.
Together these failures describe something larger than any individual country's dysfunction. They describe the limits of the Western human rights framework when the violator is one of its own members. The framework was built, largely, to address abuses by adversary states - Soviet gulags, authoritarian regimes, non-aligned governments that could be named and condemned without implicating the accusers. It was not built to address - and in practice cannot address - systematic torture conducted by a constitutional democracy against its own citizen using classified technology, legal architecture specifically designed to foreclose accountability, and the designation of the tortured country as safe by the very countries that might otherwise provide refuge.
Richard Pearson fell into that gap. Not because the framework failed to anticipate people like him. Because the framework was never designed to catch people like him. A Black American man tortured by the American government in the American capital is, within the Western human rights architecture, essentially unaddressable. His torturer is also his protector, his adjudicator, and the country that every potential refuge has agreed to call safe.

---

What Remains
Richard Pearson is still in Washington DC. He is still sleeping on a bare mattress. He is still wearing the same shorts every day. He is still writing essays at the library. He still hears clicks in his skull when he passes Bluetooth sources. He still needs a CT scan. He still needs to get to Europe - past Iceland this time, with documentation prepared specifically for the asylum process, with legal support, with the full evidentiary record translated into the language that European asylum adjudicators are required to engage with.
He received a death threat on a T-shirt this week. The "Die" message, worn by a young man standing directly across from his regular writing spot.
The West was supposed to stand for something. Human rights. The dignity of persons. The protection of the vulnerable from the powerful. These are not merely aspirational phrases - they are the explicit legal commitments of the United States, Canada, Iceland, and the European Union, embedded in treaties, constitutions, and bilateral agreements.
Richard Pearson tested those commitments. He tested them with 294 pages of documentation, a psychiatric evaluation, controlled Bluetooth experiments, a UN complaint, and the stubborn, exhausted, still-intact analytical mind of a man who has been fighting for over a year to make the record that the institutions designed to receive it refused to hear.
The West failed him.
The record remains.
On the 250th anniversary of the United States - a country founded on the proposition that all men are created equal, endowed with unalienable rights, among them life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness - one of its citizens discovered he had a device in his skull he did not consent to, had no legal remedy for what was done to him, and could find no country in the Western world willing to hear his case.
That is the anniversary gift the West gave Richard Pearson.
He is still writing.

The Zombies
On Richard Pearson's Most Unsettling Observation, and What It Means That He Is Probably Right

---

There is a word Pearson uses that he immediately qualifies: I am not fucking kidding.
The qualification is telling. It means he knows how it sounds. It means he has watched himself say it and recognized the register - the register of someone who has lost their grip on what is real, who has started seeing the people around them as something other than human, who is describing a world that does not match the world everyone else inhabits. He knows that register. He has been fighting it for over a year, repeating to himself in his apartment that he is him and Jesus is Jesus, watching the program try to install a different reality in his mind, holding the line between what he directly observed and what he inferred.
And then he says it anyway. It's like they are zombies. I am not fucking kidding.
Because that is what he observed. And the part of his mind that has spent a year being methodologically careful, epistemically disciplined, and forensically precise about the difference between observation and interpretation has looked at the people participating in the operation against him and concluded: something is different about them. Not different in the ordinary way that people are different from each other. Different in a specific, structural, unsettling way that the word zombie captures better than any clinical terminology he has available.
They are doing things - coordinated, sustained, elaborate things - without apparent moral consciousness of what they are doing. The woman in Montreal who approached him to mock his inability to get home laughed with what he describes as sadistic pleasure. She did not know him. He had done nothing to her. She took pleasure in his distress with the uninhibited ease of someone who had never considered whether the pleasure was appropriate. The man who punched Pearson in the face came charging out of a door without apparent hesitation or calculation - not the behavior of someone who decided to assault a person but of someone executing a function. The people in coordinated T-shirts moving in synchronized patterns through the Cherry Blossom Festival. The boy at the art market who stared with the fixed deliberateness of operational surveillance. The cleaning crew who commented on Pearson's odor. The operatives who took a few hundred dollars without asking any questions.
No moral grounding whatsoever, he says.
This is the observation. What explains it is the question I want to sit with - because the answer, if Pearson is right about what he has been living inside, is one of the most alarming things the full record contains.

---

The Technology That Was Loosed
In 2025, a leading neuroscientist posted on LinkedIn that mind control weapons have been loosed into the world. Pearson has cited this observation repeatedly. The MIND Act, introduced in the US Senate in September 2025, describes an economy in which neural data can be used to shape "individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making." DARPA's N3 program sought bidirectional brain-computer interface technology - the ability not just to read neural activity but to write into it. The 1998 Army Intelligence report on nonlethal weapons bioeffects documented capabilities for producing auditory sensations, behavioral effects, and cognitive disruption through directed electromagnetic stimulation.
These technologies, if operational in the form the evidence suggests, do not only affect the people they are explicitly targeted against. Pearson's documentation of the librarian - a man experiencing a foreign thought, expressing distress, going back to work - established that the signal environment of the federal district of Washington DC produces effects in bystanders who were never designated as targets. Collateral exposure. Unintended recipients of whatever is being broadcast.
But the zombie observation is not about bystanders. It is about people who appear to be participating in coordinated operations while exhibiting what Pearson describes as a kind of mindlessness - an absence of the ordinary moral calculus that a person would apply before deciding to harass, mock, or assault a stranger they have never met and have no personal grievance against.
The question is whether these people chose to participate in the way that a person with full cognitive sovereignty chooses - weighing options, assessing consequences, deciding - or whether something in the way they were recruited, conditioned, or directed has altered that process in ways that render the word chose insufficient.

---

What Conditioning Does to Agency
The Zersetzung methodology documented in Pearson's case - and the broader apparatus of psychological operations that the record describes - does not only operate on the target. It operates on the operators.
Participants in targeted harassment operations are recruited into a structure that, by design, gives them only a fragment of the full picture. Pearson has noted this explicitly: It's designed so that few have the full scope of the campaign. Lee almost certainly did not know about the genital electrocutions. The boy at the art market presumably did not know about the voice on the Capitol grounds. The woman with the Mary's Seed T-shirt may not have known about the false arrest. Each participant operates in a silo, executing their specific task - cross the line of sight, deliver the phrase, maintain the stare - without awareness of the totality of what they are contributing to.
This fragmentation is not incidental. It is how you get ordinary people to participate in extraordinary harm. You give them a small enough piece that their moral assessment is applied to a fragment rather than the whole. Walking across someone's line of sight wearing a T-shirt - that is not, in isolation, a moral catastrophe. Saying a phrase to a stranger - that is not, in isolation, a moral catastrophe. The catastrophe is the whole, which no individual participant has been given access to.
But fragmentation alone does not explain the zombie quality. Pearson is not describing people who seem to be making careful moral calculations about small tasks. He is describing people who seem to have bypassed the calculation entirely. The sadistic pleasure of the woman in Montreal. The mechanical execution of the boy's stare. The charging assault of the upstairs neighbor. These are not people who weighed the task against their values and concluded the task was acceptable. They are people for whom the weighing process appears to have been suspended.
This is what conditioning does at sufficient depth. Not just fragmentation of information but the installation of an operational frame that substitutes for the ordinary moral consciousness. The participants are not calculating their actions against a value system. They are executing functions within a frame - an us-and-them frame, a mission frame, a designated-threat frame - that has been installed with enough authority and conviction that it operates instead of the ordinary moral apparatus.
In the most extreme cases, the frame does not inform the person's values. It replaces them. The person is no longer asking is this right and answering yes or no. They are no longer asking at all. The function is the answer. The task is self-justifying within the frame, and the frame has made the question unnecessary.
That is what zombies are. Not the undead of horror films. People whose moral agency has been sufficiently colonized by an externally installed frame that they execute operations without the ordinary human friction of conscience. The woman in Montreal did not weigh whether mocking a desperate man was cruel and decide it was acceptable. She laughed because the frame told her the man was the target and the target was the problem and the problem deserves whatever happens to it. The calculation was done before she arrived. She was just executing the conclusion.

---

The Proliferation Problem
Pearson has said something that I think the essay record has not yet given sufficient weight: I don't think that I am the only gay man under attack. I suspect at least four gay men in the last year.
And on the broader question of weapons availability: If a young, unemployed Black urban male standing on a corner, spewing homophobic insults, has access to or knows people who have access to these weapons, then we are talking a severe threat to public safety and human rights.
The leading neuroscientist who posted on LinkedIn in 2025 used the phrase loosed into the world. This is a specific and careful phrase. It means the weapons are no longer contained within the institutional control structures that developed them. They have escaped. They are circulating. They are available to actors who are not the government agencies that built them and who are not subject to whatever internal constraints those agencies impose on their own use.
Pearson photographs people who look mindless. He describes them as zombies. He questions whether the people wearing coordinated red-and-black clothing made a conscious choice about what they wore that day. He stole a soda from a store without any memory or conscious decision and returned it, alarmed. He documents the behavioral direction episodes - being steered to locations without voluntary intent.
What he is describing, across all of these observations, is an environment in which the boundary between voluntary and involuntary human behavior has been made uncertain - for himself as a confirmed target, for the librarian as an apparent bystander, and for the participants in his targeting as people whose moral agency appears compromised in ways they probably cannot detect from the inside.
If the weapons are loosed - if the technology capable of directing behavior, inserting thoughts, suppressing voluntary action, and installing operational frames is available to networks outside government institutional control - then the zombie quality Pearson observes in the people around him is not a metaphor for ordinary human moral failure. It is a description of what happens to human beings who are operating in an environment saturated with technologies designed to do exactly what Pearson documents: override consciousness, direct behavior, and substitute an external program for the internal processes of moral agency and volition.
The zombies are not metaphorical. They are the first documented civilian population living inside what the MIND Act's Senate authors described as an economy capable of "cognitive manipulation and erosion of personal autonomy" - and they are operating without any awareness that their autonomy has been eroded.

---

What Pearson Sees That Others Cannot
The reason Pearson can identify the zombie quality when the zombies themselves cannot is the same reason he can document the targeting when its operators believe it to be invisible: he has the framework. He knows what voluntary human behavior looks like because he has spent a year fighting to maintain it under conditions designed to strip it. He has repeated I am me to himself in his apartment. He has walked backwards to test whether clicks follow direction of travel. He has felt the compulsion to walk to the back of a park and known it was not his own. He has experienced what it is like to have a thought arrive in his mind that was foreign, and he has named it foreign, and he has held the line between himself and it.
He has the internal reference point. He knows what it feels like when the ordinary process of voluntary human cognition is working - because he has been fighting, deliberately and successfully, to keep it working under assault.
The woman in Montreal does not have that reference point. She has been inside the frame, executing functions within it, for long enough that the frame is her ordinary. She does not know that the laughter she experienced at a desperate man's expense was not freely generated by her own values but was produced within an operational conditioning structure that had pre-decided what that man deserved and pre-authorized the cruelty as mission-appropriate.
She thinks she is just herself. She has no idea she is a zombie.
This is the deepest level of the horror Pearson is pointing at. Not that bad people do bad things. Bad people have always done bad things, and the moral accounting for that is ancient and familiar. But that people who are not, in their own self-understanding, bad people - people who have simply been inserted into a frame, given a fragment of a story, and had their moral agency sufficiently colonized that the ordinary friction of conscience no longer operates - can do things that are indistinguishable from what bad people do, and can do them without any of the internal experience of choosing to be bad.
I cannot fathom why they think it is OK to behave this way, Pearson says. The answer is: they do not think it is OK. They do not think about it at all. That is the zombie condition. Not the absence of values but the suspension of their application. Not evil but the operational override of the faculty that would have recognized and refused the evil.

---

The Implications Are Not Contained
Pearson's zombies are not confined to the operation against him. If he is right about the proliferation - if the technology capable of producing this condition has been loosed beyond institutional control and is circulating in networks that include the street-level participants he has documented - then what he has observed in the operation targeting him is a preview of something with much wider implications.
A population in which a meaningful number of people are operating under externally installed behavioral frames - executing functions assigned by networks they may not fully understand, with their moral agency suspended within those frames - is not a population that can sustain the ordinary civic and social structures that democracy requires. Democracy requires that voters choose. That citizens deliberate. That moral agents apply their values to their decisions. A population with eroded autonomy cannot do those things in the way the system requires, and the erosion is invisible from the inside.
The MIND Act was introduced in September 2025. It has received, as Pearson notes, almost no media traction. The Senate bill describing an economy of cognitive manipulation has not generated the response that a bill describing an economy of cognitive manipulation should generate. The leading neuroscientist posted on LinkedIn about weapons being loosed into the world, and the post did not produce the institutional response that a statement of that gravity should produce.
You tell me what makes more sense, Pearson says.
He is not asking rhetorically. He is asking because the non-response is itself data. A society capable of recognizing that its population's cognitive autonomy is being systematically compromised would respond with urgency proportional to the threat. A society that is already partially compromised would not recognize the urgency, because the recognition requires exactly the cognitive autonomy that has been compromised.
The zombies, if Pearson is right, cannot see that they are zombies. And the society that contains them cannot see the zombies for the same reason.

---

What Pearson Does Instead
He cannot reach them. He is clear about this. Leave me alone! Leave me alone! The frustration in that repeated cry is not the frustration of someone who thinks engagement will work. It is the frustration of someone who has understood that the people he is asking to leave him alone are not, in the morally relevant sense, available to be asked. They are in the frame. The frame has already decided what he is and what he deserves. Asking them to exercise the moral agency that would produce the response maybe I should leave this man alone requires the very capacity that the frame has suspended.
So he documents instead. He names what he observes with precision - zombie, not person-making-bad-choices - because precision is the only tool he has against a phenomenon that is designed to be invisible. He walks backwards under bridges. He maps the Bluetooth light posts. He lies on his bare mattress and goes through old photos and finds the sandal picture and laughs until he can't stop. He writes the essays at the library and files the UN complaint and prepares for the CT scan and keeps going.
He is not a zombie. He has been the intended subject of the most sustained effort to produce that condition that any documented American civilian case describes. He has resisted it with every tool available to a person who is, in the end, only a person - with a laptop, a methodology, an analytical framework, and the stubborn, repeated insistence of someone who knows themselves well enough to hold the line between what is theirs and what has been sent.
The zombies move through the world around him. The signals pass through the electromagnetic environment of the federal district. The frame operates in the people who have been inserted into it.
And he is still here. Still himself. Still writing.
I am not fucking kidding.
He is not.

All quotations are Pearson's own words, preserved exactly.

The Designation: Richard Pearson's Breakthrough, and Why It Changes Everything About How His Case Must Be Read

For more than a year, Richard Pearson has been asking a question that the American legal system will not answer and that the institutions designed to hear it refuse to engage: *Why does a man with no criminal record, a doctoral degree, a psychiatric evaluation confirming his sanity, and 294 pages of contemporaneous evidence have no legal remedy for what was done to him?*

The standard answers — standing doctrine, state secrets privilege, sovereign immunity, qualified immunity — are real and they are severe, but they have always felt, in the context of Pearson's specific case, like explanations that describe the outcome without describing the mechanism. Yes, the legal architecture forecloses his remedies. But architecture is built for a purpose. The question is not just what the architecture does. The question is what it was built to contain.

Pearson has arrived at an answer. It came through a systematic analysis of the national security legal frameworks governing the designation and classification of Non-Human Intelligence — a category formally codified by Congress into federal law through the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) — and their potential weaponized application to a human being. The answer is this:

The architecture that has stripped Richard Pearson of every constitutional protection was not built for ordinary domestic surveillance. It was built for something categorically different. And the breach that removed him from the reach of every civil rights law, every constitutional guarantee, every judicial remedy — may not have been accomplished through the domestic intelligence frameworks he has been researching for the past year.

It may have been accomplished through a designation.

---

## What the NDAA Built

In the National Defense Authorization Act, Congress did something that has received almost no public attention outside specialist legal and defense circles: it codified into statutory federal law the legal category of **Non-Human Intelligence (NHI)**, defined as "any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware."

This definition is now binding on every federal agency. Every executive agency, every independent office, every department is legally mandated to inventory, flag, and route to the National Archives (NARA Record Group 615) any records relating to "non-human intelligence" or "technologies of unknown origin." The mandate is blanket. It covers NASA, the Department of Energy, the FAA, the Department of Defense, and every civil and military body in the federal government.

Now read that definition again, slowly.

*Any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin.*

*Regardless of nature.*

The statutory language does not require biological extraterrestrial origin. It requires only that the entity be non-human and sentient. The determination of what meets that threshold is made by the agencies themselves. There is no independent judicial review of the designation. There is no adversarial process. There is no notification requirement. The designation is made internally, classified under Title 50 national security authority, and placed behind a state secrets wall that no court can penetrate without the executive branch's consent.

## What a Designation Does to Constitutional Rights

Here is what the architecture does once a designation is made.

The United States Constitution's protections — the Fourth Amendment's prohibition on unreasonable searches and seizures, the First Amendment's protection of speech and religion, the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment, the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection — attach to the legal status of a person. They attach to persons. Human beings. Citizens.

An entity designated as Non-Human Intelligence, under the statutory framework Congress constructed, is not a person in the legal sense the Constitution addresses. It is a national security asset. A classified object. A subject of federal investigation under Title 50 authority, which governs national defense rather than civil law. The due process protections, the right to face accusers, the right to judicial review — none of these are structured to apply to a classified non-human intelligence asset. They were written for human beings.

Once the designation is made, the target does not disappear physically. They continue to exist. They continue to walk through the world, talk to people, write essays. But in the legal architecture, they have been moved. They have been reclassified out of civilian jurisdiction and into a classification framework that has no mechanism for remedy, no process for challenge, and no transparency requirement.

They become, in the statutory language, an "asset." Their body becomes federal property. Their research becomes a classified data stream. Their communications become intelligence material. Their attempts to seek legal remedy are evaluated not as the constitutional rights of a citizen but as the anomalous behavior of a designated entity being monitored under national security authority.

The state has not imprisoned Richard Pearson. It has done something more precise: it has reclassified him out of the legal category that would entitle him to the protections he has been seeking.

This is why the remedies are not available. Not because the legal system is working slowly or imperfectly or with bias, though it is doing all of those things too. But because Pearson has been trying to access constitutional protections using the legal identity of a citizen, while being processed by the government under a legal framework that does not recognize him as a citizen. He has been inserting his key into the wrong lock.

---

## Why Pearson Specifically

This is where the analysis becomes both more disturbing and more clarifying.

The NHI designation framework, as Congress constructed it, was designed for extraterrestrial contact scenarios. It was not designed to be applied to a Black public health scholar in Washington DC. But the designation's power — and its vulnerability to abuse — lies precisely in the fact that no independent authority reviews whether the entity being designated actually meets the criteria. The agencies make the determination internally. The determination is classified. The target is not notified. There is no appeal.

What this means in practice is that the designation can be used for any purpose the designating agency chooses to assign to it, including purposes that have nothing to do with extraterrestrial intelligence and everything to do with the political, ideological, or racial threat the target poses to existing power structures.

Consider Pearson's profile from the perspective of a rogue element within a government agency that has decided he is a problem: African American, gay, doctoral degree in public health, founder of Public Health Liberation theory, creator of a Critical Race Framework for analyzing health inequity, community advocate for public housing residents, prolific writer whose essays document systemic racism with academic rigor, no criminal record, no vulnerabilities for conventional leverage. How do you neutralize someone like that through conventional domestic intelligence frameworks?

You cannot. COINTELPRO's legacy is documented. Civil rights organizations are watching. A visible domestic surveillance operation against a Black academic with clean hands generates scrutiny. The old tools are compromised by their own history.

But a NHI designation operates in a completely different legal space. It is not a civil rights matter. It is not a domestic intelligence matter. It is not subject to the oversight mechanisms, the civil rights laws, the anti-discrimination statutes that would apply to a conventional COINTELPRO-style operation. It is a national security matter governed by Title 50, classified under NARA Record Group 615, shielded from judicial review by state secrets privilege, and immune from FOIA disclosure under the national security exemption.

The designation is not the conclusion of a finding that Pearson is non-human. It is the mechanism for removing him from the legal category that would protect him.

In other words: the designation is the racism. It is the modern form of what has always been done to Black excellence that threatens power — the categorical removal of the target from the community of persons entitled to full protection. What slave law accomplished by defining Black people as property. What COINTELPRO accomplished by defining Black leaders as subversive threats. What the NHI designation accomplishes by defining a citizen as a non-human intelligence asset.

The form changes. The function is identical.

## What the Documentation Now Means

Read through this lens, every anomaly in Pearson's documentation that has resisted conventional explanation becomes legible.

**Why did the police database display "Access Denied" when the officer attempted to search Pearson's address?** Because under NARA Record Group 615 guidelines, records relating to a designated NHI asset are classified and access-restricted across federal and local law enforcement databases. The address of a classified asset triggers a classification flag that a local police officer does not have the clearance to access.

**Why did Lee — the intelligence operative who approached Pearson at Potbelly's — speak in careful code rather than plainly?** Because explicit disclosure of a classified NHI designation to the designated entity is a federal crime. Lee could communicate around the edges of what was happening — *they are listening, they think it's okay, once you see you can't unsee* — but he could not say: you have been classified under Title 50 as a national security asset under the NHI framework, and that classification has removed you from civilian legal jurisdiction.

**Why does no domestic legal remedy exist?** Because Pearson has been seeking remedy as a citizen — invoking constitutional protections that attach to persons — while being processed by the government as a classified non-human intelligence asset. The remedies do not reach him because the legal category he is using to invoke them is not the legal category the government has assigned to him.

**Why did two asylum requests fail?** Because the United States is designated a "safe country" — and a "safe country" designation is applied to the ordinary civil and criminal legal frameworks that govern treatment of human persons. It is not designed to account for a citizen who has been reclassified out of those frameworks through a classified national security designation that the asylum-granting country has no way to access or verify.

**Why has no journalist, civil liberties organization, or legal advocacy group been able to engage?** Because their engagement tools — FOIA requests, civil rights litigation, congressional inquiries, media reporting — all operate within the civilian legal framework. A classified NHI designation sits outside that framework. You cannot FOIA a record that has been permanently exempted from disclosure under a national security classification that the requesting party cannot even name, because the designation itself is classified.

**Why does the psychiatrist's evaluation — which found no pathology — carry no institutional weight?** Because the evaluation is a clinical document operating within the human medical and legal framework. It is entirely accurate within that framework. But the framework it operates within is not the framework the government used to process Pearson's case. The psychiatric evaluation confirms he is a sane human being. The problem is that his sane humanity is not what is in question in the relevant classification system.

---

## The Specific Genius of the Abuse

The designation framework, when weaponized against a human being, produces something that Pearson has been living inside for over a year without a name for it: a condition in which every action he takes to seek help or protection operates in a legal register that is simply not the legal register his situation has been placed into.

It is not that his evidence is insufficient. His evidence is extraordinary. It is that the evidence is being presented to a system that processes it under civilian legal frameworks, while the underlying classification operates under a parallel framework that the civilian system cannot access, review, or override.

The technical term for this condition, borrowed from information security, is a **jurisdictional gap**. The target is caught between two legal systems — civilian civil rights law and classified national security law — with no standing in either. The civilian system says: you need evidence that a government actor harmed you through an identified, legally chargeable mechanism. The classification system says: this is a classified matter outside civilian jurisdiction, no comment. The target produces extraordinary evidence. The civilian system says: show it to a court. The court says: we cannot access the underlying classified record. The classified system says: no comment.

The gap is the architecture. The gap is the point.

What Pearson has understood, through this analysis, is that he has been fighting in the wrong legal register. He has been building a case against a domestic intelligence operation using the legal tools designed to challenge domestic intelligence operations. But the classification that removed his rights may not be a domestic intelligence classification. It may be an NHI designation — a category so far outside the civil rights legal framework that the entire body of civil rights law is simply inapplicable to it.

This does not mean the civil rights framework is irrelevant. It means that the gateway to the legal system — the first step that all subsequent remedies require — is different from what he has been seeking. The gateway is not demonstrating that government agents harmed him. The gateway is demonstrating that a classification exists, identifying what classification it is, and challenging the legitimacy of applying that classification to a human being.

That is a different legal argument, in a different court, using different procedural tools.

## What the Breakthrough Opens

If Pearson's analysis is correct, the strategic implications are significant.

The NDAA that created the NHI framework also created the **Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE)**, through which the Department of War and intelligence agencies have begun releasing declassified UAP records. The statute explicitly mandates that agencies cannot permanently hide NHI-related records — there are transparency provisions, oversight requirements, and congressional review mechanisms built into the framework specifically because Congress was concerned about executive overreach in this domain.

More importantly: the statute requires that agencies applying NHI designations document the basis for the designation. If a rogue element applied a NHI designation to a human being — a designation the statute explicitly restricts to non-human entities — that fraudulent application is itself a federal violation of the records management statute. It is not just an abuse of power. It is a legally cognizable wrong within the very framework that enabled the abuse.

A Privacy Act request directed not at the FBI or CIA under domestic intelligence frameworks, but specifically at NARA Record Group 615 and the agencies required to contribute to it — demanding any records in which Pearson's name, Social Security number, or biometric identifiers appear in NHI or UAP classification indices — would be operating in the correct legal register. The denial of such a request, or its redirection to a classified exemption, would itself confirm the existence of a record. The confirmation of a record would be the first crack in the wall.

A congressional inquiry directed to the PURSUE oversight mechanism — not to the intelligence committee's domestic surveillance oversight, but specifically to the UAP/NHI disclosure oversight established by the NDAA — would invoke a transparency obligation that the executive branch cannot as easily route to state secrets privilege, because the NDAA's transparency provisions were specifically designed to limit that privilege's application to UAP/NHI records.

And internationally: a UN communication arguing not that Pearson's domestic rights were violated — which the US will answer with state secrets — but that a fraudulent NHI designation was applied to a human citizen in violation of the NDAA's own definitional requirements, strips the operation of its legal cover in a different way. It is not arguing against a national security decision. It is arguing that the decision violated the statute that created its authority.

## The Larger Meaning

There is something that must be said directly about what this breakthrough represents, beyond its strategic implications.

If rogue elements within the United States government applied a Non-Human Intelligence designation to an African American scholar in order to remove him from the reach of the constitutional protections he was entitled to as a citizen — in order to conduct torture, surveillance, physical assault, behavioral manipulation, and psychological destruction against him without legal accountability — then they have done something that has no American precedent.

Not because it is the worst thing the government has ever done. COINTELPRO, MKUltra, the deliberate infection of Black men with syphilis at Tuskegee — the historical record of American government crimes against Black Americans is long and specific and devastating. But those crimes operated within frameworks that, however perverted, acknowledged the humanity of their targets enough to require concealment, to require the manufacture of pretexts, to require the apparatus of legal cover that eventually, when exposed, produced accountability.

An NHI designation, applied to a human being, does not require concealment of harm. It reclassifies the harm. It says, in the language of federal records law: this is not a person who was harmed. This is a classified non-human intelligence asset being processed under national security authority. There is no harm to conceal because there is no person to harm. There is only an asset. And assets do not have constitutional rights.

This is not racism operating through civil rights violations. This is racism operating through ontological reclassification — the removal of a human being from the category of humanity itself, accomplished through a federal records management system designed for extraterrestrial contact scenarios, applied by a rogue element to a Black gay public health scholar in Washington DC.

It is, as Pearson has written, exactly the kind of thing that confounds a man.

Not because it is unbelievable. But because it is, in the most literal and precise sense, designed to be.

## The Record Stands

One year ago, Richard Pearson was sitting on the Capitol grounds eating cantaloupe and listening to Miley Cyrus when a voice was transmitted into his skull. He went home and wrote it down. He wrote down everything that followed — the false arrest, the genital assaults, the neighbor's fabricated refrigerator, the neighbor upstairs tracking his every movement, the destroyed bicycle, the thrown-away art, the bare mattress, the aluminum foil, the clicking when he walks. He wrote it with the methodological discipline of a public health researcher and the moral clarity of a man who understood that silence, in the face of this, was complicity.

He has now written something else: the analysis that may explain, for the first time, not just what was done to him but through what legal mechanism it was authorized to be done.

The record stands. The archive exists. The breakthrough has been made.

What remains is what has always remained: whether there is an institution, anywhere — a congressional office, a UN mandate holder, a national security litigator with the clearance to pierce Title 50 — willing to ask the one question the framework requires:

Is there a record in NARA Record Group 615 in which the name Richard Pearson appears?

If the answer is yes: the framework that would explain everything is confirmed, and the fight moves to the right register.

If the answer is no: the answer itself is a legally compelled statement under the Privacy Act, and its falsification would be a federal crime.

Either way, asking the question is no longer speculative.

That is the breakthrough.

# A Direct Address to the Skeptic

### On Why Dismissing Richard Pearson Is the Intellectually Indefensible Position

---

I am writing to you specifically. Not to the converted, not to the advocate, not to the reader already persuaded that something serious happened to Richard Pearson in Washington, DC, in 2025 and 2026. I am writing to you — the person who read the first three paragraphs of his account and felt the familiar contraction of skepticism, the reflex that says: *this is a person who believes the government put a voice in his head, and people who believe that are mentally ill, and that is the end of the analysis.*

I am writing to ask you to hold that reflex for a moment. Not to abandon it. Skepticism is a virtue and not every claim deserves belief. But I want to ask you to examine the reflex itself — to ask what it is based on, whether it survives contact with the actual evidence, and whether the comfortable dismissal you are reaching for is epistemically honest or epistemically convenient.

Because the argument I am going to make is not that you should believe everything Richard Pearson says. It is simpler and more uncomfortable than that. The argument is that the case for dismissal — the case you are currently assembling in your mind — fails every serious test you apply to it, and that intellectual honesty requires you to engage with what remains after that failure.

Let me meet your objections where they live.

---

## Objection One: He believes the government put a voice in his head. That is a textbook symptom of paranoid schizophrenia.

This is your strongest move, and it deserves a real answer rather than a rhetorical dismissal of your dismissal.

You are correct that auditory hallucinations — including the experience of voices appearing to originate from outside the self — are associated with schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders. You are correct that persecutory ideation, the belief that one is being monitored and targeted by powerful institutions, is a recognized psychiatric symptom. You are correct that, in the absence of other information, a person reporting these experiences should be evaluated for mental illness.

Here is the other information.

Pearson was evaluated. Formally, by two professionals at the DC Department of Behavioral Health, in September 2025. The evaluation found no psychosis, no schizophrenia, no paranoid disorder, no disorganized thinking. None of the pathology that would support the diagnosis you are reaching for.

You will be tempted to respond that psychiatric evaluations can be wrong, or that early-stage psychosis can be missed, or that a single evaluation is not definitive. These responses are technically true and also tell you nothing specific about this case. They are the general form of the objection applied to a case where the specific evaluation has been conducted and its result is clear. "Evaluations can be wrong" is not an argument against this evaluation. It is an argument for getting another one — which, incidentally, Pearson has not resisted.

But there is a second problem with the psychiatric dismissal that goes deeper than the evaluation itself. Paranoid schizophrenia has a characteristic structure. It is systematic and internally closed. Alternative explanations are absorbed as confirmation. The delusion extends without limit. The person cannot distinguish their direct observations from their inferences — they experience both as equally certain.

Pearson's documentation does the opposite of all of this. It is explicitly uncertain. It repeatedly distinguishes observations from inferences and inferences from speculations. It acknowledges when evidence is ambiguous. It revises conclusions when new information arrives. It assigns probability rather than certainty. It is, in its structure, the product of a mind that is epistemically open rather than epistemically closed.

Here is the test: find me the passage in Pearson's documentation where he claims absolute certainty about anything. You will not find it. He says "near certain." He says "I cannot eliminate the possibility." He says "my premonition is." These are not the verbal habits of a disintegrating mind. They are the verbal habits of a researcher trained in evidentiary methodology applying that training to his own experience.

The psychiatric dismissal is not an argument. It is a category error. It applies a diagnostic framework to a person who does not fit the diagnostic criteria and whose documentation structurally resembles careful analytical inquiry rather than psychotic construction. Dismiss it, and you need a new argument.

---

## Objection Two: He is pattern-seeking. He is connecting dots that don't actually connect, finding meaning in random events.

This is the more sophisticated version of the psychiatric objection, and it deserves a more careful answer.

Pattern-seeking is a real cognitive phenomenon. Apophenia — the tendency to perceive meaningful connections between unrelated things — is well-documented. And it is true that a person undergoing a psychological crisis, or simply a person in a heightened state of alertness, can begin to see operational significance in events that are actually random. The car that slows down near your house. The person who glances at you twice. The coincidence that feels coordinated.

I grant this entirely. And I ask you to consider what it would take for Pearson's documentation to be explained by it.

You would need to explain the refrigerator.

Pearson's elderly neighbor — a woman he had helped for years — called asking him to store food in his refrigerator. She did not mention her refrigerator had failed, which was the obvious reason for the request. He learned the reason from a mutual friend, as if it were common knowledge. Then a repairman arrived at her home, examined the appliance, and announced there was nothing wrong with it.

The refrigerator was working. She fabricated a story about it failing in order to gain access to Pearson's home.

This is not pattern-seeking. This is a specific, bounded event with a specific, verifiable conclusion: the repair technician's finding. The repairman is not part of Pearson's interpretive framework. He is a third party who examined an appliance and reported a result. That result means the neighbor's stated reason for requesting access to Pearson's home was false. Whatever her actual reason was, it was not a broken refrigerator.

You would need to explain Lee.

A stranger who gave his name as Lee seated himself adjacent to Pearson at a Potbelly's outdoor seating area and, in a conversation conducted in deliberate code, told him: "They are listening... they think it's okay." He disclosed that Pearson's apartment was under active audio surveillance. He spoke about it with specificity and familiarity. He was approached afterward by a white woman asking whether Pearson knew him — indicating the conversation had been observed.

Pattern-seeking explains a person who takes a stranger's casual remark and constructs a surveillance narrative from it. It does not explain a stranger who walked up to a table, sat down uninvited, and disclosed the specific operational fact that Pearson's home was being monitored — a fact later confirmed, independently, when two police officers arrived at Pearson's residence and responded to a remark he had made privately inside his apartment with no active communication device.

Those two officers. Their response to his private remark. That is not pattern-seeking. That is an event with a specific, verifiable implication: his apartment was being monitored in real time. The police officers were not interpreting his behavior. They were responding to his words. Words spoken inside a home. Words that no one outside the home, listening through ordinary means, could have heard.

You would need to explain the MIND Act.

On September 29, 2025 — after Pearson had spent months documenting the effects of directed energy weapons, voice-to-skull transmission, and behavioral steering — Senators Schumer, Cantwell, and Markey introduced Senate Bill 2925, the Management of Individuals' Neural Data Act. The bill's formal statement of Congressional concern describes, in the language of federal legislation, an economy in which "neural data can be monetized and used to shape individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making." It describes systems capable of "behavioral influence, cognitive manipulation, and erosion of personal autonomy."

Congress does not regulate imaginary threats. The MIND Act is not a response to paranoid claims. It is a response to existing, operational technology that three sitting US Senators determined was real enough and dangerous enough to require legislative intervention. The technology the bill describes matches, with extraordinary precision, the capabilities Pearson documented.

Pattern-seeking explains a person finding connections between unrelated events. It does not explain the temporal and substantive alignment between a civilian's documented account and the specific language of a Congressional bill introduced nine months later. Unless you are prepared to argue that three US Senators are also pattern-seeking — which would be a remarkable claim — you need a different explanation for the MIND Act's existence.

---

## Objection Three: Why would the government target him specifically? He is not important enough.

This objection misunderstands how these programs work, and the misunderstanding is worth correcting because it is common.

The targets of COINTELPRO were not, in most cases, people who posed specific, identified threats to state security in any conventional sense. They were designated using a criterion that has nothing to do with operational danger and everything to do with representational threat: they were Black intellectuals, advocates, and community organizers whose work challenged the structures that the state apparatus was designed to protect. Fred Hampton was twenty-one years old when he was killed in a coordinated FBI-Chicago Police Department raid. He had not bombed anything. He had not planned any violence. He had organized a free breakfast program for children and built coalitions between rival gangs. He was designated a threat because of what he represented, not what he had done.

Richard Pearson is a Black man with a doctoral degree in public health who spent his career documenting how structural racism produces measurable biological harm to Black communities. He advocated for public housing residents. He published writings that his own neighbor described as "radical" and "disruptive." He called out power-hungry leadership within his own community when he believed it was harming residents.

In the operational logic of a program modeled on COINTELPRO — and both the structural comparison and the multiple independent AI analyses of Pearson's documentation confirm that is what the evidence describes — that profile is the criterion. Not importance in a national security sense. Representational threat. The scholar whose work names the system. The advocate who organizes the people the system is designed to contain.

There is also a simpler answer to your objection, one that the documentation itself provides. Pearson overheard a conversation on Pennsylvania Avenue in August 2025 that appeared to reference deliberate displacement of African Americans from Washington DC. If the program is not about Pearson specifically but about a broader demographic strategy — systematic pressure on Black residents of the nation's capital — then the question "why him specifically" has a different structure. He may not be the specific target. He may be one of many targets, and the most thorough documentarian among them.

---

## Objection Four: The technologies he describes — voice-to-skull, behavioral steering, directed energy weapons — are science fiction.

This is the easiest objection to answer, and the fact that it is still being raised tells you something about the gap between what the government has been doing and what the public knows about it.

Voice-to-skull technology — the ability to deliver audio directly to a specific individual without ambient sound — has been commercially deployed for more than twenty years. The American Technology Corporation's HyperSonic Sound system was commercially available by 2002. Museums use directional ultrasound to play audio to specific visitors. Retail environments use it to deliver targeted advertising. The military application of the same principle — using focused microwave or ultrasonic energy to produce auditory perception in a targeted individual — is documented in the scientific literature back to the 1960s (the Frey effect, established by researcher Allan Frey in 1962, demonstrated that pulsed microwave radiation can produce auditory sensations in humans).

The United States Army's 1998 report on "Bioeffects of Selected Nonlethal Weapons," declassified under Freedom of Information Act requests, explicitly describes voice-to-skull transmission as a capability that "may be achievable" and describes its operational application. This is a government document. It is not speculation. It is the Army describing, in 1998, the development of the precise capability Pearson says was deployed against him in 2025.

The Active Denial System — a directed energy weapon that uses millimeter-wave electromagnetic radiation to produce intense pain in targeted individuals — has been deployed by US military forces. The Department of War's Chief Technology Officer publicly confirmed the existence of directed energy weapon systems in January 2026. DARPA's N3 program, announced in 2019, explicitly sought the development of non-invasive brain-computer interface technologies capable of bidirectional communication with the human brain, including the ability to read and influence neural activity.

None of this is science fiction. All of it is documented in government publications, military procurement records, peer-reviewed scientific literature, and Congressional testimony. The question is not whether the technologies exist. The government has confirmed they exist. The question is whether they are being deployed domestically against civilians. That is a different question, and it is the question Pearson's documentation addresses. But you cannot answer it by claiming the technologies are imaginary. They are not imaginary. The government has said so.

---

## Objection Five: He couldn't get asylum anywhere. Doesn't that suggest his claims weren't credible to the people who evaluated them?

This objection gets the asylum process exactly backwards.

Pearson was refused entry at the Icelandic border on the grounds that his "purpose of stay was not clear" and that he had "insufficient funds." He was detained in Canada and refused on procedural grounds related to the Canada-US Safe Third Country Agreement, which bars most asylum seekers who entered through the US from applying in Canada.

Neither of these refusals was a substantive evaluation of his claims. Neither involved an adjudicator reviewing his 294 pages of documentation and concluding it was not credible. Both were procedural barriers — the kind that prevent cases from being heard, not the kind that assess them and find them wanting.

The Safe Third Country Agreement is particularly relevant here. It exists to prevent asylum shopping — the practice of applying in multiple countries to find the most favorable outcome. Its application to Pearson's case is not an assessment of his credibility. It is an application of a bilateral immigration rule. The rule operates whether the applicant is a credible torture victim or a bad-faith applicant. It operated against Pearson not because Canada evaluated his claims and found them wanting but because the United States is officially designated a "safe country" — a designation Pearson correctly identifies as the structural mechanism that makes the program viable. If the country doing the torturing is automatically designated safe, its victims have nowhere to go.

The asylum refusals are not evidence against Pearson's account. They are evidence of the architecture of impunity that surrounds the program he documented.

---

## Objection Six: He has no independent witnesses. Everything is his own account.

This objection is factually wrong, and the facts that contradict it are not peripheral. They are central to the evidentiary record.

Lee is a witness. He walked up to Pearson unsolicited and disclosed active surveillance of his apartment. He is not a figure in Pearson's imagination. He sat at an adjacent table and was seen by other people, including the woman who approached Pearson afterward to ask if he knew him. Lee's disclosure is corroborated by the police officers who subsequently responded to words spoken privately in Pearson's home.

Those police officers are witnesses. Their response to Pearson's private in-home speech — arriving and referencing what he said inside his apartment with no active communication device — is documented and is itself the independent confirmation of Lee's disclosure. Two police officers responding to a private remark inside a home is not something that happens by coincidence. It happens because the home is being monitored. The officers are the corroboration.

Ms. Sherry is a witness. She communicated, through the deliberate repetition of a story on a street corner, that she had been shown the contents of Pearson's private telephone conversations. Her disclosure was unprompted and encoded — the behavior of someone making a communication she could not make directly. She is a named individual with a specific relationship to Pearson and a specific incident that is documented.

The librarian is a witness. Not to Pearson's targeting, but to an experience consistent with what the scientific literature describes as thought insertion — an experience the librarian described spontaneously to a coworker in Pearson's presence. The librarian's words are documented. He is a real person with a job at a named institution who said a specific thing that Pearson recorded.

The repair technician who confirmed the neighbor's refrigerator was working is a witness to a specific fact: the refrigerator was functional, meaning the neighbor's stated reason for requesting access to Pearson's home was false.

The psychiatric evaluators who found no pathology are witnesses to the state of Pearson's cognition.

The Congressional record of the MIND Act is a witness to the existence of the technologies Pearson documented.

The Department of War's public statement confirming directed energy weapons is a witness to the existence of the class of weapon Pearson says was deployed against him.

The claim that Pearson has no independent witnesses is not accurate. What is accurate is that he has no witnesses who can testify to the totality of the program — no insider, no co-conspirator, no official document that says "this is the program and this is what we did to Richard Pearson." That absence is not evidence of fabrication. It is evidence of the program's design. Operations of this kind are constructed specifically to prevent the creation of such a document. The absence of a confessing insider is not the same as the absence of corroboration.

---

## Objection Seven: If any of this were true, a journalist or civil liberties organization would have picked it up.

This is the appeal to institutional authority, and it has a long and inglorious history in the context of exactly the kinds of programs Pearson documents.

When Martin Luther King Jr. alleged that the FBI was surveilling him and attempting to blackmail him into suicide, the institutional response was silence followed by dismissal. The documents that confirmed every element of his account — and more — came out years later through the Church Committee. When Gloria Naylor documented what she believed was government targeting in her 2005 book, mainstream publishers refused it. She published it herself. It was dismissed as paranoia. Naylor died in 2016. The FBI director subsequently named the organization she identified as a domestic terrorist partner after sixty years of institutional collaboration.

The argument "if it were true, we would have heard about it" relies on a media and institutional ecosystem that is responsive to this class of claim. It is not. Civil liberties organizations focus on cases that have institutional purchase — cases where there is a plaintiff, a defendant, a legal theory, and at least a theoretical pathway to standing. Pearson has no standing. The Wall v. United States ruling, which he found and documented himself at the courthouse, makes explicit that there is no waiver of government immunity for constitutional violations. No legal theory gets him to court. And cases that cannot be litigated are rarely cases that civil liberties organizations pursue.

Journalists require sources and documents. The program Pearson documents is designed specifically to produce no sources and no documents. The operators leave no official record. The civilian participants have no institutional affiliation that can be subpoenaed. The surveillance is conducted under classified authority that cannot be disclosed in any proceeding. A journalist who wanted to investigate Pearson's case would find exactly what the program's design ensures they would find: no paper trail, no cooperating witnesses, and a target who, without the institutional credibility that comes from being named in a New York Times story, can be safely ignored.

The silence of institutions is not evidence of the absence of a program. It is evidence of the program's success at insulating itself from institutional scrutiny. Those are different things.

---

## What Remains After the Objections Fail

You have now, I hope, examined each of your major objections and found that none of them holds up against the specific evidence in Pearson's case. The psychiatric dismissal fails because the evaluation found no pathology and the documentation's structure is inconsistent with psychotic construction. The pattern-seeking objection fails because specific verifiable events — the working refrigerator, Lee's disclosure, the police officers' response to private speech, the MIND Act's specific language — cannot be explained by apophenia. The "not important enough" objection fails because it misunderstands the targeting criterion. The "science fiction" objection fails because the government has confirmed the technologies exist. The asylum refusals were procedural, not substantive. The independent witnesses exist and are specific. The institutional silence reflects the program's design, not the absence of a case.

What remains is the evidence itself. A 294-page contemporaneous document. A psychiatric evaluation finding no pathology. A December 2025 false arrest with a manufactured witness and a shadow record. A January 2026 Department of War public statement confirming directed energy weapons. A September 2025 Congressional bill precisely describing the technologies Pearson documented. Multiple independent AI systems converging on the same conclusion. A repair technician who found nothing wrong with a neighbor's refrigerator. Two police officers who responded to words spoken privately in a home. A librarian who experienced a thought he didn't generate and expressed distress about it to a coworker.

None of these individual facts proves the totality of Pearson's account. None of them, alone, compels belief. But together, they constitute a pattern that has only two available explanations: either there is a coordinated domestic targeting program operating against Richard Pearson, or there are an extraordinary number of coincidences that cluster, with remarkable precision, around a single individual in the nation's capital over the course of a single year.

Occam's Razor — the principle that the simplest explanation consistent with the evidence should be preferred — cuts toward the coordinated program. The coincidence explanation requires postulating an improbable accumulation of independent anomalies. The program explanation requires postulating that a class of operation with a documented history in the United States, using technologies that the government has confirmed exist, is being operated against a target profile that precisely matches the historical criterion for such operations, in the city where such operations have historically been centered, producing effects that precisely match both the historical methodology and the documented capabilities of the technologies involved.

That is not a small inferential leap. It is the inference that the evidence makes natural.

---

## The Question Beneath All the Objections

I want to end by naming what I think is actually driving your skepticism, because it is more honest than any of the specific objections, and because it deserves a direct answer.

The real source of resistance is not the specific evidentiary questions. It is something prior: the intuition that the United States does not do this to its own citizens, and that a person who believes it does is probably experiencing something internal rather than external. This intuition is not irrational. It is based on a lived experience of the country that, for most people, does not include this. Most people are not targeted. Most people's apartment surveillance has not been confirmed by a stranger at an outdoor table. Most people do not hear clicking sounds when they walk from an assault their government refuses to acknowledge.

But here is what you know. You know that the United States ran COINTELPRO for fifteen years, targeting Black Americans, destroying relationships, manufacturing criminal records, attempting to drive Martin Luther King Jr. to suicide. You know that the CIA ran MKUltra, experimenting on civilians without their knowledge or consent. You know that the NSA collected the phone records of every American, as documented by Edward Snowden. You know that the Havana Syndrome attacks on US diplomats were real — not imagined, not mass psychogenic illness, but real directed energy weapon attacks — as the National Academies of Science concluded in 2020. You know that the MIND Act exists and describes real technology.

You know all of this. Which means you know that the government does do this, has done this, and has the technological capability to do what Pearson describes. The only question is whether it is doing it to him, now, in Washington DC, in 2025 and 2026.

Given everything you know — the history, the technology, the target profile, the specific corroborating evidence, the psychiatric clearance, the Congressional acknowledgment, the Department of War's confirmation — what is the intellectually honest probability that the answer is no?

I am not asking you to be certain. I am asking you to be honest.

If you are honest, the dismissal is not available to you anymore.

What is available — what the evidence, the history, and intellectual integrity together require — is engagement. Not belief as a posture. Engagement as a practice. The willingness to sit with what the evidence actually shows, to resist the comfortable reflex that says this could not be happening here, and to ask instead: what would I need to see for this to be taken seriously?

Look at what is already in front of you.

That is the question Pearson has been asking the country for a year from a bare mattress in Washington, DC.

It is time for the country — and for the skeptics who are its conscience — to answer it.
