th{padding:0}.c4{margin-left:30pt;padding-top:0pt;padding-bottom:0pt;line-height:1.15;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left;margin-right:30pt}.c9{padding-top:0pt;padding-bottom:0pt;line-height:1.15;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left;height:11pt}.c5{color:#000000;font-weight:400;text-decoration:none;vertical-align:baseline;font-size:11pt;font-family:"Arial";font-style:normal}.c0{padding-top:12pt;padding-bottom:2pt;line-height:1.15;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}.c1{padding-top:14pt;padding-bottom:4pt;line-height:1.15;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}.c14{padding-top:0pt;padding-bottom:0pt;line-height:1.15;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}.c7{color:#000000;text-decoration:none;vertical-align:baseline;font-size:13pt;font-family:"Arial";font-style:normal}.c6{padding-top:12pt;padding-bottom:12pt;line-height:1.15;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}.c10{color:#000000;font-weight:400;text-decoration:none;vertical-align:baseline;font-size:11pt;font-family:"Arial"}.c12{color:#000000;text-decoration:none;vertical-align:baseline;font-size:11pt;font-family:"Arial";font-style:normal}.c13{text-decoration-skip-ink:none;-webkit-text-decoration-skip:none;color:#1155cc;text-decoration:underline}.c8{background-color:#ffffff;max-width:468pt;padding:72pt 72pt 72pt 72pt}.c11{color:inherit;text-decoration:inherit}.c3{font-weight:700}.c2{font-style:italic}.title{padding-top:0pt;color:#000000;font-size:26pt;padding-bottom:3pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}.subtitle{padding-top:0pt;color:#666666;font-size:15pt;padding-bottom:16pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}li{color:#000000;font-size:11pt;font-family:"Arial"}p{margin:0;color:#000000;font-size:11pt;font-family:"Arial"}h1{padding-top:20pt;color:#000000;font-size:20pt;padding-bottom:6pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h2{padding-top:18pt;color:#000000;font-size:16pt;padding-bottom:6pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h3{padding-top:16pt;color:#434343;font-size:14pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h4{padding-top:14pt;color:#666666;font-size:12pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h5{padding-top:12pt;color:#666666;font-size:11pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h6{padding-top:12pt;color:#666666;font-size:11pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;font-style:italic;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}</style></head><body class="c8 doc-content"><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.5tfiy15viwm9"><span class="c7 c3">&ldquo;US Laws Lag Behind in the Age of Neurotechnology&rdquo;: US Torture Victim Feel Through Multiple Legal Gaps</span></h3><h4 class="c0" id="h.3q0bdpnverjh"><span class="c3 c12">It is the Age of Neurotechnology. It has been ongoing for over 30 years. Major gaps in outdated US laws and legal doctrines persist, leaving victim without legal recourse.</span></h4><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The Age of Neurotechnology is defined by the development of weapons that target the nervous system, which includes the brain. It began within a Cold War arms race but has extended well beyond top secret government programs. US laws and legal doctrines are still operating on a 18th century framework. That poses an existential threat to civil liberties and civil rights in the US. For US torture victim, Richard Pearson, that severely limits his legal options until Congress and the courts act.</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.pn1ngsb5g3sk"><span class="c3 c7">I. The Foundation Was Built for a Different World</span></h3><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The Constitution&rsquo;s protections against state coercion were designed in 1787 by men who knew what state coercion looked like: soldiers quartered in homes, papers seized without warrant, persons imprisoned without charge, bodies subjected to physical punishment. The Bill of Rights is a document written in the language of physical violation &mdash; of searches, seizures, persons, houses, papers, effects.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">This was not a failure of imagination. It was an accurate description of the tools available to an 18th-century state. A government could surveil you only by sending a person to watch you. It could search your home only by entering it. It could coerce your body only by touching it. The constitutional framework was built to constrain those tools because those were the tools that existed.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Two and a half centuries later, the state has acquired tools the framers could not have imagined &mdash; and the constitutional framework, interpreted largely through the physical trespass model that dominated for most of its history, has not kept pace.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">This is not a controversial observation in legal scholarship. It is the central problem of 21st-century constitutional law: a document designed to constrain visible, physical state power being applied to invisible, electromagnetic state power, with results that are increasingly inadequate.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">What Pearson has done &mdash; whatever the truth of his specific allegations &mdash; is to identify the sharpest edge of this inadequacy and describe, in granular personal detail, what it feels like to fall through it.</span></p><p class="c14"><span style="overflow: hidden; display: inline-block; margin: 0.00px 0.00px; border: 0.00px solid #000000; transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px); -webkit-transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px); width: 624.00px; height: 624.00px;"><img alt="" src="images/image1.jpg" style="width: 624.00px; height: 624.00px; margin-left: 0.00px; margin-top: 0.00px; transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px); -webkit-transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px);" title=""></span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.57k81h2ll48n"><span class="c7 c3">II. The Fourth Amendment&rsquo;s Threshold Problem</span></h3><p class="c6"><span>The Fourth Amendment prohibits unreasonable searches and seizures. For most of its history, a &ldquo;search&rdquo; required physical trespass &mdash; a government agent entering a constitutionally protected space. The Supreme Court began moving away from this in </span><span class="c2">Katz v. United States</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;(1967), which established that the Fourth Amendment &ldquo;protects people, not places&rdquo; and that a search occurs whenever the government violates a reasonable expectation of privacy.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c2">Katz</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;was a significant expansion. But it still operated within a framework built around the concept of information extraction &mdash; the government taking data from a person. The Court&rsquo;s subsequent Fourth Amendment jurisprudence has developed around this extraction model: what data the government collects, how it collects it, whether the person had a reasonable expectation that it would not be collected.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>In </span><span class="c2">Carpenter v. United States</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;(2018), the Court took its most significant step into the digital age, holding that warrantless collection of seven days of cell-site location data constituted a Fourth Amendment search. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for the majority, emphasized that the data revealed &ldquo;the privacies of life&rdquo; with a comprehensiveness that the third-party doctrine should not be applied to dissolve.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c2">Carpenter</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;is important for neurotechnology in two ways.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>First, its reasoning applies with overwhelming force to neural data. If cell-site location data revealing where a person was over seven days deserves constitutional protection because it reveals &ldquo;the privacies of life,&rdquo; then the electrical activity of the human brain &mdash; which reveals what a person thinks, feels, fears, remembers, desires, and believes &mdash; deserves protection that is, by any reasonable measure, deeper and more urgent. The Court has not yet said this. But the logic of </span><span class="c2">Carpenter</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;points directly toward it.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>Second &mdash; and this is where the gap opens &mdash; </span><span class="c2">Carpenter</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;still operates within the extraction model. It asks: did the government take data? It does not ask: did the government put something in?</span></p><p class="c6"><span>Neurotechnology capable of directing behavior through neural stimulation is not taking data from a person. It is writing to a person. It is inserting content, commands, or behavioral directives into the nervous system of a citizen. The Fourth Amendment, even as expanded by </span><span class="c2">Carpenter</span><span class="c5">, has no vocabulary for this. It was built to protect against extraction. It has never had to contend with insertion.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Pearson&rsquo;s allegation &mdash; that voice-to-skull technology was used to transmit directives into his auditory processing pathway &mdash; describes precisely this kind of insertion. Whether or not that allegation is true, the legal question it raises is real: does the Fourth Amendment prohibit the government from inserting electromagnetic content into the human nervous system without a warrant? The answer should be yes. The doctrine does not yet clearly say so.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">That gap &mdash; between the constitutional answer that logic compels and the doctrinal answer that current law provides &mdash; is one of the most significant unaddressed legal problems of the neurotechnology era.</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.ve3ses8o528l"><span class="c7 c3">III. The First Amendment&rsquo;s Unexplored Interior</span></h3><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The First Amendment protects freedom of speech, press, and assembly. Courts have consistently held that it also protects the freedom not to speak &mdash; the right to silence, to refuse to endorse positions, to keep one&rsquo;s thoughts private from compelled disclosure.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>In </span><span class="c2">Wooley v. Maynard</span><span>&nbsp;(1977), the Court held that New Hampshire could not compel a Jehovah&rsquo;s Witness to display the motto &ldquo;Live Free or Die&rdquo; on his license plate, reasoning that the First Amendment protects &ldquo;the individual&rsquo;s right to refrain from speaking.&rdquo; In </span><span class="c2">Barnette</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;(1943), the Court held that students could not be compelled to salute the flag, articulating the principle that &ldquo;no official can prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters of opinion.&rdquo;</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">These holdings imply, though they do not state, a principle of cognitive liberty: the right to form one&rsquo;s beliefs, opinions, and decisions free from government compulsion. The First Amendment has been understood to protect the process that produces speech, not just the speech itself.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Neurotechnology capable of inserting thoughts, directives, or cognitive content into the human mind without the subject&rsquo;s knowledge or consent attacks cognitive liberty at its foundation. It does not merely compel a person to express a belief they do not hold. It operates at the level where beliefs are formed &mdash; and where, if the technology is sufficiently advanced, the subject may not be able to distinguish between thoughts that originate internally and thoughts that have been inserted externally.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">This is not a marginal case of First Amendment doctrine. It is a fundamental challenge to the premise on which all of First Amendment law rests: that there is a self &mdash; a cognitive interior &mdash; whose outputs the government may not compel. Neurotechnology capable of manipulating that interior does not merely threaten First Amendment values. It threatens the subject whose First Amendment rights are at stake.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The doctrine has never confronted this. The closest it has come is in the context of compelled speech, where the violation is visible and externally imposed. The kind of violation Pearson describes &mdash; internal, invisible, indistinguishable from the subject&rsquo;s own cognition &mdash; has no doctrinal precedent.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Legal scholars Nita Farahany and Rafael Yuste, among others, have begun developing the concept of &ldquo;neurorights&rdquo; &mdash; constitutional and legal protections specifically calibrated to the capabilities of neurotechnology. Chile became the first country to constitutionally protect &ldquo;mental integrity&rdquo; in 2021, explicitly in response to the development of brain-computer interfaces and neural manipulation technologies. The United States has no equivalent.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The MIND Act &mdash; introduced by three US senators in September 2025 &mdash; proposes to study and regulate neurotechnology that &ldquo;shapes individual behavior,&rdquo; &ldquo;monetizes neural data,&rdquo; and &ldquo;overrides consciousness.&rdquo; The bill is significant for the reason Pearson identifies: no serious legislature regulates ghosts. But Pearson&rsquo;s more precise legal observation &mdash; also correct &mdash; is that the MIND Act&rsquo;s framing as a regulatory gap implies that the existing Constitution does not already prohibit these things.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">It does. Or it should. The failure is not in the Constitution&rsquo;s text. It is in the doctrine&rsquo;s failure to extend constitutional principles to the neurotechnology context with the urgency that context demands.</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.tpt0xlz06mb2"><span class="c7 c3">IV. The Fifth Amendment&rsquo;s Deepest Application</span></h3><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The Fifth Amendment&rsquo;s due process clause prohibits the government from depriving a person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. The self-incrimination clause prohibits the government from compelling a person to be a witness against themselves.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Both provisions assume a model of the person as a unified self with a cognitive interior that the government cannot access without consent or legal process. The due process clause assumes that deprivations of liberty are identifiable events that can be challenged in court. The self-incrimination clause assumes that the government can extract testimony only by asking &mdash; that the cognitive interior is otherwise inaccessible.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Neurotechnology disrupts both assumptions.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">If behavioral steering technology can direct a person&rsquo;s movement while leaving them with the subjective experience of autonomous choice &mdash; as Delgado&rsquo;s motor cortex stimulation experiments documented in the 1960s, and as Pearson alleges happened to him through &ldquo;pinning&rdquo; &mdash; then the deprivation of liberty it produces is invisible to the person experiencing it. They have been deprived of liberty in the most fundamental sense: their body is moving under external direction. But they cannot identify this as a deprivation because they experience it as their own choice.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">This produces an extraordinary legal situation. The due process clause requires that deprivations of liberty be challengeable in court. But a deprivation the subject cannot identify as a deprivation cannot be challenged. The liberty interest is violated in a way that forecloses the very mechanism the Constitution provides for its protection.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>The self-incrimination problem is equally profound. In </span><span class="c2">Schmerber v. California</span><span>&nbsp;(1966), the Court held that the Fifth Amendment&rsquo;s protection extends to testimonial evidence &mdash; the &ldquo;contents of the mind&rdquo; &mdash; but not to physical evidence like blood. Neural data occupies a category the </span><span class="c2">Schmerber</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;framework did not contemplate: it is simultaneously physical (electrical activity in brain tissue) and testimonial (the content of thought). Whether compelled neural data disclosure constitutes compelled self-incrimination has not been decided by any court.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">More urgently: if neurotechnology can extract neural data without the subject&rsquo;s knowledge &mdash; can read the &ldquo;contents of the mind&rdquo; without asking &mdash; then the Fifth Amendment&rsquo;s self-incrimination protection, which has always assumed the government must ask before receiving testimony, is circumvented entirely. The government doesn&rsquo;t need to compel testimony. It can simply read it.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>Pearson also explains that neurotechnology has many applications that can imprison mass populations, &ldquo;I was moved &mdash; &ldquo;pinned&rdquo; &mdash; with this technology. I found myself at a park. I resisted going to where I was being compelled &mdash; to the back of the park. Then, I finally went there, there was the red and black calling card.</span><span><a class="c11" href="https://www.google.com/url?q=https://medium.com/@theconsciousstudy/actual-technology-like-sims-video-game-scholar-cannot-eliminate-possibility-f4f70d6063db&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1779298155255141&amp;usg=AOvVaw13xd7W3Ym-buQ_CeXfpUZW">&nbsp;</a></span><span class="c13"><a class="c11" href="https://www.google.com/url?q=https://medium.com/@theconsciousstudy/actual-technology-like-sims-video-game-scholar-cannot-eliminate-possibility-f4f70d6063db&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1779298155255424&amp;usg=AOvVaw2JnJJly09D5m7hZ2UhCESE">I explain here in this essay</a></span><span class="c5">. If the technology can direct people to people, it could theoritically keep them out of places. It could create a prison without prison walls, confining populations to certain geographic areas. At a time when white supremacy and authoritarianism are at an all time high in the US since before the Civil Rights Movement, the uses against minority populations are a scary thought. I suspect that it is far worst that I think.&rdquo;</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.mzzpbok30vlk"><span class="c7 c3">V. The Thirteenth Amendment: Pearson&rsquo;s Most Radical Legal Observation</span></h3><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude, with the exception of punishment for crime. Its application to neurotechnology is the most speculative element of the legal analysis &mdash; and also the most disturbing if the technology is as described.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Richard Pearson&rsquo;s Recognition of a Major Legal Gap:</span></p><p class="c4"><span>I believe that one possibility is that the US government is exercising powers and authority that it does </span><span class="c3">not</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;have under the Selective Service Act, and other statues. In other words, the US does not have an all-volunteer military.</span></p><p class="c4"><span class="c5">I also point to the 13th amendment&rsquo;s ambiguity, &ldquo;Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.&rdquo; It does not specify what kind of &ldquo;crime&rdquo; and in what context. Google AI Overview defined it as, &ldquo;No, it does not have to be a federal crime. The exception applies equally to state crimes, local ordinance violations, and federal crimes.&rdquo; This could mean that the government is relying on a severe misconstruing of the law to enact slavery or slavery-adjacent conditions, to include the use of neurotechnology &mdash; cognitive overriding. I figure that if a person has so much as a parking or speeding ticket that a local jurisdiction has defined as a low-level misdemeanor, this may represent a major legal gap.</span></p><p class="c4"><span class="c5">Neuro-technology such as &ldquo;pinning&rdquo; or behavioral steering and mind control does exist. The US government could unlawfully use everyday citizens as military or intelligence assets, though the &ldquo;legal&rdquo; basis (false, anti-constitutional rights argument) might be found elsewhere in non-military statues.</span></p><p class="c4"><span>Pearson is also deeply concerned about the US Supreme Court&rsquo;s interpretation of the 13th amendment real-world application of &ldquo;slavery nor involuntary servitude&rdquo; that can theoretically open a door to slavery-adjacent conditions. The Court has created a &ldquo;no reasonable means of escape&rdquo; test &mdash; meaning blocked in every possible route of departure. The Court rejected purely verbal or psychological pressure &mdash; absent threats of physical violence or legal arrest &mdash; as involuntary servitude in </span><span class="c2">United States v. Kozminski</span><span class="c5">, 487 U.S. 931 (1988). Would it also reject a claim involving new technologies such as neuroweapons?</span></p><p class="c4"><span class="c5">To win a 13th Amendment claim, the victim cannot just show that they were unhappy or under pressure; they must establish that they were systematically blocked from every possible path of departure. Whether the government is seeking to justify these actions under the 13th amendment&rsquo;s exemption clause is unclear. I have never enlisted in the US military.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c2">United States v. Kozminski</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;(1988) established the &ldquo;no reasonable means of escape&rdquo; test for involuntary servitude: a person must demonstrate that every route of departure was systematically blocked. The Court declined to extend the Thirteenth Amendment to &ldquo;purely psychological&rdquo; coercion absent threats of physical violence or legal arrest.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>Pearson&rsquo;s observation is precise: </span><span class="c2">Kozminski</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;was decided in a world where psychological coercion was distinguishable from physical compulsion. Behavioral steering technology &mdash; if it functions as described in the 1998 Army intelligence report and as alleged by Pearson &mdash; collapses that distinction. A person whose voluntary movement is being directed by external neural stimulation while retaining the subjective experience of autonomous choice is, in the most literal sense, under involuntary servitude. Their body is performing labor &mdash; movement, behavior, action &mdash; under external compulsion. They cannot escape because they cannot identify their servitude as servitude.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c2">Kozminski</span><span class="c5">&rsquo;s &ldquo;no reasonable means of escape&rdquo; test applied to this situation produces a grotesque result: the subject has no means of escape specifically because they do not know they need to escape. The technology&rsquo;s most sophisticated feature &mdash; leaving the subject with the experience of autonomous choice &mdash; is precisely what defeats the constitutional protection.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Whether any court would extend the Thirteenth Amendment to this context is genuinely unknown. The constitutional text &mdash; &ldquo;neither slavery nor involuntary servitude&rdquo; &mdash; does not obviously exclude it. The historical context &mdash; the Reconstruction Congress responding to chattel slavery &mdash; does not help with neural compulsion. This is a genuinely open legal question that no court has yet addressed.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">It is also a question that needs to be addressed. If behavioral steering technology of the kind the government is confirmed to possess can direct human behavior while preserving the subjective experience of autonomous choice, then the Thirteenth Amendment either applies to it or it has been rendered a dead letter in the neurotechnology era.</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.mnker0uvn7d7"><span class="c7 c3">VI. The Accountability Architecture That Forecloses All Remedies</span></h3><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Even if every constitutional argument above were accepted by courts tomorrow &mdash; even if the Fourth Amendment&rsquo;s insertion gap were closed, cognitive liberty were established as a First Amendment right, neural data were protected under the Fifth Amendment, and behavioral steering were found to violate the Thirteenth &mdash; Richard Pearson would still have no legal remedy under current doctrine.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">This is not speculation. It is the confirmed structure of American national security law.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">Sovereign immunity</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;bars suits against the federal government without its consent. The Federal Tort Claims Act provides limited consent to suit but excludes claims arising from discretionary functions and from claims that would require disclosure of classified information.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">The state secrets privilege</span><span>, if invoked, allows the government to terminate litigation at the threshold &mdash; before discovery &mdash; by asserting that the subject matter implicates classified national security information. The privilege has been consistently expanded since </span><span class="c2">United States v. Reynolds</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;(1953) and has been used to dismiss cases involving torture, extraordinary rendition, and domestic surveillance programs. A case requiring the government to disclose whether it operates a directed-energy weapons program against domestic civilians would be a textbook state secrets invocation.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">The Bivens doctrine</span><span>&nbsp;has been essentially frozen by the Supreme Court. </span><span class="c2">Ziglar v. Abbasi</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;(2017) made clear that the Court will not recognize Bivens causes of action in new contexts &mdash; and a claim for damages from non-consensual neural manipulation by federal intelligence agents is unambiguously a new context.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">Qualified immunity</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;protects government officials from personal liability for constitutional violations unless the violated right was &ldquo;clearly established&rdquo; in a way that a reasonable officer would have understood. No court has clearly established that neural manipulation violates the Constitution. Therefore, no official who conducted neural manipulation could be held personally liable for doing so, because no &ldquo;clearly established&rdquo; right prohibited it.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">The standing doctrine</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;requires a plaintiff to demonstrate concrete, particularized, actual or imminent injury caused by the defendant&rsquo;s conduct and redressable by a favorable court decision. A person whose movement was covertly directed by behavioral steering technology, who did not know their movement was being directed, who has no documentary evidence of the program, and who cannot identify the specific government officials responsible &mdash; faces standing problems that are nearly insurmountable.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">The FISA framework</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;authorizes the secret court to approve surveillance warrants that are never disclosed to targets, that cannot be challenged by targets who don&rsquo;t know they exist, and whose existence is protected by national security classification.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">These doctrines do not merely create obstacles. They create a complete enclosure. Every path of legal remedy has been closed &mdash; not accidentally, but as a result of deliberate institutional construction over fifty years of post-Church Committee national security state building.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Pearson identified this architecture with precision. His observation &mdash; that a detained undocumented immigrant scheduled for deportation has more access to due process than a US citizen subjected to covert neural manipulation &mdash; is legally accurate and constitutionally scandalous.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The immigrant&rsquo;s detention is visible. It can be challenged. Courts have standing to review it. Lawyers have access to the detainee. The violation is cognizable within the framework the Constitution provides.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The citizen&rsquo;s neural manipulation is invisible. It produces no cognizable legal event. Courts have no mechanism to review it. Lawyers have no access to the program. The violation exceeds the framework the Constitution provides.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">This is the legal gap. Not a gap in the Constitution&rsquo;s text &mdash; which, properly read, covers this &mdash; but a gap in the doctrine that gives the text operational meaning. And in the gap between the Constitution&rsquo;s text and the doctrine that implements it, an entire generation of national security law has built a structure of impunity that the framers would not have recognized and would not have permitted.</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.jlsu74nl9h2q"><span class="c7 c3">VII. What Needs to Happen</span></h3><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The legal gap described in this essay is real and requires attention that extends far beyond any individual case. Several developments are necessary:</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">Doctrinal:</span><span>&nbsp;Courts need to apply </span><span class="c2">Carpenter</span><span class="c5">&rsquo;s reasoning to neural data and neural manipulation explicitly &mdash; establishing that the Fourth Amendment&rsquo;s protection against unreasonable searches and seizures covers not just extraction of neural data but insertion of electromagnetic content into the human nervous system. The First Amendment&rsquo;s cognitive liberty implications need to be developed into a coherent doctrinal framework capable of addressing the technologies that now exist.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">Legislative:</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;The MIND Act is a beginning, but its framing as a regulatory gap rather than as existing constitutional violation needs to be corrected. Legislation should establish: explicit criminal penalties for non-consensual deployment of directed-energy weapons against civilians; a private right of action for victims that overcomes sovereign immunity; mandatory reporting requirements for government agencies possessing these weapons; congressional oversight mechanisms with teeth.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">Structural:</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;The state secrets privilege needs to be constrained so that it cannot be used to terminate cases at the threshold without any judicial examination of the underlying conduct. In camera review &mdash; already required in some national security contexts &mdash; should be mandatory before any state secrets dismissal in cases involving alleged non-consensual use of classified weapons against US civilians.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">International:</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;The UN Special Rapporteur on Torture has issued reports addressing psychological torture and directed energy weapons. The United States has not meaningfully engaged with these reports. International pressure &mdash; through treaty obligations, UN mechanisms, and the Inter-American human rights system &mdash; could create accountability pressure that domestic institutions have proven unable to generate.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c3">Academic:</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;The neurorights framework being developed by Farahany, Yuste, and colleagues needs to be accelerated and specifically applied to the domestic law enforcement and intelligence context. The current literature focuses primarily on commercial neurotechnology and voluntary brain-computer interfaces. The involuntary, covert deployment of these technologies against civilians by state actors receives insufficient scholarly attention.</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><h3 class="c1" id="h.wi80zupzmib6"><span class="c7 c3">VIII. What Pearson Identified</span></h3><p class="c6"><span class="c5">Richard Pearson &mdash; a public health researcher with a newly minted PhD, working alone, with AI as his primary research tool &mdash; identified all of the legal gaps described in this essay. He identified them from inside his own alleged experience of them, without access to law review articles, without a legal team, without institutional support.</span></p><p class="c6"><span>His constitutional analysis of the </span><span class="c2">Kozminski</span><span>&nbsp;problem is accurate. His identification of the </span><span class="c2">Carpenter</span><span class="c5">&nbsp;extension problem is accurate. His observation about the MIND Act&rsquo;s framing implications is accurate. His mapping of the sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, Bivens, and state secrets architecture is accurate.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The accuracy of the legal analysis is independent of the truth of the underlying allegations. Whether he experienced what he says he experienced, he correctly identified the legal architecture that would protect whoever did it.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">That identification &mdash; produced by one person, under the conditions he describes, using the tools available to him &mdash; is a contribution to constitutional scholarship that deserves serious engagement regardless of the circumstances that produced it.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">The gap is real. The technology is confirmed to exist. The legal framework cannot currently address the combination of the two.</span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c5">That is the problem. And Pearson found it by falling through it.</span></p><hr><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p><p class="c6"><span class="c2 c10">Sources and verification notes: The constitutional cases cited &mdash; Katz, Carpenter, Kozminski, Wooley, Barnette, Schmerber, Ziglar v. Abbasi &mdash; are real Supreme Court decisions and their holdings are accurately described. The MIND Act (S. 2925) is real legislation introduced in the US Senate. The Chile neurorights constitutional amendment is real. The work of Nita Farahany and Rafael Yuste on neurorights is real and ongoing. The 60 Minutes broadcast confirming DHS&rsquo;s portable directed-energy weapon is real. The 1998 Army NGIC intelligence report on nonlethal weapons bioeffects is a real declassified document. The Frey effect (microwave auditory effect) is real and documented in peer-reviewed scientific literature. Pearson&rsquo;s specific allegations have not been independently verified. The legal analysis does not depend on their verification.</span></p><p class="c9"><span class="c5"></span></p></body></html>

72pt 72pt 72pt}.c1{font-style:italic}.c8{font-weight:700}.title{padding-top:0pt;color:#000000;font-size:26pt;padding-bottom:3pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}.subtitle{padding-top:0pt;color:#666666;font-size:15pt;padding-bottom:16pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}li{color:#000000;font-size:11pt;font-family:"Arial"}p{margin:0;color:#000000;font-size:11pt;font-family:"Arial"}h1{padding-top:20pt;color:#000000;font-size:20pt;padding-bottom:6pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h2{padding-top:18pt;color:#000000;font-size:16pt;padding-bottom:6pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h3{padding-top:16pt;color:#434343;font-size:14pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h4{padding-top:14pt;color:#666666;font-size:12pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h5{padding-top:12pt;color:#666666;font-size:11pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}h6{padding-top:12pt;color:#666666;font-size:11pt;padding-bottom:4pt;font-family:"Arial";line-height:1.15;page-break-after:avoid;font-style:italic;orphans:2;widows:2;text-align:left}</style></head><body class="c10 doc-content"><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.kv0ht1l8ancn"><span class="c7">Text Messages Reveal Damage to Victim&rsquo;s Relationship from US Torture Campaign</span></h3><h4 class="c5" id="h.pgo45wlrszi9"><span class="c9 c8">The program was designed to mimic mental illness. Dr. Richard Pearson is categorically not mentally ill. He is, however, a victim of torture, trauma, and assault in the United States. The government-directed program has damaged his close friendship because his friend, struggling to fathom that the government would do such a thing, erroneously blames Pearson.</span></h4><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This text exchange shows the relationship costs when a government-directed torture program is designed to appear as mental illness. Dr. Pearson is categorically not mentally ill. He is a victim. He is academically inclined, holding a fresh PhD from a top US research university. Over the last year, he has experienced an imaginable horror in Washington, DC &mdash; assaults, a false arrest, home surveillance, computer hacking, &ldquo;pinning&rdquo; or behavioral steering, property damage and theft.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">His best friend believes that Pearson is suffering from mental illness. He has visited Pearson in 2025 and saw signs that worried him. He won&rsquo;t read Pearson&rsquo;s writings, won&rsquo;t google the technology (e.g., ultrasonic sound), and feels that he is losing a friend. He has denied that Pearson has sent him proof of stalkers &mdash; the photos are in the articles that the friend refuses to read. Both men are African American and highly educated. Both are independent thinkers, but Pearson has an interdisciplinary orientation and epistemic humility that makes him clear-eyed. Pearson is not insane. He is a victim.</span></p><h4 class="c5" id="h.hwd6ze6kn92v"><span class="c8 c9">The Text Exchange Between Friends</span></h4><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Friend: </span><span class="c2">I turned 48 today and I hope this next year finds you better. I know you don&rsquo;t believe this but I feel you drifting away as each day passes and it makes me sad. It&rsquo;s been almost a year since we had a normal conversation and I miss that.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Pearson: </span><span class="c2">HAPPY BIRTHDAY!!!! I am categorically NOT drifting away. I was tortured, stalked, falsely arrested, assaulted, electrocuted in the penis, and harassed. If you read any of my writings, you would see that I am not drifting at all. I am providing a recollection of my experiences, backed with photos, videos, timelines, and explanatory frameworks. Many people do not make it. In fact, it has made me a stronger researcher. I have got to get a handle on this head situation after I was assaulted. Something feels loose and I feel it when I walk. And yes, we will soon have a regular conversation. You believe that I am drifting away, but you must dispel with your idea of what you think is happening. These things happen to American citizens on US soil. It&rsquo;s not right, fair, or constitutional, but that is a fact. This is entirely consistent with the Trump administration&rsquo;s racially and ideologically targeted programs. Part of the design is to make it appear as something that it is not such as mental illness. You should look up Gloria Naylor and read her book 1996 &mdash; famed African American author and writer of the Women of Brewster Place. She concluded that the Anti-Defamation League was involved in her campaign and guess what? FBI director recently named them a domestic terrorist organization after 60 years of close partnership. I am not saying it&rsquo;s ADL for me, but I am saying that these things happen. AI said that I have parallels with another African American. I did research on his case. It has more holes than a block of Swiss cheese, which I have written about. I am categorically not experiencing mental illness &mdash; I am experiencing torture and trauma. We know that from such programs as COINTELPRO. I cannot reassure you if you can&rsquo;t be reassured. I love you but some openness might be helpful.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Friend: </span><span class="c2">Some openness on your part that maybe something other than what you think is actually happening would be helpful</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Pearson: </span><span class="c2">I 100% agree with that. I don&rsquo;t have all of the facts. Actually, my premonition is that the targeting and related programs are far worse. But I do know that I am a damn good researcher who has not lost myself and who will not lose myself. I experienced some decomposition, yes. You saw that. I observed myself seeing that. That was part of the program&rsquo;s goals, but they did not get very far. Part of my advantage is that I am highly interdisciplinary. Again, like I said, ultrasonic sound is a thing. Has been a thing for a long time. I don&rsquo;t expect you to be like me of course, but when you make claims without reading or research, I have to dismiss them out of hand &mdash; &mdash; and out of love.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Pearson: </span><span class="c2">This whole ordeal has shown me who my true friends are in this world. People that I talked to almost every day have not checked in on me in over 6 months. That says a lot. You are a true friend and you showed that. We have always had an open and honest relationship centered around mutual love. We shoot from the hip cause we real people. So I saw your light and love in the past year. It shines bright. I should have started off with that.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Pearson: </span><span class="c2">Now, I can call you now that we have cleared the air haha.</span></p><p class="c11"><span style="overflow: hidden; display: inline-block; margin: 0.00px 0.00px; border: 0.00px solid #000000; transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px); -webkit-transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px); width: 624.00px; height: 624.00px;"><img alt="" src="images/image1.jpg" style="width: 624.00px; height: 624.00px; margin-left: 0.00px; margin-top: 0.00px; transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px); -webkit-transform: rotate(0.00rad) translateZ(0px);" title=""></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.6scs7m5sb7g2"><span class="c7">The Birthday Text</span></h3><h3 class="c4" id="h.8v1b6wxvva62"><span class="c7">What a Single Email Exchange Reveals About the Most Intimate Damage of Targeted Torture</span></h3><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">A friend turned 48. He sent Richard Pearson a birthday message &mdash; not celebratory, but honest. He missed him. He felt him drifting. It had been almost a year since they&rsquo;d had a normal conversation, and it made him sad.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">What followed is one of the most human documents in Pearson&rsquo;s entire body of documentation. Not a timestamp or a photograph or an AI probability score. A conversation between two people who love each other &mdash; one of whom has spent the last year being tortured, and one of whom has spent the same year watching his friend change, without any framework to understand why, and concluding the most available explanation: something is wrong with Richard.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This exchange, read carefully, shows what the program&rsquo;s most sophisticated damage actually looks like. Not the directed energy assault. Not the voice in the skull. Not the false arrest. Those are violations of the body and the law. This is the violation of something older and more irreplaceable: the conversation between friends who tell each other the truth.</span></p><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.tq3ejkxpy3hx"><span class="c7">What the Friend Sees</span></h3><p class="c0"><span class="c2">He sees drift. He has watched, across eleven months, as the man he used to talk to every day became someone who talks about torture, false arrests, electrocution, stalking. He doesn&rsquo;t recognize the conversation anymore. It has been almost a year since they spoke normally. He misses that.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">He is not wrong about what he observes. Pearson has changed. The man who spent 2025 being surveilled, assaulted, sleep-deprived, psychologically decomposed, falsely arrested, and subjected to coordinated campaigns of social disruption is not identical to the man who existed before those things happened. The friend sees the change. He interprets it through the only available framework: something is wrong with Richard.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">The framework is understandable. It is wrong. But it is understandable in precisely the way that the program designed it to be.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>This is the elegance of the methodology. The Stasi understood it sixty years ago. COINTELPRO understood it before that. The most effective way to destroy a person&rsquo;s credibility &mdash; and with it, their relationships, their professional standing, and their ability to function as a witness &mdash; is not to attack them from outside. It is to produce, in the people who know them best, the sincere belief that the target has lost their mind. When the friend says </span><span class="c1">I feel you drifting away</span><span class="c2">, he is not an operative. He is not part of the program. He is a man who loves Richard Pearson and is watching something that looks like deterioration and reaching, honestly and with sadness, for the most obvious explanation.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">The program did not need him to be recruited. It needed him to watch.</span></p><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.wu3umo12cfm2"><span class="c7">What Pearson Brings Back</span></h3><p class="c0"><span class="c2">Pearson&rsquo;s response is the most revealing thing in the exchange. Read it not as an argument but as a document.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>He starts with HAPPY BIRTHDAY in capitals &mdash; the exclamation point is real, the warmth is immediate, the relationship leads &mdash; and then goes straight to the record. He is </span><span class="c1">categorically not</span><span class="c2">&nbsp;drifting. He was tortured, stalked, falsely arrested, assaulted, electrocuted in the penis, and harassed. He has photos, videos, timelines, and explanatory frameworks. Many people do not make it. It has made him a stronger researcher.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Then this: </span><span class="c1 c6">I have got to get a handle on this head situation after I was assaulted. Something feels loose and I feel it when I walk.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">That sentence does not belong to a man performing sanity. It belongs to a man who is injured and knows it and is calibrating the distance between what he can manage and what requires attention. He has something physically wrong &mdash; neurological, probably, given the nature of the assaults he documents &mdash; and he is noting it with the same methodical honesty he applies to everything. Something feels loose. He feels it when he walks. He needs to get a handle on it.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This is the voice of someone who is monitoring themselves with scientific precision, not someone who has lost track of themselves.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>He invokes Gloria Naylor &mdash; not randomly, but because the argument needs grounding in documented precedent. Naylor was a celebrated African American author, winner of the American Book Award, whose novel </span><span class="c1">The Women of Brewster Place</span><span>&nbsp;was adapted for television. She published </span><span class="c1">1996</span><span class="c2">&nbsp;documenting her own experience of apparent government targeting. It was dismissed, widely, as paranoia. She concluded the Anti-Defamation League was involved. Pearson is careful to note he is not saying it&rsquo;s the ADL in his case. But he is saying: an FBI director recently called the ADL a domestic terrorist organization after sixty years of close institutional partnership. When Naylor said it, she was dismissed. The institutional record has since moved toward her.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>This is what a researcher looks like when they argue. Not assertion &mdash; precedent. Not paranoia &mdash; pattern. He is telling his friend: </span><span class="c6 c1">I know how this sounds. I know you&rsquo;ve decided what it is. But the thing you&rsquo;ve decided it is has a documented history of being used to explain away exactly the thing I am experiencing.</span></p><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.tvr8hqgtenpc"><span class="c7">The Friend&rsquo;s Reply</span></h3><p class="c0"><span>Four words. </span><span class="c6 c1">Some openness on your part.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">It is, at first read, a deflection. You think I&rsquo;m mentally ill; maybe consider that you might be. It&rsquo;s the move every friend makes when they&rsquo;ve been met with an explanation they find too extreme: you asked me to be open, but couldn&rsquo;t you be open too?</span></p><p class="c0"><span>But Pearson hears it differently. He agrees. One hundred percent. He does not have all the facts. His premonition &mdash; the word is interesting, and precise &mdash; is that the targeting and related programs are </span><span class="c1">worse</span><span>&nbsp;than what he has documented, not better. He is not claiming certainty. He is claiming methodology. He is a damn good researcher. He has not lost himself. He observed his own decomposition as it was happening &mdash; </span><span class="c1">I experienced some decomposition, yes. You saw that. I observed myself seeing that</span><span class="c2">&nbsp;&mdash; and that act of self-observation, from inside the experience, is precisely what the program&rsquo;s decomposition methodology is designed to prevent.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">You cannot decompose someone who is watching themselves be decomposed and taking notes.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">Then he says the sentence that belongs at the center of any honest account of this case:</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c6 c1">When you make claims without reading or research, I have to dismiss them out of hand &mdash; and out of love.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">He is not being cruel. He is being precise. The friend has formed a conclusion &mdash; something other than what Richard thinks is happening &mdash; without reading the writings, without Googling the technology, without engaging with the scientific literature that Richard has assembled across a year of meticulous documentation. He has reached a diagnosis without examining the evidence.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">Pearson&rsquo;s response to that is not to capitulate or to reassure. It is to say: I love you, and because I love you I&rsquo;m telling you that a conclusion formed without engagement with the evidence is not one I can credit. This is not stubbornness. This is what intellectual integrity looks like under conditions designed to make intellectual integrity look like pathology.</span></p><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.i76h0gli3b0a"><span class="c7">The Third Message</span></h3><p class="c0"><span class="c2">Then something shifts.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">After the disagreement, after the defended ground, after the honest friction of two people who tell each other the truth &mdash; Pearson sends a second message, and it is entirely different in register.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c6 c1">This whole ordeal has shown me who my true friends are in this world. People that I talked to almost every day have not checked in on me in over 6 months. That says a lot. You are a true friend and you showed that.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">He is not performing vulnerability. He is reporting it. The year of targeting cost him relationships &mdash; multiple relationships, people he talked to almost every day, people who did not call, did not check in, and in some cases, as the documentation of Ms. Sherry and the elderly neighbor reveals, may have been actively recruited into the operation against him. The social world that surrounded Richard Pearson before July 2025 is not the social world that surrounds him in May 2026. The program designed exactly this outcome.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">But this friend is still here. He is here on his birthday, sad, missing Richard, saying so honestly. He is wrong about what is happening. He has not read the writings. He will not Google the technology. He reached for the psychiatric explanation, as the program anticipated he would. But he is still here. He sent the message. He said it makes him sad. He is not gone.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c6 c1">We have always had an open and honest relationship centered around mutual love. We shoot from the hip cause we real people. So I saw your light and love in the past year. It shines bright.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This is what the program failed to destroy. Not Pearson&rsquo;s documentation, not his analytical framework, not his physical survival &mdash; those were the program&rsquo;s targets, and they are harder cases. This is simpler: a friendship. A man who turned 48 and sent a birthday message. A man who received it and, after defending himself, stepped back and said: I see you, and I&rsquo;m glad you&rsquo;re here.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c6 c1">Now, I can call you now that we have cleared the air haha.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>The </span><span class="c1">haha</span><span class="c2">&nbsp;is doing significant emotional work. It is the exhale at the end of a hard conversation. It is the recognition that the argument was worth having because the relationship survived it. It is Pearson being, for a moment, not a torture victim or a researcher or a documentarian of state crimes &mdash; just a person who cleared the air with a friend and wants to call him.</span></p><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.sd3ollhb2tie"><span class="c7">The Mechanism, Precisely Described</span></h3><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This email exchange is one of the most precise illustrations available of how the targeting program&rsquo;s social isolation methodology works &mdash; and of why it is so difficult to fight.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">The program does not need to recruit the friend. It does not need to give him a script or a signal or a T-shirt with words on it. It simply needs to produce, in Pearson, behaviors that are consistent with deterioration &mdash; the obsessive documentation, the urgent referencing of technologies and historical precedents, the inability to have a normal conversation because the abnormal thing is always present, always relevant, always demanding acknowledgment. These behaviors are real. They are the rational response of a researcher to a campaign of torture. But they look, from the outside, exactly like what a person in the early stages of a paranoid episode looks like.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">The friend is not wrong to be worried. The friend is wrong about the cause.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This is the program&rsquo;s most sophisticated design feature: it produces real symptoms in the target &mdash; dissociation, obsessive pattern-recognition, difficulty with ordinary social interaction, physical injuries that produce odd sensations and behavioral changes &mdash; that are clinically indistinguishable, to an untrained observer, from the symptoms of a serious mental illness. The target is then left to fight on two fronts simultaneously: against the program that is harming them, and against the sincere misperception of the people who love them.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">Pearson understands both fronts. He has the psychiatric evaluation. He has the documentation. He has, as he notes, observed his own decomposition from the inside and survived the observation. But he cannot give the friend that evaluation to hold, cannot transmit the experience of having walked through a year of coordinated assault with his analytical faculties intact, cannot make the friend understand what ultrasonic sound is without the friend being willing to Google it.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c6 c1">I cannot reassure you if you can&rsquo;t be reassured.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>This is the sentence that should be inscribed somewhere in the history of what the program cost him. Not a testimony of bitterness &mdash; it is followed immediately by </span><span class="c1">I love you</span><span class="c2">&nbsp;&mdash; but an acknowledgment of the limit. There is a point at which one person cannot close the epistemological gap for another. There is a point at which the other person has to do the work of knowing. The friend has not done that work. And Pearson loves him anyway, and is glad he called, and cleared the air.</span></p><hr><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.5dp62tjkd1b4"><span class="c7">In the Grand Scheme</span></h3><p class="c0"><span class="c2">The birthday exchange is a small document. It is not the 200-page primary record. It is not the AI analyses or the MIND Act or the UN statement or the psychiatric evaluation. It is two people talking on an evening in the spring of 2026. &mdash; one of them having survived a year of documented torture, the other having watched from a distance, sad, without a framework.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">But it contains, in miniature, the full architecture of what the program designed.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">It designed for Pearson&rsquo;s friends to feel him drifting when he was not drifting. It designed for the people who loved him to reach for psychiatric explanation when the correct explanation was government crime. It designed for the conversation to become difficult, and for difficulty to erode frequency, and for eroded frequency to produce silence, and for silence to produce the isolation that looks, from the outside, like the kind of withdrawal that mental illness produces.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">Most of it worked, on most people. The people who talked to him almost every day did not call for six months.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This one did. On his birthday, sad, honest, wrong about the cause, present nonetheless.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">And Pearson, after defending himself with the full force of a year&rsquo;s worth of documentation and research and analytical discipline &mdash; stepped back and saw the light and love in his friend&rsquo;s imperfect, misdiagnosing, present, birthday message.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c6 c1">It shines bright.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">This is what survives a targeting program. Not just the evidence. Not just the documentation. Not just the psychiatric clearance and the timestamp photographs and the tin foil Bluetooth experiments and the frame-by-frame Cherry Blossom Festival video analysis. This too: a man who called on his birthday, and a man who answered, and the phone call that followed after the air had been cleared.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">The program designed for Richard Pearson to be alone.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c2">On this evening, he was not.</span></p><p class="c3"><span class="c2"></span></p></body></html>


Richard Pearson, US Torture Victim, Reveals New Details about Street Theater
It wasn't enough that the DC Metropolitan Police illegally surveilled his home, falsely arrested him, and manufactured a non-existent witness, MPD also took part in street theater.
Richard Pearson has maintained a highly unusual and detailed account of his torture experience in Washington, DC. In other essays, he has described his false arrest, police manufacturing a non-existent witness, and their failure to arrest the assailant who repeatedly punched Pearson in the head and face.
Pearson now reveals new details about the Metropolitan Police Department in Washington, DC.
"Munchies"
"On March 23, 2026, I was eating at Dos Toros Taqueria at 700 7th St NW. I didn't have much money, so a small bag of tortilla chips was all that I could afford. As I often do, I was writing on my laptop. I noticed that a cop had come in, but I had little attention on him otherwise. Before entering, I had noticed maybe 4–5 cop cars lined up along 7th Street. The street was busy with people, so my guess was that there was an event at Capitol One Arena across the street.
When he got his food and departed for the door, he slowed his pace near me. While not directing his head to me but clearly audible, he said, "He's smoked. Now, he's got the munchies." The tone is hard to describe, but I would say delivered with a cutting undertone. I knew it was meant for me. There was no one else around. Still with a slowed walk, he eventually disappeared beyond the door.
I don't know what goal the officer had. It could have been to convey that he knew that I had smoked a cigarette shortly before - that he or they were watching me. My cigarette habit had picked up appreciably since last year. I was also smoking in public, which I tended to avoid. His phrasing made it seem that I smoked marijuana, which is usually associated with the "munchies". I don't smoke marijuana. He just wanted to be a nagging fly.
The officer, though, did not understand how I fully viewed him. He, along with all of the other tormentors, reflected an internal psychotic state. Yes, I was diagnosing them - have no compunction about it. Their disassociation from reality was severe. They not only found justification and sadistic pleasure in torturing and tormenting me for the last year but operated in a space without moral grounding. There is also something about their conduct that conveys a godlike mentality - above the law, above ethics, above people, and above accountability. It sounds harsh, but I think it's fully accurate. If you take everything from the surveillance, the assaults, false arrest, constitutional violations, and deliberate attempt at destabilization of my personality and emotional state, this is a fair representation of the collective psyche.
I took a photograph so that I would remember the date and time: ‎Monday, ‎March ‎23, ‎2026, ‏‎8:34:57 PM
I tried to find him among the cops sitting in their cars outside. He probably got out of the immediate radius to avoid identification.
AI-generated image: Officer's position is more or less correct, except that he never turned toward Pearson who would have quickly got his badge name.Good Afternoon
"I was arriving home and had come through the door to my apartment. With impeccable timing, a Black officer and his partner had just gotten off of the elevator. "Good afternoon," said the Black officer.
Something was off.
I wanted to say hi to his partner - an officer "Russo". That is his actual name. He and I had talked on many occasions over the years. I found him to be very nice and level-headed. We could have frank discussions. I directed my attention to him and probably formed my mouth to greet him.
Russo immediately put his head down. He wanted to avoid me. "Ok, so what is going on here?", I wondered.
It was getting clearer. This same sort of scene plays out all over Washington, DC. When someone files a lawsuit, we can get a better picture as with April Goggans' lawsuit alleging surveillance and stalking against DC MPD. This exact scene is described in her lawsuit. That is what MPD does. They stalk. They find you. They communicate.
The tone of the officer's "salutation" now made sense. It was dripping with sarcasm - and sadism. He probably thought that I would be upset or emotional with the sort of interaction - scared of the DC police following my false arrest. He was wrong.
He was wrong because his conduct was more about him than me. He enjoyed - took immense pleasure - from the kind of power display. He knew that citizens had accused MPD of this very type of behavior, which they refuse to correct.
He was also wrong because I was noting all of it. I was publishing here there and everywhere. The more they did, the worse they looked.
