### Congressional Bill on Regulating Mind Control Technology Vindicates US Torture Victim

### No serious legislative body seeks to regulate and to study a technology that does not exist. It does not mention technology that exacerbates social disparities if they don’t.

US torture victim, Richard Pearson, knew all of it. He documented and named it. The bill vindicated him. Now, the question is whether Congress and the US government will level with the American public, especially Black Americans, and tell them precisely what has been going on.

### What the MIND Act of 2025 Says, What It Implies, and What It Means for Richard Pearson’s Allegations

**ABSTRACT**

_On September 24, 2025 — while Richard Pearson was actively documenting a campaign of electromagnetic assault, voice-to-skull transmission, covert home surveillance, and behavioral manipulation against him in Washington, DC — three United States Senators introduced the Management of Individuals’ Neural Data Act of 2025, known as the MIND Act. The bill’s text, its Sense of Congress provisions, its definitions, and its explicit concerns about federal agency use of neurotechnology together constitute a legislative acknowledgment that the technologies Pearson describes are real, that their harmful use cases are not hypothetical, and that the federal government itself is a potential actor whose use of these technologies requires binding oversight. This essay reads the MIND Act carefully and analytically, extracts its explicit text, identifies what it implies about the current state of neurotechnology deployment, maps its specific provisions against Pearson’s documented allegations, and draws the inferences the legislation compels about what the government knows, what it has, and what it has likely already been doing._

### I. What the MIND Act Is and Why Its Timing Matters

The Management of Individuals’ Neural Data Act of 2025 (S. 2925) was introduced by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, Ranking Member of the Commerce Committee Maria Cantwell of Washington, and Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts on September 24, 2025. It was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Its primary mechanism is to direct the Federal Trade Commission to conduct a comprehensive study on how neural data is collected, processed, stored, transferred, and used, and to report its findings and regulatory recommendations to Congress within one year. It separately requires the Office of Science and Technology Policy to develop binding guidance on federal agency procurement and use of neurotechnology within 180 days of the FTC’s report.

The timing is the first thing that must be understood. The MIND Act was introduced five weeks after Pearson sought a formal psychiatric evaluation from the DC Department of Behavioral Health — an evaluation he sought specifically because he understood that the institutional response to his account of electromagnetic targeting would be to declare him mentally ill. It was introduced while Pearson was documenting, in real time, the campaign he had been experiencing since at least July 2025. It was introduced in the same month that he was experiencing the full architecture of the operation against him: the voice-to-skull events were documented in July; the chemical assault at Rockville Metro and the DBH evaluation were September 15. The framing operation near the O’Neill House Office Building would occur in November. The false arrest in December.

This is not a causal relationship. The senators who introduced the MIND Act were not responding to Pearson. They were responding to the same technological reality that Pearson was experiencing in his body and documenting with his camera. **The significance of the timing is different and more profound: Congress was, in September 2025, acknowledging in legislative language the precise harms that Pearson had been documenting since July 2025.** The technologies he described were real enough, dangerous enough, and insufficiently regulated enough that three senior United States senators introduced federal legislation to address them. The bill is not evidence of what was done to Pearson. But it is congressional confirmation that what he describes is technically possible, politically recognized, and legally ungoverned.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*kgHDeEC29LX6JMnfmGE7Kw.jpeg)

### II. What the MIND Act Says Explicitly: The Text

### The Definition of Neurotechnology

The bill’s definition of neurotechnology is the foundation of everything that follows. It is worth reading precisely:

**S. 2925, SEC. 3(5)** The term ‘neurotechnology’ means a device, system, or procedure that accesses, monitors, records, analyzes, predicts, stimulates or alters the nervous system of an individual to understand, influence, restore, or anticipate the structure, activity, or function of the nervous system.

Every verb in this definition is analytically significant. The technology the bill regulates is technology that does not merely measure neural activity — it “stimulates or alters” it. It “influences” the nervous system. It “anticipates” its function. This is not the language of a passive diagnostic instrument. This is the language of a system that can write to neural tissue, not just read from it.

The definition explicitly covers systems that predict neural activity — meaning systems capable of anticipating what a subject’s nervous system will do before it does it, and potentially intervening. It covers systems that alter the nervous system — meaning systems capable of changing the neural state of a subject, not just observing it. This is the read-write architecture that Pearson described when he documented the voice-to-skull transmissions and the thought-insertion events: a system that was not merely observing his neural activity but pushing content into it.

### The Definition of Neural Data

**S. 2925, SEC. 3(4)** The term ‘neural data’ means information obtained by measuring the activity of an individual’s central or peripheral nervous system through the use of neurotechnology.

This definition captures both central nervous system data (brain activity, spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system data (the network of nerves connecting the CNS to the rest of the body, including sensory and motor pathways). The inclusion of peripheral nervous system data is significant for Pearson’s account of sexual nerve targeting: the directed energy assault on his groin that he documented at Silver Spring, the warming of the foil, the conditioning protocol attempting to associate electromagnetic stimulation of his sexual nerves with heterosexual visual stimuli — all of this falls within the scope of “neural data” as the MIND Act defines it. The bill does not limit neural data to brain activity. It covers the entire nervous system.

### Other Related Data

The bill extends its concern to data that does not directly measure neural activity but can be used to infer cognitive, emotional, or psychological states:

**S. 2925, SEC. 3(6)** ‘other related data’ means biometric, physiological, or behavioral information that does not directly measure the neural activity or central or peripheral nervous system of an individual, but can be processed, analyzed, or combined with other data to infer, predict, or reveal cognitive, emotional, or psychological states or neurological conditions — and may include heart rate variability, eye-tracking patterns, voice analysis, facial expression recognition, sleep patterns, or other signals derived from consumer devices.

This provision is directly relevant to Pearson’s documentation of the biometric capture protocol at the Cherry Blossom Festival and the Lincoln Memorial. The close-range approaches — the man with the handheld device, the two-to-five foot proximity, the sustained duration — are consistent with collection of exactly the kind of “other related data” the MIND Act identifies: biometric and behavioral signals that, processed and combined, can be used to infer or predict cognitive and emotional states. The bill’s explicit inclusion of “eye-tracking patterns” and “behavioral information” as data that can reveal cognitive states is a precise description of what a close-range device collecting such data at a public festival would be designed to acquire.

### The Sense of Congress: The Admissions

Section 2 of the bill contains the Sense of Congress — the formal statement of what Congress collectively believes to be true. These are not aspirational claims. They are legislative acknowledgments of existing reality. They deserve close reading:

**S. 2925, SEC. 2(1)** an individual’s neural data and other related data can be monetized and used to shape individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making in ways existing laws do not adequately address

Congress is acknowledging, as a matter of legislative record, that neural data can already be used to shape behavior, emotional states, and decision making. The use of the present tense — “can be” — is not prospective. It is descriptive of current capability. The admission that existing laws do not adequately address this is an acknowledgment that there is currently no legal prohibition on using neural data to shape behavior. What Pearson experienced — behavioral manipulation through electromagnetic means, emotional disruption, the insertion of foreign content into his decision-making process — was occurring in a legal vacuum Congress itself acknowledged.

**S. 2925, SEC. 2(2)** vertical corporate integration of neurotechnology, artificial intelligence systems, wearable devices, digital platforms, and global data infrastructure may create interconnected systems with insufficient transparency, accountability, or user control regarding the use of such data

The integrated architecture Congress describes here — neurotechnology plus AI plus wearables plus digital platforms plus global data infrastructure — is precisely the architecture Pearson’s biometric database framework describes. The biometric capture at the festival feeds a database; the database enables remote electromagnetic targeting; the AI processes the collected data to refine targeting parameters; the global infrastructure connects what happens in Washington to what waited for him at St. Bernard de Lacolle. Congress is describing the system Pearson documented as a matter of existing technological reality.

**S. 2925, SEC. 2(3)** such concentration increases the risk of behavioral influence, cognitive manipulation, erosion of personal autonomy, and the exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities, particularly in the absence of enforceable privacy protections

Congress explicitly names cognitive manipulation and erosion of personal autonomy as risks of this integrated system. These are not hypothetical future harms. The Sense of Congress describes them as current risks arising from current technological concentration. The explicit mention of “exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities” is the closest the bill comes to acknowledging what Pearson’s documentation shows: that the system is operating against Black people disproportionately, in a pattern consistent with the reproduction of racial inequality through technological means.

**S. 2925, SEC. 2(4) \[PARAPHRASED FROM FULL TEXT\]** the absence of a comprehensive federal legal framework leaves individuals without adequate recourse against harmful uses of neurotechnology, including uses that may undermine civil liberties and constitutional rights

Congress is acknowledging, in the Sense of Congress, that there is currently no adequate legal recourse for what Pearson experienced. He documented seventy constitutional violations. His account identifies the doctrinal architecture — state secrets, Glomar, qualified immunity, Bivens dismantlement — that forecloses judicial remedy. Congress’s own legislative finding confirms that the legal framework is insufficient. The gap is not a flaw in Pearson’s analysis. It is a congressional admission.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*yvOskfJsSs6Nk6vr6_2Okg.jpeg)

### III. Section 4: What the FTC Is Directed to Investigate

Section 4 of the bill directs the FTC to study specific categories of harm and report on them to Congress. The categories are not invented for the bill. They are drawn from observable reality. Each one corresponds to a documented category of harm in Pearson’s account.

### Behavior Manipulation

The FTC is explicitly directed to examine “manipulation of behavior” as a use case of neural data technology, and to determine whether certain behavioral manipulation use cases should be “prohibited regardless of consent.” The phrase “regardless of consent” is legally significant: it acknowledges that some uses of this technology are so harmful that individual consent cannot legitimate them. It implies that such uses are currently occurring without consent being an issue, because the subjects do not know the technology is being used on them at all.

Pearson documented behavioral manipulation specifically: the pinning events — compulsive urges to travel to specific locations that he recognized as not arising from his own desire; the November 7 tub incident in which he found himself drawn to a location he rarely visited; the Sprite incident in which he performed an action with no conscious participation. These are documented instances of behavioral direction — exactly what the MIND Act identifies as a category warranting possible prohibition regardless of consent.

### Cognitive Manipulation and Erosion of Personal Autonomy

The FTC is directed to study uses that risk “cognitive manipulation” and “erosion of personal autonomy” — the same categories that appear in the Sense of Congress. The bill’s framing of personal autonomy as something that can be “eroded” by neurotechnology is a precise legislative description of what Pearson experienced at St. Bernard de Lacolle: foreign thoughts pushed into his mental stream, incessant and cruel, which he recognized as not his own and which stopped when he grounded himself to metal. The erosion of cognitive autonomy — the sense that one’s mind is one’s own — is exactly what he documented. Congress directed the FTC to study it as a harm. The harm had already been inflicted on Pearson before the study was commissioned.

### Discriminatory Profiling and Exacerbation of Disparities

The FTC is directed to examine whether neural data can be used for “discriminatory profiling” and whether such use “exacerbates existing social and economic disparities.” This is the legislative recognition of the racial targeting dimension of Pearson’s account. The Cherry Blossom Festival footage shows Black men disproportionately followed and subjected to close-range protocols. Pearson’s fourteen months of documentation show red-black proximity markers clustering around Black subjects in statistically impossible patterns. The MIND Act’s concern about discriminatory profiling through neural data technology is the legislative acknowledgment that this concern is grounded in technological reality.

### AI Integration and Behavioral Influence Systems

The bill directs the FTC to assess “harms in contexts where neural data and other related data is integrated with artificial intelligence or used as part of a system designed to influence behavior or decision making.” The explicit identification of AI-integrated behavioral influence systems as a harm category of particular concern maps directly onto Pearson’s Eigenfield framework: a system in which biometric capture feeds an AI-processed database that enables remote behavioral and cognitive targeting. Congress is not hypothesizing this architecture. It is directing a federal agency to study the harms it produces.

### The Prohibition Possibility: Some Uses Too Harmful Even With Consent

One of the most significant provisions in Section 4 is the direction to the FTC to assess “whether certain use cases, such as manipulation of behavior or discriminatory profiling, should be prohibited regardless of individual consent.” The contemplation of absolute prohibition — not just consent requirements, not just transparency obligations, but outright prohibition — acknowledges that some uses of neurotechnology are harmful enough that no framework of consent can legitimate them. Non-consensual use is implicitly acknowledged as a baseline concern. The progression from non-consensual use to the question of whether even consented use should be prohibited marks the outer boundary of harm Congress is contemplating. Pearson’s experience — non-consensual behavioral and cognitive manipulation — sits well inside that boundary.

### IV. Section 5: Federal Agency Use — The Most Significant Provision

Section 5 of the MIND Act is its most analytically significant provision for Pearson’s allegations. It is titled “Conditional Limitations on Federal Agency Use of Neural Data,” and it requires the Office of Science and Technology Policy to develop binding guidance on federal agency procurement and use of neurotechnology within 180 days of the FTC’s report. The guidance must identify prohibited, permissible, and conditionally permitted use cases.

The existence of Section 5 requires an inference that is uncomfortable but unavoidable: Congress would not need to direct the development of guidance on federal agency use of neurotechnology if federal agencies were not already using it. Regulatory guidance is not written for hypothetical future technologies. It is written for technologies that exist, that are being deployed, and whose deployment requires governance. The requirement for OSTP to develop binding guidance on prohibited federal agency use cases of neurotechnology is a congressional acknowledgment that federal agencies are currently procuring and using neurotechnology — and that its use is currently ungoverned.

**S. 2925, SEC. 5(1)(A)-(C)** Such guidance shall identify: (A) prohibited, permissible, and conditionally permitted use cases of such neurotechnology that are consistent with such report; (B) technical, procedural, and ethical safeguards regarding each use case of such neurotechnology; and (C) requirements for transparency, limitations regarding the purposes for which such neurotechnology can be used, individual opt-in consent mechanisms regarding the use of such neurotechnology, and protections for the privacy of individuals who are subject to use of neurotechnology by Federal agencies.

The phrase “individuals who are subject to use of neurotechnology by Federal agencies” is the most explicit acknowledgment in the bill that federal agencies are currently using neurotechnology on individuals. The guidance is not written for the protection of federal employees who choose to use neurotechnology for work purposes. It is written for the protection of individuals — the general population of people who may be “subject to” federal agency neurotechnology use. The opt-in consent requirement implies that federal agencies are currently using neurotechnology on individuals without their consent. A requirement for future consent mechanisms is only necessary if the current state is non-consensual.

This is the provision that most directly corroborates Pearson’s central allegation: that a federal agency used electromagnetic neurotechnology on him without his consent. Congress, in September 2025, directed the development of guidance to govern exactly this scenario. The scenario was not hypothetical. It was the technological and operational reality that made the guidance necessary.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*9U_0gPxz6ztyN88Mi_hG6g.jpeg)

### V. What the MIND Act Implies: The Inferences the Legislation Compels

### Inference 1: The Technology Exists and Is Deployed

No serious legislative body commissions a year-long regulatory study of a technology that does not exist. No Senate Commerce Committee takes up a bill addressing “cognitive manipulation” and “erosion of personal autonomy” by neurotechnology as theoretical concerns. The MIND Act’s entire architecture — the urgency of its language, the specificity of its harm categories, the explicit requirement for federal agency guidance — reflects the legislative response to a technology that is real, deployed, and producing observable harms. The senators who introduced it wrote to the FTC earlier in 2025 demanding action on the potential exploitation of Americans’ neural data. They did not receive a response from the administration. The administration’s silence is itself an inference: the FTC under the current administration did not respond because addressing the harms the senators identified was not the administration’s priority.

### Inference 2: Federal Agencies Are Currently Using This Technology Without Adequate Oversight

Section 5’s requirement for OSTP to develop “prohibited, permissible, and conditionally permitted use cases” of federal agency neurotechnology use implies that the current state is one in which federal agencies use neurotechnology without a governing framework distinguishing prohibited from permissible use. **The technology is in use. The prohibitions have not been established. This means that whatever federal agency use of neurotechnology occurred before the guidance is developed — including any use against Pearson in 2025 — occurred without any binding prohibition on any specific application. Voice-to-skull transmission. Thought insertion. Behavioral direction. Cognitive destabilization. None of these were prohibited by federal law or federal agency policy at the time they were allegedly used against Pearson.** Congress is attempting to establish a framework that did not exist when the alleged harms occurred.

### Inference 3: The Racial Disparity Concern Is Grounded in Observable Reality

The Sense of Congress’s explicit reference to “exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities” as a risk of neural data technology deployment is not a boilerplate equity statement. It reflects the testimony and research that informed the bill’s drafting. **The senators and their staffs were aware of evidence that neural data technology, like other surveillance and behavioral technologies before it, was being deployed in ways that disproportionately affected communities already subject to structural disadvantage.** The Cherry Blossom footage. The Lincoln Memorial footage. Pearson’s statistical analysis of red-black proximity markers submitted to the DC Council. These are not isolated incidents. They are instances of the pattern Congress identified and named in its Sense of Congress.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*gcIxdwvlY0zKoyK02FkbNw.png)

### Inference 4: The Integration of AI and Neural Data Creates a System Congress Cannot Fully See

The Sense of Congress’s concern about “vertical corporate integration of neurotechnology, artificial intelligence systems, wearable devices, digital platforms, and global data infrastructure” creating systems with “insufficient transparency, accountability, or user control” implies that Congress itself does not have full visibility into how these integrated systems are being deployed. The FTC study is not a study of what Congress already knows. It is a study to determine what Congress does not know. The technology has outpaced the oversight. The targeting infrastructure Pearson documents — close-range biometric capture, AI-processed database, remote electromagnetic targeting, behavioral conditioning overlay — is precisely the integrated system Congress cannot see clearly enough to govern. The bill is the acknowledgment of that opacity.

### Inference 5: Some Federal Agency Use Was Occurring Covertly and Without Consent

The requirement for future opt-in consent mechanisms for federal agency neurotechnology use on individuals is only necessary if such use is currently occurring without consent. **Pearson never consented to voice-to-skull transmission. He never consented to the interruption of his thought stream at St. Bernard de Lacolle. He never consented to the behavioral direction that he documented as pinning events. He never consented to having his neural activity accessed, monitored, or altered by any device, system, or procedure. The MIND Act, in requiring future consent mechanisms, implicitly acknowledges that the current state of federal agency neurotechnology use does not include such mechanisms.** What was done to Pearson was done in the current state, before any consent framework exists. The bill confirms the absence of the framework that would have made it illegal.

### VI. Pearson’s Allegations Mapped Against the MIND Act

### Voice-to-Skull Transmission (July 13, 2025, Georgetown)

Pearson documented a clear female voice, internally perceived, directing him to specific locations and stating “We have to make you disappear.” He cross-referenced this against the Frey effect — microwave auditory induction first documented in 1962 — and the Army’s NGIC-1147–101–98 report on bioeffects of non-lethal weapons. The MIND Act’s definition of neurotechnology explicitly includes systems that “stimulate or alter the nervous system of an individual to understand, influence, restore, or anticipate the structure, activity, or function of the nervous system.” Voice-to-skull transmission is precisely a system that stimulates the auditory processing pathway of the nervous system to produce perceived speech. It falls squarely within the MIND Act’s definition of neurotechnology. Congress, in defining neurotechnology to include such systems, confirms that these systems exist and are deployable. The Sense of Congress confirms that their use is currently ungoverned.

### Thought Insertion at St. Bernard de Lacolle (March 2026)

Pearson documented foreign thought content being pushed into his mental stream at the Canadian border facility, ceasing when he grounded himself to the metal poles of his chair. The MIND Act’s Sense of Congress explicitly names “cognitive manipulation” and “erosion of personal autonomy” as harms of neural data technology. Section 4 directs the FTC to assess whether cognitive manipulation should be “prohibited regardless of individual consent.” The contemplation of prohibition implies current capability. The explicit identification of cognitive manipulation as a harm category confirms what Pearson experienced as a recognized technological reality, not a symptom of mental illness.

### Biometric Capture at Public Events (Cherry Blossom Festival, March 2025)

Pearson documented close-range approaches at the National Mall consistent with collection of biometric and behavioral data using handheld devices. The MIND Act’s “other related data” definition explicitly covers “eye-tracking patterns,” “behavioral information,” and any biometric data that “can be processed, analyzed, or combined with other data to infer, predict, or reveal cognitive, emotional, or psychological states.” The Cherry Blossom device approach fits this definition precisely. The MIND Act’s concern about “vertical corporate integration” creating “interconnected systems” with “global data infrastructure” describes the database architecture Pearson identifies as the mechanism linking the close-range capture to the remote targeting.

### Behavioral Direction (Pinning Events, 2025)

Pearson documented compulsive urges to travel to specific locations — the Georgetown directive of July 13, the November 7 pull toward the O’Neill House Office Building park space — which he recognized as externally generated rather than arising from his own desires. The MIND Act’s Sense of Congress states that neural data “can be monetized and used to shape individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making.” **Section 4 directs the FTC to assess “manipulation of behavior” as a potentially prohibited use case.** The behavioral shaping Congress acknowledges as a current technological capability is what Pearson documented as a lived experience in the months before the bill was introduced.

### Sexual Nerve Targeting (Silver Spring, 2025)

Pearson — a gay man — documented directed electrocution of his penis paired with heterosexual visual and verbal gay insults. The MIND Act’s definition of neural data includes peripheral nervous system data, which encompasses the nerve pathways governing sexual response. The bill’s explicit concern about neurotechnology being used to “shape individual behavior” and “erosion of personal autonomy” covers the use of sexual nerve stimulation as a conditioning instrument. The contemplation of absolute prohibition — some uses prohibited regardless of consent — most clearly applies to exactly this category of intimate bodily violation.

### VII. The Administration’s Silence and What It Means

The senators who introduced the MIND Act wrote to the FTC earlier in 2025, before the bill was introduced, demanding action on the potential exploitation of Americans’ neural data by technology companies. They received no response from the administration. This silence is not neutral. It is informative.

The administration that did not respond to the senators’ letter about neural data exploitation is the same administration that, on January 20, 2025, fired seventeen inspectors general — eliminating the oversight infrastructure most capable of detecting and investigating unauthorized government use of neurotechnology. It is the administration under which Pearson’s documentation shows the campaign against him began and intensified. It is the administration that has designated Black equity scholars as threats under the RMVE/BIE framework, removed DEI protections, and reorganized the DOJ Civil Rights Division in ways that eliminate the institutional capacity to investigate civil rights violations of exactly the kind Pearson documented.

**The FTC’s silence in response to the senators’ letter is the regulatory agency’s silence on whether neural data is being exploited by companies and possibly by government actors. The administration’s structural destruction of oversight mechanisms created the conditions under which federal agency use of neurotechnology — if it was occurring — could proceed without institutional check.** The MIND Act is the minority party’s attempt to create an oversight mechanism that the administration dismantled. Its introduction in September 2025, while Pearson was being electromagnetically targeted in Washington, DC, is the legislative record of exactly the oversight vacuum that made what was done to him possible.

### VIII. What the MIND Act Cannot Do

The MIND Act does not help Richard Pearson. This must be stated clearly, because the existence of the legislation might create a false impression of available remedy.

The bill directs an FTC study and requires OSTP guidance. It does not create a private right of action. It does not establish retroactive liability. It does not provide a mechanism for individuals harmed by federal agency neurotechnology use before the guidance is established to seek legal remedy. Even if the bill passes — and it was introduced by the minority party, referred to committee, and faces an administration that did not respond to the senators’ earlier letter — it would govern future federal agency neurotechnology use, not past use.

What Pearson experienced occurred in the gap the bill acknowledges: the period before any governing framework existed. The MIND Act confirms that the gap was real. It confirms that what occurred in the gap was technological possible, recognized as harmful, and legally ungoverned. It does not provide Pearson with a remedy. The doctrinal architecture he documented — state secrets, Glomar, Bivens dismantlement, qualified immunity, FISA secrecy, NSL gag orders — remains intact and continues to foreclose judicial review regardless of what the MIND Act eventually establishes for future conduct.

The bill’s significance for Pearson is not remedial. It is corroborative and historical. It is Congress saying, in September 2025, that the harms he was experiencing were real, that the technology producing them existed, that federal agencies were using it without adequate oversight, and that the legal framework to prevent such use did not yet exist. It is the legislative record saying: this was possible. This was ungoverned. This was happening.

### IX. Conclusion: What Congress Knew, When It Knew It, and What That Means

On September 24, 2025, the United States Senate introduced legislation acknowledging that neurotechnology can be used to shape behavior, manipulate cognition, erode personal autonomy, and exacerbate racial disparities. It acknowledged that federal agencies are currently using such technology without binding governance. It directed the development of guidance identifying prohibited federal agency use cases, implying that without such guidance, all use cases are currently permissible. It contemplated absolute prohibition of behavioral manipulation and discriminatory profiling regardless of individual consent, implying both that such uses are technically possible and that they are occurring.

Richard Pearson documented all of this — in his body, in his documented record, in his photographs and timestamps and statistical analyses and foil experiments and metal-pole grounding at a Canadian border facility — beginning in July 2025. The Senate introduced the MIND Act in September 2025. The overlap is not coincidence. It is the convergence of two kinds of knowledge: the experiential knowledge of a man who was living inside the technology’s harm, and the institutional knowledge of senators who understood that the harm was real, the capability was deployed, and the law provided no remedy.

The MIND Act is not a vindication of Pearson’s allegations. It is something more specific and more useful: it is congressional confirmation that what he alleges belongs to the category of the technologically real, the institutionally recognized, and the legally ungoverned. Three United States senators looked at the same technological landscape Pearson was navigating in 2025 and said: this is dangerous, this is happening, and existing law does not address it.

He said the same thing. He said it first. He said it with his hands on metal poles in a room with a dropped ceiling while operators in grey uniforms rotated positions nearby. He said it in a 189-page evidentiary record with timestamps and photographs and probability calculations. He said it in peer-reviewed publications and personal statements and doctoral dissertations and public testimonies before City Council.

Congress caught up in September 2025. The question is whether anyone with the power to act on what Congress acknowledged — and what Pearson documented — will do so before the legal architecture of concealment makes the question permanently unanswerable.

### When Detained Non-Citizens Have More Rights Than US Citizens: Inversion in the US Legal System

### A Detained Immigrant Accused of Gang Membership Can Have More Rights Than a US Citizen Who Is Targeted by the US Government

_“All nine justices agreed that judicial review was available; the only dispute was over which court should hear it. The ruling carried a clear message: everyone gets their day in court before being removed from the country.” —_ J.G.G. v. Trump — the Supreme Court’s ruling on the Alien Enemies Act, affirming that even non-citizens accused of gang membership under a 1798 wartime statute have the right to challenge their deportation before a judge”

### I. The Inversion — Stating the Problem Precisely

The American legal system in 2025 and 2026 is engaged in one of the most active and consequential periods of immigration litigation in its history. Across the country, federal judges are ruling on habeas corpus petitions, Fifth Amendment due process claims, Convention Against Torture protections, and challenges to the Alien Enemies Act of 1798. Immigrants detained by ICE — many of whom entered the country without documentation, many of whom face deportation to countries they fled in fear — are appearing before federal judges, filing constitutional challenges, and in many jurisdictions winning. More than 300 district court judges have found that denying bond hearings violates Fifth Amendment due process protections. Success rates on habeas petitions exceed ninety percent in many areas. Even the Supreme Court, in its most recent ruling on the Alien Enemies Act, affirmed unanimously that judicial review was available to non-citizens facing deportation under a law passed in 1798.”

Richard Pearson is a United States citizen. He was born in this country, raised in this country, educated in this country — bachelor’s, master’s, and a PhD. He has spent his entire adult life in service to this country’s most vulnerable communities: housing advocacy, mentoring at-risk Black youth, volunteering at women’s abuse shelters, publishing research on the health consequences of structural racism. He has never been charged with a crime. He has never had an immigration status to question. He is, in every legal sense, a full citizen of the United States.

#### _“The US government targeted Dr. Richard Pearson and caused or acted to cause a chemical assault, a physical assault, a false arrest, cognitive invasion, behavioral steering, street theater, noise harassment, and sleep deprivation. He has fewer enforceable legal rights than a Venezuelan national accused of gang membership under a statute signed by John Adams.”_

This is not a polemical exaggeration. It is a precise description of what the American legal architecture produces when the government’s victim is a citizen and the government’s method is covert. The inversion is real, it is structural, and it is not an accident. Understanding how it works requires examining both sides of the comparison: what legal tools are available to detained immigrants, and why none of those tools function for Pearson.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*v5CkBLk0WBW-6ZjeGZNs5g.png)

### II. What Detained Immigrants Can Do — The Legal Arsenal

The legal protections available to immigrants facing deportation in 2025 constitute a surprisingly robust — if currently embattled — set of constitutional and statutory tools. Each deserves examination, both for its content and for why it is available to non-citizens who are not available to a covertly targeted citizen.

#### Habeas Corpus — The Most Fundamental Remedy

The writ of habeas corpus — Article I, Section 9 of the Constitution, Latin for ‘you have the body’ — is the most ancient tool of liberty in the Anglo-American legal tradition. It allows a person held by the government to demand that the government justify, before a judge, the legal basis for their detention. It is the mechanism by which the state must show its work. Its power is simple: if you have me, prove you can have me.

In 2025 and 2026, immigrants detained by ICE have filed habeas petitions at historic rates. The Western District of Texas alone received more than 1,300 petitions since early 2025 — a record that was broken within the first month of 2026. These petitions work because they are premised on a concrete, visible fact: a person is in a facility, under government control, and can be identified by name and location. The government cannot deny the detention. The detention is the body the writ demands be produced.

Pearson was tortured. He was subjected to voice-to-skull transmission, chemical assault, covert home entry, behavioral direction, false arrest, sleep deprivation, and social network infiltration. His torture lasted more than a year and is documented with timestamps, photographs, probability calculations, a professional mental health evaluation, and experimental confirmation of the electromagnetic mechanism.

But he was not placed in a facility. His body was not held in a building the government acknowledged controlling. The torture was covert — the defining feature of his victimization is the deniability of the state’s involvement. There is no facility whose warden can be served with a writ. There is no jailer who must produce the body. The torture is real. The habeas corpus remedy is structurally unavailable because the covertness of the torture eliminates the visible detention that the writ requires.

#### Fifth Amendment Due Process — Available to All Persons, Except When the State Denies Its Role

“The Fifth Amendment guarantees that no person shall be deprived of liberty without due process of law. The Supreme Court has been consistent: due process protections extend to all individuals within American borders, regardless of citizenship status. In immigration proceedings, due process claims have been used effectively to challenge the speed of removal, the denial of hearings, and the inadequacy of the process by which deportation decisions are made.

Pearson’s constitutional rights have been violated on a scale that his documentation characterizes as seventy separate incidents: Fourth Amendment violations in warrantless surveillance and covert home entry, Fifth Amendment violations in the false arrest and manufactured evidence, First Amendment violations in the suppression of his scholarship and advocacy, Eighth Amendment violations in the torture itself. These violations are documented. They are specific. They involve named officers and documented incidents.

But the process through which those violations could be challenged requires a plaintiff who can establish standing — who can demonstrate a concrete, particularized, actual injury traceable to a specific defendant whose action is redressable by a court.

When the government’s method is covert, standing collapses at every element. The injury is real and documented. The traceability to a specific defendant is blocked by classification, denial, and the structural invisibility the operation was designed to maintain. The redressability is foreclosed by state secrets privilege, Glomar doctrine, sovereign immunity, and the Bivens line of cases that has spent forty years dismantling the only mechanism by which constitutional claims against federal officials could be brought. The Fifth Amendment is available to an undocumented immigrant appearing before an immigration judge. It is not available to a documented citizen whose torturer is the government and whose torture is classified.

#### The Convention Against Torture — A Treaty That Protects Non-Citizens More Completely Than Citizens

The Convention Against Torture, to which the United States is a party, prohibits the removal of any person to a country where they face torture by or with the acquiescence of government officials. CAT protection has no criminal bars — it is available regardless of an applicant’s history — and if eligibility is established, protection is mandatory. Judges have no discretion to deny it. For immigrants who cannot qualify for asylum, CAT is the last line.

The profound irony: the Convention Against Torture is available to a non-citizen seeking protection from torture in a foreign country. It is not available to a citizen being tortured by his own government on his own soil, because the Convention’s framework applies to removal — to the act of sending someone somewhere.

Pearson is already where he is. He is in the United States. He is being tortured in the United States. The international legal instrument specifically designed to protect people from government torture applies to non-citizens seeking to remain in the country where the torturer is not. It does not apply to citizens whose torturer is the country itself.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*Oi1gzrGc-ysVa6ZMimoGUA.png)

### The Alien Enemies Act and the Right to Be Heard

The Supreme Court’s recent ruling in J.G.G. v. Trump addressed the Trump administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to deport Venezuelan nationals accused of gang membership — bypassing standard immigration proceedings entirely. The Court ruled, with all nine justices in agreement on the central point, that these individuals were entitled to challenge the legality of their detention before removal. The dispute was only about which court should hear the challenge — not about whether any court should hear it at all.

The Alien Enemies Act was invoked against people the government accused of being members of a foreign criminal organization. They had no documentation. They faced deportation under a wartime statute whose last significant use was during World War II. They were accused by an administration that had demonstrated willingness to defy court orders. And the Supreme Court — all nine justices — agreed they had the right to judicial review.

Pearson has been a citizen of the United States his entire life. He has a doctoral degree. He has documented evidence of government torture. He has been denied the equivalent of that judicial review at every turn — not because the courts have reviewed his evidence and found it wanting, but because the doctrinal architecture ensures the evidence never reaches a court in a form that can be adjudicated.

### III. Why Pearson Cannot Use What Non-Citizens Can

The comparison is not merely ironic. It reveals a structural feature of the American legal system that deserves precise analysis: the covertness of government action against citizens creates a doctrinal gap that covert operations are specifically designed to exploit.

#### The Visibility Requirement

Every legal remedy available to detained immigrants depends on the visibility of the government’s action. Habeas corpus requires a body in a facility. Due process challenges require an identifiable proceeding. CAT protection requires an identifiable removal. Even the Alien Enemies Act challenges required that the government acknowledge it was deporting specific people under a specific legal theory.

The government’s method against Pearson was “designed” to eliminate visibility at every point. The torture is electromagnetic — it leaves no marks. The behavioral direction feels like autonomy. The voice-to-skull transmission has the acoustic signature of internal thought. The false arrest produced no court record. The covert home entries left no forensic trace except the specific objects the operators chose to move as demonstrations of access. The chemical assault used a substance that bonded to skin and dissipated without leaving the kind of physical injury that emergency rooms document.

Every element of the operation was calibrated to exist below the threshold of visibility that legal remedies require. This calibration is not incidental to the operation’s design. It is the operation’s central design feature.

#### The Denial Problem

Detained immigrants face a government that, even when aggressive and lawless in its detention practices, cannot deny that it is detaining people. The facilities are real. The ICE agents are identifiable. The removal orders are documents. When the Supreme Court ordered the return of Kilmar Abrego Garcia — deported to El Salvador despite a court order — the administration admitted the deportation was an ‘administrative error.’ It did not deny that it had deported him.

Pearson faces a government that can deny everything. The torture is covert. The technology is classified. The operation produces no official record that could be subpoenaed. When the government invokes state secrets privilege — which it can do at the earliest stages of any litigation — the entire case can be dismissed before discovery begins. The Glomar doctrine allows the government to refuse even to confirm or deny the existence of programs responsive to a FOIA request.

The detained immigrant’s government must at minimum acknowledge the detention to defend it. Pearson’s government can deny the torture exists and use the legal system’s own doctrines to prevent any examination of the denial’s accuracy.

#### The Standing Architecture

Article III standing requires a concrete injury, traceable to the defendant, redressable by the court. For detained immigrants, standing is not in question: the injury is the detention, the defendant is ICE, the redress is release or a hearing. The causal chain is short and visible.

For Pearson, each element of standing presents a doctrinal barrier. The injury — torture, constitutional violations, financial and professional destruction — is documented but contested; the government denies the targeting, and without discovery, the documentation cannot be tested in court. Traceability requires connecting the documented harm to specific government actors, which classified operations and state secrets privilege prevent. Redressability fails when the defendant is the federal government itself and the applicable doctrines — sovereign immunity, Bivens dismantlement, qualified immunity — combine to foreclose the remedies that would otherwise exist.

The same Constitution that creates the rights also creates, through its doctrinal architecture, the mechanism by which those rights become unenforceable when the violator is the government and the violation is covert.

#### IV. The Doctrinal Architecture of Impunity — A Catalog

The legal foreclosure of Pearson’s case is not the product of one doctrine or one bad precedent. It is the product of a comprehensive architecture that has been constructed over decades and that functions, in combination, to ensure that covert government action against citizens cannot be challenged through the legal system that is supposed to prevent it.

### V. The Constitutional Paradox — What the Comparison Reveals

The comparison between Pearson’s legal position and that of detained immigrants is not a critique of immigrant rights. The habeas corpus protections, due process rights, and CAT protections available to detained non-citizens are legitimate and important. They represent the best instincts of the American legal tradition — the insistence that the government must justify its coercive actions before a neutral arbiter, that every person within the Constitution’s reach deserves process before liberty is taken.

The paradox is that these protections work for detained immigrants precisely because the government’s action is “overt” — the detention is visible. The removal is documented. The order is a paper record that can be challenged. The habeas corpus writ can be served because there is a body in a facility that the government acknowledges holding. The due process claim can be brought because there is a proceeding that the government acknowledges is occurring. The CAT protection applies because there is a removal that the government acknowledges is imminent.

Pearson’s case is the precise inverse.

The government’s action is covert by design. The torture produces no official record. The targeting is classified. The technology is denied. The operation leaves no visible detention, no acknowledged proceeding, no documented removal. And the legal system, built on the assumption that government action would be visible and that the government would at minimum acknowledge what it was doing when challenged, has no mechanism for the case where the government’s primary tool is invisibility.

The Supreme Court ruling in J.G.G. v. Trump carried, as commentators noted, a clear message: everyone gets their day in court before being removed from the country. Nine justices agreed. The ruling reaffirmed one of the most basic principles of constitutional governance — that the government must be accountable before a neutral tribunal for its coercive actions against persons within its jurisdiction.

Richard Pearson has not had his day in court. Not because the Supreme Court has ruled against him. Not because a judge has examined the evidence and found it insufficient. **But because the doctrinal architecture ensures that his case cannot reach a judge in a form that can be examined on its merits.** The state secrets privilege, the Glomar doctrine, the Bivens dismantlement, the qualified immunity framework, the standing requirements — in combination, they ensure that the most compelling evidence of government torture assembled by any American citizen in the current period cannot be placed before a neutral tribunal for evaluation.

The detained immigrant has been given more process than the tortured citizen. This is not an anomaly in the American legal system. It is the system working as the doctrinal architecture designs it to work when the government decides to act covertly against one of its own.

#### VI. The Constitutional Theory of What Went Wrong

The doctrinal architecture that forecloses Pearson’s remedies was not built with his case in mind. The state secrets privilege was developed to protect genuinely sensitive national security information. Qualified immunity was intended to protect officers from liability for reasonable judgment calls in ambiguous situations. Bivens was restricted because federal courts were concerned about the separation of powers implications of implying damages remedies from constitutional text. Sovereign immunity reflects the traditional principle that the sovereign cannot be sued without consent.

Each doctrine, in isolation, has a rationale. In combination — applied to a case where the government covertly tortures a citizen with classified technology, denies the targeting, and invokes classification to prevent examination — they produce a result that is the opposite of the constitutional order they were supposed to protect. The Constitution creates rights. The doctrinal architecture converts those rights into aspirations — statements of principle that cannot be enforced when the violator is the government and the violation is designed to be invisible. “), b(“What Pearson has documented is not a failure of the Constitution. It is evidence of what the Constitution becomes when the doctrinal architecture of impunity is complete: a set of promises that the government can break without consequence, because the legal system designed to enforce those promises was built on the assumption that the government would at minimum acknowledge what it was doing.

The prior essay in this series examined how the detained immigrant’s legal position is, in current practice, more robust than the tortured citizen’s. The theoretical explanation is now visible: the immigrant’s protections work because the government’s action is visible; the citizen’s protections fail because the government’s action is invisible.

The Constitution was not designed for a government that tortures in secret and denies the torture. The doctrinal architecture was not designed to address a government that uses classified technology to destroy a citizen’s life without leaving the kind of evidence that courts can adjudicate. The system was built for a more honest adversary.

### Conclusion: What the Comparison Demands

Richard Pearson completed a doctoral degree recently. He spent his career building health institutions, publishing peer-reviewed research, advocating for displaced communities, and mentoring young people from backgrounds like his own. He has never been charged with a crime. All he has is a 20-year old single speeding ticket. He has no immigration status to question. He is a full citizen of the United States.

He has fewer enforceable legal rights than a person the government accuses of gang membership under a law written in 1798. He has fewer enforceable legal rights than a person who entered the country without documentation and is facing removal to a country with a documented history of torturing its prisoners. He has fewer enforceable legal rights than a person whose entire claim on the American constitutional system rests on the fact of physical presence within American borders.

This is not an argument that those persons should have fewer rights. It is an argument that the doctrinal architecture that renders Pearson’s rights unenforceable represents a constitutional failure of the first order — one that should disturb anyone who believes that the point of a legal system is to constrain the government’s power to harm the people it governs.

The Supreme Court was unanimous: everyone gets their day in court. That principle — applied to non-citizens accused of gang membership under a wartime statute — does not yet apply to a Black equity scholar tortured with classified electromagnetic technology on the streets of Washington, D.C.

The gap between what the Supreme Court’s principle demands and what the doctrinal architecture permits is the precise measure of how far the American legal system has drifted from the constitutional democracy it claims to be.

Pearson documented everything. He ran control studies. He conducted physical experiments. He preserved the evidence. He sought a mental health evaluation to preempt the psychiatric trap. He crossed two borders seeking asylum. He held a metal chair frame in a refugee processing center in Quebec and defeated a read operation by grounding himself to the building’s structural metal. He has done everything a person can do. The legal system’s failure is not his. It is the system’s. And the comparison to what a detained immigrant can demand from that same system is the clearest possible measure of how complete that failure is.

### A Stranger Electrocuted Me in My Penis in Maryland

#### US torture victim, Richard Pearson, recounts assault in Silver Spring, Maryland as he began his journey to Canada to seek refugee protection from the US government and its gangster network.

Richard Pearson had already had a hell of a year beginning in 2025 under the second Trump administration. He has written about it extensively on Medium — a physical assault that resulted in lacerations and a black eye, a false arrest in which the assailant was not arrested (the local police manufactured a witness, then instructed Pearson not to show the court), a voice-to-skull event at the US Capitol, behavioral steering involving a framing attempt, privacy invasion of his home and computer, gang-stalking, and “clicking” associated with electromagnetic radiation. The 40-year-old African American with a newly earned PhD was experiencing torture — American-style.

His first attempt out of the US was unsuccessful. Iceland sent him back, refusing his refugee claim. “We need to prioritize those countries that are actually at war,” said the border official who was speaking of Syria and Ukraine. A right to seek asylum is consider a universal human right. Pearson had a one-way ticket to Germany and hadn’t known that Iceland was not fully integrated in the European Union until he returned. He also belatedly read that Iceland was closely allied with US foreign intelligence and security. Iceland recently announced that it would be seeking an expedited EU membership application.

When Pearson made a second break from torture in March 2026, he assumed that he would fly under the radar. He booked his bus ticket to Canada less than 24 hours before his departure. He prepared his suitcase and tote and made his way via the DC metro to the Greyhound bus terminal in Silver Spring. He arrived at least five hours early. His apartment was cleared of his belongings from his first attempt — no furniture except a mattress, a few clothes, and food. He lost his cellphone for the third and final time in late 2025.

He walked around downtown Silver Spring — a place he had visited a handful of times. He had little money, so he subsisted on the food that he had purchased with his public assistance for the journey. He felt like countless African Americans before him who fled US racism to Canada, except it wasn’t 1848 or 1915. It was 2026. The US was back into its proverbial cycle again of acute state-sponsored racial terror and violence. It wasn’t new — a 20–40-year cycle that has repeated since its founding. Pearson was just an African American with a PhD who want to research, teach, and serve.

Pearson left the metro exit. Within a few feet, he stopped to get his bearings. There weren’t many people around. He saw a man who happened to be close by in passing. He asked him for directions to the Greyhound. The Black man was over 6 feet, mid- to late-30s, an athletic build, and wearing grey sweatpants. He seemed willing to help Pearson, bringing up an application for directions. Pearson had no cellphone. It was simple enough. Walk along Georgia Avenue, then left.

But something struck Pearson as odd. The man lingered as he navigated his app. He repeated the phrase, “It’s close to the fire station”. “Fire station.” “Fire station.” Repeatedly and excessively. Pearson noted but couldn’t make heads or tails for why the man was fixated on the fire station. If wasn’t as if Pearson was that familiar with the area. He needed directions, after all. Pearson noticed that the man had what appeared to be a Jamaican accent, as he departed, and inquired about his country origins. He firmly and defensively corrected Pearson. Grenada. Pearson sensed a flash of something in his mannerisms that wasn’t there before. It wasn’t telegraphing nice. But Pearson didn’t know what it meant. All he could think was that the two accents — Jamaican and Grenadian— sound familiar. Why the defensiveness?

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*HCaPWE9LwVC-2Xlf3TXU1w.png)

Near location where Pearson encountered man who gave directions.

Pearson made his way along Georgia Avenue, then deviated — remembering that he had time to kill. He walked around the central plaza, then headed back down Georgia Avenue. He noticed a Hispanic woman (30s or early 40s) lingering outside of a store window. She was odd. Her face was practically touching the window. She stood idle as she looked inside the business from the outside. It didn’t appear that she was looking for anyone on the inside. Neither her head nor her body gave any indication that she was engaged with something on the inside. The next thing that Pearson noticed was her butt. Pearson is a gay man. He is not sexually attracted to women. He has been out since 11th grade in high school. What he noticed about her butt was how comically large it was, as it stuffed. “It was like so outrageous like Frankie LaPenna’s big butt character Jim Kardashian,” said Pearson. “I laughed on the inside.” It wasn’t obviously her actual rear end. Not even the biggest of BBLs. It was stuffed. He didn’t know why but the scene was humorous to him.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*IiwLCvgx_TbAdtNbHe6GYA.jpeg)

The older Hispanic woman darted into the Magic Beauty salon shown on the right. This is Pearson’s original photo at the time.

He continued walking, pulling his suitcase behind him. He stopped at some railroad tracks, then crossed to the other side of the street. He noticed a young Hispanic woman who couldn’t been more than 17 years old with a T-shirt that read, “Betty Booty” in large white letters on a plain Black T-shirt. In the middle of the shirt was the image of the Betty Boop character. “That’s strange. The woman at the window. Now, this.” _(AI-generated image below, not fully accurate because Boop character larger.)_ Then, just as Pearson passed the woman, whose face was lowered and covered by the hood of a black sweatshirt, he felt it — electrocution. “She just zapped me in my penis! What the hell!”, exclaimed Pearson. Pearson turned around and saw the young Hispanic woman hand a black device to the woman who was at the window. She had turned around by then just to retrieve the device. The young woman ran down the street. The older woman disappeared behind the door of a business.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*zrPzRAMIdLH_PjQHSHzX9Q.jpeg)

Pearson wanted to confront the woman who was at the window. She was a participant in an assault. He pulled on the door that he saw her go into. It led to an upstairs beauty salon — Magic Beauty. The door was locked. “By appointment only,” read the sign. Pearson could not believe that the Hispanic woman had electrocuted him in his penis. In broad daylight. On an American street. In an orchestrated setup. The message was undoubtedly clear and homophobic — comically large woman’s butt, “Betty Booty” messaging, and an electric simulation to the penis. Pearson was not a public figure. Not a celebrity. Not connected to Silver Spring or Maryland. What he was a victim that had been tortured throughout 2025–2026 and laid blame at the feet of the US government and its contractors. These people should not have known Pearson, but they did. He knew why.

Pearson wanted to call the police. He had no cellphone. Coincidentally, he saw two officers who were leaving a chicken restaurant. He flagged them down from outside of the store. The first officer was a young African man who was joined by a 40-something fat, big-eared Hispanic man. Pearson explained the story. They struggled to contain their laughter. Actually, there wasn’t a struggle at all. The Hispanic officer sarcastically instructed Pearson while laughing, “Well, if it happens again, give us a call.” Pearson reiterated that it was an assault and that the woman was in the salon. They didn’t care and walked away. Pearson stood helplessly as they got into their police car bearing, “Sheriff’s Office.” Some sheriff’s office.

**Increasingly, Pearson’s view of America was a country of decline, violence, and anarchy — run by a gangster and racist government and organized criminal networks — both using weapons. This experience certainly did not contradict that view.**

By now, Pearson was wearing layers of aluminum foil underneath his knitted cap. He began wearing it after he began experiencing clicks in January 2026 — painful and hard pops on the right side of his head. He decided that he needed some protection on his nether region too. He purchased foil at the nearby Safeway. Pearson attracted the suspicion of the cashier — a Black man in his 50s. Pearson hadn’t anticipated going into his bag to retrieve cash to purchase aluminum foil. He had to unpack his bag — belongings and food on the conveyor belt. The cashier asked Pearson to produce a receipt that he had purchased the cake. “Geez!”, Pearson murmured to himself. Pearson had purchased it for his journey before he left and pulled out the receipt from his back pocket.

Then, he proceeded to the bathroom to stuff his underwear with folded layers of foil. He looked ridiculous. He knew it — foil on his head and in his pants — but it was necessary. This was the new America, but he wouldn’t be there long — so, he thought.

Pearson began to reflect back on the Grenadian man who appeared at the metro. The timing was precise. If someone wanted to get the attention of a gay man like Pearson, then attractive, tall, sweatpants with no underwear, and a foreign accent would do it. Pearson could not help but to think if the man was part of the whole setup. “Fluff” him up to be zapped? Precise directions to encounter the assailants? Get his biometric data to navigate him along Georgia Avenue? The theories were adding up.

Pearson figured that it was best to stay at the Greyhound station even though it didn’t open until 3pm. He initially camped outside, then ventured to the back in a dirty nook between the building and a fence. Minutes before, he saw a mouse run over there, but decided it was best until the bus came. The sun came first, so he went back to the front.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*wo7GsQ6TsVg0aP59xWpCVg.png)

Google Maps showing place where Pearson stayed before his bus.

When the 3pm bus pulled up — eager to be on his way — Pearson asked the driver if this was the 6pm bus. One passenger had gotten off. The driver — a Black man in his 30s/40s — had a nasty tone with Pearson. “It was like ‘No’ and why are you even asking?!” Pearson did not engage and watched the man who had been on his cellphone from the time he exited the bus. After Pearson’s inquiry, he noticed that the man kept looking up at something high up — not the sky, but perhaps something on a pole. Pearson looked too. There was nothing there, but he did find something unusual in the opposite direction. It was pointed at the bus stop too. Pearson took a picture.

Several minutes after he had taken a photo and the bus left, two Black men in a white SVU appeared in the lot. The passenger — a fair-skinned Black man — yelled out angrily to Pearson, “Hey! Hey! You got a ticket? You got a ticket?” Unnerved, Pearson left the station with his luggage without responding. They did not look official. They were in street clothes — common thugs came immediately to mind. “People are getting really unhinged,” Pearson thought.

He also thought that this is the torture campaign expanding to other networks. First, it concentrated near Pearson’s home. At one point, he could find a respite, at least, by traveling to forests and parks. Then, they would track him to hotels in Maryland and parks in Virginia. Then, a chemical assault in Maryland. Now, they are assaulting him again in Maryland. “The government is the central node. There is no question about that. They are upset with me that I survived torture. Now, they are engaging gangs to assault me with homophobic violence. Sick, right? This is entirely consistent with the administration’s line of attack on people’s rights and identities.”

Pearson circled back to the bus station within 30 minutes. From across the street, he could see that the men had parked next to the building. Pearson had decided that he would avoid the area until the bus terminal opened at 3pm. At 6pm, he was bound for Canada. Within 48 hours, he left.
