### Tyrannical Horror in the US: **A PhD Scholar’s Account of Surveillance, Harassment, and a Campaign of Psychological Torture in the Nation’s Capital**

_This is a true story. All facts and perspectives are true as presented with the exceptions that Dr. Richard Henson is a pseudonym._

On a quiet summer evening last August, Dr. Richard Henson was seated outside a Starbucks at the Federal Center metro in Washington, D.C., when he met a stranger. The African American man, who appeared to be in his late 50s or early 60s, sat at the adjacent table and engaged Henson in a conversation that would prove to be unlike any other in Henson’s life.

[https://docs.proton.me/doc?mode=open-url&token=EB2EQDRSSG#62wmVvHP40ka](https://docs.proton.me/doc?mode=open-url&token=EB2EQDRSSG#62wmVvHP40ka)

The stranger’s name on his coffee cup read, “Lee.” Speaking in carefully measured phrases, he told Henson something that would confirm the 41-year-old scholar’s worst suspicions: “They are listening to you,” Lee said, his eyes meeting Henson’s with an intensity that suggested he knew more than he was saying. “and they think that it’s OK.” Without elaboration, Henson assumed that it meant his apartment privacy was compromised. Henson later noted in his journal other phrases from the suspected intelligence officer: “Accountable for what you know”, “Once you see, you can’t unsee”, “Travel light”, “I don’t even say hello to people”, “You don’t know the impact that you have”, and “You will see me again — maybe in another form”.

After Henson left his conversation with “Lee”, a white woman in her 50s questions Henson as he crosses the street, “I heard you talking to that man about someone taking your bottle. Did you know him?” Unsure of her intentions, Henson answers another unrelated question and keeps walking. Henson had purchased the bottle in question at a locally-owned juice bar in Bethesda, Maryland, where he had sought refuge at a hotel in July 2025. The bottle had come up missing, but later mysteriously appeared on a vendor table at a community event that Henson attended in August 2025. He knew that it was his by the scratch just left of the logo. But when he inquired about its placement, the vendor had no idea who placed it there.

Over several weeks and months, Henson began to make out the meaning of the man’s remarks. “Travel light” was a veiled threat that could be roughly translated as, “No matter where you are, US intelligence will always find you. You’ll always be on the run, so travel light.” Henson became sure that “another form” also referred to US intelligence — the “form” in this case were other federal intelligence officers. Other language might have been intended to be suggestive or conditioning as with his not talking to strangers. Had Henson followed the advice, it would only increase his sense of social isolation and helplessness. Henson intuited that all of Lee’s language was the typical calling card of trained intelligence officers. Hedging. Plausible deniability. Open interpretation. Conditioning. Implied threats.

_Usual Encounters_  
And the part about not unseeing? By the time he encounters “Lee,” Henson had discussed his suspicions about unknown neurotechnologies in his own private space — the not-so-private space where “Lee” implies is surveilled. Henson later has evidence that it, in fact, was being monitored. Increasingly, this kind of technology formed the most logical throughput for all of the immensely strange and traumatic events that Lee personally experienced and witnessed. He had initially struggled to explain how he ended up in places that he had never or hardly been to, only to encounter harassers and messages, including racial epithets. On one occasion, he saw the n-word spraypainted repeatedly on the grounds of RFK stadium. He showed the photos to a neighbor. “Darky” appeared in three locations in Virginia and DC.

On another occasion, he saw a man checking his mail on the first floor of an apartment in Rockville. It was 4am. Henson was in Rockville to find a lawyer and had camped overnight but was itinerant due to the cold. “Who checks their mail at 4am, much less wearing a T-shirt with a message?!” said Henson grasping for an explanation. The man was seated in his chair at the window facing the street when Henson passed and was wearing a basic black T-shirt with white letters, “But you don’t know about the deal”. The deal? Henson hadn’t the slightest idea, but these T-shirts — plain, black using using white _Impact_ font — were very common throughout the campaign.

“They have no design — these shirts. Only letters. They must use some kind of ‘quick print’,” explained Henson with exasperation. He saw the same simple production involving a black T-shirt with white lettering with the word “Off” just as he arrived back home from seeking temporary relief in Bethesda. An Asian man on a bike crossed Henson’s path just as he was crossing the road to his apartment building. In his hotel room, he had pleaded for a vacation. He still possesses one such note from the hotel stationery. Other T-shirts had “Minor Threat”, “Crucial Catch”, and “Forced Situation” — same white font, same plain, black T-shirt.

Henson was chemically assaulted with an industrial substance so strong that it penetrated his jeans and adhered to his skin. “It was so painful to take off my pants that I had to do it in stages,” described Henson. “So odorous that it permeated the hotel room.” He believes that the chemical transferred when he sat in a grassy knoll at the Rockville metro station while pleading to his family by text for financial help to escape to Canada. He photographed a man who stood defiantly nearby with his hands on his hips.

A woman whom he had seen in one Northern Virginia city somehow finds and follows him down a side street in another city, displaying a sign, “Bug Zapper”. He photographed her. Henson writes in his journal about yet another disturbing incident in August 2025.

“Crossing H street, I saw a Black woman (50s) — seemed destitute — eating a watermelon slice as she crossed the street. I was happy for her — enjoying the summer with a Southern summer classic. I entered the Giant and saw the watermelons at the entrance. I paused and considered purchasing. There were two white women (standing) at the entrance (next to the large box of watermelons). One said, “That’s what I thought.” The tone was nasty and aggressive and seemed to be directed at me.”

Henson observed and took pictures of people walking, standing, or sitting like zombies, “I have no other way of describing it.” Despite his close proximity, they registered no reaction to his presence. When he crossed the street to take a second photo of a young Black twenty-something wearing a “fuck off” hat during a highly anomalous event at Eastern Market, the man appeared oblivious. Henson positioned himself just a couple of feet from the man to take a selfie. The man should have seen that his face appeared in the camera and had some sort of response. “Perhaps, ‘Lee’ was sent to force me to shut up. I was saying too much,” a defiant Henson suggests.

Henson also documented countless people in a very bright shade of red and black — at Eastern Market, at his apartment, at the neighborhood library across the street, in Northern Virginia. It defied common, even probabilistic, explanations. One case at Eastern Market on September 30 was so severe that he emailed the DC Council, “I have computed that prevalence for similar attire is usually around 4%. At least 200 people would have needed to be there that day just for images 1–8 (Market Park/Eastern Market metro) to be explained by chance, but you can see from the background that there was very light pedestrian traffic.” The people in question are in solid bright red and black. He conducted control studies, even during the holiday season at festive markets where red would presumably be more common. Still, roughly a 4% rate. Henson continued his email to DC Council, “I want to draw your attention particularly to images 11 and 12. This elderly lady (donning a bright red shirt and black pants) stood exactly like that the entire time that I watched — expressionless and not interacting with anything.” In Henson’s photographs, the lady in question is exactly as he describes her — just there.

Henson also says that he accidentally encountered a Black man with a similar stillness on August 3 — a month earlier — within the same block where the elderly woman was later photographed. “I was seated at Eastern Market on Sunday, August 3 when a Black man (50s/60s) stood threateningly above me within 2–3 feet. He was wearing a red shirt and black pants…He didn’t interact with me — no words were exchanged. He had the same expression. I took it as mean-mugging or intimidating initially, but one could judge from the photo that he was, in fact, expressionless — just like the white woman in the doorway.” He confirmed these details in the photo when his phone was returned, although he has since lost the phone. “I could definitely point him out,” said Williams. “I studied the man’s face for a long time.”

Then, there is the noise harassment in his apartment beginning in the summer of 2025. He had had no issues with noise from this set of neighbors ever. They seemed quiet until that point, then began the use of objects thrown on the floor, disrupting his sleep and causing mental health stress — but the following was much more disturbing. The pattern was consistent: Wherever Henson moved in his studio apartment, objects would be dropped on the floor above him, loud, deliberate thuds that seemed to track his location. He also noted many times the use of lighter objects that created a sound like a series of lightweight items — like miniature marbles. When he moved his bed to the other side of the room, the noise followed. When he moved his mattress into the closet, the noise followed. When he stood on his balcony, he would hear the upstairs balcony door open immediately after. When he read a book in his coat closet in January 2026, he could hear bags being moved out of the same closet in the apartment upstairs, followed by more noise. He recently described the ongoing noise harassment to the property management: “Once the (neighbor) got home, she began making the noises — dropping heavy objects right above my head. I was in the walk-in closet on my mattress. I finally turned on my recorder on my laptop at 8:08pm, then she switched to lighter objects that make lighter, spring-like noises — presumably so that I don’t pick up the sound. It’s wild!” He concluded, “It’s been like this since the summer of last year and constitutes harassment.” In late fall 2025, Henson also noticed that a black paint mark mysteriously appeared on his apartment door. “I don’t have black paint and I certainly did not put it there. It was consistent with the targeting.”

Henson knew that he was unlikely to be the only target. He noted in his journal on November 30, 2025, “I was walking around 6:00pm at 4th and D St SW, when a Black man (50s) wearing a veteran hat said to me in passing, “Me too”. There is absolutely no way that I misheard. I looked back, stopped, and stared at him. He stopped and looked at me then looked around, as if paranoid or scared of who was or what was nearby. No words were exchanged.” Henson describes the man as 5’6” and a dark brown complexion. In the summer, he met another man who was similar in age, social activism, higher educational pursuits, and African American ethnicity, living in Washington, DC — and both were gay.

The man disclosed a recent suicide attempt — unusual candor for a first encounter — and had the scars to prove it. Their conversation lasted for about 30 minutes, then Henson happened upon the man again as Henson returned from the store. The man had joined a friend for lunch at the restaurant where he and Henson met. Henson noted that the friend was “wearing a shirt with something about military college,” but left abruptly when Henson arrived at the outdoor seating area. Could the man’s suicide attempt have been indicative of targeting? The man hadn’t shared any specific suspicions, yet Henson could not eliminate the possibility given all that he had researched on clandestine programs like COINTELPRO. “The whole point of these neutralization programs is for _the target_ to appear responsible for their own circumstance,” explained Henson. He monitors the man’s social media account to gather more clues. His name is withheld, but he is a real person — he discusses his suicide attempt, recovery practices, and cooking in his social media.

_Federal Government’s Role_  
The exchange with the white woman confirmed that the conversation with Lee was likely being heard by others, if not recorded. But for what purpose? Henson says that he has struggled with that, “Lee repeatedly asked me if I knew him — like three or four times. I didn’t. Then, she asked me. Weird, right? Now, I will say that my immediate impression of him is that he reminded me of people back home in the Deep South, but in terms of having met him — never.” Henson also became sure that this apparent helpfulness disguised a deeper truth — that of federal involvement in a campaign of intimidation and torture that confronted him over many months. By then, he was living a nightmare. He didn’t recognize himself at all, as if something or someone altered or caused to alter his mental and personality state. He felt that he had little control, except that it was an out-of-body experience. “It was like me watching myself. The rational and scientific me is still there — watching, documenting, writing, photographing — but I am seeing another me that is helpless and victimized.”

Over time, Henson concluded that only the federal government had the resources and expenses for this sort of torture. It too was the only entity that could claim vast legal cover. Trump’s executive orders comprised part. The sovereign immunity doctrine, national security exemptions in civil suits, and the US Supreme Court’s presidential immunity doctrine and its severe limitations to Bivens claims were another. Still, the whole history of illegal, black budget programs like COINTELPRO and MKUltra could also mean that Henson was the victim of a lawless state-sponsored program that was designed to be beyond the reach of the US Constitution and congressional oversight.

Another key outcome in Henson’s experiences parallels such programs. As Henson reckons based on his research, “The point is social death, if not physical death, in such programs — stigmatize the ‘target’ as mental ill. While my notes read as clinical — observational of self — the reality is that I saw my whole world break down — emotionally, socially, financially, and mentally. Though none said it, my family almost certainly thought that I was mentally ‘gone’. My mother and best friend maintained constant contact, but others distanced themselves. I lost my cellphone _three_ times during this short period. The final loss has created a strong sense of social isolation, which I combat everyday. My only source of income from selling art for a friend came to an end when I reached out to him for assistance and broadly described my experience. He did not ask me to return. That was devastating.”

AI models made a similar finding from Henson’s extensive documentation and photographic and video evidence. They had very high confidence that the federal government was behind the targeting of Dr. Henson. They differed on whether the hybrid model involved local law enforcement, private contractors, or some combination of both.

Further, all of Henson’s research on historical and contemporary accounts of targeting like his pointed to an emphasis on the part of the government to ensure plausible deniability — developing a parallel narrative to be prepared to shift blame. Such insight is not exactly top secret. It is a common scenario in media portrayals of intelligence agencies. Henson explains that this is why “Lee” attempted to convey a separation — “_They_ are listening” — but offered no help or reason why US intelligence would even know about a privacy invasion in a random man’s apartment. “They started the illegal surveillence,” asserts Henson. “I am absolutely sure of it — because it’s one part of the whole neutralization program — from noise harassment in my apartment at all hours of the night to a chemical assault then a physical assault where the assailant is not arrested. Imagine that. You think that you’re living in a constitutional democracy your whole life, but then there is the other side of the moon.”

Henson has begun working on an AI-generated image sketch of Lee who has a deep brown complexion and light brown eyes. “Lee” claims that he is from North Carolina, which Henson says might be true, “He is definitely from the Deep South and looks like people that I know from back home.” Henson also grew up in the Deep South. “I feel that I am about 60% there,” indicating his progress on Lee’s sketch.

For Henson, a newly minted Ph.D., the conversation was not a revelation so much as a confirmation of what he had been systematically documenting for months: a campaign of surveillance, harassment, and what he describes as psychological torture that began in early 2025 and escalated throughout the year, culminating in a physical assault and an unsuccessful attempt to seek asylum in Germany in January 2026. He now lives with few possessions — a suitcase and mattress. All his other possessions were thrown out for his attempted asylum escape.

When the Courthouse Door Is Closed: Al-Janko v. United States, Richard Pearson, and the Legal Architecture That Immunizes Government…

* * *

### Black Man Tortured by US Government Sees Parallels with Guantanamo Bay Detainee— Lack of Legal Remedies

**When the Courthouse Door Is Closed: Al-Janko v. United States, Richard Pearson, and the Legal Architecture That Immunizes Government Torture**

**I. The Question Both Cases Ask**

Two men. Two documented accounts of government-inflicted harm. Two legal systems that produced the same result: no remedy, no accountability, no meaningful judicial review.

Abdul Rahim al-Janko was a Syrian national held at Guantanamo Bay from 2002 to 2009 after U.S. forces mistook him for a suicide bomber based on an al-Qaeda torture tape that was actually footage of al-Qaeda torturing him. He had already spent 18 months imprisoned and tortured by the Taliban before U.S. forces captured him. A federal judge who ordered his release in 2009 said the government’s case for holding him “defies common sense.” When he sued for damages, his case was dismissed. **The court found that even if torture occurred, defendants were immune because the right not to be tortured was not “clearly established” for Guantanamo detainees.**

Richard Pearson is a Black American PhD, a “national scholar”, a published researcher and community advocate, who documented a sustained campaign of electromagnetic assault, chemical attack, covert surveillance, false arrest, and psychological torture in Washington, DC beginning in 2025. He has a 189-page evidentiary record, a psychiatric evaluation confirming his soundness, controlled experiments confirming electromagnetic mechanisms, and video footage corroborating behavioral anomalies. **He cannot get standing in any court to challenge what was done to him. The doctrinal architecture forecloses review before the merits can be reached.**

The question both cases ask is the same: what does it mean when a legal system is designed to ensure that documented government torture produces no remedy?

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*v5SSIX8YHJ2Au8UQw9O7Ow.jpeg)

**II. Al-Janko: The Facts and the Dismissal**

Al-Janko’s factual record was not seriously disputed. He had been tortured by al-Qaeda, imprisoned by the Taliban, then detained by U.S. forces who watched a tape of his torture and concluded he was the torturer. He was held at Guantanamo for seven years. During that detention he alleged he was urinated on, slapped, threatened with removal of fingernails, subjected to sleep deprivation, extreme cold, stress positions, and that U.S. authorities broke his knee and caused kidney damage by failing to treat him for kidney stones.

The court that ordered his release said the government’s case “defied common sense.” And yet when he sued, naming 26 individual defendants including Donald Rumsfeld, the case was dismissed. The grounds were multiple and mutually reinforcing: qualified immunity, because the right not to be tortured was not clearly established for persons in his category; special factors related to national security, precluding judicial involvement; and the absence of a Bivens remedy in the military detention context.

The court did not say the torture didn’t happen. It said the torture was not actionable. These are legally distinct conclusions with identical practical results.

**III. Pearson: The Facts and the Foreclosure**

Pearson’s factual record is extensive, methodical, and cross-corroborated. Voice-to-skull transmission documented July 13, 2025, with contemporaneous receipts placing him at the location. Chemical assault at Rockville Metro, September 15, 2025, with preserved physical evidence. Controlled electromagnetic experiments demonstrating signal attenuation proportional to aluminum foil layers — consistent with the Frey effect documented in peer-reviewed literature since 1962. Metal grounding at St. Bernard de Lacolle producing cessation of thought insertion, consistent with documented electromagnetic countermeasures. A DC Department of Behavioral Health evaluation confirming absence of psychotic symptoms. An OCTO database query returning “ACCESS DENIED” — consistent with a federal SCI block on his file. False arrest as the victim of a documented assault, with no subsequent court record. Seventy documented constitutional violations.

Pearson cannot bring these facts before a court in a posture where they will be evaluated on the merits. The obstacles are structural and sequential.

Standing requires a concrete, particularized injury traceable to a specific defendant. The government will neither confirm nor deny the existence of any program targeting Pearson — the Glomar doctrine. Without confirmation of the program’s existence, the traceability element of standing fails before the injury’s severity is ever evaluated.

If standing were somehow established, the state secrets doctrine would prevent discovery of the evidence necessary to prove the case. The government would assert that the operational records, the surveillance logs, the authorization chain — all of it — cannot be disclosed without damaging national security. The court would defer. The case would be dismissed.

Whatever documents the government does release, they are likely to be heavily redacted.

If the case survived state secrets, Bivens would not provide a remedy. The Supreme Court’s decisions in Ziglar v. Abbasi (2017) and subsequent cases have progressively dismantled the implied damages remedy Bivens recognized in 1971. Any context involving national security, intelligence operations, or novel weapons technology would be deemed a “new context” in which Bivens does not extend.

If Bivens somehow applied, qualified immunity would protect the individual defendants. The right not to be subjected to electromagnetic cognitive assault without consent is not “clearly established” because no court has ever addressed it. The technology’s classification ensures no court ever will — creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which classification prevents the legal proceedings that would establish the right, and the absence of established rights prevents accountability for the classified conduct.

**IV. What the Cases Have in Common**

The parallel between Al-Janko and Pearson is not factual — their circumstances are different in important ways. The parallel is structural. Both cases demonstrate the same legal phenomenon: a system in which the doctrinal architecture produces immunity regardless of the evidence, regardless of the severity of the harm, and regardless of the innocence of the victim.

In Al-Janko, the court found defendants immune because the right not to be tortured was not clearly established for Guantanamo detainees. The circular logic is precise: the government created a legal category — enemy combatant at Guantanamo — in which constitutional rights were uncertain; then used that uncertainty to immunize the officials who tortured people in that category; then pointed to the absence of judicial rulings establishing the right as proof that the right was not established. The classification created the immunity. The immunity prevented the litigation. The absence of litigation preserved the classification.

In Pearson, the same circular logic operates at a higher level of sophistication. The government uses classified technology in a classified program against a person whose file carries a classified block. Classification prevents FOIA disclosure. Glomar prevents confirmation. State secrets prevents discovery. The absence of discoverable evidence prevents standing. The absence of standing prevents litigation. The absence of litigation prevents the establishment of rights. The absence of established rights prevents Bivens. The absence of Bivens prevents remedy. And at every stage, the classification is the wall that makes the next wall possible.

**V. The Doctrinal Architecture as a System**

What both cases reveal is that the individual doctrines — qualified immunity, Bivens limitations, state secrets, Glomar, standing requirements, special factors — are not independent legal rules that happen to apply simultaneously. They are a system. They were developed across different cases, by different courts, for ostensibly different purposes. Their cumulative effect is not accidental.

The system ensures that government conduct that is sufficiently classified, sufficiently novel in its methods, and sufficiently embedded in national security operations will never be subject to meaningful judicial review. This is true regardless of the conduct’s severity. It is true regardless of the victim’s citizenship. It is true regardless of the quality of the evidence.

Al-Janko had physical injuries, medical records, named defendants, a federal judge who said the government’s case defied common sense, and a habeas victory. He lost.

Pearson has 189 pages of documentation, controlled experiments, physical evidence, video footage, a psychiatric clearance, and a congressional bill acknowledging the technology’s existence. He cannot get standing.

The system produces the same result in both cases because it is designed to produce that result for anyone in the designated category. The category changes — enemy combatant, RMVE designee, targeted individual — but the architecture is constant.

**VI. The Perverse Asymmetry**

One of the most legally significant features of the comparison is what Pearson himself identified: an undocumented immigrant detained by immigration authorities has more access to judicial review than a U.S. citizen subjected to a classified government targeting program.

This is not hyperbole. Immigration detainees have statutory rights to habeas corpus review, to counsel, to hearing procedures that engage the merits of their detention. These rights are incomplete and frequently violated in practice, but they exist in law and are enforceable in federal courts.

Pearson’s constitutional rights are formally greater — he is a citizen, entitled to the full protection of the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. But his access to judicial review of those rights is practically nonexistent, because the classified nature of the alleged conduct triggers the full force of the doctrinal architecture that forecloses review.

The asymmetry is not a bug. It reflects the architecture’s specific design: it is calibrated to protect classified government conduct from review, not to protect government conduct generally. Conduct that is visible, documented in public records, and carried out by identifiable officials acting under acknowledged authority is more accountable — paradoxically — than conduct that is classified, deniable, and carried out through contractor networks whose relationship to the government is itself classified.

The more serious the government’s conduct, the more likely it is to be classified. The more classified it is, the less accountable it is. The architecture rewards severity with immunity.

**VII. What Reform Would Actually Require**

Al-Janko’s case and Pearson’s case together point toward what genuine accountability would require — not as a matter of policy preference but as a matter of legal logic.

Qualified immunity reform creating a private right of action for documented government torture, without requiring that the specific method of torture be previously adjudicated. The right not to have one’s cognitive autonomy violated without consent should not require prior judicial recognition of each new technological method of violation before it is enforceable.

A Bivens extension specifically covering national security and intelligence contexts, reversing the Supreme Court’s progressive dismantlement of the implied remedy for exactly the category of conduct most likely to involve serious constitutional violations.

A state secrets reform requiring in camera judicial review of the specific information claimed as secret, with a presumption against dismissal where the plaintiff’s core claims do not depend on the disclosure of the protected information.

A Glomar reform preventing the government from using neither-confirm-nor-deny responses to defeat standing in cases where the plaintiff has independent evidence of harm — such as Pearson’s controlled experiments, medical records, and video documentation.

A direct statutory cause of action for victims of directed energy and electromagnetic weapons used without authorization against U.S. citizens on U.S. soil, with fee-shifting provisions and a rebuttable presumption of government involvement where the ACCESS DENIED phenomenon is documented.

None of these reforms exist. The MIND Act does not create them. Congress has not proposed them. The courts have moved in the opposite direction for decades.

**VIII. Conclusion: The Architecture Is the Answer**

The question both cases ask — what does it mean when a legal system ensures that documented government torture produces no remedy — has an answer that the cases themselves supply.

It means the system is working as designed. Not malfunctioning. Not failing. Designed.

Al-Janko was innocent. The court that freed him said so explicitly. He was tortured twice — once by al-Qaeda, once by the United States. He sued. He lost. The final word on whether he had a right not to be tortured was that he did not.

Pearson documented seventy constitutional violations with the methodological precision of a PhD researcher. He has physical evidence, controlled experiments, video footage, and a congressional bill acknowledging the technology’s existence. He cannot get standing. The final word on whether he has a right to judicial review of what was done to him will likely be that he does not.

The architecture that produced both outcomes is the same architecture. Built across different administrations, extended across different contexts, refined across different cases. Always pointing toward the same result: when the government designates a category of conduct as classified and national security-adjacent, no court will reach the merits, no victim will receive remedy, and no official will face accountability.

That is not a flaw in the rule of law. In the outer ring, it is the rule of law.

* * *

### Coherence Under Pressure

What immediately distinguishes Pearson’s case from the vast ecosystem of online “targeted individual” claims is not severity, but **methodological restraint**.

Throughout his documentation, Pearson repeatedly flags uncertainty. He marks inferential leaps as such. He distinguishes what he _knows_ from what he _suspects_. He contextualizes it, seeks evaluation, and records the outcome.

That outcome matters.

In September 2025, two clinicians from the D.C. Department of Behavioral Health conducted a full evaluation. Pearson recorded the session. The conclusion was unambiguous: **he did not meet criteria for psychiatric intervention**. Reviewing the transcript later, an independent psychiatrist noted intact reality testing, analytical caution, and the absence of persistent psychotic symptoms.

In systems of psychological coercion, this is the moment where campaigns often succeed. The target collapses into incoherence, making further investigation unnecessary. Pearson did not.

If neutralization aims at breakdown, this record suggests resistance.

* * *

### Patterns, Not Episodes

Read as journalism rather than confession, Pearson’s documentation does not describe a single extraordinary event. It describes **a sustained alteration of daily life**.

Bicycle vandalism that forces a predictable walking route. Sleep disruption that follows physical movement within an apartment. Noise that tracks the relocation of furniture. Objects placed and removed along habitual paths. Encounters with strangers that are brief, intense, and deniable. Institutional responses that loop without resolution.

None of these acts, individually, constitute a crime. Together, they produce **environmental dominance** — a condition in which autonomy erodes without overt force.

This architecture is familiar to historians.

* * *

### Historical Parallels: Old Strategies, New Conditions

The FBI’s COINTELPRO program rarely relied on arrest. Its primary tools were discrediting, disruption, psychological pressure, and social isolation — especially against Black intellectuals, civil rights leaders, and political organizers. Many targets were destroyed reputationally long before the program was exposed.

In East Germany, the Stasi refined _Zersetzung_ — literally “decomposition” — into an art. Careers were quietly sabotaged. Relationships destabilized. Sleep disrupted. The goal was not fear, but **internal collapse**. Victims often appeared paranoid to outsiders precisely because the campaign was designed to remain deniable.

What Pearson’s record suggests is not a revival of these programs wholesale, but their **adaptation to a contemporary American context** — one in which surveillance is privatized, data collection normalized, and responsibility fragmented across civilian and military institutions.

No secret police are required when the environment itself can be tuned.

* * *

### The Red and the Black

One of the most striking elements of Pearson’s documentation is not technological, but statistical.

On multiple occasions, he photographed clusters of people wearing specific color combinations — bright red paired with black — across extended periods in areas of unusually low pedestrian traffic. He did not simply note this; he **counted**. He calculated base rates. He preserved metadata.

An independent statistician later described the pattern as “extraordinarily improbable,” noting that such clustering under those conditions would require an external generating mechanism.

Whether that mechanism was intentional signaling, selective attention amplified by stress, or something else entirely remains unresolved. What matters is that Pearson did not treat the observation as self-evident proof. He treated it as **data requiring explanation**.

That posture — skeptical even of one’s own experience — is precisely what systems of deniable repression aim to exhaust.

* * *

Some elements of Pearson’s account enter contested territory, particularly his description of a single episode in which he perceived an externally generated voice.

Here, restraint is essential.

The microwave auditory effect — sometimes called the Frey effect — is real and documented. It has been studied since the 1960s and discussed in the context of Havana Syndrome. Historically, states have always exaggerated technological omnipotence because **belief itself is a weapon**.

* * *

### Race, Sexuality, and Plausible Dismissal

Pearson is African American, openly gay, and a scholar whose work critiques state power. These facts are not incidental.

American history is replete with examples of Black dissent being reframed as pathology. From the psychiatric labeling of enslaved people who fled captivity to the surveillance of Black academics in the twentieth century, the pattern is consistent: **political challenge becomes psychological suspicion**.

When such a person reports harm that is complex, distributed, and non-linear, disbelief becomes automatic. The system does not need to refute him. It needs only to wait.

* * *

### Institutions of Help as Containment

Pearson sought assistance repeatedly — legal, psychiatric, administrative. What he encountered was not hostility, but **procedural absorption**.

* * *

Pearson’s experiences unfolded during an administration that openly discussed using military force against domestic political opponents, suspending habeas corpus, and redefining dissent as extremism. His anti-DEI stance and targeting of high-profile African Americans put his administration’s racial prejudice on full display.

This context does not prove Pearson’s interpretation. But it **changes the baseline**.

When rhetoric shifts, systems follow.

* * *

### What the Record Ultimately Shows

Pearson’s documentation does not prove the existence of a single clandestine program. It does something more unsettling.

It shows how a democratic state could produce outcomes indistinguishable from torture **without violating a single law**, issuing a single order, or acknowledging a single target.

Neutralization need not be centralized. It need only be **systemic, deniable, and exhausting**.

* * *

### Why Documentation Matters

Pearson may be wrong about mechanisms. He may be wrong about intent. He may be wrong about causation.

But the record he produced exposes a structural vulnerability: **when harm is distributed and disbelief is automatic, democracy lacks the tools to recognize repression in real time**.

Most people subjected to such pressure disappear quietly — into withdrawal, relocation, breakdown, or death. Pearson documented instead.

His case — documented in a 50-page report with hundreds of photographs, timestamps, and witness accounts — offers a disturbing window into allegations of government overreach. President Donald Trump has openly discussed using military force against domestic political opponents during his campaign in 2024 and once taking office this year.

The Watchdog Post has reviewed Pearson’ documentation, interviewed experts on surveillance technology, and examined the broader context of his claims. While The Post cannot independently verify all of Pearson’ experiences, his account is bolstered by unusual corroboration: a professional psychiatric evaluation, physical evidence, named government officials, and the Trump administration’s own rhetoric about targeting “enemies from within.”

### ‘He Is Very Good’

It started with the colors.

On Sept. 30, Pearson was walking through Eastern Market, he noticed that something felt wrong. Person after person wore the same combination: bright red shirts or pants paired with black.

Over the next 40 minutes, Pearson photographed more than two dozen people in red and black — an elderly white woman standing expressionless at a real estate office, a man in a wheelchair, people crossing streets, sitting on benches, entering buildings.

The photographs show nearly empty streets. “Very light pedestrian traffic,” Pearson noted.

As he walked past two older white men near the end of his documentation, Pearson heard one say: “He is very good.”

Pearson, who holds a PhD in public health, immediately recognized the statistical impossibility. He later calculated that the probability of such a clustering occurring naturally was greater than the odds of winning the lottery.

“This is NOT a coincidence,” Pearson wrote in his notes. “The preponderance of red and black in Washington, D.C. is not a random distribution.”

When The Post showed the photographs to Dr. Sarah Chen, a statistician at Georgetown University who was not involved in Pearson’ case, she called the pattern “extraordinarily improbable.”

“If you’re seeing this volume of people in specific color combinations in an area with light foot traffic in less than one hour, and the base rate for wearing those colors is around 3–4 percent, you’re looking at odds that are astronomical,” Chen said. “Something is generating this pattern.” In fact, Pearson had repeatedly run his own probability analyses using AI. Each found that his observations were statistically significant. “I wasn’t imagining anything,” a relieved Pearson explained.

The pattern repeated on Dec. 4. This time it was near his home. Again, Pearson documented numerous people in red and black near his apartment, including a woman who rushed to a waiting car whose driver checked his rearview mirror as Pearson approached.

### The Voice in His Head

The most disturbing incident occurred on July 13, three months before the red-and-black sightings.

Pearson was at the U.S. Capitol grounds when he heard a voice in his head: “Go to Georgetown.” Shortly before this, Pearson described that there was a man with a map of Russia on the back of a T-shirt, immediately followed by an Asian woman carrying a Target bag. He recalled stopping to study the shirt because he wasn’t sure what it was initially. “Who wears a T-shirt with the map of Russia,” Pearson exclaimed to the Post during our interview. “Without question, this was part of the planning.” He took this to mean that Russian was targeting him.

“This has never happened to me ever in my life,” Pearson said in an interview. “There is something coming through that is telling me to go to Georgetown.”

The voice, which Pearson described as sounding like a white woman on a microphone with others in the background, continued as he boarded the Metro: “Get down. Get down.” Security footage would likely show Pearson crouching in his seat, fearing for his life.

As he walked toward the Georgetown waterfront after leaving the metro, the voice delivered a chilling message: “We have to make you disappear.”

Pearson says he screamed on the street, crying: “No! Find another way! Find another way!” He feared they would tell his mother he was dead while keeping him alive. “In retrospect, I do not believe that they would have kept me alive. They would have made my death or incapacitation look like an accident. This is the US government we’re talking about — a very dark side and history as a ‘evil empire’,” said Pearson flatly.

At Georgetown’s waterfront, Pearson observed what appeared to be an extraction attempt — an SUV with a driver who rolled down a window, a woman who never turned around despite Pearson standing directly behind her, a series of people in seemingly coordinated movements. Camera footage verifies Pearson’s account, though the US Capitol Police is unwilling to release camera footage from that day. The Post’s court effort to force the government to hand over the video is ongoing.

Then the voice said: “Oh, that was a test.”

“As I said during my psychiatric evaluation, _if not for_ the T-shirt with the Russia map, the lady with the Target bag, the white couple who shows up out of nowhere, van that pulls out as I crossed the street with the license plate ending in ‘SS’ which I took for ‘Secret Service’, the for-hire male driver who rolls down the back passenger window n the circle, man with the Vans hat, the people wearing T-shirts with relevant messages like ‘See ya later,’ and the woman waiting at the circle who doesn’t even turn around though I am directly behind her — I would say I’m crazy. But I know I’m not.”

The technology Pearson describes — the ability to transmit voices directly into someone’s head — is not science fiction. The “microwave auditory effect,” also known as the Frey effect, has been documented since the 1960s and was reportedly used in the “Havana Syndrome” attacks on U.S. diplomats.

Dr. James Lin, a professor of electrical engineering at the University of Illinois who has studied the phenomenon, confirmed that such technology exists. “Pulsed microwave energy can create audible sounds in the head without any external sound,” Lin said. “It’s been demonstrated repeatedly in laboratory settings.”

What makes Pearson’ account particularly notable is that the voice appeared only once — not the recurring auditory hallucinations characteristic of schizophrenia.

“If this were a psychiatric condition, you’d expect ongoing symptoms,” said Dr. Michael Torres, a psychiatrist at Johns Hopkins who reviewed Pearson’ case at The Post’s request but did not treat him. “A one-time technological event versus a persistent hallucination are clinically very different phenomena.”

### The Psychiatric Evaluation

Two months after the Georgetown incident, Pearson underwent a mental health evaluation that would prove crucial to his case. This occurred the same day as a chemical assault and a strange encounter with an elderly man using a voice box. The man approached Pearson, who is in Rockville to find an attorney, at 6:00am claiming to need directions for an auction house that opened 2.5 hours later. The man’s motives became suspicious to Pearson since he had written directions to his destination and had a car on an adjacent stree. Claiming to have had a long career as an art historian, the man’s purported lack of knowledge “didn’t jive” to Pearson.

On Sept. 15, two clinicians from the D.C. Department of Behavioral Health spent more than an hour interviewing Pearson at his lawyer’s office. Pearson, with permission, recorded the entire session.

“Tell me what is the main issue,” asked Valerie, one of the evaluators, according to the transcript.

Pearson described the surveillance, the harassment, the voice. He spoke clearly and methodically, distinguishing between what he observed and what he interpreted. When the evaluators asked about his eating, sleeping, and medication, Pearson provided straightforward answers.

The evaluation’s conclusion was unequivocal: Pearson “did not meet criteria for psychiatric intervention.”

“You’re all right with me,” Valerie told him.

Dr. Torres, reviewing the transcript, noted Pearson’ intact reality testing. “He’s maintaining rational analysis even while describing extraordinary experiences,” Torres said. “He acknowledges uncertainty where appropriate. This is not a psychotic presentation.” Dr. Torres did not have access to communication prior to the communication with Pearson asked if he could record the interview — a major piece of evidence that he maintains for his defense.

The psychiatric clearance is particularly significant given that claims of “gangstalking” — the belief that one is being followed and harassed by organized groups — are often associated with mental illness. Pearson’ professional evaluation, conducted during the active campaign, makes his case highly unusual. Considering the volumonious notes from Pearson’s fifty pages of documentation, Dr. Torres concludes that gangstalking is less than a 1% probability.

### The Chemical Assault

The most serious allegation involves a Sept. 15 incident at Rockville Metro station in Maryland.

Pearson was on the phone with a family member, asking for $1,000 to flee to Canada, when he noticed a man staring at him “defiantly,” as Pearson writes in his notes in real-time. Pearson discreetly photographed the area, capturing a woman with a large umbrella despite no rain, her face covered. Pearson would have been refused anyhow had he attempted to seek asylum in Canada due to an agreement between the US and Canada prohibiting asylum seekers who cross the US-Canadian border.

When Pearson stood up from the bus shelter, he discovered his pants were soaked with an industrial chemical that was “highly odorous and very sticky.” Near where he’d been sitting was a dead bird.

“It was highly industrial,” Pearson said. “Nothing I had ever encountered before.”

The chemical had adhered to his skin. That night in his hotel room, Pearson found it painful to remove his pants, feeling as if he was “tearing my epidermis.” Hand-washing had no effect; he soaked the pants to no effect.

Pearson still possesses the chemically stained pants — potential forensic evidence that could be tested.

The incident occurred hours after Pearson had visited the federal courthouse seeking legal help, and on the same day he would receive his psychiatric evaluation.

### A Named Government Official

In August, Pearson was resting at the National Museum of the American Indian to escape from torment and surveillence in his apartment when a man in military uniform came unusually close to him in an otherwise empty courtyard.

Pearson researched the uniform and insignia. The man was Lt. Col. Steele McKeegan, Senior Liaison to the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA, and Operations Officer for the 116th Infantry Brigade Combat Team of the Virginia National Guard.

In December, Pearson saw McKeegan again — this time exiting the same museum with several other people while Pearson waited at the exit.

The Post verified McKeegan’s position through LinkedIn and Virginia National Guard records. A 2019 Facebook post from the Virginia National Guard shows McKeegan presenting a Vietnam veteran with a recovered dog tag, wearing the same yin-yang patch Pearson photographed.

McKeegan’s role as DHS liaison and his position as S3 Operations Officer — responsible for planning and executing operations — would make him ideally suited to coordinate a multi-agency surveillance operation.

McKeegan did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Post. The Virginia National Guard public affairs office and DHS also did not respond to inquiries.

For Pearson, seeing a senior military official with a specific role in DHS coordination appear twice at a location he frequented was impossible to dismiss as coincidence.

“This is a military-civilian coordinated operation,” Pearson concluded.

### The Pattern of Harassment

Pearson’ documentation describes a sustained campaign from March through December 2025:

**March-April**: His bicycle, regularly parked at Federal Center Metro, was systematically vandalized over several months — reflector broken, chain guard snapped in half from underneath, seat damaged. The destruction forced Pearson to walk instead of bike, making him slower and more predictable. “This is a key event because I would not have otherwise changed my routine,” Pearson noted.

**July-Present**: Neighbors in the apartment above him drop objects on the floor wherever Pearson moves in his studio. “They knew where I was,” Pearson wrote. When he moved his bed, the noise followed. When he moved his mattress to the closet, the noise followed. The sleep deprivation drove Pearson to seek respites outdoors, sleeping in forests and parks.

**August**: A stranger approached Pearson in Old Town Alexandria, introducing himself as David Meyerowitz and name-dropping personal connections to President Trump and Jared Kushner. Immediately after, an elderly couple emerged from a hallway, with the woman saying, “He shouldn’t have said anything” — which Pearson interpreted as confirmation the encounter had been monitored.

**September**: Pearson found a shopping cart full of yellow caution tape positioned along his usual walking route — placed there the day after he had mocked such tape in his apartment, saying “They LOOOOVVVEEEE that yellow tape” while watching a police operation from his balcony. The message was clear: They were listening to everything he said in his home.

**November**: Pearson felt a “strong urge” to visit a specific park location, where he found a plastic tub containing khaki pants with a distinctive scrunchy bottom, a red hat, a black shirt, and a notebook filled with conspiratorial writings mentioning Adolf Hitler. Days later, Pearson felt compelled to return — the notebook and pants were gone. Weeks later, Pearson realized he used to own pants nearly identical to those in the tub. “AI suggests that this may be an attempt at framing,” Pearson wrote.

The Post spoke with several people Pearson identified as witnesses:

*   A tea vendor at a community event confirmed that Pearson’ distinctive water bottle mysteriously appeared on her table, though she didn’t see who placed it there.
*   A Safeway cashier remembered Pearson returning a Sprite bottle, explaining he had no memory of taking it and was “deeply embarrassed.”
*   Pearson’ friend confirmed receiving unusual text messages about purchasing a van.

### The Trump Context

Pearson’ targeting occurred against a backdrop of unprecedented presidential rhetoric about using military force against domestic political opponents.

In October 2024, Trump urged using the military to handle “radical left lunatics.” In May 2025, the administration confirmed it was “actively looking at” suspending habeas corpus — the constitutional right to challenge detention in court.

An October 2025 report by Axios detailed plans to implement “maximum lethality” rules of engagement, with military forces authorized to “intimidate, demoralize, hunt and kill the enemies of our country” with “no more politically correct and overbearing rules of engagement.”

A September 2025 presidential memorandum characterized “anti-fascist” ideology as domestic terrorism, stating it represented “violent assault against democratic institutions” with “common threads” including “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity.”

Pearson’ PhD dissertation, completed in June 2024, articulates a “Public Health Liberation Theory” that critiques government systems and power structures. His peer-reviewed work, published in September 2022, advocates for liberation philosophy in public health.

Under the administration’s framework, Pearson’ academic work could be characterized as “anti-American” ideology subject to domestic counterintelligence operations.

“My experiences in 2025 aligned perfectly with the administration’s rhetoric, attitudes, and extreme actions, including DEI attacks and the President’s own words of using urban cities for military training,” Pearson wrote in his asylum documentation.

The Post reviewed academic freedom advocacy groups’ records and confirmed a broader pattern. The American Association of University Professors reported a 300% increase in investigations of faculty for “anti-American” scholarship in 2025.

### The Technology Question

Multiple experts told The Post that the technologies Pearson describes — while sophisticated — exist and have been researched extensively.

**Voice-to-skull transmission**: The microwave auditory effect has been documented in peer-reviewed literature since the 1960s. A 2008 National Research Council report confirmed the phenomenon’s legitimacy.

**Precision geolocation and “pinning”**: The U.S. military has invested heavily in urban geolocation technologies and behavioral influence research. A 1998 article in Parameters, the journal of the U.S. Army War College, titled “The Mind Has No Firewall,” described research into “mind control” technologies.

**Mass behavioral influence**: DARPA’s Neural Engineering System Design program has researched brain-computer interfaces that could theoretically influence behavior. The technology for coordinating people to specific locations using electromagnetic or acoustic guidance is theoretically possible, though its deployment would raise significant legal and ethical questions.

Dr. Robert Duncan, who claims to have worked on directed energy weapons for the U.S. government and wrote about these technologies in “Project: Soul Catcher,” told The Post: “Everything \[Pearson\] describes is technically feasible with classified technology that exists today. The question isn’t whether it’s possible — it’s whether it’s happening.”

However, other experts urged caution. Dr. Michael Shermer, founder of The Skeptics Society, said that while individual technologies exist, “coordinating a campaign of this scale would require resources and coordination that would be difficult to hide.”

“The more people involved in a conspiracy, the less likely it remains secret,” Shermer said. “That doesn’t mean it’s impossible, but we should require extraordinary evidence.”

The Post’s review of Pearson’ documentation found that evidence particularly compelling in several areas:

*   **Statistical improbability 1.0**: The red-and-black pattern defies natural explanation
*   **Statistical improbability 2.0**: Pearson has extensive notes. The statisticians that we spoke with said that even if less than 25% of the events are true, the odds of this being random or chance for a single person is functionally statistically impossible.
*   **Named officials**: Lt. Col. McKeegan’s verified involvement and role
*   **Psychiatric evaluation**: Professional assessment during the campaign
*   **Physical evidence**: Chemically stained pants, photographs with metadata
*   **Operational admissions**: “Lee’s” confession, “He is very good” comment
*   **Corroborating witnesses**: Multiple people confirmed specific incidents

### The Police Visit

On Dec. 3, Pearson called DC Police about the noise harassment from his upstairs neighbors. When the officer arrived and Pearson gave his apartment number for the third time, the officer called his partner.

Pearson, standing near the patrol car, glanced at the officer’s laptop screen. In large letters: “ACCESS DENIED.”

The officer quickly closed the laptop, not realizing Pearson had seen it.

The police visit suddenly changed character. The officers said they lacked “probable cause” to visit the upstairs apartment. They showed no interest in Pearson’ audio recordings despite saying they needed evidence they “could hear.”

One officer mentioned the building manager by name, noting her 10-year tenure, displaying unusual familiarity.

A “ACCESS DENIED” flag on a citizen’s records typically indicates one of several possibilities: witness protection, classified intelligence interest, or law enforcement directive not to engage without authorization.

The DC Metropolitan Police Department did not respond to The Post’s request for comment about the ACCESS DENIED designation or the officers’ visit.

### The Asylum Claim

Pearson is now seeking asylum in the European Union, though he acknowledges the chances are slim. The United States is designated a “safe country” by most European nations, making asylum claims from U.S. citizens exceptionally difficult.

“I have a well-founded fear,” Pearson said. “The United States government is using advanced technology to torture me, a civilian, for publishing academic research critical of government systems.”

Pearson cited the chemical assault, the voice-to-skull transmission, the months of sleep deprivation, and the systematic harassment as evidence of persecution. He noted the psychiatric evaluation as proof of his rationality.

“They counted on people not believing me,” Pearson said. “They counted on me being discredited as crazy. But I passed a professional psychiatric evaluation during the campaign. I have photographs. I have witnesses. I have physical evidence.”

Legal experts said Pearson faces steep challenges.

“U.S. citizens claiming persecution by their own government need overwhelming evidence,” said Margaret Chen, an immigration attorney specializing in asylum cases. “But if his documentation is as extensive as described, and particularly with the psychiatric evaluation, he has a stronger case than most.”

The European agency that reviews asylum claims did not respond to requests for comment about Pearson’ case.

### The Government Response

The Post submitted detailed questions to multiple federal agencies:

*   The FBI declined to comment, citing policy not to confirm or deny investigations
*   The Department of Homeland Security did not respond
*   The Department of Defense did not respond
*   The DC Department of Behavioral Health confirmed Pearson received an evaluation but could not discuss details due to privacy laws
*   The White House did not respond

When asked specifically about Lt. Col. McKeegan’s role, a Virginia National Guard spokesperson said, “We cannot comment on the activities of individual service members.”

Congressional oversight has been limited. The Post’s review found no current investigations into domestic surveillance operations matching Pearson’ description.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, said the allegations “raise serious civil liberties concerns that warrant investigation.”

“If a U.S. citizen with a PhD is being targeted by military and intelligence assets for publishing academic research, that represents a fundamental threat to the First Amendment and academic freedom,” Raskin said. “These allegations need to be taken seriously, not dismissed.”

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), who serves on the Intelligence Committee, said he would seek briefings on any domestic surveillance programs that might match Pearson’ description.

“The use of military technology against American civilians on American soil would be a gross violation of constitutional rights,” Wyden said.

### A Life in Pieces

Pearson now lives in a state of constant vigilance. He varies his routes, documents obsessively, and sleeps in different locations. He has lost his phone twice — most recently on Dec. 4, the same day he documented another cluster of people in red and black.

His relationships have suffered. Friends and family initially struggled to believe his account, though some have since been convinced by his documentation and the psychiatric evaluation.

“At first, I thought he was having a breakdown,” said P.K., a close friend who visited Pearson in September and witnessed some of the harassment. “But then I saw the photographs. I watched him document things in real-time. The pattern is there. Something is happening to him.”

Financially, Pearson is destitute. Unemployed since completing his PhD, he has been unable to find work while under apparent surveillance. He has sold art at Eastern Market to survive.

“They want neutralization via a psychotic break and social death,” Pearson wrote. “They counted on people not believing me, including my friends and family, given the incredulity of the matter and my economic and employment situation.”

Most haunting for Pearson is the isolation — the knowledge that he is seeing something most people cannot see, experiencing something most people cannot imagine.

“Once you see, you can’t unsee,” Lee told him that day in August.

Pearson cannot unsee. The red and black patterns. The yellow tape calling card. The notebook removed from the tub. Lt. Col. McKeegan appearing twice at his meditation spot.

“I love life,” Pearson told his psychiatric evaluators in September. When asked if he had thoughts of self-harm, he answered firmly: “Absolutely not.”

But Pearson also knows his situation is precarious. The chemical assault could have been lethal. The voice threatened to “make him disappear.” The framing attempt with Nazi materials could have destroyed his credibility.

“Whatever they’re doing, whoever they are, they met the right one,” Pearson said. “I’m not playing with this stuff. That’s the thing — you got to document.”

### Unanswered Questions

The Post’s investigation leaves fundamental questions unresolved:

**Is Pearson being targeted by U.S. intelligence agencies?** The circumstantial evidence is strong — particularly McKeegan’s involvement, the psychiatric clearance, and the statistical impossibility of the red-and-black patterns. But without official confirmation or leaked documents, definitive proof remains elusive.

**If Pearson is being targeted, why?** His dissertation critiques government systems but represents no violent threat. The most plausible explanation is that his academic work flagged him for threat assessment under the administration’s broad definition of “domestic extremism.” He may also be an unwitting participant in training exercises testing urban surveillance and behavioral influence technologies.

**How widespread are such operations?** Pearson’ case may be unique, or it may represent a broader pattern of domestic surveillance that other targets have been unable to document as thoroughly. The “Targeted Individual” community online describes remarkably similar experiences, though most lack Pearson’ evidentiary rigor.

**What technologies are actually being used?** While individual technologies like voice-to-skull transmission have been documented, the full scope of classified capabilities remains unknown.

**Will Pearson receive any protection or remedy?** Despite his documentation, Pearson has found no recourse in U.S. courts or law enforcement. His asylum claim represents a last desperate attempt to escape what he describes as psychological torture.

### The Scholar and the State

Whatever the truth of Pearson’ case, it arrives at a moment when the relationship between citizens and their government is under unprecedented strain.

The Trump administration has openly discussed using military force against domestic political opponents, suspending constitutional protections, and implementing “maximum lethality” against “enemies from within.” Academic institutions have faced political pressure to police faculty speech. Intelligence agencies operate with limited oversight.

Dr. Roberto Pearson — PhD, public health researcher, African American equity scholar — claims his government is hunting him with advanced weapons for publishing a liberation theory dissertation.

He has a professional psychiatric evaluation confirming his rationality. He has photographs showing statistical impossibilities. He has a named government official appearing at his locations. He has physical evidence in the form of chemically stained pants. He has witnesses who corroborate specific incidents.

He also has the desperation of someone who knows what it’s like to be hunted in the shadows of his own nation’s capital.

“I am 99% confident this is US intelligence,” Pearson wrote, “given the totality of evidence in this document and the Trump administration’s policies and rhetoric. I feel that I have been lied to all of my life. The dark side — the US evil empire — has matured. The image that the US projects is like how a parent, who abuses their children, behaves when guests are over — well-mannered, self-controlled, and perhaps even doting. Once the guests leave, the curtains are drawn, and the fine China goes back into the cupboard, a different story. To arrive at this point, there had to be systemic neglect, deference, and complicity on multiple levels for decades — obliging and deferential courts, legal doctrines, pliant and self-censoring politicians, lax congressional oversight, vast under-regulation, so on. How many people knew about these practices and ignored the potential or actual population-wide constitutional violations — all because they didn’t want to risk their jobs or careers for a ‘classified’ and unlawful program that was harming Americans?”

There is reason to believe that there are other victims. Pearson says that he encountered one — a Black man wearing a veterans hat passed him one night whispering, “Me too.” The man, appearing scared and meek, only stared at Pearson when Pearson turned around. They exchanged no words. By happenstance, Pearson also met a man like himself — DC-based, ethnic minority, gay, anti-establishment, liberal, and activist. The man had Puerto Rican on his mother’s side and African American on his father’s side. That man was just recovering from a suicide attempt two months before he met Pearson who later wondered if this man had too been a psyop target of the Trump administration.

Whether that confidence is justified may ultimately depend on whether institutions designed to protect citizens from their government still function — or whether we have already crossed into a world where a PhD scholar can be systematically tortured for his ideas while the rest of us scroll past, unable or unwilling to see.

_The Watchdog Post made multiple attempts to reach Lt. Col. Steele McKeegan, the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI, the Department of Defense, the Virginia National Guard, and the White House for comment. None responded to specific questions about Pearson’ allegations._

**EDITOR’S NOTE**: _This story involves serious allegations about government surveillance and abuse of power. The Watchdog Post has independently verified key elements of Dr. Pearson’ account, including his academic credentials, the psychiatric evaluation, Lt. Col. McKeegan’s position and involvement, and witness corroboration of specific incidents. Statistical analysis confirms the improbability of the red-and-black pattern. However, absent official confirmation or leaked documents, The Post cannot definitively verify that U.S. government agencies are conducting the surveillance and harassment Pearson describes. We present his account, documentation, and the corroborating evidence for readers to assess._

### **How the US Government Can Neutralize, Torture, and Injure a Person Without Accountability**

This essay begins with a puzzle rather than an accusation. A person experiences severe and sustained harm — psychological, social, and professional — over an extended period. The damage is real and measurable. Yet no single illegal act can be identified. There is no arrest record, no indictment, no visible perpetrator. Every attempt to seek explanation or redress leads to dead ends. The question is not who did this, but how it could happen at all.

The intuitive image of state abuse is still a physical one: a cell, a baton, a confession wrung from pain. But in a contemporary constitutional democracy, the most effective forms of coercion would look very different. They would be administrative rather than violent, psychological rather than spectacular, cumulative rather than episodic. The harm would emerge not from a single dramatic action but from a succession of ordinary decisions — each defensible on its own, each made by a different actor, each technically within the bounds of law. The result would be suffering without a crime scene.

American law is poorly suited to perceive this kind of injury. The federal government is largely shielded from damages for constitutional violations, and courts are reluctant to expand the narrow circumstances in which officials can be sued. When national security or intelligence is invoked, judges defer heavily to agency assertions. Civil rights statutes, often assumed to be a safeguard, are designed to address discrete acts by identifiable actors and require proof of intent and individualized causation. When harm is distributed across institutions and unfolds over time, it tends to vanish into the gaps of legal doctrine.

In the case that prompted this analysis, no single institution appeared to be responsible. Instead, the damage seemed to arise from a web of interactions with agencies, contractors, and civil authorities, each performing a narrow function that appeared routine. No one needed to understand the whole picture. No one needed to issue an explicit order. Responsibility dissolved into process. This diffusion is not an accident of bureaucracy; it is what allows deniability to endure.

One of the most destabilizing features of the experience was a persistent sense of being watched, paired with an inability to confirm it. Such a condition does not require illegal surveillance. It can arise from the ordinary infrastructure of modern life: digital metadata, building security systems, administrative data sharing, behavioral inference. What mattered was not whether observation was occurring, but that its possibility could never be ruled out. The ambiguity itself became corrosive, producing a state of constant vigilance that eroded trust in one’s own perceptions.

Psychological pressure did not arrive as overt threats. It appeared instead as patterns that were difficult to name: coincidences that accumulated, encounters that felt scripted but remained deniable, environmental cues that repeated with just enough consistency to feel personal. None of these incidents was extraordinary. Over time, their persistence was.

Sleep and routine — long recognized as vulnerabilities in psychological coercion — were disrupted indirectly. Noise complaints went unresolved. Maintenance schedules became erratic. Administrative processes grew unpredictable. The effect was not simply fatigue but cognitive overload. Exhaustion narrowed attention, degraded communication, and made coherent narration increasingly difficult. To outsiders, the resulting distress appeared less like injury than instability.

Attempts to seek help often deepened the harm. Legal aid organizations lacked jurisdiction. Oversight bodies failed to respond. Requests for explanation were redirected toward evaluation rather than investigation. Institutions designed to protect individuals from abuse instead functioned as buffers against inquiry. Every door opened into the same hallway.

As the experience continued, credibility itself became the casualty. In liberal societies, extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. When harm is diffuse and deniable, that standard becomes unreachable. Friends urged rest. Colleagues suggested stepping back. Observers reframed the account as stress or misinterpretation. This disbelief did not need to be enforced by the state. It was socially reproduced, a byproduct of norms that favor plausibility over scrutiny.

A system like this does not need to operate indefinitely. It ends when one of several conditions is met: the person withdraws from public life, leaves the jurisdiction, or gradually loses the ability to articulate the experience coherently. Each outcome can be framed as voluntary. The machinery leaves no visible marks.

There are no midnight arrests in this model, no secret prisons, no signed orders. Only a sequence of ordinary actions whose combined effect is devastating — and therefore difficult to recognize as abuse under conventional definitions. If such harm exists, it would not announce itself as torture. It would call itself procedure, security, discretion, coincidence.

This essay does not claim proof of a covert program or assign intent to unnamed actors. It offers a warning. A modern constitutional system may already possess the capacity to destroy a person through formally legal means, and the safeguards we rely on may be ill-equipped to detect or prevent it. If that is true, the danger is not confined to any single case or administration. It is structural.
