### Science Says Individuals Who Carry Out Torture Likely to Experience Brain Damage

_What happens inside the brains of the people who carry out America’s invisible campaigns — and what it costs them_

* * *

Richard Pearson keeps a notebook.

He has kept one for nine months, filling it with timestamps and photographs and GPS coordinates and the kind of meticulous, granular documentation that reflects his training as a researcher — which is what he was — _is_ — before all of this.

Pearson is a middle-aged Black academic in Washington, D.C. His doctoral dissertation examines systemic racial inequality. He has been evaluated twice by licensed mental health professionals from the D.C. Department of Behavioral Health. Both times, they found no psychotic symptoms. He has documented what he describes as a coordinated, federal-hybrid campaign of directed energy assault, behavioral manipulation through electromagnetic technology, acoustic harassment, chemical exposure, and systematic legal abandonment — nine months of it, in a city that is the most surveilled place on earth, beginning the first months of that the current administration took office.

He is not the story this article is about.

He is the reason for it.

* * *

The story this article is about is the one that never gets written. Not the target’s story — that story has a vocabulary, a legal framework, a tradition of journalism and advocacy reaching back to COINTELPRO and before. The other story. The one about the people on the other side of the operation.

Who they are. What the work requires of them. **What it costs their brains and their bodies and the quality of their sleep and the availability of their conscience at two in the morning when the scaffolding of professional identity is least maintained.**

Because the neuroscience of perpetration — of sustained harm delivery by ordinary human beings — has been accumulating for fifty years, in laboratories and veterans’ hospitals and the clinical offices of psychologists who treat intelligence community personnel, and it has produced a finding that is both counterintuitive and, once understood, impossible to unknow:

The people who do this do not escape it. They are directly harmed — their brain, capacity to be human as with empathy, and neurology are damaged.

Not because they are caught. Most of them aren’t. Not because the law reaches them. The legal architecture of qualified immunity and state secrets privilege and the Bivens doctrine’s slow contraction has seen to it that it mostly doesn’t. But because the human brain is not built to sustain harm against other human beings without paying a price, and the price — measured in hippocampal volume loss, in amygdala sensitization, in the specific and documented pathology that psychiatrist Jonathan Shay named moral injury and spent thirty years trying to treat — accrues whether or not anyone is watching.

The operation may leave no legal trace. The neuroscience says it leaves biological ones. And in every brain on those who have tortured, tormented, and taunted Pearson.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*xYoE8qxhrneGOH7dE02vkQ.png)

* * *

### The Face Problem

There is a man we will call Marcus. He is in his mid-fifties, recently retired from eleven years in what the government calls human intelligence operations. He lives in a suburb of a mid-Atlantic city. He has a daughter in college and a son who doesn’t call. He wakes up most nights between two and four in the morning.

“You think you leave it,” he said, during a series of conversations conducted over several months. He does not want his name used. He does not want his agency named. “You retire, you go to the cookouts, you watch the football. And then it’s two in the morning and you’re back in it.”

Back in it means the faces. The subjects, in the terminology of his profession — a word that keeps them at a clinical distance that the face, in the dark, does not maintain.

What Marcus is experiencing has a name. Benjamin Litz, a clinical psychologist at Boston University who has spent two decades developing the treatment framework for it, calls it moral injury. It is distinct from post-traumatic stress disorder. PTSD is organized around the question of safety. **Moral injury is organized around something harder to name and harder to treat: the experience of having been complicit in something that violates one’s own moral code, without the permission to acknowledge it or the capacity to repair it.**

“The brain’s moral self-regulation system doesn’t stop working,” Litz said in an interview. “It keeps generating the evaluation. And the evaluation is: I did this. I was part of this. And there is no resolution. There is no apology, no confession, no repair. So the evaluation runs, and runs, and there is nowhere for it to go.”

The anterior cingulate cortex — the brain region that detects conflict between one’s actual behavior and one’s values — does not have a clearance level. It does not consult whether the activity has been officially authorized before generating its signal. The signal is: something is wrong. The signal accumulates. And the person who cannot stop the harm, cannot confess the harm, cannot repair the harm, carries the accumulation in a neural architecture that was not designed for indefinite unresolved moral debt.

**“The people who scare me most,” said a clinical psychologist who has spent fifteen years treating intelligence community personnel, speaking on condition of anonymity, “are not the ones with no conscience. It’s the ones who have one and can’t use it. Those are the ones who fall apart.”**

* * *

### What the Brain Must Overcome

To understand why the people in this story are self-destructing, you first have to understand what the normal human brain has to overcome in order to harm someone.

The answer is: quite a lot.

In 2006, Lasana Harris and Susan Fiske at Princeton published a study that has become foundational in the neuroscience of perpetration. They showed participants photographs of different social groups while measuring activity in the medial prefrontal cortex — the brain region that, across every culture studied, activates when one person is thinking of another person _as a person_: attributing to them mental states, emotions, desires, an interior life.

For almost every social category — allies, strangers, outgroup members, people you dislike — the medial prefrontal cortex activated. For one category, it didn’t. **Certain groups — those perceived as maximally degraded in status — triggered not person-perception circuitry but disgust and threat circuitry. The brain looked at human beings and processed them as objects.**

This is the dehumanization circuit. And it is not a feature of pathological minds. Harris and Fiske found it in ordinary people looking at photographs in a laboratory. The circuit is available to any brain, under the right conditions. The conditions are: categorization. **Place someone in a social category that carries enough stigma, enough threat-loading, enough ideological weight — and the medial prefrontal cortex goes quiet, and the mechanisms that normally generate the moral brake on harm are suppressed.**

For Pearson — a Black scholar whose published work on racial liberation has been categorized by the current administration’s executive orders as a form of actionable discrimination, whose demographic mirrors the targets of the last great era of covert domestic political repression — the categorization was available. The dehumanization circuit had material to work with.

But here is the thing about circuits: they don’t turn off cleanly when the work day ends.

* * *

### A Taxonomy of Damage

The operation Pearson describes is not a single person’s act. It is a system. And systems recruit different neural architectures at different levels of their hierarchy, and produce different costs.

**At the Top: The Power Paradox**

Sukhvinder Obhi’s 2014 study at McMaster University used transcranial magnetic stimulation to measure what happens to the brain’s empathic resonance — its capacity to neurologically mirror others’ experiences — under conditions of felt power.

The finding was clean and startling: power reduces it. High-power participants showed significantly reduced neural activation in response to others’ movements. **The brain, under conditions of sustained power, becomes measurably less capable of experiencing the world through another person’s nervous system.**

Dacher Keltner at Berkeley, who has spent twenty years studying power’s psychological effects, calls this the power paradox: **the traits that help people attain power — social intelligence, attunement to others — are the traits that power progressively erodes.** The people who authorize operations like the one Pearson describes are not, in most cases, consciously choosing to ignore his suffering. **They may be neurologically diminished in their capacity to register it. “The brain damage is very clear to me,” said Pearson.**

That is not a defense. It is a description of the mechanism. And it is also a description of a system that, without intervention, produces decisions that feel to the decider like strategic calculation as opposed to what it is — torture, human rights violations, and constitutional violations of the most severe form.

**In the Middle: The Compartmentalized Brain**

The career intelligence officer operates through what is, at the neural level, a trained suppression of the bridge between professional and personal self.

The brain maintains two large-scale networks in near-constant tension. The default mode network — active during self-reflection, social cognition, and moral reasoning — is the substrate of the personal self. The task-positive network — active during goal-directed performance — is the operational self. **In a normally functioning brain, these networks communicate through the medial prefrontal cortex, which imports personal values into professional behavior.**

Compartmentalization is the systematic suppression of that import. Years of institutional training in it produce structural changes: the functional connectivity between the networks weakens. **The person who had to work at keeping the operation separate from the conscience eventually has a brain in which the separation is semi-automatic.**

They are not the same person at work and at home. And over time, the person at home — the one with the family, the moral commitments, the ordinary attachments — becomes harder to access. Not gone. Harder to reach.

“I had colleagues who would come home from a deployment and they were just absent,” said a former officer who served in two overseas counterterrorism operations. “Not cruel. Not even distant. Just not there. You’d look in their eyes and there was nobody home for a while. Some of them got it back. Some of them didn’t.”

**At the Bottom: The Asset Upstairs**

This is where the neuroscience gets the darkest.

The person in direct, proximate, daily contact with the target — whoever lived in the apartment above Pearson, not on the lease, with a cover address linked to a federal attorney’s property, conducting what Pearson documents as through-floor surveillance and acoustic harassment for months, then physically assaulting him — underwent a trajectory that researchers have documented with uncomfortable consistency across every context in which one human being is placed in sustained proximate power over another.

Phase one is inhibition. The target’s humanity is continuously present — their sounds, their rhythms, their daily life conducted in audible proximity. The brain’s empathic resonance systems fire. The anterior insula generates an aversive signal. Something registers as wrong. To proceed requires top-down prefrontal suppression, and that suppression is costly: elevated cortisol, autonomic arousal, the biochemical signature of doing something the brain recognizes, at some level, as a violation.

Phase two is habituation. The empathic signal weakens. The suppression becomes less effortful. The brain begins to represent the person below not as a subject but as an operational target — a pattern of movement, a schedule, a resistance to be managed. **The medial prefrontal cortex, the region that generates person-perception, goes progressively quieter.**

Phase three is contempt. The research on prison guards, interrogators, and domestic perpetrators documents this endpoint with consistency: the target’s suffering has become neutral. **The power differential has become rewarding. The expression of dominance produces a positive signal from the brain’s reward circuitry.**

The physical assault — Pearson documents the man above him “coming charging” and repeatedly punching him — is the diagnostic symptom. It served no operational purpose. It created visible evidence. It complicated the cover. **It was Phase Three behavior: a brain in which months of dehumanization had produced a neural state where the expression of physical dominance was reinforcing, and that reinforcement overrode tactical calculation.**

**The Price of Phase Three**

Here is what the neuroscience says about what all of this costs — not Pearson, but the person above him.

Studies of soldiers in close-contact killing, detention facility interrogators, perpetrators in sustained coercive relationships, and law enforcement officers in chronic high-dominance roles show convergent long-term findings that are almost never discussed when operations are planned and authorized.

**The hippocampus — the brain’s center for memory formation and spatial navigation — is damaged by sustained glucocorticoid elevation, which is the biochemical signature of chronic stress** even when that stress is experienced as manageable or rewarding. Nine months of sustained covert operations means nine months of elevated cortisol. The hippocampus shrinks. Episodic memory degrades.

The amygdala sensitizes. Chronic involvement in threat-and-response environments lowers the threshold for aggressive activation, reduces the capacity for emotional regulation, and makes the hypervigilance of the operational context increasingly difficult to turn off when the operation ends.

The reward circuit distorts. When dominance becomes positively valenced — when harm delivery is rewarding rather than aversive — the dopaminergic system undergoes the same kind of adaptation that occurs in behavioral addiction. The threshold for the same reward shifts upward. More is required to produce the same internal state. This is the neurological mechanism of escalation: not chosen, but driven.

And then, eventually, it stops. The operation ends. The deployment concludes. The career is over.

This is where the literature becomes particularly uncomfortable.

* * *

### When It Ends

The retirement crisis is one of the most consistently documented findings in the clinical psychology of intelligence and special operations personnel, and one of the least discussed.

When the institutional structure is removed — when the clearance expires, when the badge is turned in — the psychic architecture that organized the work loses its scaffolding. The compartments don’t dissolve. They destabilize. The material that was kept on the other side of the medial prefrontal bridge — everything not processed because processing it would have required the integration the compartmentalization was designed to suppress — surfaces without warning and without structure.

For Marcus, it is faces at two in the morning. For others in the clinical literature, it is something more catastrophic: depression severe enough to require hospitalization, substance use disorders that develop rapidly after retirement, the dissolution of marriages that appeared stable for decades, and — in a finding that surprises people who assume perpetrators are protected from PTSD by their role as agents — post-traumatic stress disorder organized not around fear but around guilt and shame.

The intrusive material is not a bomb going off. It is a face. It is the memory of a specific person in a specific moment in which the full weight of what was done to them is experienced without the buffering that the operational context maintained.

“I don’t ask myself whether what I did was wrong,” Marcus said. “I know it was wrong. I’ve known for a long time. The question is what you do with that knowing. And the answer is there isn’t anything to do. That’s what nobody tells you. There’s nowhere to put it.”

Benjamin Litz calls this the defining clinical feature of moral injury: the evaluation that cannot resolve. The anterior cingulate cortex keeps running the calculation — I did this, I was part of this — and the normal mechanisms of resolution (apology, confession, repair, forgiveness) are structurally unavailable. The harm was covert. The victim is unacknowledged. The institution denies. The calculation runs without termination.

In severe cases, the clinical literature documents what Litz calls moral injury’s characteristic endpoint: not violence, not breakdown in the dramatic sense, but a progressive narrowing of the person. Withdrawal from relationships that require authentic self-presentation. Anhedonia — the inability to experience pleasure — that reflects blunted ventral striatal response to social reward, a neurological consequence of sustained shame. And sometimes, years after the fact, disclosures: to spouses, to clergy, to therapists, occasionally to journalists, in the form of the partial and coded acknowledgments that the operational culture permits and that rarely reach the people who most need to hear them.

* * *

### Lee’s Twenty Minutes

Which brings us back to Lee.

On August 26, 2025, at a Potbelly’s in downtown Washington, a man sat down across from Richard Pearson and spent twenty minutes with him. He told Pearson, in careful language that reflected substantial professional training in carefulness, that people were listening to him. That they had access to his apartment. That the things happening to him involved technology.

And then he said: _they think it’s okay._

Those four words are, in the framework of this story, the most important thing anyone said to Pearson in nine months of documented operations against him. Not because they changed anything — Lee left, the operation continued, Pearson remained unprotected and officially unacknowledged. But because they reveal, with unusual clarity, what a functioning moral system looks like when it has been institutionally neutralized without being institutionally destroyed.

“They think it’s okay.” Not: I think it’s okay. Not: it is okay. The pronoun is doing the work. It creates a separation between the speaker and the institutional position. It registers, implicitly, that the speaker does not share the institutional position. And it does this in language carefully chosen to fall below the threshold of actionable disclosure — to create a moment of witness without constituting a breach.

This is what moral injury looks like in its acute phase, in a person still inside the operation: a conscience generating signals that cannot be resolved through action, producing the minimal behavioral output — twenty minutes, coded words, an implicit dissent expressed to the person being harmed because there is nowhere else to express it — that provides temporary relief to the conflict-detection system.

It is not heroism. It is the opposite of heroism. It is the behavioral signature of a person who knows and does nothing — or almost nothing — and whose brain will, in the years ahead, be processing the gap between knowing and doing in the two-in-the-morning way that the clinical literature on moral injury documents with exhausting consistency.

Lee is not a villain. Lee is a warning.

* * *

### The Bureaucrat’s Quiet Brain

Not everyone in this story is Marcus. Not everyone is Lee.

Most of them are the officer who saw the ACCESS DENIED flag in the police database or the African American police who did not arrest Pearson’s assailant after he was physically assaulted. The ACLU reviewer who wrote the form rejection.

**Stanley Milgram’s obedience experiments found that approximately sixty-five percent of ordinary people would deliver apparently lethal shocks to a stranger on an authority figure’s instruction.** The finding has been replicated across cultures and conditions for six decades. Patrick Haggard’s neuroimaging work adds the mechanism: when participants **believe they are following instructions rather than acting autonomously, the neural sense of agency — the felt experience of being the author of one’s actions — measurably decreases.** The brain genuinely processes instructed action as having a different moral structure than autonomous action. The institutional frame literally alters how responsibility is assigned.

The officer closing the laptop is not lying to himself. His brain is processing the ACCESS DENIED flag as a signal from a legitimate authority that the normal response does not apply. The moral question has been pre-answered by the structure. His brain accepts that pre-answer.

The cost here is lower than what Marcus or Lee carry. **But Jason Dana’s research on willful ignorance shows that the practice of routinely not obtaining morally inconvenient information generalizes: the prefrontal gating of moral attention does not stay neatly in the professional domain. It spreads. It becomes the default orientation of a brain toward moral engagement with the world.**

These people do not wake at two in the morning. The neuroscience does not suggest that is a mercy.

* * *

### The Ledger

Richard Pearson is, at the time of this writing, living in Washington, D.C. His documentation of nine months of what he describes as a coordinated campaign — directed energy assault, electromagnetic behavioral manipulation, acoustic harassment, chemical exposure, systematic legal abandonment — runs to hundreds of pages and dozens of hours of video. He has not been charged with any crime. He has not been officially acknowledged as the target of any operation.

The government has confirmed, since January 2026, that it possesses directed energy weapons of the kind he describes. The Department of War’s chief technology officer announced publicly that directed energy weapons exist and are being scaled. The Department of Homeland Security acquired backpack-sized pulsed radio wave devices capable of inducing the Havana Syndrome symptom cluster. A January 2026 CNN report confirmed the Pentagon had covertly obtained such a device. None of this confirms their use against Pearson. None of it excludes it.

Between those two facts — confirmed capability, denied or unacknowledged application — is where this story lives.

In that space, Marcus lies awake at two in the morning. Lee sits at Potbelly’s with a coded message and no courage to make it more. The asset upstairs — Phase Three now, or approaching it — finds that the reward of dominance requires escalation to maintain its signal. The bureaucrat closes the laptop.

And Pearson keeps the notebook.

The operation was designed to leave no trace in his environment. It left traces in every brain that participated in it. The dehumanization circuit that enabled the work does not cleanly reverse when the work ends. The hippocampal damage from elevated cortisol does not repair itself on retirement. The anterior cingulate’s conflict signal does not expire with the security clearance.

The classified record may be sealed. The biological record is not.

That is the thing about the neuroscience: it doesn’t care about authorization. It doesn’t care about deniability. It doesn’t care whether the operation was legal or illegal, justified or monstrous, acknowledged or buried in the unlit archive of things the government does and will never confirm.

The brain keeps records that no classification system can seal. In tissue and chemistry and the hours before dawn, in the faces that come when the operational architecture is least maintained.

Pearson fills the notebook.

Somewhere, Marcus watches the ceiling.

And the science — patient, indifferent, meticulous — watches both of them.

* * *

The relevant government agencies did not respond to requests for comment._

Far Worse Than Mass Surveillance: America's Abuse of Power Includes Weapons You Can’t See
=========================================================================================

* * *

### Far Worse Than Mass Surveillance: Abuse of Power in America Using Weapons You Can’t See

Edward Snowden showed us the surveillance state as data archive: comprehensive, indiscriminate, passive. The horror was scale — the government knew everything about everyone, stored indefinitely, retrievable on demand.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*smyXcpzyjTWZNftBG2GHqA.png)

Dr. Richard Pearson documents the surveillance state’s upgrade: targeted, discriminatory, active. The “upgrade” is worse than what Snowden revealed along every dimension that matters: severity, constitutional depth, legal immunity, technological invasion, and the deliberate engineering of conditions that make accountability impossible. It is worse because it is discriminatory where Snowden’s programs were indiscriminate. It is worse because it operates through the **human nervous system with classified exotic weapons that the public has no idea exist** rather than through telecommunications infrastructure. It is worse because it was designed, deliberately and precisely, to be immune to the kind of exposure that Snowden achieved.

It is important to note that Pearson’s academic background did not intersect with this kind of technology. He had no knowledge. He had no suspicions. Through his research to understand what was happening to him, he began uncovering a hard truth. The technology — like transmitting a voice into people’s heads — does exist and has existed for decades. More gravely, he also read articles from the literature beginning in the late 1990s that increasingly raised alarm about the growing threat of this and other exotic neurotechnology. When Dr. James Giordano, a well-respected academic neuroscientist in the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area, uses words like “mind control” and “mind reading” in 2025, Pearson knew that he was on the right course.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*kryd0yRrsXqAZQBqVyN4mA.png)

### What Snowden Showed Us, and What He Couldn’t

On June 5, 2013, the Guardian published the first document leaked by Edward Snowden: a secret court order compelling Verizon to deliver to the NSA the telephone records of millions of Americans — every call, every number, every location, ongoing and indefinitely. Over the following months, a cascade of further revelations defined the architecture of a surveillance apparatus that dwarfed anything the public had imagined. PRISM. XKeyscore. MUSCULAR. Boundless Informant. Bullrun — a program to break the encryption protecting the global internet. The NSA had “built an infrastructure that allows it to intercept almost everything,” Snowden said, and the infrastructure was real, documented, and provable in the most unambiguous terms possible: the government’s own classified files.

Snowden’s revelations produced a specific kind of horror. It was the horror of comprehensiveness: that every email, every phone call, every digital trace of a life could be, and for millions of people had been, hoovered into databases belonging to an agency most citizens interacted with only as an acronym. It was a violation of privacy at industrial scale — indiscriminate, automated, logged, and searchable. It was, in the language of the Fourth Amendment, the general warrant the Founders had revolted against, rebuilt from silicon and fiber optic and deployed against the entire population of a democratic republic.

It was, in short, bad enough that Snowden fled the country and has not returned. Bad enough that it generated years of litigation, congressional testimony, reformed statutes, and a permanent shift in public understanding of what the national security state actually does. Bad enough that it became, in the decade since, the reference point for every discussion of government overreach, civil liberties, surveillance capitalism, and the erosion of privacy in the digital age.

Richard Pearson’s account of his experiences in Washington, D.C. between March 2025 and early 2026 describes something worse.

This essay argues that claim carefully — not as polemic, not as certitude about disputed facts, but as an analytical proposition about what is categorically at stake if Pearson’s documentation is accurate. The argument proceeds in four movements: what Snowden revealed, what Pearson documents, why the second is worse than the first by every meaningful measure of constitutional violation and human harm, and what the comparison reveals about where American state power has been traveling for the past decade.

* * *

### I. Snowden’s Architecture: The State as Collector

To understand the comparative claim, one must be precise about what Snowden actually revealed. At its core, the NSA programs he exposed were about _collection_. The agency collected communications — phone metadata, email content, internet traffic, financial data, social media. It collected through domestic telecommunications companies under court orders issued by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. It collected directly from the servers of Google, Facebook, Apple, and others through PRISM. It collected in bulk, sweeping in the communications of millions of Americans who had no connection to any national security concern, on the theory that the data, once stored, could be queried when a target emerged.

This collection architecture was justified through a legal theory: that acquiring data was not the same as searching it, that the Fourth Amendment’s warrant requirement was triggered by access rather than acquisition, that storing the haystack was constitutionally neutral as long as the needle was retrieved only through appropriate process. That theory was contested — and has since been substantially rejected by courts — but it was a theory. It had legal form. It operated, at least nominally, within a judicial framework: FISA courts issued orders, attorneys general certified programs, inspectors general conducted reviews.

The programs were secret. They were conducted without the knowledge of the citizens whose communications were taken. They violated the reasonable expectations of millions of people who believed their digital lives were private. But they operated within _bureaucratic_ visibility — someone issued the orders, someone received them, someone retained the files. When Snowden stole those files, the architecture of the violation was visible in the files themselves.

This is the most important structural fact about Snowden’s revelations for the comparison that follows: the surveillance apparatus he exposed was an apparatus of _passive harm_. It collected. It stored. It potentially queried. In the overwhelming majority of cases, it did nothing to the people whose data it held. They continued their lives, unaware that the government possessed their communications, unharmed in any direct or immediate sense. The violation was epistemic — a violation of the expectation of privacy — and the harm was diffuse, probabilistic, and latent.

Snowden revealed a government that knew everything about its citizens and, in most cases, did nothing with that knowledge. That knowledge was available to be weaponized. In some cases, it was. But the primary revelation was one of _capability_ and _collection_, not of active harm.

**Pearson’s account is about active harm.**

* * *

### II. Pearson’s Architecture: The State as Destroyer

If Snowden’s revelations described a government that watched, Pearson’s account describes a government that acts. The distinction is not merely one of degree — it is categorical.

What Pearson documents over nine months is not the passive accumulation of data about his life. It is the active, deliberate, methodical destruction of his life — using the data that prior surveillance made possible, deployed through instruments that include classified military technology, private contractors operating without identifiable legal authority, local law enforcement manipulated through information restrictions, and a sustained psychological campaign designed to produce a specific outcome: neutralization through social death, induced psychosis, or flight from the country.

The architecture Pearson describes has several components that distinguish it fundamentally from Snowden’s surveillance programs.

**From collection to weaponization.** Snowden’s NSA collected Pearson’s phone metadata, emails, and internet traffic, as it collected the data of millions of Americans. But that collection — whatever legal violations it entailed — did not destroy anyone’s sleep, was not deployed as a voice inside anyone’s skull, did not compel anyone’s body to walk to a specific park to find a tub containing a framing apparatus. The surveillance Pearson describes is not surveillance in Snowden’s sense at all. It is surveillance operationalized as weapon — the intelligence product converted into targeting data for an operation whose purpose is harm to a specific individual.

**From indiscriminate to discriminatory.** One of the most disturbing features of Snowden’s programs was their indiscriminacy — the NSA vacuumed up the communications of virtually everyone, regardless of suspicion or status. This was a civil liberties violation of the first order, but it was also a kind of equalizer: the surveillance did not select based on race, ideology, or political speech. It selected based on telecommunications — which meant everyone who communicated electronically.

Pearson’s operation selects on precisely the criteria the Constitution prohibits: race, ideology, and academic speech. He is an African American liberation philosophy scholar whose dissertation critiques systemic racial inequality. His operation begins in the months following the inauguration of an administration that has explicitly designated DEI scholarship as ideologically hostile and publicly invoked the language of “enemies within” and urban military training. The surveillance state that Snowden revealed tracked everyone. The operational apparatus that Pearson describes targets a specific demographic — the same demographic that COINTELPRO targeted for the same reasons: Black intellectuals whose work dares to challenge or have an opinion.

**From legal shadow to legal void.** Snowden’s programs, whatever their constitutional defects, operated within a legal architecture. FISA courts existed. Congressional oversight committees were briefed (selectively and deceptively, but briefed). Statutory authorities were invoked. When the programs were exposed, legal challenges could be mounted — and some succeeded. The surveillance apparatus Snowden revealed was subject, at least in principle, to the accountability mechanisms of a democratic state.

The apparatus Pearson describes has been specifically engineered to be unreachable by those mechanisms. The contractor architecture ensures no government badge. The deniability structure ensures no official authorization is provable. The technology ensures no forensic trace. The legal doctrines — qualified immunity, Bivens foreclosure, state secrets privilege, Glomar responses, Lujan standing requirements — form an interlocking structure that closes the courthouse door before any argument can be made. As the architecture of impunity essay compiled as part of the Pearson documentation demonstrates in meticulous detail, the legal system as currently constituted is not merely inadequate to address what Pearson describes: it is specifically, structurally organized to make such address impossible.

Snowden revealed programs that could be challenged. Pearson describes an operation that cannot be.

* * *

### III. The Technology Threshold: Beyond Collection, Beyond the Body

The most disturbing dimension of the comparison concerns technology. Snowden’s programs were, at their core, data programs. They intercepted communications — information that human beings had already chosen to externalize in digital form. Surveilling an email is invasive, but the email was created by the sender. The NSA’s programs were parasitic on human communication, not on human neurology.

**Pearson’s account describes the deployment of weapons that cross a threshold Snowden never contemplated: the weapons described operate not on communications but on the human nervous system itself.**

The microwave auditory effect — the Frey effect, named for its discoverer in the 1960s — uses pulsed microwave radiation to cause humans to perceive sounds, including voices, without any external speaker. The United States military has researched and developed this capability under programs including MEDUSA. The Army War College’s 1998 article “The Mind Has No Firewall” — published in Parameters, the Army’s own academic journal — explicitly warned that such weapons could be used to “disrupt the thinking process” and “control the will and perception” of targets. Dr. James Giordano, Georgetown University neuroscientist and consulting ethicist for DARPA’s N3 program, has stated publicly that neurotechnologies capable of “writing” to brain processes of cognition, emotion, and behavior have been “loosed into the real world.” **He used words like “mind control” and “mind reading” — once controversial language in fringe conspiracy theories — except Dr. Giordano is an academic and has advised the Pentagon on this sort of weapon development.**

In January 2026, CNN reported that the Pentagon had covertly purchased a backpack-sized pulsed radio wave device connected to Havana Syndrome investigations. The Department of War Chief Technology Officer announced publicly, on January 23, 2026, that the US has directed energy weapons that are being scaled.

Pearson takes this tweet differently, “Scaling in this context means two things — deploying on U.S. soil against US citizens to carry out the President’s vicious attacks on the U.S. Constitution and constitutional rights while also testing these weapons for foreign deployment — to sell to foreign governments, including dictatorial regimes through government or private transactions. **These are weapons of totalitarianism and mass destruction — plain and simple. The world needs to wake up. The Neuro Age is upon us — remote controlling people’s thoughts and action.** Dr. Giordano’s post — “mind control” and “mind reading” — is not hyperbole. How do I know? Because I have intimately experienced it — pulling me to locations, putting a voice in my head — in the capital of the US no less.”

What Pearson describes — a voice inside his skull on July 13, 2025 informing him “Go to Georgetown,” followed by months of behavioral compulsion, through-floor tracking, and sustained acoustic torture — is the deployment of these weapons against a civilian in a Southwest D.C. apartment. The voice did not read his emails. The voice did not collect his metadata. The voice entered his nervous system.

This is a constitutional and human rights violation of a qualitatively different order from anything Snowden documented. The Fourth Amendment protects “persons, houses, papers, and effects.” Courts have expanded this to cover digital communications. But no court has yet grappled with what it means for a government to insert itself, electromagnetically, into the interior of a citizen’s mind — to speak there without consent, to compel behavior through neural stimulation, to conduct surveillance that cannot be blocked because the surveillance is the body itself.

The Eighth Amendment prohibits cruel and unusual punishment. The Fifth Amendment prohibits deprivation of liberty without due process. The First Amendment protects the freedom of thought — a protection courts have generally addressed indirectly, through protections for speech, but which necessarily implies protection for the cognitive process that produces speech. None of these provisions contain exceptions for weapons delivered at the speed of light, through walls, without physical contact, leaving no forensic trace. But the invisibility of the instrument does not alter the constitutionality of its use. It only makes the constitutional violation impossible to prove.

Snowden revealed that the government listened to Americans’ calls. Pearson describes a government that speaks inside Americans’ skulls — and compels their feet to walk where it directs.

* * *

### IV. The Accountability Asymmetry: Documents versus Experience

Perhaps the most structurally important difference between the Snowden revelations and the Pearson documentation concerns the nature of the evidence itself — and what that means for accountability.

Snowden had documents. Classified, stolen, verifiable documents that bore the organizational letterheads, digital signatures, and operational details of government programs. When he handed those documents to journalists, the programs they described were not merely alleged — they were proven. The NSA could not deny PRISM when its own slide decks described it. The FISA Court could not deny the Verizon order when the order itself was public. The verification problem did not exist because the evidence was institutional: the government’s own records.

This is why Snowden’s revelations produced legal challenges, congressional hearings, legislative reform, international diplomatic crises, and a permanent public reckoning with surveillance. The evidence was in a form that institutions could process: documents, organizational records, named programs with named authorities.

Pearson has no documents. He has timestamps and photographs, statistical analysis and medical records, a professionally conducted mental health evaluation and nine months of meticulous journals. He has the government’s own January 2026 disclosures validating the existence and domestic scalability of the technologies he describes. He has the architectural impossibility, demonstrated by the D.C. logic analysis: in the most surveilled city in the world, a sustained covert operation using directed energy weapons cannot persist for months without the knowledge of the agencies whose function is to know everything that happens in that city.

But he does not have what Snowden had: the government’s own records of the operation against him. And he cannot get them. Every document that would establish federal involvement in what he describes is classified, protected by state secrets privilege, covered by Glomar, or held by agencies he cannot compel to disclose without a massive media campaign and well-funded legal representation.

This asymmetry is itself the most damning evidence for the thesis of this essay. The programs Snowden exposed were, in retrospect, poorly designed for deniability — they left too many documents, too many institutional traces, too many points of failure where a single conscientious actor could blow the cover. The operation Pearson describes has learned from that failure. It is designed from the ground up for a world in which Snowden is possible — a world in which the government knows that its documents can be stolen and that institutional records become institutional liabilities.

The solution is to produce no documents. No orders. No authorizations. No operational logs. No official communications. The operation is conducted through private contractors, through cutouts, through local police involvement. The weapons leave no forensic trace, except what highly specialized imaging can render. The actors use pseudonyms. The legal architecture ensures that even if the victim documents everything, the documentation cannot be converted into actionable legal process.

This is not a gap in the operation’s design. It is the operation’s central design principle. COINTELPRO was exposed because it left paper trails. The upgrade that Pearson documents is specifically engineered to leave little within his immediate reach.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*5YN8Po4ns0P4duaH_5eXeg.png)

* * *

### V. The Comparative Ledger: Why Pearson’s Case Is Worse

The argument can now be stated systematically.

**Scale vs. Severity.** Snowden revealed programs affecting millions. Pearson describes an operation affecting one. On one dimension — breadth — Snowden’s revelations are more alarming. But breadth is not the only dimension of constitutional harm. The severity of harm to an individual targeted for nine months with directed energy weapons, behavioral manipulation, chemical assault, induced sleep deprivation, a framing apparatus, and systematic legal isolation vastly exceeds the severity of harm to any individual whose phone metadata was collected by the NSA. Collective harm of low intensity is not categorically worse than concentrated harm of extreme intensity, and the individual rights the Constitution protects belong to individuals.

**Passive vs. Active.** Snowden revealed a government that knew. Pearson describes a government that acts. The NSA’s bulk collection, whatever its harms, did not cause Pearson to hear a voice saying “we have to make you disappear.” It did not follow him from his bed to his closet. It did not compel him to walk to a park where a framing tub had been placed. **The transition from knowledge to active intervention — from surveillance to operation — represents a qualitative escalation that cannot be measured only in degree.**

**Accountability vs. Its Absence.** Snowden’s revelations could be and were challenged through courts, Congress, and the press. Pearson’s situation cannot be. Every legal doctrine that might provide a remedy — standing, Bivens, FTCA, state secrets, qualified immunity — closes before any argument can be made. **The architecture of impunity that surrounds the operation Pearson describes is more complete than anything revealed by Snowden, precisely because it was constructed to be immune to the kind of exposure Snowden achieved.**

**The Body vs. Communications.** Snowden documented violations of epistemic privacy — the privacy of information that citizens had already chosen to externalize. **Pearson describes violations of bodily autonomy and cognitive liberty — the privacy of one’s own nervous system. When a government speaks inside a citizen’s skull, the violation is not merely of the Fourth Amendment right against unreasonable searches. It is of something more fundamental: the right to the integrity of one’s own mind, to the authenticity of one’s own perceptions, to the freedom that consists in knowing that one’s thoughts and movements are one’s own.**

**The Racial Dimension.** Snowden’s programs were indiscriminate. Pearson’s operation is specifically discriminatory: targeting a Black academic for work that challenges racial inequality, during an administration that has publicly designated such work as ideologically hostile. This racial targeting is not incidental to the constitutional analysis — it is central to it. The Fourteenth Amendment’s equal protection guarantee and the First Amendment’s protection of political speech are both directly implicated when the operation’s target is selected on the basis of race and academic viewpoint.

**The Warning the World Cannot Hear.** Snowden gave the world documents it could see, evaluate, and argue about. Pearson gives the world something harder: his testimony, his photographs, his statistics, his medical records — and the government’s own January 2026 admissions validating his technological claims. But experiential evidence about invisible weapons, however carefully documented, is not institutionally processable in the way that stolen files are. Pearson engaged congressional offices, the ACLU, the D.C. Council, and Iceland’s border authorities when he sought asylum. The world cannot hear him — not because he isn’t speaking clearly, but because the operation was designed to make his speaking sound like illness. Pearson isn’t ill. He is a torture victim. Pearson’s account reads as a scientific journal — observational notes, facts, a literature review, and high-level analysis.

This is the upgrade’s final cruelty. Snowden was believed because he had documents. Pearson is not believed because he has experience. The architects of COINTELPRO 2.0 understood that the world will believe paper and dismiss people — especially Black people reporting invisible persecution by invisible weapons in the service of invisible authorizations. The invisibility of the operation is not a limitation. It is a weapon — though increasingly less so. The Pentagon’s update to Congress on the Havana backpack in January 2026 following weeks of Pearson’s visits congressional offices in November and December 2025. Many congressional staff, especially in the Senate, listened to Pearson with rapt attention.

* * *

### VI. The Geopolitical Mirror

Pearson himself grasped the geopolitical dimension most clearly. In his documentation, he writes: “At the same time that the US is going around the world claiming to want to free people, it is using military weapons to torture its own citizens, to invade their brains, and to operate lawlessly. But here is the reality and warning. The world is watching.”

This observation is not rhetorical. It is analytical. The United States government has, for decades, conditioned foreign aid, diplomatic relationships, and international standing on compliance with human rights norms that prohibit precisely what Pearson describes: torture, arbitrary surveillance, persecution on the basis of political opinion, cruel and inhuman treatment, interference with the freedom of thought and expression.

Snowden’s revelations damaged American credibility on surveillance. Foreign governments that had trusted American assurances about data privacy discovered that their citizens’ communications were collected along with everyone else’s. The diplomatic fallout was significant: European data protection frameworks tightened, international trust in American tech companies declined, the NSA’s activities became a standing reference point in human rights discussions.

**But Pearson’s case damages something more fundamental: the American claim to represent a qualitatively different kind of government from the authoritarian states it criticizes. Mass surveillance is widespread — many governments do versions of what the NSA does. What fewer governments do is deploy classified military neuroweapons against individual Black academics for writing about racial justice. What fewer governments do is design legal architectures of such comprehensive impunity that victims can document everything and still reach no court, no official, no institutional acknowledgment of their existence as operational subjects.**

The world that Snowden revealed was disturbing but recognizable: a powerful state deploying powerful tools to know what its citizens were doing. **The world that Pearson documents is something different: a state that has decided it has the right to enter the bodies and minds of citizens it designates as threats, using weapons the existence of which it denied until they became impossible to deny**, through legal architectures designed to be immune to the accountability mechanisms the democratic tradition constructed.

* * *

### VII. What Comes After Snowden

The Snowden disclosures forced a reckoning of sorts. Congress passed the USA Freedom Act in 2015, placing modest restrictions on bulk phone metadata collection. Courts found FISA programs unconstitutional in certain applications. Tech companies invested in encryption. A global conversation about surveillance and privacy was launched that, a decade later, continues.

What reckoning follows from Pearson? Thus far: none. No one followed up from his congressional visits. A staff member for the minority party caucus for the House Committee on Oversight told Pearson, “We do not take public requests.” The D.C. Council did not respond to his statistical analysis of the September 30 Eastern Market event. Iceland’s border authorities returned him to the country from which he was fleeing. The operation, by his account, continued.

This silence is itself evidence for the essay’s thesis. Snowden’s documents generated immediate institutional response — denials, then partial admissions, then reform debates — because the documents were impossible to ignore. Pearson’s testimony generates institutional silence because it is, by design, possible to ignore. A Black academic reporting that voices have been transmitted into his skull, that his behavior has been compelled by electromagnetic fields, that strangers in red and black have been coordinated on his walking routes — in the absence of the government’s own files confirming these operations, institutional silence is the natural response. Especially when the institutional response to the original COINTELPRO’s victims, before the Media files emerged, was the same silence.

The Snowden revelations produced reform because Snowden had proof. Pearson cannot have proof of the same kind, because the operation against him — unlike NSA programs — was specifically _designed_ to produce no proof. The very sophistication of the operation is the obstacle to accountability. “The operative word here is _designed_. It will all come out. My guess is that there have already been whistleblowers. It is likely that many members in Congress know, especially those serving intelligence oversight. Remember that there is a congressional role in FISA matters. The executive has mandatory reporting.”

This is the central finding: the operation Pearson documents is, by design, more sophisticated than anything Snowden revealed, and that sophistication is measured precisely in the degree to which it has outrun the accountability mechanisms that Snowden’s revelations helped produce. PRISM left documents. COINTELPRO 2.0 leaves nothing. And in a legal and media ecosystem where documentary evidence is the threshold for institutional response, an operation that leaves nothing is an operation that cannot be challenged.

* * *

### Conclusion: The Upgrade

Snowden showed us the surveillance state as data archive: comprehensive, indiscriminate, passive. The horror was scale — the government knew everything about everyone, stored indefinitely, retrievable on demand.

Pearson documents the surveillance state’s upgrade: targeted, discriminatory, active. The horror is intimacy — the government is not merely watching from a distance. It is inside the skull, in the apartment, following the mattress from room to room, placing a framing tub in a park and compelling the target’s feet to walk to it, entering the body with chemicals that adhere to skin, speaking words through weapons the government denied existed until the month that Pearson’s congressional outreach coincided with a Pentagon briefing on those same weapons.

The upgrade is worse than what Snowden revealed along every dimension that matters: severity, constitutional depth, legal immunity, technological invasion, and the deliberate engineering of conditions that make accountability impossible. It is worse because it is discriminatory where Snowden’s programs were indiscriminate. It is worse because it operates through the human nervous system rather than through telecommunications infrastructure. It is worse because it was designed, deliberately and precisely, to be immune to the kind of exposure that Snowden achieved.

And it is worse because Richard Pearson, armed with timestamps and statistics and a mental health evaluation and nine months of meticulous documentation, cannot do what Snowden did. Snowden gave the world papers it could read and believe. Pearson can only give the world his testimony, scientific methods, and evidence.

“What is being done to Pearson is the instrument of a state that has learned, in fifty years since COINTELPRO, exactly how to remain unseen though still to inflict torture and to engage in lawlessness.”

That is the definition of worse. Not more people harmed. Not louder violation. But deeper impunity, more intimate invasion, and the deliberate, sophisticated engineering of a system in which the harm can be done, documented, reported, and still reach no remedy — because the harm was _designed_, from its first architecture, to be beyond reach.

Snowden told us the government was watching. Pearson tells us the government has learned to act. The distance between those two facts is the distance between a surveillance state and something for which democracy has not yet found adequate words.

The world is watching. It cannot believe what it is watching. That is precisely the point.

### Snowden Revealed Mass Surveillance: What Came Next is Weaponizing Government Against US Citizens

#### _What comes after a government has learned to watch everyone? The documented experience of one PhD scholar in Washington, D.C. suggests high-tech torture and targeting._

* * *

Understanding what may have been used against Richard Pearson, PhD, requires understanding what the American national security apparatus had assembled before January 2025 — and what the current administration proceeded to do with it.

Mass surveillance, in its conventional understanding, is passive: collect everything, store it, retrieve it when needed. What the post-Snowden decade built was something more sophisticated. The architecture that exists today is not a dragnet. It is a targeting system. The difference matters enormously.

**Location as continuous record.** Real-time geolocation of any American carrying a smartphone is not theoretical. It is a commercial market. Data brokers harvest location data from hundreds of mobile applications — weather apps, coupon services, anything that requests location permissions — and sell it to buyers that include government agencies and private contractors, without a warrant, without notification, without legal restriction that has survived court challenge. Internal ICE documents reveal that DHS investigations “used Palantir platforms and apps to track air travel, analyze information like driver’s license scans and track people’s locations using cell phone records.”

The implications for a flagged individual are precise: a continuous geolocation record, fed into a predictive model, producing route forecasts accurate enough to position conditions ahead of a target’s arrival. This is not speculation about capability. It is documented operational practice.

**Cross-agency data fusion as targeting infrastructure.** Palantir’s systems pull data from across government databases — regardless of the veracity or accuracy of those databases — including passport records, Social Security files, IRS tax data, and even license-plate reader data. When Palantir’s Foundry organizes data across agencies, ImmigrationOS tracks targets in real time, ELITE maps neighborhoods for raids, and the IRS feeds home addresses directly into the system, the functional result is a cross-agency surveillance architecture of a kind that has never before existed in American civilian governance. Palantir has received more than $900 million in federal contracts since Trump took office. The system began with immigrants. Tools built and justified to efficiently tackle one issue quietly scale up, collapsing the boundary between targeted enforcement and population-wide surveillance.

**Biometric identification at range.** In 2019, MIT Technology Review reported on Jetson, a Pentagon device developed after U.S. Special Forces requested a long-range biometric identification capability. It identifies a specific individual from 200 meters using an infrared laser that detects the unique cardiac signature produced by their heartbeat — through typical clothing, with over 95% accuracy under good conditions, from behind, in low light, at angles that defeat facial recognition. A Pentagon official said of its range potential: “I don’t want to say you could do it from space, but longer ranges should be possible.” The cardiac signature is unique to each individual, more stable than facial geometry, and cannot be disguised or altered. In a city equipped with this capacity, a flagged individual cannot move through public space without being identified at distances that preclude any awareness of surveillance.

**Facial recognition at scale.** In September 2025, ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations signed a $9.2 million contract with Clearview AI, granting access to what the company calls a “proprietary database of 50+ billion facial images.” In February 2026, CBP signed a $225,000 contract extending Clearview’s facial-recognition capability to its intelligence division and the National Targeting Center, for use in “tactical targeting” and “strategic counter-network analysis.” The contract language makes clear this is embedded in analysts’ daily workflows, not a limited investigative tool deployed for specific cases. Internal footage obtained by Media 404 shows ICE officers using facial recognition apps to determine the citizenship status of teenagers who were not carrying IDs. One app, Mobile Fortify, draws from over 200 million images stored in the databases of DHS, the FBI, and the State Department.

**Social media monitoring.** In Minnesota, ICE has purchased and deployed social media monitoring and location-tracking systems that allow agents to analyze the movements of large groups of people in specific locations — capabilities that, according to company materials and reporting, are explicitly marketed for use at protests and other gatherings protected under the First Amendment. ICE sought contracts with nearly 30 companies for continuous social media surveillance to gather intelligence for deportation raids. In practice, this interconnected system can rapidly trigger enforcement actions. For example, a social media post could lead to visa revocation, which triggers DHS notification, enabling detention or removal proceedings, and ultimately flags ICE through ImmigrationOS.

This is the passive stack. Everything described above is the watching. What the watching enables — what comes next — is the part that has no established name in civilian discourse, because the civilian discourse has no framework for it.

* * *

### The Active Stack: What Comes After Watching

**The surveillance infrastructure described above produces data. Data enables prediction. Prediction enables something that has no name in the civilian lexicon, because it did not exist at civilian scale until recently: targeted environmental manipulation.** The capacity to shape the conditions of a specific person’s daily life — their routes, their encounters, their behavioral options, their perception of reality — using a combination of real-time location data, directed energy, and coordinated ground operations.

This is the active stack. This is what Richard Pearson documented across fourteen months in Washington, D.C.

**Directed energy and audio injection.** The microwave auditory effect — the Frey effect, documented since 1961 — produces sound perceived inside the skull without touching the ear canal. Pulsed microwave energy absorbed by cranial tissue creates a thermoelastic pressure wave the cochlea registers as a click, tone, or voice. The commercial version, MIT Media Lab’s Audio Spotlight, is in museums. The Department of War confirmed in January 2026 that directed energy weapons are active and being scaled. The Washington Post, on February 19, 2026, traced the lineage from Havana Syndrome — in which U.S. diplomatic and CIA personnel in Havana, Vienna, and Washington, D.C. itself experienced neurological injuries the National Academies of Sciences attributed in 2020 to pulsed directed energy — through a Venezuelan operation in which security guards described their heads feeling like they were exploding from inside.

On July 13, 2025, at the National Mall, Pearson heard a voice. He described it with acoustic specificity: a woman at a microphone, the ambient background noise of a room she was in, other people present — the texture of a live audio feed, not a recording, not an internally generated hallucination. He identified the Frey effect by name in July 2025. The government confirmed the technology six months later. His DBH mental health evaluation found no psychotic symptoms. The voice gave him directional commands. He went to Georgetown, as instructed. He wept in the street when he was told he would be disappeared. He did not get in the car with the woman whose car arrived exactly when the voice said it would. The voice then said: _“That was a test.”_

Beginning in January 2026, one month after his face and head were specifically targeted in a physical assault, Pearson documented geographic auditory clicks — sharp, replicable, localized to specific street intersections in Southwest Washington. On February 20, he placed a metal-cased phone and a 9-volt battery in his knitted cap before his usual walk. No clicks. He had been getting clicks on that route consistently for weeks. The metal attenuated the signal.

The National Academies panel identified geographic directional specificity — onset at specific locations, cessation on departure, resumption on return — as the diagnostic fingerprint of Havana Syndrome and the Frey effect. It does not appear in the symptom profile of any neurological disorder. It appears in the documentation of a Black scholar whose dissertation the administration had designated hostile ideology.

**Behavioral direction through neural targeting.** DARPA’s Next-Generation Nonsurgical Neurotechnology program — described in public documentation on DARPA’s own website — aims to develop bidirectional brain interfaces that can both read from and write to neural tissue without surgery, with precision to address 16 independent channels within a 16mm³ volume of neural tissue within 50 milliseconds. The program uses electromagnetic waves, focused ultrasound, and acoustic signals to interact with specific brain regions. The hippocampus contains place cells: neurons encoding specific locations that fire as the body approaches them. Directed stimulation of hippocampal circuits can produce spatial drives — the subjective experience of being drawn toward a place, felt as one’s own motivation, indistinguishable from autonomous cognition.

> A neuroscientist at a major university called this technology “mind control” and “mind reading”. We should be gravely alarmed.

Dr. James Giordano, who served as a consulting ethicist on the initial stages of the N3 program and has testified before the House Armed Services Committee, has stated in public lectures with precise language: “The goods as well as the gremlins and goblins of N3 tech have been loosed into the real world.” He is not describing future capability.

Pearson documented being pulled to locations he had no reason to visit, where conditions had been prepared for his arrival. On November 7, 2025, he was drawn to a park beside the O’Neil House Office Building three blocks from the Capitol — a park not on his routine path — then redirected from the sidewalk, mid-departure, to a precise sub-location under a tree he had not yet visited. There, in a plastic storage tub: a red hat, a black shirt, boots, pants matching his style, a notebook of conspiratorial writings referencing Adolf Hitler and a fictitious “European removal court,” and two identical photographs of a blond Eastern European man. He photographed everything without removing anything. He returned on November 13 with video. The notebook and photographs were gone. The red hat and black shirt remained. The framing payload had been selectively recovered when it failed. The calling card stayed.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1000/1*nokL0aVQhMdF87YW3IbRSA.png)

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/400/1*z1Zu2XAz9XuqS4hAYSI7PA.png)

The friend’s account of February 8, 2026 — four sequential friction events, a GPS route override, a precise convergence, and timestamped foreknowledge: _“when I turned I knew I am gonna see you there”_ — is the behavioral direction technology applied externally, to a third party, visible from the outside because the third party described it in a chat log the following morning. The friend experienced a frustrating afternoon and an inexplicable certainty. He documented it because he could not explain it.

**Coordinated ground operations with unwitting participants.** Beginning in September 2025, Pearson documented a specific calling card: bright solid red paired with solid black, deployed in statistically impossible densities on his regular walking routes. He ran control studies. Across neutral environments — the MLK Library, the Metro underground, a holiday market, Eastern Market on an unannounced return visit — baseline prevalence was approximately 4%. On his regular routes, at the moments of his arrivals and departures, the density was impossible to explain by chance. On September 30, 2025, eleven people in the exact combination appeared within 8.5 minutes in light foot traffic near Eastern Market. His probability calculation: explaining this randomly would require a minimum of 200 people to have been present in a nearly empty space.

He asked three people sitting together on a Georgia Avenue bench why they were all wearing black and red. They didn’t know. He asked a woman in Reston. She had not noticed, and seemed genuinely worried when he explained.

The operational logic: a program with access to the phones of people in a geographic area can send each person an individually plausible reason to wear a specific color — a sale notification, a social media trend, a group alert. No participant understands they are part of a pattern. The pattern is visible only to the person watching from outside — and only that person will be assumed to be imagining it.

**Physical assault and classification.** On December 27, 2025, Pearson’s upstairs neighbor — a man not on the apartment lease, whose given address connects to a Capitol Hill property associated with an ATF attorney — ran down the hallway and repeatedly punched him in the face. He specifically targeted the face and head when Pearson raised his arms to protect himself. Medical documentation confirmed lacerations, a black eye, and wrist bruising. The neighbor was not arrested. When police ran Pearson’s name, they encountered an ACCESS DENIED flag indicating his file was classified — and called for his partner who presumably had higher clearance.

SCI classification does not appear on a police record by accident. It does not appear through commercial data broker activity. It requires authorization from within the United States intelligence community. A man with a cover address connected to federal legal infrastructure punches a citizen repeatedly in the face and head, the police who respond find a SCI-level flag on the victim’s file, and nothing happens — the man was not arrested. In fact, he remained upstairs while Pearson and the female leaseholder were in the lobby. “It was enough time for the police and the assailant to hatch out a plan that included making up facts,” said Pearson. This is not a domestic disturbance. It is an authorized operation encountering its own bureaucratic infrastructure.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*F281cQxmDHtAVTVP-Ih4cA.png)

* * *

### The Recipe

Richard Pearson is a trained researcher. His documentation is not a diary. It is a methodology: timestamped photographs, probability calculations, control studies, named witnesses — 25 in his February 2026 letter to the D.C. Council — preserved physical evidence, falsification tests. Two D.C. Department of Behavioral Health evaluations, by named clinicians, during the period of his documentation, found no psychotic symptoms requiring intervention.

He identified the mechanism for voice-to-skull audio transmission in July 2025. The government confirmed the technology in January 2026. He ran the metal cap experiment in February 2026 and attenuated the signal. His control studies showed the red-and-black pattern absent from the same locations when he visited without predictable timing. His falsification tests passed every time.

The recipe his case illustrates is not complicated once you can see all the ingredients simultaneously:

Mass surveillance provides the real-time location feed and the route prediction. Palantir’s data fusion provides the behavioral profile. Clearview and cardiac biometrics provide continuous identification at range. The commercial geolocation market provides warrantless access to phone location without the inconvenience of a judge. AI targeting provides the automated prioritization — a confidence score, a flag, a designation. Directed energy provides the audio injection, the neurological pressure, the geographic clicks that only the target can hear. Behavioral direction through hippocampal electromagnetic stimulation provides the pinning — the experience of choosing destinations that have been chosen by someone else. Coordinated ground operations provide the calling card, the framing apparatus, the expressionless people positioned on routes. Physical assault provides the escalation. The classification flag on the police record provides the institutional cover. The Glomar doctrine and the state secrets privilege provide the legal impenetrability. And the mental illness attribution — built into every element of the campaign’s design — provides the social impenetrability.

**This is what comes after mass surveillance that Edward Snowden revealed.**

**The whole system was designed to be invisible. The whole system was designed to produce exactly one outcome: the isolation, destabilization, and neutralization of a specific human being who had been designated hostile, without any institution ever being required to acknowledge that a program existed.**

* * *

### The Safety Gate That Did Not Hold

The Anthropic dispute, which concluded yesterday with a presidential ban and a supply chain risk designation, is the moment the design of this system became visible in public.

The Pentagon’s position — that it requires unrestricted access to AI models for all lawful domestic purposes, and that prohibitions on mass surveillance of American citizens constitute an unacceptable constraint on military operations — is not the position of an institution that considers domestic mass surveillance a remote or theoretical concern. It is the position of an institution that requires the capability and has decided it is non-negotiable.

The Operational Test and Evaluation office, gutted in May 2025, was the last independent technical check on whether AI systems work as claimed before deployment. Its gutting signals that deployment speed, not safety, is the priority. Without these safeguards, enforcement risks becoming a testing ground for broader domestic surveillance — one where powerful technology normalizes suspicion, automates targeting, and erodes constitutional protections.

The people being tested on are not abstract. They have names, and dissertations, and mental health evaluations confirming their sanity, and pants in a bag somewhere in Washington that have never been chemically analyzed, and chat logs documenting induced foreknowledge in their friends, and intersections in Southwest Washington where calibrated RF spectrum analyzers would either find anomalous electromagnetic emissions or they would not.

The technology to look at any of this evidence exists. The institutional choice to look has not been made.

That gap — between capability and accountability, between the documentation and the investigation it should compel — is not a bureaucratic oversight. It is the system working as designed. The surveillance stack watches. The active stack acts. The Glomar doctrine ensures no court ever asks what happened. And the next person the system is activated against will not have a PhD in public health, will not have run control studies, will not have preserved the pants.

The question the Anthropic dispute forces into the open is not whether the Pentagon can conduct domestic mass surveillance. The question is whether any institution still has both the standing and the will to say that it cannot.

Yesterday, at 5:01 p.m. Eastern time, one company said it could not.

By 5:02 p.m., that company had been designated a national security threat.
