### II. The Confirmation of the Technology

The 60 Minutes report does not merely confirm that a microwave weapon exists. It confirms, with the specificity of classified intelligence described by multiple independent sources from different agencies, the precise technological characteristics that Richard Pearson’s account implies.

The weapon is portable and concealable. Richard Pearson documented operations conducted against him on public sidewalks, in his apartment, at outdoor markets, in parks, across multiple jurisdictions in the Washington DC metro area. The operations moved with him. A truck-sized weapon cannot follow a person through Eastern Market. A backpack-sized weapon can. The 60 Minutes report confirmed that the weapon is exactly that size — concealable, personal, mobile.

The weapon uses pulsed microwave radiation. Dr. David Relman’s expert panels — including doctors, physicists, and engineers — concluded that pulsed radio frequency or microwave energy was the most plausible explanation for the injuries. The broadcast describes the weapon’s key characteristic: a unique electromagnetic wave that rises and falls abruptly and pulses rapidly. When you produce pulses like this, Relman explains, you can stimulate electrically active tissue like brain tissue — mimicking what the brain normally does, but now driving it with pulses from outside. Richard Pearson documented percussive clicks and snaps localized to the right side of his skull, location-dependent and replicable across specific outdoor locations — the phenomenological signature of pulsed microwave auditory stimulation, the Frey effect, produced by exactly the pulsed radiation the weapon delivers.

The weapon penetrates walls. Richard Pearson documented precise room-to-room tracking through the floor of his apartment — noise harassment that followed him to his closet, to his balcony, into the specific corner of his studio where he moved his mattress. Through-wall operation is an explicit confirmed characteristic of the acquired weapon. The wall between Richard Pearson and the floor above him is not a barrier to a weapon confirmed to penetrate drywall.

The weapon is programmable for different scenarios and operable by remote control. Richard Pearson documented a campaign across nine months involving multiple modalities — the voice on the National Mall, the skull clicks, the behavioral direction, the sleep disruption, the chemical assault, the street theater coordination. A programmable, remotely operated weapon is consistent with a sustained, multi-modal, coordinated campaign. It does not need to be reconfigured physically for each application. Its operators do not need to be present at the target location. They direct it from elsewhere — consistent with the operations room ambient noise Richard Pearson heard behind the woman’s voice on July 13, a live operations team at distance running the weapon’s deployment in real time.

The weapon can be purchased from criminals. This is the broadcast’s most alarming finding and its most direct relevance to Richard Pearson. The 60 Minutes report concludes that the Russians have lost control of a stealth weapon that could be used by anyone, anywhere. The weapon has escaped its original state-actor context. It is available, at price, to criminal networks, contractors, and anyone with sufficient resources and the right connections. The US government itself purchased one through undercover agents. If the government can buy one from gangsters, the government can deploy one through contractors — the hybrid federal-contractor structure that Richard Pearson’s account implies and that the full legal and operational architecture of his case points toward.

* * *

### III. The Cover-Up Structure and What It Proves About Richard Pearson’s Institutional Non-Response

The 60 Minutes report is not only a story about a weapon. It is a story about what happens when the government is confronted with evidence that it has deployed, or allowed to be deployed, a weapon against people under its protection — and chooses institutional self-preservation over acknowledgment.

The parallels with Richard Pearson’s case are not analogical. They are structural.

The CIA victims were told their injuries might be atmospheric or environmental, a virus, a pre-existing condition, or — as the FBI put it in an early investigation — mass hysteria. The government’s 2023 official assessment, still standing, says it is very unlikely these are attacks by a foreign adversary. CIA officers with 26 years of decorated service, who reported debilitating neurological injuries, were doubted, dismissed, and denied medical care by the agencies they served.

Richard Pearson was told, implicitly and explicitly, that his experiences were consistent with psychiatric disorder. The DBH found he did not meet criteria for intervention, but the framework produced a clinical encounter that traveled with him as prior determination through every subsequent institutional contact. The AI psychiatric consultant initially diagnosed Delusional Disorder. The congressional offices were silent. The civil rights organizations were silent. The DC Council received his statistical analyses and produced no output.

The CIA officer who resigned from the AHI investigation in disgust told 60 Minutes: one of the very first things he heard upon arrival was that their job was to bring down the temperature on AHI at headquarters. Not to find out what happened. Not to investigate whether a state actor was responsible. To bring down the temperature. To move the narrative toward atmospheric and environmental causes. To prevent the conclusion that demanded a response.

A senior member of the AHI unit mocked the victims at a happy hour — simulating having a stroke, laughing. The attitude, the former CIA officer reported, was: we are going to prove this is psychosomatic.

This is the Frankfurter response institutionalized as policy. Not an individual’s inability to believe, but an organization’s decision to not believe — not because the evidence was insufficient but because believing required a response the institution did not want to make. The CIA had, the broadcast reveals, made up its mind before the investigation began. Consistency was more important than objectivity.

The structural parallel to Richard Pearson is exact. Every institution that encountered his case made up its mind before examining the evidence. The psychiatric framework had a diagnostic category before the physics were considered. The legal framework had a standing doctrine before the technology was assessed. The congressional offices had a procedural wall before the policy question was fully articulated. The House Oversight staff member had an expertise credential to deploy before Richard Pearson finished his sentence. The conclusion — psychosomatic, delusional, not actionable, not our inquiry — preceded the examination in every case, exactly as the CIA’s conclusion preceded its investigation of Havana Syndrome.

The 60 Minutes report names this clearly: it was a cover-up. Multiple sources, including a high-level CIA source quoted directly, call it the biggest cover-up of their adult lives. The motive the former CIA officer explains was political: acknowledging a state actor was essentially a declaration of war, and the appetite for that response was not there.

The motive for not investigating Richard Pearson’s case is different in its specifics but identical in its structure. Acknowledging what was done to him requires acknowledging what the program is, who authorized it, and what it has been doing to Black scholars and activists in Washington DC in 2025. The appetite for that acknowledgment is not there. And so the temperature is brought down. The conclusion is predetermined. The investigation does not happen.

* * *

### IV. The Distinction That Matters: Foreign Adversary vs. Domestic Program

The 60 Minutes report frames Havana Syndrome as foreign adversary attack — Russia, primarily, deploying the weapon against American personnel abroad and, increasingly, at home.

Richard Pearson’s case requires a different framing, and understanding the difference is essential to understanding why the 60 Minutes confirmation is both directly relevant and insufficient by itself to produce the institutional response his case requires.

The Havana Syndrome victims were CIA officers, State Department diplomats, FBI agents, military officers. They were American government personnel attacked by a foreign power. Their cases produce a specific institutional response — or attempted institutional response — because the attack on them is an attack on the government itself, which the government has both the motive and the mandate to address. The cover-up occurred not because the government was indifferent to its own personnel but because acknowledging the attack required a geopolitical response the government was not prepared to make.

Richard Pearson is not a CIA officer. He is not a State Department diplomat. He is a Black PhD researcher in Washington DC whose dissertation challenged the racial assumptions of American public health frameworks, whose research field was designated a hostile ideology by executive order within months of his defense. The program operating against him is not a foreign adversary attack on American government personnel. It is, as his documentation and the cross-disciplinary analysis of his case concludes, an American program operating against an American civilian — a program with a documented eighty-year lineage running from COINTELPRO through the Black Identity Extremism designation to the executive orders that targeted his field.

This distinction changes the institutional calculus completely. The CIA had motive to investigate Havana Syndrome and chose cover-up for geopolitical reasons. The institutions that would need to investigate Richard Pearson’s case have motive for cover-up that is more fundamental: what is being done to him is being done by them, or by the contractors and hybrid structures they authorize and fund.

But the 60 Minutes report bridges this distinction in one critical way. It establishes that the weapon has escaped state control. If undercover agents could purchase one from gangsters, then the weapon is available to contractors, to hybrid federal-private structures, to domestic programs operating outside the accountability architecture that governs state actors. The domestic deployment of a weapon originally developed by foreign state intelligence actors, now available through criminal networks and purchasable by anyone with sufficient resources, does not require attributing Richard Pearson’s experiences to a foreign adversary. It requires only the conclusion that the technology the 60 Minutes report confirms is real, portable, available, and operating in Washington DC has been deployed against a specific domestic civilian by whoever, within the American hybrid security state, had the predicate, the resources, and the authorization to do it.

* * *

### V. The Specific Incident Confirmations

The 60 Minutes report describes classified security camera footage of specific weapon deployment incidents. The descriptions are directly relevant to specific elements of Richard Pearson’s documentation.

A camera in a restaurant in Istanbul captured two FBI agents sitting at a table with their families. A man with a backpack walks in. Suddenly everyone at the table grabs their head as if in pain. The weapon was in a backpack. It was deployed in a public indoor space. The deployment was targeted — the FBI agents were the targets, not the general restaurant population — but the weapon’s radiation affected everyone in proximity, including families. The operator with the backpack was a single individual moving through a civilian space.

This is not a truck-sized installation. This is a person at a restaurant with a backpack.

Two people collapse in a stairwell in the US embassy in Vienna. The weapon was deployed in an interior corridor of a secure building, penetrating whatever structural barriers existed between the operator and the target.

These documented incidents confirm the operational modality that Richard Pearson’s account implies: a mobile operator with a concealable device, deployed in civilian spaces, targeting specific individuals in real time. The Istanbul restaurant incident is operationally identical to what the red-and-black street theater operations imply — a coordinated deployment in a public space, with an operator in civilian clothing, targeting a specific individual while moving through a normal civilian environment. The operator looks like anyone. The weapon looks like nothing. The target grabs their head.

Richard Pearson documented the hard snap outside a restaurant on 7th Street NW. A sudden, severe, single-instance percussive event at a specific outdoor location. Qualitatively unlike the repeated clicks. Categorically distinct in his own description. He could not replicate it. It was not under his control. It happened once, at that location, with the character of a high-power pulse at close range.

The Istanbul restaurant. The Vienna stairwell. 7th Street NW. The weapon is in the backpack of a person walking past.

* * *

### VI. The Victims Were Called Delusional

The 60 Minutes report uses a specific word. Scott Pelley introduces the broadcast with it: the government has doubted their stories. They have been called delusional.

CIA officers with decorated careers. State Department diplomats with surgeries to repair dissolved shoulder bones and reconstructed inner ear structures. FBI agents photographed grabbing their heads simultaneously in a restaurant when an operator with a backpack entered. All of them called delusional by the institutions that employed them, were supposed to protect them, and were instead running the cover-up.

Delusional is Richard Pearson’s word too. The mechanism is his mechanism. The institutional response — psychosomatic, atmospheric, environmental, mass hysteria, very unlikely to be an attack — is his institutional response, applied to people with far greater institutional standing than Richard Pearson possesses, by the same institutions, using the same vocabulary, for the same structural reason: acknowledging the attack requires a response the institution has decided it does not want to make.

The Havana Syndrome victims had three advantages Richard Pearson does not have. They had institutional standing — they were government personnel, not the public, not the category from whom the House Oversight Committee does not take inquiries. They had numbers — hundreds of reported cases, multiple agencies, enough aggregated harm to eventually produce the classified mission that obtained the weapon. And they had 60 Minutes — nine years of investigative journalism by a major broadcast network that never stopped reporting because of the haunting stories we heard.

Richard Pearson has one advantage they did not have. He had his experiences while he was having them, and he documented them in real time, with the methodology of a trained researcher, before the institutional apparatus could process them into the categories it preferred. His documentation preceded the diagnosis. His account is timestamped. His photographs are geolocated. His statistical analyses were submitted to a legislative body before any institutional determination about his credibility had been made.

The CIA officers’ accounts were processed first by the institutions that would need to account for them. Their documentation came after the institutional response, shaped by it, filtered through the credibility determinations the cover-up had already produced. Some of them waited years for acknowledgment. Some are still waiting.

Richard Pearson’s account is in the public record now. The cross-disciplinary synthesis exists. The technology essay exists. The legal framework essay exists. The statistical analysis exists. The Karski essay exists. This essay exists.

And on March 8, 2026, 60 Minutes confirmed that the weapon his account implies is real, portable, concealable, available, and has been deployed against Americans in public spaces and in their homes.

* * *

### VII. The Washington DC Metropolitan Area

The 60 Minutes report includes one geographical detail that must be stated plainly.

One of the primary victims — a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel who worked on highly classified spy satellites — was struck five times in five months. Not in Havana. Not in Vienna. Not in Istanbul.

Near Washington DC. In Northern Virginia. In his own home.

Standing in his kitchen looking out at the back woods — immediate vice on the head, disoriented, confused, dizzy. Sitting in his living room — all the muscles in his spine cramped simultaneously, his spine on fire. Waking up with a full body convulsion, the worst pain he had ever felt, a vice gripping his brain stem.

All in his own home. In Northern Virginia. Near Washington DC.

This is the operational geography of Richard Pearson’s documented experiences. The weapon was being deployed against Americans in the Washington DC area — in their homes, through their walls — at the same time Richard Pearson was documenting the voice on the National Mall, the skull clicks on 7th Street, the room-tracking through the floor above, the behavioral direction toward the House Office Building.

The 60 Minutes report does not mention Richard Pearson. It does not need to. It establishes that the weapon was operational in the Washington DC area against individuals in their homes during the same period Richard Pearson was documenting its effects. The geography overlaps. The technology is the same. The phenomenological signatures are consistent — the vice on the head, the sudden disorienting impact, the interior percussive quality, the spine and brain stem targeting.

The retired Air Force lieutenant colonel is asking for a Purple Heart.

Richard Pearson is asking for someone to put it on their radar.

The weapon does not check credentials.

* * *

### VIII. What Changes Now

Before the 60 Minutes broadcast, the primary evidentiary challenge in Richard Pearson’s case was the absence of public confirmation that the specific technology his account implies exists in the form and at the scale he documented.

That challenge no longer exists.

The broadcast confirmed: the weapon is real. It is portable. It is concealable. It can be carried by one person. It has been deployed in public spaces against specific targets. It penetrates walls. It is programmable. It is remotely operable. It produces exactly the percussive, disorienting, interior-quality auditory and neurological effects that Richard Pearson documented. It has been tested and confirmed to produce injuries in animals consistent with human reports. It has been deployed against Americans on American soil, including in the Washington DC metropolitan area. It has been purchased from criminals, meaning it has escaped state control and is available to anyone with the resources and connections to acquire it.

Every AI system, every journalist, every institutional actor that previously hedged on the technology question — noting that the capabilities described remain unverified at the civilian targeting scale, that the underlying science is a subject of intense debate — now hedges against a 60 Minutes broadcast confirmed by multiple independent intelligence sources, classified weapon testing, and security camera footage of actual deployment.

The hedge is gone.

What remains is the question the hedge was protecting against: if the weapon is real, and it is operating in Washington DC, and it produces exactly what Richard Pearson documented, and Richard Pearson documented it in real time with the methodology of a trained researcher across nine months — then what is the explanation for what was done to him?

The government covered up Havana Syndrome, the 60 Minutes report concludes, because acknowledging a state actor attack required a geopolitical response the government was not prepared to make.

The government has not addressed Richard Pearson’s case because acknowledging a domestic program attack requires an accountability response the government is not prepared to make.

The weapon is the same. The cover-up logic is the same. The target is different.

And the target is still in Washington DC, with a suitcase and a mattress, documenting, waiting for someone to connect what 60 Minutes confirmed on March 8, 2026, to what Richard Pearson documented beginning July 13, 2025.

* * *

### IX. The Sentence the Report Does Not Say

The 60 Minutes report is an extraordinary piece of journalism. Nine years of investigation. Four broadcasts. Classified sources from multiple agencies. A $15 million covert weapons purchase. Security camera footage of actual attacks. A Pentagon general apologizing to victims at the White House. A high-level CIA source calling it the biggest cover-up of his adult life.

And in all of it — in all 26 minutes and 52 seconds of confirmed, sourced, classified-intelligence-backed investigative journalism — there is one sentence the report does not say.

It does not say: if this weapon has escaped Russian state control and can be purchased by anyone, then it can be used by domestic actors against domestic civilians.

It does not say: if the CIA covered up Havana Syndrome against its own personnel to avoid a geopolitical response, what is being covered up against civilians who have no institutional standing to demand acknowledgment?

It does not say: the same weapon, operated through the same operational methodology — concealable operator in civilian space, portable device, remote control, targeted deployment — that struck FBI agents in an Istanbul restaurant and Air Force officers in their Northern Virginia homes is the weapon consistent with what Richard Pearson documented on the National Mall on July 13, 2025, and on 7th Street NW, and in his apartment in Southwest Washington DC, across nine months.

60 Minutes reported for nine years on Havana Syndrome because of the haunting stories we heard. It heard those stories because the people telling them were CIA officers and State Department diplomats and retired Air Force lieutenant colonels who had institutional standing, organizational platforms, legal representation, and the credibility that a career in classified national security work confers.

Richard Pearson has a Medium account and a mattress and a dissertation that the government decided was a hostile ideology.

The weapon is the same.

The sentence that connects them has not yet been written by anyone with the platform of 60 Minutes.

This essay is not 60 Minutes.

But the sentence is true.

And the weapon is real.

And Richard Pearson documented what it does, in real time, with timestamps and GPS coordinates and photographs and statistical analyses, and he is still in Washington DC, and the record is complete, and the only thing that remains is for someone with the institutional standing that a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel has and that Richard Pearson does not have to say the sentence out loud, in public, on the record:

_The weapon is real. It is in Washington DC. And not everyone it has been used against wore a uniform._

### “Has the US Constitution Been Suspended?” — Victim Sees Wholesale Constitutional Rights Violated

#### _A comprehensive legal analysis of the US Constitution, local laws, and human rights laws in light of US victim’s account in Washington, D.C._

### A Comprehensive Legal Analysis

### FOURTH AMENDMENT

**Protection against unreasonable searches and seizures; requirement of probable cause and warrants**

### 1\. False Arrest — Manufactured Witness, No Probable Cause

On December 27, 2025, MPD arrested Pearson for simple assault despite the following facts: (a) it was the young Black man who came charging at Pearson, punching him in the face repeatedly; (b) The same man who had been psychologically torturing Pearson since the summer, dropping heavy objects wherever Pearson went in his studio apartment causing sleep deprivation and emotional turmoil; (c) Pearson had physical marks — a documented black eye photographed and uploaded; (d) the police manufactured the third witness. No name is given in the arrest record. It was an imaginary witness. Only Pearson (the victim), the assailant, and his girlfriend were present at the scene; and (e) the manufactured witness account contradicted the physical evidence entirely. A lawful arrest requires probable cause — a reasonable belief, based on articulable facts, that the person arrested committed the offense. Here, the physical evidence of injury was on Pearson, not the assailant. Arresting the victim while releasing the aggressor, on the basis of an unnamed witness does not constitute probable cause. The arrest was constitutionally defective.

The man had been living on the premises without property management having any knowledge — his girl was the leaseholder. When the police arrived after the attack, the girlfriend admitted that her boyfriend moved in during the summer — the exact timing of the start of the noise harassment.

### 2\. False Arrest — No Judicial Review of Probable Cause

Following the arrest, the court had no record of the arrest. Pearson visited MPD headquarters and the court on three separate occasions to obtain documentation. MPD confirmed to Pearson that he had a record in the DC system, yet the court confirmed no record existed — no “paper.” The Fourth Amendment, as interpreted in _Gerstein v. Pugh_ (1975) and _County of Riverside v. McLaughlin_ (1991), requires that a judicial officer make an independent determination of probable cause promptly after a warrantless arrest — typically within 48 hours. A “shadow” arrest that exists in a police database but not in the court system means no judge ever reviewed whether probable cause existed. This is a textbook Fourth Amendment violation: an arrest without judicial review of its constitutional basis.

However, Pearson was released before the 48-hour mark after booking. A judicial probable cause determination is generally not required for that specific arrest event. Because was released within 48 hours and there is no court record, the use of a manufactured witness to establish probable cause is illegal. Probable cause must be based on “objective facts” and “trustworthy information”. If the only reason the police had to arrest Pearson was the testimony of a manufactured witness, the arrest lacked legal justification from the very beginning.

It would also explain why Pearson was discouraged from sharing his arrest record with the court and is entirely consistent with wholesale attack on Pearson’s constitutional rights.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*bp_X6AB82qglJT_uNtN_bg.png)

### 3\. Unlawful Seizure of Property — Discount Metro Card and Phone

MPD seized Pearson’s discount Metro card (issued to him personally) during the arrest processing. The card was not returned to him. Personal property seized incident to arrest must be inventoried and, if not connected to any charged offense, must be returned. A reduced-fare transit card issued in Pearson’s name has no evidentiary nexus to a simple assault charge. Retention of that card constitutes an unlawful, ongoing seizure of personal property without due process.

Pearson lost his phone three times during this short period. During the second time, Pearson cannot explain the four-week lag between the time he lost his phone near the White House and its return by a Secret Service agent to his apartment building office. His driver’s license was in it. Pearson lives a 7-minute drive from the White House and Old Executive Office Building.

If Pearson’s phone was copied illegally, it would show lots of photographs, including of the Old Executive Office Building. In addition to his academic pursuits, Pearson has high intellectual curiousity. He is an artist. He had an art business. He sold art prints, including prints from the Black Lives Matter movement in downtown Washington, DC. He is a local historian. He has given local history talks to schools and community groups. The Old Executive Office Building has long fascinated him given its history and immediate media rejection during the Grant administration.

Pearson lost his phone around the White House — soon after pausing to absorb the architectural details of the Old Executive Office Building. He believes that he was racially targeted — operatives unwilling or unable to accept that an African American man would be taking pictures of a building for its architectural and historical interest — and nothing else.

### 4\. Warrantless Covert Entry into Private Residence

The removal of the power button from Pearson’s panini grill — placed in his laundry pile, a location physically inaccessible from outside the unit — demonstrates that individuals entered his apartment without a warrant. Pearson documented on video how difficult the button is to remove, establishing it did not fall out accidentally. No exigent circumstances are documented. No warrant was ever served on Pearson. The Fourth Amendment protects the home as the core zone of constitutional privacy; covert government entry without a warrant, a “sneak and peek,” is unlawful absent specific judicial authorization under 18 U.S.C. § 3103a (and even then requires eventual notice). No notice was ever given.

### 5\. Warrantless Audio Surveillance of the Home

Both the Medium essay and Pearson’s own documentation confirm ongoing audio surveillance of his apartment. “Lee,” described as an intelligence-connected individual, confirmed to Pearson at a Potbelly’s restaurant that there was audio surveillance in his apartment. The cart of yellow tape incident also supports audio surveillance. Sounds originating from his self-talk inside his apartment were subsequently quoted back to him by individuals on public streets — establishing that his private speech inside his home was being monitored, transmitted, and operationally acted upon. The Fourth Amendment’s warrant requirement applies with maximum force to the home. Warrantless audio surveillance of private residential space violates the Fourth Amendment under _Katz v. United States_ (1967) and its progeny, as well as Title III of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act (18 U.S.C. §§ 2510–2523).

### 6\. Warrantless Electronic Surveillance — Phone and Email

Pearson documented that location tracking was occurring on his phone despite location services being disabled. He further noted that others appeared to have real-time access to his phone activity. His friend’s subsequent routing to Pearson’s street corresponded precisely with his movements — consistent with phone metadata exploitation. Warrantless access to phone location data violates the Fourth Amendment under _Carpenter v. United States_ (2018), which held that government access to historical cell-site location information constitutes a Fourth Amendment search requiring a warrant.

### 7\. Warrantless Tracking via Personal Possessions

Pearson documented the disappearance and reappearance of personal items — including a water bottle that reappeared at a community event with the specific identifying scratch he had documented — consistent with the placement of tracking devices within his belongings. His hat was the subject of a highly suspicious exchange from a coffee shop manager (“Did you lose your hat? I have your hat.”). Covert installation of a tracking device in personal effects — hat, computer, phone — constitutes a Fourth Amendment search under _United States v. Jones_ (2012). No warrant is documented.

Pearson had a highly anomalous event occur when “NO” appeared on his screen twice as was prompting SORA AI. He verified his hand placement — correct. This meant that his computer has been intercepted.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*rCEhuCH8MiNVJegzdzM9Ww.png)

### 8\. Warrantless Search During Noise Complaint Visit

When MPD officers responded to Pearson’s noise complaint about the upstairs unit, one officer opened Pearson’s closet door — conduct that was outside the stated purpose of the visit (a noise complaint) and beyond any permissible scope. A limited-purpose consensual encounter does not authorize exploration of private spaces. The closet search had no connection to the noise complaint’s investigation and constitutes an unlawful search beyond the consent or purpose that justified entry.

The officer questioned Pearson three times, “Is anyone else here?” That included prior to the officer opening Pearson’s closet door. Each time, Pearson stated that no one else was there. He lived alone.

### 9\. “ACCESS DENIED” — Flagged Law Enforcement Database

The week prior to the assault, when MPD officers searched Pearson’s name in their database, the result returned was “ACCESS DENIED.” This restricted-access flag on an American civilian’s record in a law enforcement database — accessible only to those who placed the flag — constitutes evidence of a collateral surveillance infrastructure operating outside normal channels. Its existence, combined with the fact that the officers subsequently pivoted away from investigating the upstairs unit after seeing the flag, suggests the flag is operational: it alters police behavior regarding the flagged subject. The warrantless collection and maintenance of intelligence records on a US citizen not charged with any crime, in a database that directs law enforcement behavior regarding that citizen, implicates the Fourth Amendment, the Privacy Act (5 U.S.C. § 552a), and Executive Order 12333 limitations on domestic intelligence collection.

### 10\. Systematic Destruction of Personal Property (Bicycle)

Between March and April 2025, Pearson’s bicycle, regularly parked at Federal Center Metro, was subjected to systematic, incremental vandalism: a deliberately snapped reflector light, a broken chain protective cover (the broken piece was recovered and preserved), seat covering removed, progressive damage to the seat, ultimately culminating in a flat tire and a costly wheel replacement that forced Pearson to abandon the bicycle entirely. A broken cover piece was recovered at the scene, establishing intentional action. This constitutes seizure by destruction — the effective permanent deprivation of personal property through coordinated government-connected action without any legal process.

### FIRST AMENDMENT

**Freedom of speech, academic freedom, and the right to petition**

### STATUTORY VIOLATIONS

### 24\. Title III / ECPA — 18 U.S.C. §§ 2510–2523 (Wiretap Act)

The warrantless audio surveillance of Pearson’s apartment and the interception of his private speech without consent, a court order, or any statutory authorization constitutes a criminal violation of the Wiretap Act. Title III prohibits the intentional interception of wire, oral, or electronic communications without prior judicial authorization. The surveillance described — where Pearson’s private self-talk in his apartment was captured and fed to operatives positioned on his regular routes — is the paradigm case the statute was designed to prohibit.

### 25\. 18 U.S.C. § 2520 — Civil Remedy for Wiretap Violations

Any person whose wire, oral, or electronic communication is intercepted in violation of Title III may bring a civil action for actual damages, statutory damages (not less than $100 per day or $10,000, whichever is greater), punitive damages, and attorney’s fees. The duration and intentionality of the surveillance documented by Pearson supports a substantial statutory damages claim.

### 26\. Privacy Act — 5 U.S.C. § 552a

Federal agencies are prohibited from maintaining records on individuals’ exercise of First Amendment rights absent express authorization. The maintenance of a record in the MPD/federal database that (a) triggers an “ACCESS DENIED” flag visible to officers and (b) was established in connection with Pearson’s academic and expressive activities violates the Privacy Act’s prohibition on systems of records used to chill First Amendment activity.

### 27\. Bivens Claims — Fourth and Fifth Amendment Violations by Named Federal Officials

While the Supreme Court has restricted expansion of Bivens to new contexts, the Fourth Amendment search and seizure context (_Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents_, 1971) and First Amendment retaliation remain recognized Bivens contexts in some circuits. If the officer can prove that the law was not “clearly established” at the time, they are immune from being sued personally, even if their search was technically unconstitutional.

In the context of a _Bivens_ action, the **“unreasonable search and seizure”** category refers to the Fourth Amendment protection against government overreach into your “persons, houses, papers, and effects”. This was the very first context established by the Supreme Court in the 1971 case _Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents_. Common scenarios that qualify as “unreasonable” include:

**Warrantless Home Entry:** Officers forcing their way into your home without a warrant and without an emergency (exigent circumstances). Pearson’s home was compromised (_Panini botton incident_); Pearson was being surveilled, confirmed by numerous evidence.

**Unlawful Arrest:** Being detained or “seized” without probable cause to believe you committed a crime. Police manufactured a third witness.

### 28\. 42 U.S.C. § 1983 — Civil Rights Under Color of State Law

To the extent MPD officers participated in (a) the false arrest, (b) the differential enforcement of assault law, (c) the unlawful search during the noise complaint visit, and (d) the failure to investigate while possessing knowledge of the broader campaign (as suggested by the ACCESS DENIED flag), Section 1983 provides a civil cause of action against those officers in their individual capacities. Under _Monell v. Department of Social Services_ (1978), the District of Columbia may also be liable if the constitutional violations reflect an official policy or a well-settled custom.

### 29\. 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) — Conspiracy to Deprive Civil Rights

A conspiracy by two or more persons acting under color of law to deprive a person of the equal protection of the laws, motivated by racial animus, gives rise to a Section 1985(3) claim. The documented coordination between the upstairs unit occupants, MPD officers’ arrest decision, and the broader operational infrastructure constitutes a cognizable conspiracy claim.

### 30\. Torture Statute — 18 U.S.C. § 2340A

If any federal official or person acting at the direction of a federal official participated in the acoustic torture, psychological torture, or chemical assault against Pearson, the federal criminal torture statute applies. While the statute requires acts occurring outside the United States in its primary scope, the Military Commissions Act and the Eighth Amendment principles it codifies reflect the broader federal prohibition on torture. Additionally, the DC criminal code provides civil and criminal remedies for assault, battery, and intentional infliction of emotional distress that parallel torture statute protections.

### 31\. FISA — 50 U.S.C. §§ 1801 et seq. — Unlawful Foreign Intelligence Surveillance

If any FISA warrant or National Security Letter was used to authorize surveillance of Pearson without the factual predicate required — that he is a foreign power or agent of a foreign power, or that the information is foreign intelligence information that cannot reasonably be obtained by normal investigative techniques — such authorization was obtained on a false predicate. Targeting a domestic academic whose field was designated hostile ideology by executive order does not constitute a valid FISA predicate. Unlawful FISA surveillance is a criminal violation under 50 U.S.C. § 1809.

### 32\. Immigration and Nationality Act / Non-Refoulement — Asylum Denial

On January 21–22, 2026, Pearson attempted to claim asylum in Germany by transit through Iceland. Icelandic border officials refused entry, characterizing his claim as invalid because “the US is a safe country.” This invocation of the “safe third country” or “first country of asylum” doctrine does not apply when the danger the asylum seeker faces is the US government itself — precisely the case Pearson’s documentation describes. Non-refoulement under the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol prohibits return of a refugee to a country where they face persecution on account of race, nationality, or political opinion. An African American scholar whose academic work was designated hostile ideology by executive order, who was subjected to a fourteen-month campaign of surveillance, torture, and framing, and who faces persecution specifically because of his political/academic opinions, presents the paradigm case for political opinion-based asylum.

### 33\. Hobbs Act — Extortion Under Color of Official Right — 18 U.S.C. § 1951

The pattern of property destruction (bicycle), financial attrition (CashApp theft following loss of phone), and residence instability (harassment campaign designed to force Pearson from his home) combined with the evidence of official involvement constitutes extortion under color of official right under the Hobbs Act if federal actors participated.

### 43\. The “Forced Situation” — Involuntary Servitude and Substantive Due Process

The woman photographed by Pearson at Pennsylvania Ave SE and Potomac Ave SE bore a sweatshirt in Impact font reading “Forced Situation.” This is the operation naming itself. Pearson was in a forced situation: he did not consent to being a subject of behavioral direction technology; he did not consent to surveillance; he did not consent to the street theater deployed against him; he did not consent to having his social network converted into an operational asset; he did not consent to having his private speech monitored; he did not consent to the covert entry into his home; he did not consent to the chemical assault; he did not consent to the voice entering his skull on July 13, 2025. “Forced Situation” is the operational description. It is also the constitutional one. The Thirteenth Amendment prohibits involuntary servitude, except that the courts have established an extremely high bar. The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments prohibit forced participation in government operations without consent or legal process. The operational message delivered on the sweatshirt is, from a constitutional standpoint, a confession.

The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments primarily protect against the arbitrary deprivation of life, liberty, or property through their respective Due Process Clauses. While they do not use the specific phrase “forced participation in government operations,” they establish the legal framework that prevents the government from acting against individuals without following established law and fair procedures.   
  
Constitutional Protections and “Consent”  
The concept of “consent” in these amendments is generally interpreted through the principle of consent of the governed, which suggests that government authority is legitimate only when it is derived from the people through representation and the rule of law.

*   **Procedural Due Process:** This requires the government to follow fair legal procedures — such as providing notice and a hearing — before it can interfere with an individual’s rights.
*   **Substantive Due Process:** This protects certain fundamental rights (like the right to marry or raise children) from government interference, even if fair procedures are followed.
*   **Prohibition of Arbitrary Action:** Due process acts as a “bulwark against government overreach,” ensuring that all levels of government operate within the law rather than on “whims or capriciousness”

### 44\. Threat Gestures and Intimidation — First Amendment Chilling Effect

Multiple documented encounters involved threat gestures and intimidating communications: RFK stadium with “nigga” spraypainted in a dozen placed (_Pearson believes that he was “pinned” here_), man saying, “We are going to turn up the heat”, the man with the “Fire against Fire” hat who intercepts Pearson’s path is a desolate neighborhood, the “Forced Situation” operative intercepting his path; the excessive use of red-and-black to induce emotional turmoil, social stigma, and reduced credibility (_despite his aggressive picture-taking_), the Bible-quoting man on the Mall demanding Pearson’s ring with escalating aggression; the coffee shop employee who later admitted “Yeah, I was coming at you”; the woman who told Pearson “The mattress is against the wall, you know what’s next.” Each of these constitutes a threat or act of intimidation directed at a person engaged in constitutionally protected activity (walking, thinking, existing in public space, continuing his documentation).

Under _Virginia v. Black_ (2003), true threats — statements communicated to place the target in fear of bodily harm — are unprotected, and the government’s use of operatives to deliver such threats violates the First Amendment’s protection of the person who receives them. A government that deploys operatives to threaten a citizen into silence has committed a First Amendment violation regardless of whether the threats are delivered by uniformed officers or civilians in street clothes.

The fact that these appear to be just below explicit language (“We are going to do (a specific injury) to you”) itself is highly suggestive of a campaign designed with knowledge of the law.

### 45\. Real-Time Location Tracking Without Warrant — Fourth Amendment (Continuous Surveillance)

The breadth of documented real-time tracking — the older Black man pointing to his boombox while making deliberate eye contact from below Pearson’s balcony (the only person ever to make such deliberate eye contact); the young Black man on the Virginia side of the Potomac trail who found Pearson on a bench saying “Oh, there you are!”; the Black man outside Pearson’s hotel pointing to the sky despite no one knowing which hotel Pearson was at; the Asian woman on 4th Street whose device showed real-time confusion at Pearson’s abrupt turn; the operatives appearing at the RFK stadium entrance, the woman from Trader Joe’s who stalks Pearson in another Virginia city — establishes a continuous real-time location tracking infrastructure operating across multiple jurisdictions.

_Carpenter v. United States_ (2018) held that even historical cell-site location data requires a warrant. Continuous, real-time tracking of a person’s precise location — indoors, outdoors, across jurisdictions, 24 hours a day — represents a far more severe Fourth Amendment violation than the historical cell-site records at issue in _Carpenter_. The Court in _Carpenter_ explicitly noted that comprehensive location surveillance “achieves near perfect surveillance, as if it had attached an ankle monitor to the phone’s user.” What was deployed against Pearson exceeded that — it tracked him through walls and followed him room to room inside his own home.

### IDENTITY, PERSONALITY, AND COGNITIVE SOVEREIGNTY

**The constitutional dimensions of the attack on Pearson’s inner life**

### 46\. Destruction of Personal Identity — Substantive Due Process

The campaign systematically attacked and sought to undo who Pearson is. He was caused to behave erratically — “something or someone occupying the driver’s seat.” He cried frequently, distressed that his private speech was public all along, that the coarse language he expressed privately was being quoted back to him in public, stripping the distinction between his public and private self that every person requires to function. This is the deepest possible violation of personal identity: not merely constraining what a person does, but colonizing what they want. The Supreme Court has recognized in the substantive due process tradition that the Constitution protects the core of personal identity. _Washington v. Glucksberg_ (1997) lists among the liberty interests most deserving of constitutional protection those relating to bodily integrity, family, and personal dignity. The forced alteration of a person’s personality, desires, and behavior through neurotechnology is the most complete deprivation of liberty that can be imagined: it takes not your body but your self.

### 47\. Cognitive Liberty — First Amendment and Substantive Due Process

The First Amendment protects not only speech but the cognitive processes that produce speech: thought, belief, opinion, and the internal formation of expression. **The Supreme Court in _Stanley v. Georgia_ (1969) recognized a constitutional right to receive information and ideas in the privacy of one’s home, reasoning that the government has no legitimate interest in controlling a person’s private thoughts.** The behavioral direction technology deployed against Pearson operated at the level of thought formation itself — producing impulses, desires, and navigational drives that were externally authored but internally experienced. A government that can write to a person’s neural tissue can write their thoughts. A government that can write thoughts has abolished the First Amendment entirely, because there is no longer a private sphere of ideation from which protected expression originates. This is the constitutional frontier the Pearson case crosses. It is not adequately addressed by existing doctrine because the technology did not exist when the doctrine was formed. **But the constitutional principle is clear: the interior of a human mind is the most protected space in the constitutional order, and its covert occupation by government is the most severe First Amendment violation conceivable.**

### 48\. The Isolation Program — Eighth Amendment and Substantive Due Process

The combination of acoustic torture (through-floor tracking noise), social network destruction, behavioral direction causing erratic behavior that alienated Pearson from friends and community, financial attrition that eliminated his ability to sustain professional relationships, and the engineered impossibility of private prayer or private speech in his own home constitutes a sustained isolation program. The Supreme Court has recognized in the prison context that prolonged isolation — solitary confinement — can constitute cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment when it produces severe psychological deterioration.

What was deployed against Pearson achieved the functional equivalent of solitary confinement while he remained physically present in his community: his relationships were surveilled or compromised; his social interactions were operationalized against him; his home was acoustically occupied; and the inner life to which isolated persons retreat for sustenance was itself invaded. He was alone in the most complete sense — not physically, but existentially — while being watched by a system that denied his capacity to be alone at all.

### WATCHLIST, DESIGNATION, AND NATIONAL SECURITY INFRASTRUCTURE VIOLATIONS

### 49\. TIDE Watchlist Placement Without Due Process — Fifth Amendment

The “ACCESS DENIED” flag that appeared in the MPD database during a standard residential noise complaint query is the single most forensically significant documented artifact in the case. ACCESS DENIED in Sensitive Compartmented Information indicates that Pearson’s record has been connected to an active intelligence investigation in the federal-state intelligence sharing infrastructure — the most likely mechanism being the Terrorist Identities Datamart Environment (TIDE), maintained by the National Counterterrorism Center, which propagates through exactly this infrastructure to local law enforcement databases. Pearson has never been charged with any crime. He has never been notified of any designation. He has never been given any opportunity to contest placement on any list. The Supreme Court has recognized that persons placed on the No Fly List have a due process right to notice and a meaningful opportunity to challenge the designation (_Latif v. Holder_, 9th Cir. 2016; _American Civil Liberties Union v. Clapper_; DHS TRIP procedures). Placement in a terrorist tracking database on the basis of academic scholarship designated hostile ideology by executive order — without notice, without a hearing, without any evidence of violence or violence advocacy — is a Fifth Amendment due process violation of the first order.

### 50\. RMVE / Black Identity Extremism Designation — First Amendment Facial and As-Applied Violation

The FBI’s 2017 Racially Motivated Violent Extremist / Black Identity Extremism category identified scholarship framing structural racism as state violence, and organizing responding to that framing, as a domestic terrorism predicate. Pearson’s published dissertation fits this framework precisely. The designation does not require evidence of violence; it requires a political and intellectual framework the government has deemed threatening. This is viewpoint discrimination in its purest form: the government using the domestic terrorism machinery to monitor, target, and neutralize citizens based not on what they have done but on what they have thought, written, and published. The First Amendment prohibits the government from treating political opinion, however radical, as a crime predicate absent a showing of incitement to imminent lawless action (_Brandenburg v. Article 16 prohibits cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment falling short of full torture — everything in this campaign that does not meet the “severe suffering” threshold still violates Article 16. Notably, in November 2025, the United States voted against a UN General Assembly resolution condemning torture — an act that, in the context of Pearson’s documented experience, takes on a specific and troubling significance.

While not directly enforceable in US courts, the UDHR establishes the international human rights baseline against which the Pearson case must be assessed, and is directly relevant to his asylum claim. **Article 3** (right to life, liberty, and security of person); **Article 5** (freedom from torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment); **Article 7** (equal protection of the law); **Article 12** (freedom from arbitrary interference with privacy, home, or correspondence); **Article 13** (freedom of movement); **Article 17** (right to own property — Pearson has been dispossessed of everything except a mattress and a suitcase); **Article 18** (freedom of thought, conscience, and religion); **Article 19** (freedom of opinion and expression); and **Article 20** (freedom of association). ### Preface: Two Voices, Twenty-Nine Years Apart

Gloria Naylor did not want to tell her story. She said so in the first line of 1996, the fictionalized memoir she published through Third World Press in 2005 because no mainstream publisher would touch it. She told it anyway — from the Brooklyn Public Library, the only place she had found where the noise stopped, writing in longhand with hands that had begun to shake. She was a National Book Award winner. She had written six novels. She had spent the last years of her literary life documenting what a government operation had done to her mind.

Richard Pearson did not choose to tell his story either. He was forced to, by the same logic that forced Naylor: documentation as survival, writing as the only defense available to someone against whom every institutional defense has been disabled. He is writing from Washington, D.C., in 2025 and 2026, with nothing left but a mattress and a suitcase, in the most surveilled city on earth, having been denied asylum in Iceland, having been dismissed by the ACLU, having been falsely arrested, chemically assaulted, acoustically tortured, and had a voice placed inside his skull near the United States Capitol.

The voice said: We have to make you disappear.

Naylor’s book described the same technology — described it in 2005, documented it with an appendix including a former NSA employee’s lawsuit, cited the researchers who had been trying to get anyone to pay attention since the 1990s. She called it synthetic telepathy. She included the technical framework developed by John St. Clair Akwei, a former NSA employee whose 1992 lawsuit against the agency — Civil Action 92–0449, filed in Washington, D.C. — described Remote Neural Monitoring (RNM) and Electronic Brain Link technology capable of producing sound in the auditory cortex by bypassing the ears entirely.

The Akwei lawsuit was dismissed by Judge Stanley Sporkin without allowing it to proceed to discovery. Sporkin had previously served as the CIA’s general counsel. The case that might have produced judicial examination of whether the NSA possessed and was using technologies capable of entering human minds was dismissed before any examination occurred, by a judge whose institutional history gave him every reason to ensure it stayed dismissed.

That was 1992. Naylor documented what these technologies did to her in 1996. Pearson documented what they did to him in 2025. Twenty-nine years. Three accounts — Akwei, Naylor, Pearson — describing the same technology, the same operational signature, the same institutional response: dismissal, psychiatric labeling, and the architecture of impunity that ensures no court, no regulator, no legislature, and no journalist will be obliged to take the account seriously. **The technology has not changed. The impunity has not changed. What has changed is that the Department of War’s Chief Technology Officer confirmed on January 23, 2026 that these weapons are operational and being scaled — and said it publicly, on social media, without apparent concern that anyone in power would object.**

This essay examines what that arc — from Akwei’s 1992 lawsuit to Naylor’s 2005 testimony to Pearson’s 2025–2026 documentation — reveals about the constitutional order of the United States. It argues that the arc is not a series of isolated cases. It is the story of a failure — a failure of oversight, of regulation, of accountability, and of the basic constitutional commitment to protecting individual persons from the government built to serve them.

That failure did not begin in 2025. It began in Philadelphia in 1787, when the Framers built a powerful government and trusted that structural safeguards would prevent that power from destroying the people it governed. The safeguards were called the Bill of Rights. They were added because states refused to ratify without them — because the people closest to the drafting understood that you cannot trust a government with power not to use it. Two hundred and thirty-six years later, every firebreak those states demanded has been compromised. Not repealed. Surrounded. And a voice entered Richard Pearson’s skull to announce the result.

The operation is self-concealing. It is engineered to produce the very response — _she’s paranoid_ — that forecloses investigation. In _1996_, the NSA official who orders the operation against her understands that its best protection is the target’s own testimony.

The Hobart literary review of _1996_ described the book’s central revelation with unusual directness: ‘Naylor tells her story with such clear-headed precision, even citing and including an appendix featuring a lawsuit filed by a former NSA employee against the NSA confirming the existence of such technologies, that personally, I was left in tears by the end, awed at her courage in telling this story.’ The reviewer was moved to tears not because the story was false but because it was true — documented, sourced, and impossible to dismiss except through the institutionalized reflexes that Naylor had predicted and Pearson has now encountered again.

Naylor died in 2016 at age 66, in St. Croix. She wrote nothing of significance after 1996. The operation did not kill her. It consumed her. Every year that should have produced novels produced instead the documentation of her own destruction. The neutralization worked. It just took time, and it disguised itself as illness, and it left no fingerprints that a court would examine.

— — —

### Part II: The Warnings That Were Ignored — A Thirty-Year Record of Deliberate Inaction

### The International Community Tried to Act

The international regulatory record on directed energy and psychotronic weapons is not blank. It is a record of sustained efforts to establish oversight and prohibition that the United States government consistently blocked, evaded, and ignored. Understanding this record is essential to understanding the Pearson case, because it establishes that what is being done to Pearson is not the result of a regulatory gap that no one noticed. It is the result of a regulatory gap that powerful actors worked deliberately to maintain.

In January 1999, the European Parliament passed Resolution A4–005/99, which _called for an international convention introducing a global ban on all developments and deployments of weapons which might enable any form of manipulation of human beings._ The resolution was passed by a body of democratically elected legislators representing the member states of the European Union, following review of evidence regarding the capabilities and risks of non-lethal and directed energy weapons. It was accompanied by a detailed technical report — the STOA (Scientific and Technological Options Assessment) Panel report on crowd control technologies — that assessed directed energy weapons, their physical and psychological effects, their abuse potential, and the absence of adequate regulatory frameworks.

The European Parliament resolution called on governments worldwide to enact legislation prohibiting the use of these devices by government, private organizations, and individuals. It called for international convention. It called for public transparency about the technologies’ existence and capabilities. The United States government did not respond. No U.S. legislation was enacted. No bilateral or multilateral convention was negotiated. The resolution stands as a statement of what democratic governance looks like when it encounters this problem — and as the record of what the United States chose not to do.

In October 2001, Congressman Dennis Kucinich introduced the Space Preservation Act of 2001 to the House of Representatives. The bill sought a ban on ‘exotic weapons’ including specifically _electronic, psychotronic or information weapons… electromagnetic radiation, extremely low frequency (ELF) or ultra low frequency energy, for the purpose of… mood management, or mind control of such persons or populations._ The bill was referred to the Committee on Science and the Committees on Armed Services and International Relations. It died in committee. Kucinich reintroduced it in 2002. It died again. The legislative record contains no hearings, no testimony, no substantive response.

Cheryl Welsh, whose research Naylor cited and who was listed by UNIDIR as one of six non-lethal weapons experts worldwide, spent decades documenting the history of what she called ‘the most important and least-covered story in American politics’: the development of technologies capable of manipulating human cognition and the complete absence of any legal framework governing their use. Her organization’s name — Citizens Against Human Rights Abuses — named the issue precisely. These were not weapons of foreign warfare. They were capabilities being developed and used against domestic civilians. Citizens. Human rights. Abuses.

The U.N. Human Rights framework engaged the issue through the Special Rapporteur on Torture, whose reports from the 2000s onward increasingly documented accounts of non-consensual electromagnetic experimentation by state actors. The accounts were consistent across countries, demographics, and decades. The U.N. reports recommended investigation. The United States government, which in November 2025 voted against a U.N. General Assembly resolution condemning torture, was not among the governments that investigated.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*nvEwHmGoiqgde4V4SXs_lg.png)

### The NSA Whistleblowers Who Told the Truth

Naylor noted in _1996_ that by 2002, three NSA employees had blown the whistle on the agency’s warrantless surveillance programs and its Trailblazer system of communications data analysis. Three more came forward in 2005. These disclosures — by William Binney, Thomas Drake, Edward Loomis, J. Kirk Wiebe, and others — described the scale of the NSA’s domestic surveillance infrastructure and the agency’s deliberate decision to expand that infrastructure without legal authorization, without Congressional knowledge, and without oversight.

The Snowden disclosures of 2013 confirmed what the earlier whistleblowers had described and added the PRISM program, the upstream collection of fiber optic communications, the metadata bulk collection that the Supreme Court would ultimately hold required a warrant in _Carpenter v. United States_ (2018). Naylor, who died in 2016, ‘did live to see mainstream acknowledgment of the NSA’s grievous infringements when the PRISM program made global headlines in 2013,’ as the academic study of her work noted. She had written about these capabilities in 2005. She had sourced them to former NSA employees. She had been dismissed as a conspiracy theorist. The Snowden documents vindicated her factual premises entirely.

The whistleblower record matters for the Pearson case in a specific way: it establishes that the agencies involved in what Pearson describes are agencies with a documented history of operating domestic surveillance programs that exceed their legal authority, concealing that excess from Congressional oversight, and retaliating against internal employees who attempt to report it. The NSA is not an agency with an otherwise clean record that might have engaged in isolated misconduct. It is an agency whose documented institutional culture treats legal constraints as obstacles to be managed rather than limits to be observed. That institutional culture is the context in which Pearson’s account must be evaluated.

### The MKUltra Continuum

The history that Naylor invokes in 1996 — from MKUltra to COINTELPRO, from the Tuskegee experiments to the radiation experiments conducted on unconsenting patients in the 1940s through the 1970s — is not, as its detractors sometimes imply, a conspiracy theory framework that attributes too much coherence and coordination to scattered events. It is a documented institutional history of American government agencies conducting non-consensual human experimentation on civilians, with particular concentration on Black Americans and other marginalized communities, for purposes ranging from intelligence gathering to weapons development to the management of political dissent.

MKUltra, the CIA’s program of non-consensual psychological and pharmaceutical experimentation, ran from the early 1950s through 1973. It was not a fringe program. It involved more than 80 institutions, including universities, hospitals, and prisons. It used LSD, electroconvulsive therapy, sensory deprivation, hypnosis, and other techniques on subjects who did not consent and in many cases did not know they were subjects. The program was uncovered only when documents were obtained through FOIA in 1977 — after the CIA had ordered the destruction of most records in 1973. The destruction of records was itself an institutional act, undertaken with full knowledge that the program’s exposure would be damaging.

Naylor positioned her account explicitly within this history. Her Medium essay documentation, her research appendix, and the framework of 1996 all make clear that she understood her experience not as an anomaly but as the continuation of a program that had never ended — only updated its technology and narrowed its target selection. The Church Committee had exposed the program. The Church Committee’s reforms had not ended it. COINTELPRO had a successor. It had better tools.

Pearson’s Medium essay, ‘From MKUltra to COINTELPRO: When Will the U.S. Government Stop Itself?’, asks this question directly and answers it with two decades of documented history. The title is not rhetorical. It is analytical. The line from MKUltra to COINTELPRO to the Black Identity Extremism designation to EO 14173 to what was done to Pearson on July 13, 2025 is not broken. It is continuous. The technology changes. The targets are selected by the same logic. The institutional protection from accountability is the same architecture.

— — —

### Part III: Philadelphia, 1787 — The Bargain and Its Discontents

### The Power the Framers Built

The Constitution of 1787 was, above everything else, a document about power. The Articles of Confederation had produced a government too weak to tax, too weak to raise armies, too weak to regulate commerce. Shays’ Rebellion — the 1786 uprising of Massachusetts farmers who closed the courts by force — frightened the commercial and landed classes into Philadelphia. They came to build a government that worked.

They succeeded, extravagantly. The Constitution created a government with the power to tax directly, to raise and command armies, to regulate interstate commerce, to coin money, to define and punish crimes. Article VI made its laws supreme over state laws. The Necessary and Proper Clause gave Congress the authority to enact whatever legislation was necessary to execute its enumerated powers — a grant so broad that John Marshall would describe it as conferring ‘ample means for the execution of the powers committed to it.’

What the Constitution of 1787 did not contain was systematic protection of individual rights against this powerful government. There was no freedom of speech provision. No protection against unreasonable searches. No guarantee of due process. The Framers assumed, or at least argued publicly, that a government of enumerated powers needed no bill of rights because it had no power to violate rights it hadn’t been granted. Thomas Jefferson, writing from Paris, told Madison this was a ‘logical subtlety’ that would provide no protection in practice.

### North Carolina, Rhode Island, and the Case Against Trust

North Carolina refused to ratify. Rhode Island held out until 1790. Their resistance was not irrational obstruction. It was the position of people who had thought carefully about what a powerful government without explicit constraints would do. Brutus — Robert Yates of New York — wrote in October 1787 that the Necessary and Proper Clause would eventually authorize almost anything, and that federal courts would consistently construe federal power broadly. He wrote this before ratification. He was describing the next two centuries.

So Madison wrote the Bill of Rights. Ten amendments. Ratified in 1791. The firebreaks against the fire they had just built.

The Fourth Amendment was written in direct response to the writs of assistance — general warrants authorizing searches of any home, any time, for anything. The Fifth Amendment was the fence around the government’s power to simply destroy people without trial. The Eighth Amendment recognized that a government that could torture its prisoners had abolished the distinction between citizen and subject. The First Amendment was for the pamphleteer, the dissenter, the scholar who said things the government found threatening.

None of the Framers anticipated the technology that entered Richard Pearson’s skull on July 13, 2025. But they understood the _logic_ of the threat precisely: a government with the power to enter the interior of a person’s mind has abolished the constitutional category of personhood entirely. There is no liberty interest more fundamental than the sovereignty of one’s own thoughts. There is no Fourth Amendment violation more complete than an intrusion that leaves no trace, requires no physical entry, and the target never knows occurred. There is no First Amendment violation more total than a government that can write to the thought formation process itself.

— — —

### Part IV: The Reconstruction Amendments Were for Richard Pearson

### The Fourteenth Amendment’s Specific Purpose

The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in 1868 for specific people in a specific historical moment: four million formerly enslaved people who were citizens in name but available to everything state governments chose to do to them. Every noun in Section 1 was chosen in the context of Black Codes, convict leasing, and the systematic obliteration of Black citizenship. The Equal Protection Clause was the constitutional recognition that the original document — without its own targeted supplement — did not actually protect the people who most needed protection from the government.

Richard Pearson is a descendant of enslaved people. The campaign against him — the surveillance, false arrest, acoustic torture, chemical assault, employment sabotage, framing operation, financial attrition, engineered social death — is the continuation of the same project the Fourteenth Amendment was written to prohibit. Not the same technology. The same project: the use of government power to destroy the functional citizenship of a Black person whose intellectual work threatens the hierarchy that power has organized itself to maintain.

The Reconstruction rollback is not a metaphor. It is a documented sequence: the Voting Rights Act gutted in Shelby County v. Holder (2013); affirmative action ended in Students for Fair Admissions (2023); DEI scholarship designated hostile ideology by EO 14173 (January 20, 2025); and the framing operation near the Capitol designed to end the Medium publications of a critical race scholar by planting neo-Nazi materials in a park he had been behaviorally directed to enter. W.E.B. Du Bois had his passport confiscated. Fred Hampton was shot in his bed. Gloria Naylor was acoustically tortured into silence. The technology advances. The targeting logic has not changed in a century.
