### Part V: How the Firebreaks Were Removed — The Doctrinal History

### The Architecture of Impunity, Stage by Stage

The transformation of the Bill of Rights from enforceable constraints into nominal promises did not happen in a single act. It happened across seven decades, in a sequence of decisions each defended as technically narrow and procedurally justified, that together produced a legal architecture in which the government can violate any right it chooses and face no accountability — judicial, legislative, or institutional. The sequence is important precisely because it shows the outcome was not accidental. It was constructed. And the Pearson case sits at its completion.

**Stage One: Reynolds (1953) — The National Security Exception Built on Fraud**

_United States v. Reynolds_ created the state secrets privilege on a fraudulent predicate: the government told the Supreme Court the crash report contained classified information. It contained evidence of negligence. Declassified forty years later, it revealed the fraud. The Court, informed, declined to revisit. The doctrine that protected the lie stands. Every government lawyer who needs a lawsuit to disappear has had this tool for seventy years. _Reynolds_ is not merely a bad precedent. It is the foundational proof that the national security exception will be used to protect the government from accountability, not to protect genuine national security, whenever the two conflict — and the Court will permit it.

**Stage Two: FISA (1978) — The Secret Court That Hears One Side**

The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act was enacted three years after the Church Committee finished documenting COINTELPRO. The connection was direct and intentional: Congress had seen what warrantless surveillance of civil rights leaders, Black activists, journalists, and academics produced, and FISA was supposed to be the answer — a judicial check on executive surveillance power in the foreign intelligence context.

The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court became something else. It is a one-sided proceeding in which the government presents evidence and argument without any opposing party, without adversarial testing of its factual representations, without any mechanism for the target to know the proceeding occurred. The FISC cannot know what the government is not telling it. It cannot test the government’s characterizations against alternative explanations. It hears one voice and issues an order.

The approval rate across the court’s history is approximately 99.97 percent. In fiscal year 2023, the government submitted 1,096 applications. The court approved 1,030 in full and modified 62. It denied 3. This is not judicial oversight. It is judicial decoration — the institutional form of a check without its substance. The Church Committee designed FISA to impose meaningful constraint on the executive. What was built was a mechanism that provides the _appearance_ of judicial authorization while ensuring the government is never actually refused.

FISA’s structural defect is compounded by its post-9/11 expansions. The PATRIOT Act (2001) removed the requirement that foreign intelligence collection be the primary purpose of surveillance, making FISA usable in cases that previously required ordinary criminal warrants. The FISA Amendments Act (2008) added Section 702, authorizing warrantless collection of communications of non-U.S. persons abroad with ‘incidental’ collection of Americans’ communications — a category that the NSA’s upstream collection programs used to capture essentially all international communications passing through U.S. fiber optic infrastructure. The FISC approved those programs. Its legal reasoning was classified for years.

For the Pearson case, the FISA court’s role is not peripheral — it is structural. If a FISA order exists targeting Pearson, it was issued on representations he cannot access, cannot challenge, and cannot know. The court that issued it heard only the government’s version of who he is. It did not hear that he is a public health scholar who eats cantaloupe on the Mall and advocates for public housing residents. It heard a threat assessment, a designation, and a targeting predicate.

Pearson is a curious intellectual. He likes art as much as research. His activism is as much a part of his identity as much as his love of gay culture. He can easily glide between discussion of constitutional doctrines to regression analysis. Pearson is a product of the US education system — a man whose racialized identity and knowledge absorption and synthesis became the basis for targeting.

If a FISA order existed, it was presented with the government’s narrative shaped for authorization, from the only party permitted to speak. As the essay elsewhere establishes, _even if FISA authorization exists, it cannot authorize torture, behavioral direction, chemical assault, framing, or the systematic destruction of a person’s cognitive sovereignty_. But the FISC’s existence provides institutional cover that makes the question of what was actually authorized impossible to litigate — because the order is classified, the predicate is classified, the legal theory is classified, and the target has no mechanism to appear before the court that purports to have authorized his destruction.

FISA also created a self-sealing information system that compounds every other doctrinal barrier. Clapper prohibits standing without proof of surveillance. FISA prohibits disclosure of whether surveillance occurred. Glomar prohibits confirming or denying the existence of programs. NSL gag orders prohibit recipients from informing targets. The FISC’s classified opinions prohibit public examination of the legal theories authorizing the programs. Each barrier reinforces every other. Pearson cannot prove the FISA order exists. He cannot prove it doesn’t. He cannot get the documents. The documents are protected by the order whose existence cannot be confirmed. The circle is _architecturally_ closed — designed, not accidental.

**Stage Three: The Immunity Doctrines Proliferate (1982–2017)**

_Harlow v. Fitzgerald_ (1982) transformed qualified immunity from a good-faith defense into a near-absolute barrier to accountability. Officials are immune unless they violated ‘clearly established’ law — established with sufficient specificity that every reasonable official would know the specific conduct was unconstitutional. In practice: if the government does anything new, there is no clearly established precedent, so immunity attaches. The doctrine structurally rewards innovation in abuse. The more novel the violation, the more complete the protection. For voice-to-skull targeting, hippocampal place cell activation, behavioral direction through vestibular stimulation, and through-wall acoustic tracking — technologies confirmed as operational in January 2026 but without a body of prior case law — qualified immunity provides absolute protection at the moment of most severe violation.

_Ziglar v. Abbasi_ (2017) essentially ended Bivens claims in new contexts, foreclosing the constitutional cause of action against federal officials for rights violations wherever Congress has not explicitly authorized suit — and directing plaintiffs to Congress as an ‘alternative political remedy.’ The same Congress that has not held a single hearing on the domestic deployment of directed energy weapons against civilians, has not enacted any statute governing their use, and has not responded to thirty years of documented warnings, is offered as the functional substitute for judicial enforcement of the Bill of Rights. The recommendation is not a remedy. It is a deflection. Bivens was the mechanism by which the Constitution enforced itself against the people who violated it. Its practical elimination leaves the Constitution with no enforcement agent in exactly the contexts where enforcement is most urgent.

The Federal Tort Claims Act’s exceptions complete the immunity architecture for institutional liability. The intentional tort exception (28 U.S.C. § 2680(h)) bars suits against the United States for most intentional misconduct by law enforcement. The discretionary function exception (§ 2680(a)) bars suits for policy decisions or conduct involving judgment and choice. Together, these exceptions ensure that the United States itself — as distinguished from individual officials — cannot be held liable for designing and executing a systematic campaign of covert violence against a civilian. The DC federal courthouse produced exactly this result for Pearson: _‘The United States simply has not rendered itself liable under the FTCA for constitutional tort claims.’_ The sentence is accurate. It is also the description of an accountability-free zone created by statute and maintained by judicial deference.

**Stage Four: The Information Architecture Seals (1990s–Present)**

The Glomar doctrine — originating in the CIA’s 1975 claim that it could neither confirm nor deny the existence of a ship used to recover a Soviet submarine — has expanded to cover the existence of any surveillance program, any FISA order, any NSL, any classified targeting decision. The doctrine means Pearson cannot obtain documents confirming or denying the operations against him because confirming or denying their existence is itself classified. He cannot challenge what he cannot name. He cannot name what he cannot document. He cannot document what the government will neither confirm nor deny. The doctrine is _epistemically totalizing_: it prevents the acquisition of the knowledge necessary to exercise any of the other rights.

National Security Letters — issued by the FBI without judicial approval, accompanied by automatic indefinite gag orders — allow the collection of communications records for anyone the FBI designates a national security concern, without any judge reviewing the designation, and with criminal penalties on the recipient for informing the target. The Second Circuit in Doe v. Mukasey (2008) held the automatic indefinite gag order mechanism raised serious First Amendment concerns but did not strike the program down. For Pearson: every communications provider he has used — telephone, internet, financial — almost certainly received NSLs. None can tell him. He cannot challenge what he cannot know was issued. The designation is permanent unless the FBI decides to rescind it. There is no mechanism for the target to initiate reconsideration.

The TIDE watchlist and its propagation through law enforcement databases produced the ACCESS DENIED flag that appeared when MPD officers searched Pearson’s name during the noise complaint visit — the week before his physical assault. An ACCESS DENIED response to an MPD officer’s database query carries a specific technical meaning: a Sensitive Compartmented Information block attached to Pearson’s file, restricting access to personnel with a defined need-to-know above local police clearance. This is not a bureaucratic anomaly. It is the physical instantiation of his targeting in the infrastructure of daily law enforcement. It altered how every officer who encountered him would treat him, permanently, without his knowledge, without notice, without a hearing, without any mechanism for challenge or correction.

**Stage Five: Standing Doctrine Becomes a Perfect Trap (2013)**

_Clapper v. Amnesty International USA_ (2013) is the case that closes the circle. The Supreme Court held that journalists, lawyers, and human rights workers who communicated with foreign sources targeted by Section 702 surveillance lacked standing to challenge the surveillance — because they could not prove with sufficient certainty that they had been surveilled. The proof was classified. The classification was permanent. The Court required ‘concrete, particularized’ injury — the standard requirement for Article III standing — which is structurally impossible to satisfy when the government’s entire architecture ensures no target ever learns they were surveilled.

Justice Breyer’s dissent in _Clapper_ identified the logical problem precisely: ‘the government has strong incentives to surveil petitioners. It has the capacity to do so. It is doing so. And the majority holds they cannot challenge it because they cannot prove it.’ The majority’s response was to tighten the standing requirement rather than acknowledge that the standing doctrine had been used to construct an accountability-free zone. The result is the constitutional equivalent of a hall of mirrors: the violation produces the injury; the injury cannot be proven because the violation is classified; the inability to prove the injury bars standing; the absence of standing bars discovery of the proof; the absence of proof perpetuates the inability to establish standing. The target is trapped inside the hall of mirrors with no exit.

**Stage Six: Pearson’s Below-Threshold Theory — The Most Sophisticated Innovation**

Pearson identified, in his own analysis of what was being done to him, a dimension of the impunity architecture that is more sophisticated than any of the doctrinal mechanisms above — because it operates not in law but in operational calibration. He called it, in substance, the ‘below-threshold’ problem: the deliberate engineering of each individual act of harm to remain below the level at which it would, standing alone, trigger a legally cognizable claim.

The theory works as follows. Civil standing under Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is traceable to the defendant and redressable by a favorable court decision. Each individual component of the campaign against Pearson was calibrated — deliberately, he argues, and the operational precision of the campaign supports the argument — to remain just below the threshold that would independently satisfy each element. A noise complaint: not an assault. A reflector snapped from a bicycle: not property destruction sufficient for a civil action. A car taking off from a parking space when he walks past: not stalking under any statute’s threshold. An officer opening a closet door during a noise complaint visit: arguably within the scope of a safety sweep. Objects moved in his apartment: nothing missing, no provable entry. The ‘Lee’ confirmation at Potbelly’s: an ambiguous conversation, not sworn testimony. Each act, individually, is below the legal threshold at which a court would be required to take it seriously.

The genius of the below-threshold design — and it is a design, not an accident — is that it requires the target to present the _aggregate_ to establish the constitutional violation, while legal doctrine requires the target to prove _specific_ violations with specific evidence traced to specific defendants. The aggregate is the evidence. The doctrine demands the specific. The gap between what the evidence shows and what the doctrine requires is precisely the gap into which the campaign disappears. No single act crosses the threshold. The totality — fourteen months, across multiple jurisdictions, involving dozens of coordinated actors, with consistent operational signatures and documented physical evidence — is the violation. But totality-of-circumstances analysis is reserved for very specific Fourth Amendment contexts, is unavailable in most civil rights frameworks, and is structurally hostile to the kind of claim Pearson would have to make.

The below-threshold architecture also exploits the psychiatric trap at the doctrinal level. When a plaintiff presents a court with a pattern of individually sub-threshold acts and argues that the aggregate constitutes a constitutional violation, the court’s analytical reflex — reinforced by the absence of any statutory or doctrinal framework for evaluating such claims — is to treat the pattern-recognition itself as evidence of disordered thinking. The law has no category for ‘systematic campaign of sub-threshold acts coordinated to avoid legal accountability.’ The absence of the category is the protection. Pearson’s documentation of the pattern — timestamped, photographed, cross-referenced, exhaustively cross-checked with control studies — is the attempt to force the pattern into visibility against a legal framework designed to keep it invisible. The September 15, 2025 DBH evaluation that confirmed his rationality is the preemptive answer to the doctrinal reflex: the person presenting this pattern is not disordered. The pattern is real. The framework for engaging it does not exist.

The below-threshold theory connects directly to the FISA architecture. If a FISA order exists, the government’s lawyers have designed the operational parameters of the campaign with full knowledge of what thresholds must not be crossed. The voice-to-skull transmission on July 13, 2025 — _‘We have to make you disappear’_ — crossed a threshold. It produced evidence: Pearson’s contemporaneous documentation, his physical and emotional response, his immediate reporting. The operation appears to have been designed to ensure that this kind of threshold-crossing was exceptional rather than routine — that the campaign’s daily operational texture consisted of acts calibrated to produce cumulative harm while maintaining individual deniability. This is not the product of unsophisticated actors. It is the product of legal counsel who understood exactly what the thresholds were and exactly what operational parameters would keep the campaign below them.

The below-threshold theory, taken seriously, reveals the deepest flaw in the remedial architecture: it was built to respond to discrete, identifiable, attributable violations. It was not built to respond to a campaign of coordinated, sub-threshold acts designed by people who understood the remedial architecture and calibrated their conduct accordingly. The Bill of Rights was written by people who had experienced overt government abuse — general warrants, quartered soldiers, public prosecutions. It was not written by people who anticipated a government with the legal resources, the operational sophistication, and the institutional longevity to design abuse specifically to evade the constraints they were putting in place. That is the government Richard Pearson encountered. That is what the firebreaks were not built for. That is why they are gone.

**Stage Seven: The Remedial Architecture’s Final Collapse (2013–2025)**

The arc from _Clapper_ (2013) through _Ziglar_ (2017) through the firing of the twelve inspectors general on January 20, 2025 represents the final stage of remedial collapse. _Clapper_ forecloses standing. _Ziglar_ forecloses Bivens. The FTCA exceptions foreclose sovereign immunity waiver. State secrets forecloses discovery. Glomar forecloses document access. NSL gag orders foreclose source disclosure. FISA secrecy forecloses challenge to the authorization. Qualified immunity forecloses individual official liability. The below-threshold calibration forecloses pattern-of-conduct claims. And the removal of the twelve inspectors general removed the internal feedback mechanism — the one institutional actor whose statutory independence and access to classified programs would have permitted identification and reporting of exactly what was done to Pearson.

Each of these closures was defended, when challenged, as a technical procedural adjustment made for legitimate institutional reasons. The aggregate is not a technical procedural adjustment. It is the elimination of every mechanism by which the most powerful government in human history can be held accountable for what it does to the least powerful people it has decided to target. The Supremacy Clause says the Constitution is supreme law. The architecture described above is the government’s answer to that claim: supreme in text, unenforceable in practice, for the people who most need it enforced.

— — —

### Part VI: The Contextual Crisis — Why Every Institution Has Failed Simultaneously

### The Congressional Failure: Neuroweapons Without Law

Congress has not regulated neuroweapons. Not because no one asked. The European Parliament called for international convention in 1999. Kucinich introduced the Space Preservation Act in 2001 and 2002. Naylor’s 1996 documented the technologies in 2005 with a former NSA employee’s lawsuit in its appendix. Pearson knocked on dozens of congressional office doors in December 2025. Within weeks, the administration briefed Congress on directed energy systems. The DoW CTO announced scaling on January 23, 2026. The Washington Post published on the arms race in February 2026.

No statute defines what directed energy weapons may or may not be used for domestically. No statute requires judicial authorization for their use against a civilian. No statute establishes a due process requirement for targeting. No statute provides a cause of action for a victim. No statute establishes criminal penalties for unauthorized use. No hearings have been held. Twenty-five years after the European Parliament acted and after Naylor published, the United States Congress has produced no legislative response to the existence of these capabilities whatsoever.

This is not a gap that no one noticed. Cheryl Welsh noticed it in 1992. Akwei filed suit about it in 1992. The Association of National Security Alumni reported on it in 1992. Julianne McKinney documented it in 1992. The European Parliament addressed it in 1999. Kucinich legislated about it in 2001. Naylor published about it in 2005. The gap is thirty years of deliberate inaction in the face of documented, sourced, repeatedly-raised evidence that these capabilities exist and are being used against civilians without any legal framework.

The word for _thirty years of deliberate inaction in the face of repeated documented warnings_ is not ‘gap.’ It is not ‘oversight.’ It is a choice. Someone, repeatedly, decided not to act. Pearson is, in part, the consequence of that choice.

### The Media Failure: The Story That Was Always There to Tell

Mainstream publishers refused _1996_. No mainstream publication amplified Naylor’s account when it was published by Third World Press in 2005. The academic study of her work notes, with precision, that she was accused of ‘anti-Semitism’ rather than engaged on her documented factual claims. The dismissal was institutional: the account was too explosive, too specific, too sourced for comfortable rejection, so it was labeled and ignored. A National Book Award winner publishing a documented account of NSA directed energy operations against her home and mind was not covered. The gap in the record is not an absence of story. It is an absence of institutional will to cover it.

Pearson published on Medium because no publication would take him. He submitted to the United Nations because domestic institutions had no mechanism for receiving his account. He knocked on congressional office doors in person because no journalist was going to knock on them for him. The framing operation near the Capitol was designed to produce a mugshot that would end the Medium publications — correctly assessed as his only remaining mechanism for reaching anyone who might act.

The press failure is not primarily moral. It is structural. The economic destruction of investigative journalism has eliminated the resources and reduced the institutional courage necessary to fight the legal battles that covering this story requires. State secrets privilege blocks document access. NSL gag orders prevent sources from speaking. Qualified immunity limits the civil litigation that generates documents. And the economic crisis of journalism has eliminated the resources and courage to fight those battles for a story that will generate legal threats from the most powerful intelligence agencies in the world. The incentive structure ensures silence.

### The Technology Failure: What the Framers Could Not Have Imagined

The constitutional design rested on natural limits. Physical limits: a government that required soldiers to search homes could only search so many homes. Informational limits: a government that required human informants could only know what humans could observe. Cognitive limits: a government that could only influence people through speech could only reach people who encountered its speech. Directed energy weapons, voice-to-skull transmission, hippocampal place cell activation, behavioral direction through vestibular stimulation — the capabilities confirmed as operational by the DoW in January 2026 — abolish every assumption the Framers made about these limits. The Fourth Amendment protects the home from physical entry. It has no provision for electromagnetic entry that leaves no trace. The First Amendment protects freedom of thought. It has no provision for thought being authored by an external party whose authorship is invisible to the thinker.

Naylor understood this in 2005. She wrote about ‘synthetic telepathy’ — the precise technical term for the voice-to-skull capability that Akwei’s lawsuit had described. She wrote that it ‘bypasses the ears and speaks directly to the auditory cortex.’ She wrote that the target ‘initially assumes schizophrenia’ because the symptom profile has been engineered to produce exactly that assumption. She was describing, in 2005, what was done to Pearson in 2025. The technology is the same technology. The operational protocol is the same protocol. The defense — _she’s crazy_, _he’s crazy_ — is the same defense. The Department of War confirmed the weapons in January 2026 and no one arrested anyone.

— — —

### Part VII: The Return — 1788, 1868, 1964, and Now

### The Debate That Never Ended

Patrick Henry’s question was: what happens when the government decides that someone must disappear? He asked it about a hypothetical government with conventional powers. The answer — the Bill of Rights — provided constitutional language for the prohibition, legal mechanisms for its enforcement, and a public culture of rights.

The answer is failing. Not because the language changed. Because the mechanisms have been removed and the culture has been fragmented. We are back at Henry’s question, but now the government asking it has voice-to-skull technology, a secret court, a legal architecture that forecloses every remedy, and no regulatory framework because Congress decided thirty years ago, and has decided again every year since, not to create one.

The Reconstruction debate — whether the Fourteenth Amendment’s promise would be enforced — was answered by the Civil Rights Movement. It took a century after ratification, a movement that produced martyrs, and a Supreme Court briefly willing to enforce what it had ignored for sixty years. That answer is being systematically dismantled. We are in a second Reconstruction rollback, equipped with technologies the Framers could not have imagined, implemented through a legal architecture the Reconstruction drafters did not build meta-safeguards against, targeting a descendant of enslaved people whose scholarship examined structural racism as state violence.

### The Civil Rights Movement’s Lesson for This Moment

The Civil Rights Movement understood that legal architecture alone does not produce change. Brown v. Board was decided in 1954. Most Southern schools remained segregated for a decade. What changed was political mass action making the cost of non-enforcement higher than the cost of compliance — through television coverage of Birmingham, of Selma, of systematic violence against peaceful protesters that made the gap between constitutional promise and constitutional reality visible and politically decisive.

The ecosystem required to force enforcement of the rights Pearson’s case invokes does not currently exist. Congress is not acting. The press is not investigating. The courts have removed most remedial mechanisms. The public is fragmented, precarious, and exhausted. The institutional memory of what COINTELPRO required to expose — the stolen FBI files from the Media, Pennsylvania field office in 1971, the Church Committee, years of litigation — is not operative in the current political moment.

That is the depth of the crisis. The mechanisms that historically corrected the gap between constitutional promise and constitutional reality are themselves compromised. The crisis is not just in the rights. It is in the correction mechanisms.

### What Two Testimonies, Twenty-Nine Years Apart, Demand

The convergence between Naylor’s 1996 and Pearson’s 2025–2026 account is the most important evidentiary fact in both cases. They did not know each other. They did not read each other before experiencing what they experienced. They documented the same technology, the same operational signature, the same institutional response, the same goal.

The 1957 assertion by the Soviet dissident poet Boris Pasternak — that individual witnesses to state crimes are the most important form of historical evidence, because the state destroys documents but cannot destroy the people who experienced what the documents would have shown — applies precisely here. Naylor was a witness. Her documents are 1996 and its research appendix, the Akwei lawsuit, the Welsh research, the McKinney report. Pearson is a witness. His documents are the timestamped photographs, the preserved pants, the DBH evaluation, the congressional letters, the UN submissions, the Medium essays.

Dismissing either account requires dismissing both, because they are too similar to dismiss independently. The details that a fabricator could not reliably produce — the specific noise campaign protocols, the vehicle formation logic, the home-intrusion-as-message without theft, the object placement as signal, the psychiatric trap as structural feature of the operation — appear in both accounts, a decade apart, from two Black intellectuals in different cities who had never discussed their experiences. The _signature_ is the same because the _program_ is the same. Naylor said so in 2005. Pearson is saying so in 2025. The Department of War confirmed the weapons exist in 2026.

The question is no longer whether these capabilities exist. The DoW CTO answered that. The question is whether they are being used against American civilians without legal authorization, without judicial oversight, without due process, without Congressional regulation, without any accountability mechanism — and whether the United States government will continue to treat the answer to that question as a matter for _neither confirm nor deny._

North Carolina and Rhode Island refused to ratify the Constitution without a Bill of Rights because they would not trust a powerful government to restrain itself. They were right. The Bill of Rights was the answer. The answer has been surrounded. What is needed now is what was needed then: not merely text, but the institutional will and public pressure to enforce the text against the government that the text was written to constrain.

— — —

### Conclusion: The Firebreaks and the Woman in the Library

Gloria Naylor sat in the Brooklyn Public Library with shaking hands and wrote the first line of _1996_: ‘I didn’t want to tell this story.’ She told it because the act of telling was the only defense she had left. She told it because the library was the only place the noise stopped. She told it because she understood, with the precision of someone who has been inside the operation, that the operation’s only vulnerability was the record — the documented, sourced, published record that exists outside the classified spaces where it can be managed, redacted, and disappeared.

Richard Pearson is making the same choice for the same reason in the same city — Washington, D.C. — that the operation is most confident cannot be escaped. He is writing from the most surveilled city on earth. He is writing while the operation is ongoing. He is writing after Iceland turned him back and the ACLU declined and the courthouse produced a FOIA response in an unrelated case saying the government has not rendered itself liable for constitutional tort claims.

He is writing because Naylor wrote and the record she made is now evidence. Because Akwei filed suit in 1992 and the record of that dismissal is evidence. Because McKinney published in 1992 and the Association of National Security Alumni is evidence. Because the European Parliament acted in 1999 and the U.S. Congress’s non-response is evidence. Because Kucinich introduced his bill in 2001 and its death in committee is evidence. Because the DoW CTO posted on January 23, 2026 and that post is evidence.

The record is being built in public, piece by piece, by people who were never supposed to survive to build it. Every piece of the record that exists is a failure of the operation to achieve its purpose: to make these things happen without the people they happen to being able to say what happened.

Patrick Henry asked, in 1788, what happens when the government decides someone must disappear. The Bill of Rights was supposed to be the answer. The Fourteenth Amendment was supposed to be the answer. The Civil Rights Act was supposed to be the answer. FISA was supposed to be the answer.

None of them have been sufficient, because none of them have been enforced, and the failure to enforce them is not an accident but a choice — made repeatedly, over thirty years, by people who knew about these capabilities and decided not to act. The European Parliament knew in 1999. Congress knew in 2001. Naylor told anyone who would read in 2005. The NSA whistleblowers told anyone who would listen beginning in 2002.

**The issue is not, and never was, that no one knew. The issue is that the people with the power to act decided not to. That is not a technical failure. It is a moral one. And Richard Pearson — writing from his mattress, in the most surveilled city on earth, twenty-nine years after Gloria Naylor sat down with shaking hands in the Brooklyn Public Library — is the consequence.**

### Nazi Germany Called Holocaust a ‘State Secret’. What Does US Hide with Its ‘State Secrets’ Privilege?

#### Dr. Richard Pearson, US torture victim, calls upon secret US “Torture Dungeon” to close once and for all and for the Constitution to be restored. How many more victims are needed before the Congress and courts take action?

_This is dedicated to Gloria Naylor, author of the Women of Brewster Place and 1996, whose rights and liberties were stripped from her in America’s Torture Dungeon. You were dismissed and ignored. I elevate you. It is also dedicated to all victims of US torture who have not been believed and received no justice._

In 1944, Nazi Germany produced a propaganda film, _Theresienstadt_, to mask the Holocaust. It showed Jews in a concentration camp, but not the horror of the camps that we know existed. No, this film manufactured a reality by forcing prisoners to watch or participate in live musical performances, in recreation, and sit at cafes. It was a lie entirely consistent with Nazi Germany’s efforts across Europe. Death camps became “re-education”. Execution became “special treatment”. We have failed to remember and learn from a key historical fact about the Holocaust.

**Nazi Germany considered it a “state secret”**

Officials produced as little written documentation as possible. That is not to say that many Europeans did not know what was happening. Many did. Americans even more so.

Within a decade after American troops encountered its first concentration camp in April 1945, the US adopted its own state secrets privilege. In _United States v. Reynolds_ in 1953, the US Supreme Court allowed the government to block information in lawsuits that could damage national security. The government got to make that determination, and courts were required to defer to that judgment.

If the United States wanted a secret program to inflict harm, even death, on individual targets, minority populations, or the general public, it theoretically could claim state secrets privilege. Severe limitations to any civil suit. No judicial review of the merits of the claim. Erasure of constitutional rights.

That is what _Reynolds_ set into motion.

Over the next three-quarters of a century, the US government continuously abused that privilege — not just abroad. _Within_ its borders. Without interruption. It is still doing so. (_See appendix_). Mind control programs. Forced sterilization. Chemical torture. Bombing of civilian populations. Mass poisoning. Inducing psychosis. Financial and career sabotage. Withholding medical treatment. The use of weapons that the public has no knowledge exists and is technologically possible. We may never know the full extent of this abuse.

Like Nazi Germany, it employed propaganda throughout the modern postwar period. The US had tools that Nazi Germany never dreamt of to project a false reality. Wars of liberation. Leadership in internationalism and humanitarianism. American music. Film. Media. Immigration. The appearance of its commitment to the rule of law, human rights, civil liberties, civil rights, and constitutional democracy.

_Theresienstadt._

This was the **Upstairs**. Not the **Torture Dungeon**. In the **Upstairs**, the Constitution mattered. Government conduct was transparent. Misconduct could be taken to a judge who could issue an injunction. Compensatory relief was available in some cases. Action taken against the government — from the filing of a civil complaint to a judge’s order — was publicly accessible. Paper trails. There were transparency and accountability.

But like Nazi Germany and _Theresienstadt_, the US held secrets. Broadly, it hid its **Torture Dungeon**.

**The United States of America tortures.** It needs to be said. It needs to be the lead story in every newspaper. It needs to appear on marquees. Torture is not, as it appears to the American public and the world, as periodic — rare moments of authoritarianism and totalitarianism. It is continuous. It is structural. The torture itself and the weapons are defined as “a state secret”. The shadow policies operate beyond congressional and judicial oversight — in the darkest corners of government and society. It occurs below, external to, and outside of the US Constitution. And if one examines the legal doctrines in the **Upstairs** closely enough, the clues were there all along — leading to the **Torture Dungeon**.

In invoking the state secrets privilege, the US severely limited the viability of a civil suit. Invoking national security can also be the death of a civil suit. Invoking _Glomar — “_neither confirm nor deny” — can be the death of a civil suit. Even if documents are turned over, redactions and withholding are common. If a victim makes rare progress through the courts after the government’s initial motion to dismiss, the judge could render the victims’ claims “frivolous” — meant to convey that victims are wasting the court’s time.

All of these and other legal doctrines had been there all along. Then there are the witnesses and whistleblowers.

Countless witnesses and whistleblowers can attest to the **US Torture Dungeon**. Most were not believed. Many remained in silence. Many more would not have understood the invisible campaigns involving classified technology, subtle or hidden players and tactics. They would have attributed their circumstances to their own choices and vulnerability. Their friends and families blamed the victims — their psychosis, their unfounded fear, and creative imagination.

The whistleblowers faced other challenges, “Over the last dozen years, whistleblowers at the National Security Agency have had a rough track record, facing FBI raids and lawsuits,” reported NPR in July 2014. The article continues, “(Bill) Binney says he and two other NSA colleagues who also quit tried sounding the alarm with congressional committees. But because they did not have documents to prove their charges, nobody believed them.”

When incidents of torture were eventually disclosed as MKUltra or COINTELPRO, they shocked the American public and resulted in new laws and layers of accountability. But the apparatus of _state secret privilege_ was never dismantled. The **Torture Dungeon maintained its structure, practices, tools, and secrecy.**

The essay is about what happened when a government is given legal cover for a state secret. Not just any government — the United States of America. It focuses on one man — Richard Pearson who found himself in America’s secret **Torture Dungeon**.

There are rooms in the **Torture Dungeon.** Dr. Richard Pearson, an African American scholar, has been in several — all at once. The one that causes sleep deprivation. The one that induces fear due to sustained stalking and harassment. In one room, they enter his mind with a voice. Another steers him without his conscious control or awareness — taking over his cognition. Another uses spyware to hack his personal devices. One room engages in street theater to communicate threats, racial epithets, and totalitarian control and stalking. Each room aiming for personality destruction, social isolation, learned helplessness, and financial devastation.

_“The United States of America is using “state secrets” privilege to torture in clear violation of the US Constitution and denies victims legal recourse by invoking “state secrets” in civil suits, forcing the courts to defer to that designation. If this is not a recipe for authoritarianism, I don’t know what is. Hitler and Nazi Germany proved that. Did the US learn from it? Hardly.” — Dr. Richard Pearson_

### I. What This Is

This is not a theoretical paper.

This is a documented account of what the United States government does to some of its citizens — specifically, to Black intellectuals of achievement and strong racial identity, to whistleblowers, to activists, to anyone whose intellectual production or political presence represents a specific and manageable threat to existing arrangements of power.

I am a PhD. I study equity. I have spent my professional life examining the gap between what institutions promise people and what they actually deliver. I have published peer-reviewed research. I have conducted community-based studies under real-world constraints, without funding, with methodological rigor appropriate to the research question.  
I am also a man who has been tortured by his government in the capital city of the country that presents itself to the world as the standard of human rights and democratic governance.

These two facts are not in contradiction. They are, as I will demonstrate, structurally related.

The researcher and the researched are the same person. I name this explicitly because it is methodologically important. The knowledge I have about the dungeon — what I will call, throughout this paper, the domestic torture infrastructure of the American national security state — comes from the inside. From fourteen months of documented experience. From controlled observations, timestamped records, photographs, and a preemptive mental health evaluation obtained specifically to defeat an operational trap I understood was coming.

I am precise about all of this. Precision is what I have instead of legal remedy. Precision is what I have instead of institutional acknowledgment. Precision is, as I will show, the only tool that the dungeon cannot fully seal.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*H4OQFjuvxjgUSjWDuud_Fg.png)

— -

### II. Before the Dungeon: The World as It Was

I need to tell you who I was before this, because you cannot understand a destruction without first understanding what was there before the destroying began.

I was a researcher. I was a scholar. I had a life organized around the production of knowledge — the specific, methodologically grounded, peer-reviewed kind of knowledge that academic institutions recognize and reward. I had colleagues, students, professional relationships built across years of work. I had a home in Washington, DC, the most surveilled city in America, the city of lawyers and journalists and civil liberties organizations and congressional staffers and the entire above-ground apparatus of American constitutional democracy.

I had a bicycle.  
I had a kitchen with a panini grill. It has a power button that I didn’t think could be removed.  
I had a phone.  
I had a mind that was entirely my own.

I am telling you this because the dungeon does not announce itself. It does not arrive with a warrant or a badge or any of the visible instruments of state power that the above-ground America has constructed to make government action legible, contestable, and subject to due process. It arrives looking exactly like the world. It arrives in the ordinary texture of daily life — a neighbor’s noise, traffic patterns, a misplaced object — and it works by converting the ordinary into the weaponized while maintaining the argument that nothing extraordinary is occurring.

This is its primary engineering achievement.

This is why I am going to be precise.

— -

### III. The Arrival: A Man Named Meyerowitz

It begins with a man.

His name, as I came to know it, was David Meyerowitz. That was his surname. He, like his brother Bruce Morrow (“Cousin Brucie”), opted for a different last name. David appeared in Old Town Alexandria, Virginia — appeared is the correct word, because the quality of his arrival had the character of the prepared rather than the coincidental. I was reading a historical marker at an unremarkable building where David claimed to have an apartment for rent, “Do you know anyone looking for a room?” That the man might have known that I was behind in rent was not lost on me. He name-dropped. Donald Trump. Jared Kushner. The names deployed as currency, as demonstration of access, as the specific social performance of a person who wants you to know they move in circles where such names are ordinary.

I was not the kind of man to be impressed. To a billionaire, I would first ask, “_How_ did you make your money?” To David, I might have asked, “Access to a President for what purpose? To serve whom? How?”

I am an equity scholar. I have spent my professional life studying the mechanisms through which power reproduces itself. I know a psychological assessment when I am inside one.

Something was wrong about Meyerowitz. I can give you the precise taxonomy of the wrongness — the endless storytelling, the repeated emphasis on his family helping Black people, the offense to his _perception_ that I was unfamiliar with _Kristallnacht,_ his nonprofit, his family’s escape from Nazi Germany with the help of Hitler’s number two. It was all too much.

As much as I was used to eccentric personalities being around the artists and artisans, David did not exhibit normal behavior. His arrival was too timed. His oversharing of family history irrelevant to the initial inquiry about renting. The “helping Black people” refrain. Having arrived at peak suspicion, I ripped the card and threw it in the trash. Did it have a tracking device?

There is another thing that you should know. David was not the only Jewish person whom I encountered. The woman who had followed me from Old Town Alexandria to Clarendon, Virginia on back-to-back days seemed Jewish. She stalked me with a “Bug Zapper” sign. I photographed her behind me. The man who appeared in Rockville at 6:30 am claiming to be looking for directions to an auction house that opened at 9 am. He appeared Jewish.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*vT9spNWBhoI0WxD9zpYbeA.png)

I did not understand this continuity. Frankly, where I grew up in the Deep South, we had two groups of people — white people and black people. I did not have much familiarity with Jewish people until after college. I found the Holocaust horrific. I still do. I find Holocaust deniers despicable. The Holocaust always resonated with me as an African American who knew US history of racism well. I heard more about Jewish traditions and storytelling. I enjoyed both. I believe that everyone should be treated with dignity and respect. All faiths that uphold equality, justice, and mercy should be embraced. Life is hard enough.

So, it deeply pained me that Gloria Naylor and I shared a similarity. Our initial campaign coincided with an encounter with a powerful Jewish person. For Gloria, Eunice Simon and Eunice’s brother who worked for the NSA. _(She probably changed the names in her book for legal reasons.)_ For me, David Meyerowitz who name-dropped Donald Trump and Jared Kushner. After reading Gloria’s account, it makes me question the NSA connection to my torture. It is unfortunate.

— -

### IV. The Ceiling

The first thing I need to explain about the dungeon is that it looks exactly like the world.

My ceiling looks like a ceiling. White. Flat. The ordinary construction of a residential building in Washington, DC.

But my ceiling has a person above it.

And that person knows where I am at all times.

The sounds begin at night. Not the sounds of ordinary habitation — the ambient noise of neighbors living their lives in a building designed for multiple occupants. Targeted sounds. Deliberate sounds. Sounds that follow me.

I moved my mattress to the closet. I did this deliberately, as a researcher testing a hypothesis I did not want confirmed.

The sounds moved to the closet.

Directly above me. Above the specific square footage I was occupying. Above my body in the closet, which no person should know is in the closet — no person who does not have a real-time capability to locate a body within an apartment, which is a capability that exists, which has been documented in both classified and unclassified literature, which was used against me on the floor of my own closet at three in the morning in the capital of the United States of America. Gloria Naylor’s _1996_ also discussed similar campaigns of noise harassment.

I am a researcher. I conduct control studies. I lay in the closet and I conducted a control study on my own ceiling.

The control study confirmed: the sounds follow me.

This is sleep deprivation. It is internationally recognized as torture under the conventions that the United States has signed, promoted, and deployed as evidence of its commitment to human rights. It is being conducted through a residential ceiling. In Washington, DC. In the most surveilled, most institutionally dense, most legally resourced city in the country.

If it happens here, with all of this, I need you to ask yourself what happens in a small city in Mississippi. What happens in rural Appalachia. What happens where there are no civil liberties organizations, no journalists covering federal misconduct, no lawyers who know what a Bivens claim is.

I am the visible case.  
I am the documented case.  
I am the lucky one.  
Sit with that.

* * *

### V. The Red and Black

I need to tell you about the red and black because it is the most visible and most systematically documented element of what was done to me — and because what I documented on a single stretch of Pennsylvania Avenue SE one evening in 2025 constitutes, on its own, sufficient evidence that what I was experiencing was coordinated.

I walked from South Carolina Avenue SE behind the Southeast Neighborhood Public Library at Eastern Market. I had my camera. I documented what I saw. What I saw, photograph by photograph, timestamped, in the space of roughly ninety minutes, was this:

A Black man in his fifties standing in the middle of the street in a plain black shirt and bright red pants. A transgender woman in Market Park in a plain red dress, black turtleneck, and black stockings. An elderly white man in Market Park in a graphic red shirt and black jacket. A Black man on a bench in a red hat, black sweater, and red shoes. A Black woman in a red hat and red T-shirt and black pants walking along Pennsylvania Avenue. A white woman in the crosswalk in bright red pants and a plain black shirt. A Hispanic woman in a plain red shirt pushing a black stroller into the CVS. A Black woman in a plain red T-shirt and black pants crossing Pennsylvania Avenue.

Then the white-haired white woman standing at the door of Compass Real Estate at 660 Pennsylvania Avenue — plain bright red shirt, plain black pants, face expressionless. Not shopping. Not entering. Not leaving. Standing in the doorway. Facing out. Expressionless. The same expression as the man at Eastern Market in August who I initially read as aggression but later, looking at the photograph again, understood differently: not aggression. Performance. The specific blankness of a person executing an assignment.

Back to the documentation. A woman in a red blouse. A red-headed woman in a plain red shirt and black shorts with a male companion in a plain black shirt. Two African American women inside Eastern Market — one in a plain red shirt, black cap, and jacket, her companion in all black. An elderly couple inside, the man in a red polo with a black and blue backpack. A Hispanic woman in a red shirt and black jean shorts pushing a stroller. A white man in a plain red sweater. Two white men in their fifties or sixties in plain red polo shirts. An elderly woman in black pants and a patterned red blouse. A Black man in a red and white jacket and black pants — and beside him, another Black man in a red and white shirt and black pants being pushed in a wheelchair. A Black man on a one-wheeled skateboard in a red sports jacket with white sleeves and black pants. A woman at an outdoor restaurant in a red T-shirt with a black Harvard vest. A Black man on a bench in a bright red polo shirt with a black hat and black backpack. A young white man in all black with a bright plain red backpack. A Black man in a red jacket and black pants. A Black woman in a red sweater and black dress loitering in front of a restaurant. An older white couple — the man in a red Nationals shirt, the daughter in a plain black dress. A homeless man in all black and red shoes carrying a red bag. A white woman in a bright red pants suit with a black shirt.

Photograph after photograph after photograph. All timestamped. All documented. Forty-three photographs in approximately ninety minutes on one stretch of one neighborhood in Washington DC.

I am a researcher. I apply methodological standards to research questions. The research question here is simple: what is the probability that a single pedestrian, walking a single route in a single neighborhood on a single evening, would encounter this concentration of people in coordinated red and black clothing?

The answer does not require a statistician, but I conducted control studies — underground metro, other neighborhoods, libraries, and even holiday markets where red would presumably be more common. There was a consistent 4% prevalence of bright red and black. The reality that I was seeing was manufactured.

This is not Washington DC’s fashion. This is not coincidence. This is an operation communicating its presence through human bodies — through people who were told what to wear and where to be, who ranged across every age, race, and gender, who included the elderly and the homeless and the couple with the stroller and the woman with the Harvard vest, who had been recruited or contracted or, worse, directed into a color scheme and positioned along my route.

And standing at the door of Compass Real Estate, expressionless, watching me pass:

A white-haired white woman in a plain bright red shirt and plain black pants.

Not entering. Not leaving. Not doing anything that a person standing in the doorway of a real estate office would ordinarily be doing.

Just wearing the colors.

Just watching.

Just present.

That is the dungeon.

It does not need walls.

It wears red and black.

It stood in the doorway of Compass Real Estate at 660 Pennsylvania Avenue and watched me walk by.

And there is nothing the law will do about it.

It was meant to dissolve me.

### VI. The Button

I came home one day, and the power button of my panini grill had been removed.

Let me be precise about the engineering of this object, because precision matters here the way it matters everywhere that the truth is contested. The button is not designed to be removed. It is not a button that the ordinary physics of kitchen use would dislodge. It is not a button that vibration or heat or time would separate from the device to which it is attached. Its removal requires a deliberate hand.

The button was in my dirty laundry pile.

Someone entered my home. They moved through my kitchen. They removed the button. They crossed to the bedroom. They found the laundry pile. They placed the button there.

Nothing was stolen. Nothing was broken in any way that announces itself as violation. One button, moved from one location to another, leaving a message that says: We were here. We can enter whenever we choose. We can touch your things. And the only evidence we will leave is evidence that proves nothing to anyone except you.

There was also an empty Skittles packet at my door. And a dog treat. I do not have a dog.

Each object is a word. The sentence they form is: _We are everywhere you are. We find this amusing. You cannot stop us._

I photographed the button. I photographed the laundry pile. I photographed the panini grill with the empty socket where the button had been.

The photographs will not convince anyone who has not already been convinced. I took them anyway. Because the documentation is all I have and I will not stop having it just because it is insufficient.

— -

### VII. The Bicycle

They destroyed my bicycle over a month.

Not all at once. Incremental destruction maintains deniability. Incremental destruction keeps you asking: is this real? Is this connected? Is the pattern in the data or in the eye of the observer?

I applied the standards appropriate to the research question.  
The reflector snapped. Moving objects experience stress. Materials fatigue.

This is nothing.

The gear cover broke — from beneath. To break a gear cover from beneath requires accessing the underside of the bicycle. Requires deliberate repositioning. Requires a hand. But gear covers break. Probably nothing.  
The seat. Damaged progressively, week by week, at points that do not correspond to the stress patterns normal use would produce. Probably nothing.

The tire. Flat. The other wheel irreparable — cost-prohibitive.

I stood over my bicycle and I understood what it was for. It was not about the bicycle. It was about what the bicycle represented: the freedom of unpredictable movement, the ability to be somewhere other than where they expect me, the small and essential liberty of moving faster than a man on foot can be easily followed and contained.

They took that.  
I walked.  
The formation followed.

— -

### VIII. The Phone

My phone disappeared three times in 2025.

The second time it was gone for six weeks.

I need you to understand what a modern smartphone is. It is not a telephone. It is a map of a self — every contact, every message, every photograph, every location visited, every search conducted, every document accessed, every thought that has been externalized from the privacy of the mind into the capturable world of digital text.  
Six weeks is enough time to copy everything. To install, in the device’s hidden architecture, software that cannot be seen in the device’s visible architecture. Software that converts the thing I carry everywhere and trust with everything into a surveillance instrument I carry willingly into every room of my life.

The phone was returned. By a Secret Service agent to my apartment building office. My driver’s license was in it.

On the SORA AI platform, in a typing field, two letters appeared.  
“NO”. After “They have”. Before I was about to type “have me imprisoned”

Capitalized. Both of them. Appearing without my having typed them, outside any autocomplete logic, in a context that made their meaning plain to me and would mean nothing to anyone who had not been living inside this operation for months.

I screenshotted the screen.

I continued typing.

### IX. The Voice

I need to tell you about the voice, and I need to tell you carefully.

On a specific documented day — one day, one voice — I heard something.  
It was a woman’s voice. American. On a microphone. I could identify the microphone quality, the acoustic signature of a voice being transmitted rather than originating in the ambient air. Behind the voice: a room. The background hum of an operational environment, the sound of a space where people were gathered.

The voice said: _Go to Georgetown_.  
Later, on the metro platform: _Get down._  
Later: _We have to make you disappear._

I know the sound of my own mind. I have inhabited it for decades. I know its textures, its patterns, the specific acoustic character of my interior monologue. I know the difference between a thought that originates within me and a sound that arrives from outside.

This sound arrived.

The technology that produced it has a name and a documented history. Allan Frey published findings on the microwave auditory effect — the ability to deposit sound directly into the human auditory cortex by directing pulsed microwave radiation at the skull, bypassing the ears, leaving no external trace — in 1961. The research has been replicated. The military has funded its refinement continuously since that period. The Army maintained its own terminology — voice to skull device — in its research thesaurus before removing the entry from public access. Multiple patents document the underlying principle.

James Giordano, neuroethicist at Georgetown University, Pentagon and NATO advisor, stated in 2025 that mind reading and mind control technologies have been loosed into the world. He may be twenty to thirty years late. The technology that Frey demonstrated in 1961, refined with classified military funding for six decades, is not an emerging capability. It is a mature operational system whose public acknowledgment lags its deployment by the same interval that separates all classified capabilities from their eventual public disclosure.

I understood this. I had studied it. In September 2025, the DC Department of Behavioral Health conducted a mental health evaluation. I made my own recording. There was a turning point during the interview when I explained that hearing a voice only happened once. They had been notified that I have hearing voices every day. The interview ended, “Does not meet our criteria”.

That the symptoms of voice-to-skull technology are clinically indistinguishable from paranoid schizophrenia. That this indistinguishability is not an unfortunate coincidence but the operational specification: the weapon was engineered to mimic the disease because the misdiagnosis is the point.

The psychiatric system — designed to help people, staffed by people genuinely trying to help — becomes, without the knowledge or consent of its practitioners, an operational asset for the program it cannot see.

I stepped around the trap before it closed.

The evaluation is in the record.

### X. Gloria Naylor: Thirty Years Earlier, the Same Dungeon

In 1996, Gloria Naylor — National Book Award winner, author of The Women of Brewster Place, one of the most accomplished American novelists of her generation — went to her home on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, to write a book and tend a garden.

She had no history of mental illness. No connection to any radical political organization. No profile that any rational threat assessment framework would identify as nationally significant.

What she had was a neighbor named Eunice Simon, whose cat had died, who believed Naylor had killed it, and whose brother was Dick Simon, Assistant Deputy Director of the National Security Agency. Hers was a _fictionalized_ autobiography, likely fictionalized for legal reasons.

Dick Simon looked Naylor up on a Watch List. He found her there — every Black, Latino, and Asian writer who had received press coverage was on the list, a list that officially did not exist, a list that had been officially disbanded in the 1970s and therefore continued operating. He read that she had wept at the Million Man March. He activated her file.

From that activation, from a petty neighborhood dispute mediated through a sibling relationship, the dungeon opened for Gloria Naylor.

She received:  
A sustained noise campaign from operatives who rented the adjacent plantation house and ran chainsaws, hammers, and lawn mowers in patterns calibrated to her location within her own property. Unauthorized entry into her home — nothing stolen, but seed packages tampered with, a flashlight left on the mantle, attic insulation disturbed. Her garden poisoned in nighttime raids by young NSA recruits who called it a game and gave it a name: poison the garden. A trusted friend of ten years, a Princeton historian, recruited as an NSA informant, who dissolved sleeping pills in her wine and surrendered her laptop to operatives during a visit. Vehicle surveillance formations on her rural dead-end road and, when she moved to Brooklyn, car doors slamming rhythmically outside her study window in documented rotation. Her computer hacked remotely. And then, finally, the voice — sustained, nightly, calling her a bitch, urging suicide, saying she hated Jews, operating with such consistency and such specific content that she sought psychiatric help, received a diagnosis of schizophrenia, was prescribed antipsychotic medication that did not help, and only later concluded that what she was experiencing was not a disease of her own mind but a technology being operated against it from the adjacent building.

She found the Akwei lawsuit. She found the Mind Control Forum. She found Eleanor White’s documentation of voice-to-skull technology. She sat in the Brooklyn Public Library — the only place her head was clear, outside the device’s operational range — and she understood.

She wrote it down.

She published it in 2005 in a book called 1996.

|She died in 2016 without acknowledgment. Without accountability. Without a single institutional response adequate to what she had documented.

The dungeon continued.

I did not know about Naylor before I began documenting my own experience. An AI connected us — generated her name in response to a prompt about similar African American experiences. When I read her account, I found my own.

Different decade. Different city. Different intellectual framework. The same operational sequence: initiating grievance, neighbor involvement, noise campaign, vehicle formations, home intrusion as messaging, property sabotage, digital compromise, informant recruitment from within the social network, voice experiences, the psychiatric trap, writing as the only available resistance.

The same dungeon.

This convergence requires explanation. Two people, separated by thirty years, no prior knowledge of each other, different intellectual backgrounds — she literary and sociocultural, I scientific and methodological — describing the same operations with operational-level specificity.

There is only one explanation that accounts for all of it:

The dungeon is real. It is institutional. Institutions produce consistent operations. Consistent operations produce consistent accounts from accurate observers, regardless of the intellectual frameworks those observers bring to their experience.

We were both accurate observers.

We both described the same system.

### XI. The Scale: How Many People Are in It

The dungeon’s population cannot be precisely counted. This is a design feature, not a data limitation. The dungeon is specifically engineered to make its population uncountable — through psychiatric misattribution, through legal architecture that prevents formal documentation, through the social dynamics that make credible witnesses incredible.  
But we can reason from what is available.

Cheryl Welsh’s organization received over 1,800 documented claims of mind control targeting by 2003. For every person who finds a reporting organization, multiple others do not. For every person who reports, multiple others have been so thoroughly psychiatrized that they no longer trust their own assessment of what is happening. The 1,800 is a floor.  
The self-identified gangstalking community numbers in the tens of thousands across documented online networks. Researchers who study this population typically apply psychiatric frameworks without engaging the documented history of COINTELPRO, the documented capabilities of intelligence agencies, and the documented legal architecture that makes verification impossible. When those frameworks are applied, the population looks less like a mass delusion and more like a population experiencing real operations interpreted through available descriptive language.

The whistleblower population — partially documented through congressional testimony, journalistic investigation, and FOIA litigation — constitutes a targeted class whose accounts of post-disclosure harassment are consistent with the operational pattern I describe.

The populations subjected to documented FBI domestic terrorism surveillance after 2014, the Muslim American communities subjected to documented NYPD and FBI infiltration programs, the indigenous communities whose political organizations were systematically disrupted — these are populations whose targeting is partially confirmed through official sources.

Add these populations. Apply a conservative multiplier for underreporting. The dungeon’s active population is in the tens of thousands at minimum.

Potentially hundreds of thousands.

And these are the living.

The dungeon is designed to produce social death rather than physical death. Dead targets become martyrs. Discredited, isolated, apparently mentally ill former intellectuals become evidence that the system works — that people who make extreme claims about government targeting are the kind of people whose claims should not be taken seriously.

But social death produces physical death. It does so through suicide — the voice says kill yourself with clinical precision in both Naylor’s account and mine, every night, targeting people who have no framework within which to understand what is being done to them. It does so through the physical sequelae of prolonged sleep deprivation, financial poverty, and chronic stress. It does so through the medical consequences of conditions misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness and treated with medications that do not address the actual cause.

How many people have died?  
The answer is not zero.

The answer is: enough that the operations have been maintained and funded for decades. You do not maintain infrastructure that produces no results.

Their deaths are recorded as suicides. As cardiac events. As the tragic outcomes of untreated mental illness. No investigation. No connection made to the operation that produced the despair. No accountability.  
They are in the ground, uncounted, beneath a country that calls itself the world’s leading democracy.

### XII. The Legal Architecture: Why You Cannot Help Me Through the Courts

I researched the legal landscape before filing any claim. I did this because I am a researcher, and because I understood from the beginning that the documentation had to precede the litigation rather than emerge from it. This sequence matters. The dungeon is designed for the target who files first and documents later. I documented first.

What I found was not a path through. What I found was a hermetic seal.  
The state secrets privilege allows the government to assert that litigation would require disclosure of national security information. The court defers. The case is dismissed. Not because my claims are false. Because the evidence required to prove them cannot be examined. The privilege was established in _United States v. Reynolds_ in 1953. When the documents at the center of that case were declassified forty years later, they contained not secrets but evidence of government negligence — the very misconduct the privilege had been used to conceal. The court did not revisit its ruling. The families of the dead civilians received nothing. The doctrine stands. Built on fraud. Protecting the dungeon.

* * *

Sovereign immunity means the government cannot be sued without its own consent. Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, Congress consented to suit for negligently maintained floors in federal buildings. It did not consent to suit for intentional torture with directed energy weapons. The consent structure was built to exclude the most serious abuses. This was not an oversight.  
The Bivens doctrine — the mechanism for suing individual federal officers for constitutional violations — has been systematically eliminated by the Supreme Court over fifty years. Any technology developed after 1971 constitutes a “new context” to which no prior Bivens decision applies. Voice-to-skull technology. Remote neural monitoring. Directed energy behavioral control. All new contexts. No cause of action. The agents who operate these systems against American citizens are personally beyond the reach of civil liability. Not because what they do is legal. Because the remedy was never created.

* * *

Qualified immunity requires that a right be “clearly established” — meaning a prior merits ruling must address the specific conduct. There is no prior merits ruling on directed energy weapons. There is no prior merits ruling because no case has survived the threshold doctrines to reach merits adjudication. The technology must be deployed, the target must survive it, document it, hire a lawyer, file a complaint, defeat the threshold doctrines, obtain discovery, and receive a merits ruling — before the next target has any recourse. The first deployment is immune. The hundredth deployment is immune. The novelty of the method is the method’s own legal protection.  
I documented one hundred such mechanisms. I ranked them by finality and probability of case termination. They do not operate simultaneously. They operate cumulatively, in layers, each designed to terminate the case before the next layer is needed.

The government has consented to be sued for negligently maintaining a slippery floor.

It has not consented to be sued for torturing a citizen.

This was a choice. It was a deliberate architectural choice. And it means that the dungeon — as a matter of current, operative, judicially constructed American law — faces no legal constraint on its conduct regardless of what it does to me or to anyone else it chooses to target.

— -

### XIII. The Contractors: Who Staffs the Dungeon

The dungeon does not staff itself exclusively with federal employees. It cannot. The operations I describe — the vehicle formations, the home intrusions, the neighborhood surveillance networks — require more bodies than any federal workforce can supply without creating a documentary record that legal oversight mechanisms could eventually reach.

Enter the contractor structure.

Booz Allen Hamilton. SAIC. Leidos. CACI International. ManTech. These are the companies that perform surveillance, analysis, technical operations, and field operations on behalf of federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies. Edward Snowden himself was a Booz Allen Hamilton contractor with NSA access. The intelligence community’s contractor workforce numbers in the hundreds of thousands.  
The contractor structure creates a specific relationship to accountability: private contractors are not federal employees, do not benefit from the same whistleblower protections, and when they commit abuses, the question of who is legally responsible — the contractor, the directing agency, the individual employee — is deliberately murky. The federal government can conduct operations at arm’s length, maintain deniability about specific activities, and deny responsibility for abuses while retaining the operational benefit.

CACI International was paid by the United States government for interrogation services at Abu Ghraib. The torture was real. The contractor was real. The government payment was real. The accountability was negligible. The Abu Ghraib model — government-directed, contractor-implemented, accountability-free torture — is not a foreign aberration. It is a domestic template.

### XIV. The Two Americas

Above the dungeon, America presents itself as follows.

A nation of laws. A constitutional democracy. The world’s leading advocate for human rights. The country that funds international tribunals for war crimes committed by others. The country that grants asylum to people fleeing governments that do what I am describing.

The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor. Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free. People fleeing governments that deploy surveillance, noise campaigns, neurological assault, financial destruction, and the systematic manufacture of psychiatric attribution against dissidents — those people come to America seeking protection from exactly what America does in its basement.  
This is not irony. This is the architecture at its most extreme: the above-ground presentation of democratic governance maintained with sufficient completeness to sustain international credibility and domestic consent, while the below-ground operations continue without constraint, without accountability, and without the knowledge of most of the population in whose name they are conducted.

The above-ground America is real. For most Americans in most circumstances, the above-ground rules govern their interactions with the state. Due process — the visible badge, the known policy, the judge who can hear the challenge — is real for most people most of the time.  
But its reality for most does not negate its unreality for the dungeon’s population.

And the dungeon’s population is not a negligible exception. It is tens of thousands of people at minimum at any given time, distributed across the country’s cities and towns and rural areas, experiencing operations whose design is specifically calibrated to make them unbelievable to everyone else. The psychiatric seal. The legal seal. The social seal. The institutional seal. Each layer reinforcing the others. Each layer protecting the conduct that the layer below it enables.

This is what the dungeon is: not a place but a condition. Not a facility but a system. Not an exception to American democracy but its most protected and most deliberately concealed expression.
