### A Documented Record of State-Sanctioned Abuse, Torture, and Systemic Violence in the Post-War United States and Its Proxies

* * *

### I. Nuclear, Radiological & Chemical Weapons Testing on Human Populations

*   **Trinity Test fallout (1945)** — The first nuclear detonation showered New Mexico communities, predominantly Hispano and Native, with radioactive fallout. Residents were never warned, evacuated, or compensated. Cancer rates in the region remain anomalously elevated.
*   **Atomic bomb tests over Marshall Islands (Operation Crossroads, Castle Bravo, et al., 1946–1958)** — 67 nuclear weapons detonated over Marshallese homelands. Castle Bravo (1954) was 1,000 times more powerful than Hiroshima. Populations were forcibly relocated; many were returned to contaminated atolls as unwitting guinea pigs to measure radiation uptake. The AEC monitored them as “the closest thing to control human subjects.”
*   **Nevada Test Site “Downwinders” (1951–1992)** — Over 100 atmospheric tests rained fallout on Utah, Nevada, and Arizona. Communities — again, disproportionately Mormon, Navajo, and rural — were told the tests were safe. A 1997 National Cancer Institute study found at least 75,000 excess thyroid cancer cases.
*   **Operation Plumbbob (1957)** — 29 nuclear detonations; approximately 18,000 U.S. troops forced to maneuver near ground zero without radiation protection as part of psychological and tactical experiments.
*   **Operation Teapot & Tumbler-Snapper** — Soldiers trenched within yards of detonations; some were ordered to march toward the blast site immediately after detonation.
*   **Human plutonium injection experiments (1945–1947)** — At least 18 patients at University of Chicago, Rochester, UC San Francisco, and Oak Ridge hospitals were injected with plutonium by Manhattan Project scientists without consent. Many were terminally ill; some were not.
*   **Uranium injections (1946)** — Army doctors injected patients at Rochester with uranium solutions to study kidney toxicity thresholds.
*   **Total Body Irradiation experiments (1950s–1970s)** — Cincinnati General Hospital, funded by the DOD, administered whole-body radiation to cancer patients, mostly low-income Black Cincinnatians, primarily to study combat incapacitation effects rather than for therapeutic benefit.
*   **Operation Sea-Spray (1950)** — U.S. Navy sprayed _Serratia marcescens_ and _Bacillus globigii_ over San Francisco from offshore vessels. Dozens were hospitalized; one man died. The Army denied responsibility for 20 years.
*   **Army biological aerosol tests in subways (1966)** — Army researchers released _Bacillus subtilis_ var. niger (a simulant) into New York City subway ventilation systems; millions of commuters inhaled the agent unknowingly.
*   **Operation LAC (1957–58)** — Army aircraft dropped cadmium sulfide particles over 33 states from South Dakota to the Gulf Coast to model aerosol dispersion patterns.
*   **Operation Dew / Big Itch / Big Buzz** — Open-air releases of mosquitoes, fleas, and other vectors to test biological weapon delivery systems over U.S. and Caribbean territories.
*   **Project SHAD / Project 112 (1962–1973)** — At least 134 tests of biological and chemical agents — VX nerve agent, sarin, plague, tularemia — conducted on U.S. Navy ships, exposing thousands of sailors who were never informed.
*   **Agent Orange (Vietnam, 1961–1971)** — 20 million gallons of dioxin-contaminated herbicide sprayed over South Vietnam. At least 400,000 Vietnamese died or were disabled; 500,000 children born with defects. U.S. veterans denied compensation for decades while chemical companies (Dow, Monsanto) withheld internal toxicity data showing known risks.
*   **FEMA / Pentagon “Continuity of Government” radiological preparedness experiments** — Post-Katrina evidence of civilian population radiological exposure modeling that treated urban populations as modeling variables.

* * *

### II. Mind Control, Psychological Torture & Behavioral Weaponization

*   **Project CHATTER (1947–1953)** — U.S. Navy program testing mescaline and other drugs as truth serums on human subjects, inspired directly by Nazi experiments.
*   **Project BLUEBIRD / ARTICHOKE (1950–1956)** — CIA programs using hypnosis, barbiturates, amphetamines, and physical coercion to produce amnesia, false confessions, and programmable behavior. Conducted on prisoners, mental patients, and foreign nationals.
*   **MKUltra (1953–1973)** — 150+ subprojects across 80 institutions including 44 universities, 15 research foundations, 12 hospitals, and 3 prisons. Used LSD, heroin, mescaline, methamphetamine, electroconvulsive therapy, sensory deprivation, hypnosis, verbal and sexual abuse, and induced trauma. Most records destroyed by CIA Director Richard Helms in 1973. At least two known deaths: Frank Olson (thrown from a 13th-floor window) and Harold Blauer (lethal mescaline injection).
*   **Ewen Cameron / MKULTRA Subproject 68 (Montreal, 1957–1964)** — CIA-funded psychiatrist at McGill University subjected patients to chemically-induced sleep for weeks or months, massive electroshock (30–40x standard dose), drug cocktails, and psychic driving (looped audio messages played through helmets). Patients arrived with mild depression; many emerged with complete amnesia, permanent regression to childlike states, and destroyed identities. Canada paid reparations; the U.S. did not.
*   **Operation Paperclip (1945–1959)** — Over 1,600 Nazi scientists, engineers, and physicians — including SS officers and those who conducted experiments at Dachau and Auschwitz — recruited by the U.S. government, given new identities, and integrated into military and intelligence programs. War crimes records were falsified.
*   **Subproject 54 (“Black Witch”)** — Studied inducing concussions and amnesia through non-detectable means; no known survivors identified.
*   **Project OFTEN (1962–1973)** — CIA and Army study of occultism, drug-induced states, and exotic toxins as means of behavioral control.
*   **Psychic Driving on Veterans (VA hospitals, 1950s–60s)** — Techniques developed under Cameron were replicated at U.S. VA hospitals on veterans without consent.
*   **Sensory deprivation research (McGill, NIMH, CIA funding)** — Isolation tank and sensory deprivation experiments developed into SERE (Survival, Evasion, Resistance, Escape) training and later reverse-engineered into CIA “enhanced interrogation” techniques post-9/11.
*   **SERE reverse-engineering (2001–2007)** — The DOD’s JPRA (Joint Personnel Recovery Agency) reversed SERE training — designed to help soldiers _resist_ torture — into an active torture program. Psychologists James Mitchell and Bruce Jessen, contracted by the CIA, designed the program and were paid $81 million.

* * *

### III. Biological & Medical Experimentation Without Consent

*   **Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972)** — 399 Black men with syphilis in Macon County, Alabama were studied by the U.S. Public Health Service for 40 years. They were told they were being treated for “bad blood,” actively denied penicillin after it became the standard cure in 1947, and followed to autopsy. When discovered by journalist Jean Heller in 1972, 28 men had died of syphilis, 100 of complications, 40 wives were infected, and 19 children were born with congenital syphilis.
*   **Guatemala STD experiments (1946–1948)** — U.S. PHS researchers deliberately infected Guatemalan prisoners, psychiatric patients, soldiers, orphans, and sex workers with syphilis, gonorrhea, and chancroid — sometimes through open wounds — without any consent. Approximately 1,300 people infected; 83 confirmed deaths. Funded by the NIH; concealed until 2010.
*   **Willowbrook Hepatitis experiments (1956–1970)** — Children with intellectual disabilities at Willowbrook State School on Staten Island were deliberately infected with hepatitis to study disease progression and vaccine candidates. Parents were coerced into consent by threatening to deny their children admission.
*   **Stateville Penitentiary Malaria Study (1944–1946)** — Hundreds of Illinois inmates infected with malaria. Researchers included Nathan Leopold of the Leopold and Loeb case.
*   **Holmesburg Prison experiments (1951–1974)** — Dermatologist Albert Kligman (later famous for inventing Retin-A) conducted hundreds of experiments on Philadelphia prisoners: dioxin exposure, radioactive isotope injections, psychoactive drug testing for the Army, carcinogen patch tests for Dow Chemical, and pathogen inoculations for Johnson & Johnson. Kligman reportedly said on first entering Holmesburg: “All I saw before me were acres of skin.”
*   **Fernald State School experiments (1946–1953)** — MIT researchers fed radioactive iron and calcium to intellectually disabled children in oatmeal, funded by the Atomic Energy Commission and Quaker Oats, to study nutrient absorption. Parents were told children were joining a “science club.”
*   **Vanderbilt Nutrition Study (1945–1946)** — Pregnant low-income women given radioactive iron cocktails by Vanderbilt University without informed consent; several children later developed cancer.
*   **VA electroshock and drug experiments (1950s–1970s)** — Veterans used as experimental subjects for antipsychotics, LSD, and electroconvulsive therapy without informed consent at multiple VA hospitals.
*   **DOD LSD field tests on soldiers (1950s–60s)** — Thousands of military personnel administered LSD without knowledge in Army Chemical Corps experiments at Edgewood Arsenal; others given BZ (a powerful hallucinogen) and nerve agents including VX and GB.
*   **Edgewood Arsenal experiments (1948–1975)** — 7,000 U.S. soldiers exposed to over 250 chemical agents: nerve agents, blister agents, psychoactive compounds, and riot control agents.
*   **Syphilis experiments on Guatemalan orphans** — Children in Catholic orphanages used as infection vectors; nuns reported some were used repeatedly.
*   **CDC “Let Them Eat Cake” lead paint studies (2001)** — Johns Hopkins Kennedy Krieger Institute intentionally placed Black children in homes with known varying lead paint levels to study abatement thresholds, without disclosing risk to families. A Maryland court compared it to Tuskegee.
*   **COVID-19 prison experiments** — During the pandemic, federal and state prisons maintained infection conditions that functioned as involuntary exposure studies, with outcomes tracked by public health systems.
*   **Unethical pharmaceutical trials on incarcerated populations (ongoing)** — Despite post-Nuremberg reforms, prison pharmaceutical testing continued through the 1970s and loopholes allow ongoing exploitation of captive populations.

* * *

### IV. Forced Sterilization & Reproductive Violence

*   **Eugenic sterilization under state laws (1907–1970s)** — Thirty-three states enacted compulsory sterilization statutes. The _Buck v. Bell_ (1927) Supreme Court decision upheld them; Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote “three generations of imbeciles are enough.” Approximately 60,000–65,000 Americans sterilized — disproportionately poor, immigrant, disabled, and Black.
*   **California’s eugenic program** — The most aggressive in the nation: approximately 20,000 people sterilized, providing a model that Nazi physicians explicitly studied and cited.
*   **Puerto Rican mass sterilization / “La Operación” (1930s–1970s)** — U.S.-administered program resulted in roughly one-third of Puerto Rican women being sterilized, often through coercion, misinformation, or without understanding the permanence of the procedure. By 1968, Puerto Rico had the highest per-capita sterilization rate in the world.
*   **Native American sterilization via Indian Health Service (1970–1976)** — A GAO investigation revealed the IHS sterilized 3,406 Native women in a four-year period in just four of twelve service areas; broader estimates range from 25,000 to 50,000 women sterilized during the decade. Many were minors; many signed consent forms during labor under threat of losing welfare benefits or child custody.
*   **North Carolina Eugenics Board (1929–1974)** — Among the most aggressive state programs; operated until 1974, targeting Black women and girls. North Carolina became the first state to pay reparations ($10 million) to survivors in 2013.
*   **California prison sterilizations (2006–2010)** — At least 148 female inmates at Valley State Prison and California Institution for Women were sterilized, many without proper informed consent. A state audit confirmed “deficiencies” in the consent process. No criminal charges were filed.
*   **ICE detention sterilizations (2020)** — Whistleblower Dawn Wooten alleged a gynecologist at the Irwin County Detention Center in Georgia was performing hysterectomies on immigrant women at an extraordinary rate, often without clear informed consent or medical necessity. Congressional investigations confirmed high rates of unexplained procedures.
*   **Mississippi appendectomy** — The informal practice of performing unnecessary hysterectomies on Black women in Southern teaching hospitals for medical student training; named and described by Fannie Lou Hamer, who was herself sterilized without consent in 1961.

* * *

### V. Domestic Surveillance, Political Repression & Infiltration

*   **COINTELPRO (1956–1971)** — The FBI’s Counter Intelligence Program targeted the Communist Party, Socialist Workers Party, Puerto Rican independence movement, American Indian Movement, Black Panther Party, Nation of Islam, SCLC, SNCC, and antiwar organizations. Tactics included: informant infiltration, forged letters to incite internal conflict, “snitch-jacketing” (falsely labeling members as informants to provoke violence), blackmail, fabricated evidence, and coordination with local police to conduct raids. Fred Hampton, 21-year-old Black Panther chairman, was killed in a pre-dawn FBI-coordinated raid while asleep; internal documents later revealed the FBI paid the informant who provided the floor plan.
*   **FBI surveillance and harassment of Martin Luther King Jr.** — Wiretapped for years; J. Edgar Hoover called him “the most dangerous Negro in America.” The FBI sent King an anonymous letter explicitly urging him to commit suicide days before he received the Nobel Peace Prize. The Senate Church Committee later called this “one of the most shameful chapters in the history of the Bureau.”
*   **Operation CHAOS (CIA, 1967–1974)** — Illegal CIA domestic surveillance of over 7,200 American citizens and 1,000 organizations including antiwar groups, civil rights organizations, and journalists. Created a database of 300,000 names.
*   **HTLINGUAL / Mail Opening Program (1953–1973)** — CIA and FBI opened, photographed, and resealed first-class mail of American citizens for 20 years. Over 215,000 letters were opened; targets included senators, congressmen, businessmen, and artists.
*   **Operation SHAMROCK (1945–1975)** — NSA intercepted every international telegram sent from or to the United States, with cooperation from RCA, ITT, and Western Union. Three major companies handed over millions of cables daily for 30 years.
*   **Operation MINARET (1967–1973)** — NSA watchlist-based surveillance of American antiwar activists, Black Power leaders, and journalists, including Muhammad Ali, Jane Fonda, Dr. Benjamin Spock, Senator Frank Church, and journalists.
*   **Red Squads (1900s–1990s)** — Municipal police intelligence units in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, and elsewhere operated decades-long infiltration and harassment operations against labor unions, socialist organizations, civil rights groups, and LGBTQ+ organizations. The NYPD’s BOSSI (Bureau of Special Services) had files on over one million people.
*   **NSA STELLARWIND / PRISM / XKeyscore (2001–present)** — Post-9/11 bulk collection of domestic phone metadata, email content, internet browsing history, and social media data without individual warrants, revealed by Edward Snowden in 2013. The FISA Court later ruled the phone metadata program illegal.
*   **FBI “Black Identity Extremist” (BIE) designation (2017)** — The FBI created a fabricated domestic terrorism category to justify surveillance of Black activists in the post-Ferguson era, with no statutory basis and no criminal conduct required for targeting.
*   **Muslim community surveillance (NYPD Demographics Unit, post-9/11)** — NYPD’s Intelligence Division, with CIA assistance, conducted mass surveillance of Muslim communities across the Northeast, mapping mosques, restaurants, schools, and student groups with no predicate criminal activity. Revealed by the AP in 2011.
*   **Fusion Centers surveillance overreach** — Post-9/11 “terrorism fusion centers” across all 50 states compiled intelligence on political demonstrators, environmental activists, veterans’ groups, and Tea Party organizations with no criminal nexus.
*   **Joint Terrorism Task Force targeting of climate activists** — FBI JTTF infiltrated and designated environmental activists (including Standing Rock water protectors) as domestic terrorists while coordinating with pipeline companies.
*   **Chicago Police Homan Square black site** — Off-the-books interrogation facility operated by the Chicago Police Department where detainees were held incommunicado, shackled to walls, denied access to lawyers, and in some cases subjected to physical coercion. The Guardian documented over 7,000 detainees processed through the site.

* * *

### VI. Torture, Detention & Rendition

*   **Operation Phoenix (Vietnam, 1965–1972)** — CIA-designed program that tortured, “neutralized,” and assassinated an estimated 20,000–40,000 Vietnamese civilians suspected of supporting the NLF. William Colby, later CIA director, acknowledged before Congress that many killed were not proven combatants. Techniques included waterboarding (called “the water treatment”), electric shock, and the “tiger cages” at Con Son prison.
*   **School of the Americas / WHINSEC (Fort Benning, 1946–present)** — U.S. military training institution whose graduates include some of the most documented torturers and death squad commanders in Latin American history: Roberto D’Aubuisson (El Salvador death squads), Hugo Banzer (Bolivian dictator), Manuel Noriega, Leopoldo Galtieri (Argentina’s Dirty War). In 1996, the Pentagon was forced to release training manuals that explicitly recommended torture, blackmail, and execution. Over 60,000 Latin American military officers trained.
*   **Operation Condor (1975–1989)** — U.S. State Department and CIA coordinated intelligence sharing, operational support, and logistics for a network of South American dictatorships — Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, Brazil — that disappeared, tortured, and murdered an estimated 60,000 people, including American citizens. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger authorized U.S. participation; his cables were declassified in 2001.
*   **Abu Ghraib (2003–2004)** — Systematic torture, sexual humiliation, rape, and murder of Iraqi detainees by U.S. military personnel. The Taguba Report confirmed these were not isolated incidents but the product of command climate, intelligence directives, and private contractor involvement (CACI International). Only low-ranking soldiers were prosecuted.
*   **CIA “Enhanced Interrogation” Program / Black Sites (2001–2007)** — Senate Intelligence Committee report (2014) documented that the CIA subjected at least 119 detainees to: waterboarding (Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 183 times), “rectal rehydration” without medical justification (acknowledged as a control technique), sleep deprivation for up to 180 hours in stress positions, walling, confinement in small boxes, mock executions, threats to rape and murder detainees’ family members, hypothermia, and “rough takedowns.” The program produced no unique intelligence not obtainable through legal means, according to the Committee’s findings. The CIA misled Congress and the White House about the program’s scope and effectiveness.
*   **Guantánamo Bay (2002–present)** — Over 780 people detained; the majority released without charge. Ongoing indefinite detention without trial for remaining detainees. Documented force-feeding of hunger strikers (recognized as cruel and degrading treatment under international law), prolonged isolation, and religious humiliation. Military commissions have produced fewer than a dozen convictions.
*   **Extraordinary Rendition Program** — CIA abducted individuals from at least 54 countries and transported them to third-party nations (Egypt, Syria, Morocco, Uzbekistan, Thailand) known to practice torture. German citizen Khaled El-Masri was kidnapped by mistake, held and tortured for five months; the CIA knew within a month he was the wrong person and held him anyway.
*   **Drone assassination program / Targeted killing (2001–present)** — Over 14,000 U.S. drone strikes across Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Yemen, Somalia, Pakistan, and Libya. Bureau of Investigative Journalism estimates 8,000–16,000 civilian deaths. The Obama administration’s “signature strike” program authorized killing unidentified individuals based on behavioral patterns (“military-age males” in “conflict zones”). The kill list (“disposition matrix”) was reviewed by the President in weekly meetings. No judicial oversight; no due process. American citizens Anwar al-Awlaki and his 16-year-old son Abdulrahman were killed in separate strikes; neither was charged with a crime.
*   **JSOC assassination and detention networks** — Joint Special Operations Command operated parallel detention facilities in Iraq (“Camp Nama”) and Afghanistan with documented use of torture, sleep deprivation, and homicide. Operated outside the Army Field Manual and the Geneva Conventions.
*   **Manning, Torture by Isolation (2010–2011)** — Chelsea Manning was held in solitary confinement at Quantico for 11 months under conditions a United Nations Special Rapporteur on Torture formally called “cruel, inhumane, and degrading.” Manning was kept in a 6x8 foot cell 23 hours per day, forced to stand naked during inspections, and denied meaningful human contact.

* * *

### VII. Indigenous Peoples: Genocide, Cultural Destruction & Ongoing Dispossession

*   **Federal Indian boarding schools (1869–1970s)** — Over 400 federally funded schools forcibly removed an estimated 150,000 Native children from their families. Children were forbidden to speak their languages, practice their religions, wear traditional clothing, or use their Native names under penalty of physical punishment. Sexual, physical, and psychological abuse was widespread and systemic. A 2022 Interior Department investigation identified at least 53 burial sites at former school properties.
*   **Carlisle Indian Industrial School** — The model institution under Richard Pratt, whose stated philosophy was “Kill the Indian, save the man.” Children were regularly worked as unpaid agricultural and domestic labor, “leased out” to white families, and subjected to military-style discipline and physical punishment. Death rates were high; Carlisle’s cemetery holds the remains of children who died far from home.
*   **Termination Policy (1953–1968)** — Congress unilaterally terminated federal recognition of over 100 tribes, ending trust protections and forcing the sale of tribal lands. 1.4 million acres of Indian land were lost. Health services, education funding, and treaty rights were stripped.
*   **Relocation Program (1950s–1960s)** — Federal program relocated approximately 100,000 Native Americans from reservations to cities (Chicago, Los Angeles, Denver, San Francisco) with promises of housing and jobs that rarely materialized, creating urban poverty and disconnecting people from their communities and support systems.
*   **Water rights theft and dam construction** — Federal dam projects flooded the homelands of dozens of nations without consent: Garrison Dam (Three Affiliated Tribes, 1953), Kinzua Dam (Seneca Nation, 1960s), Tellico Dam (Cherokee, 1979). Over 1 million acres of tribal land flooded.
*   **Uranium mining on Navajo Nation (1944–1986)** — 4 million tons of uranium ore extracted from Navajo land using Navajo workers who were never told of radiation risks. Hundreds of abandoned mine sites remain unreclaimed. Diné communities continue to suffer elevated rates of cancer, kidney disease, and birth defects. EPA cleanup has been slow and incomplete for decades.
*   **DAPL / Standing Rock (2016–2017)** — U.S. Army Corps of Engineers rerouted the Dakota Access Pipeline from north of Bismarck (rejected due to proximity to the city’s water supply) to directly under the Missouri River, above the Standing Rock Sioux reservation’s water supply. Water protectors — peaceful protesters — were subjected to water cannons in sub-zero temperatures, rubber bullets, acoustic weapons, mass arrest, and FBI/JTTF surveillance.
*   **Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW)** — Indigenous women are murdered at 10 times the national average. FBI case files show extraordinary non-prosecution rates. The National Crime Information Center has no specific category for MMIW cases, making the scope systematically unmeasurable. Many perpetrators operate with impunity on the jurisdictional boundaries between tribal, state, and federal authority.
*   **Forced relocation of Diné (Navajo-Hopi Land Dispute, 1970s–present)** — Over 12,000 Navajo people forcibly relocated from Big Mountain / Black Mesa in what has been called by some human rights scholars the largest forced relocation of Native Americans since the Trail of Tears, driven by competing energy extraction interests.

* * *

### VIII. Forced Sterilization & Reproductive Violence (expanded above — see Section IV)

* * *

### IX. Environmental Racism & Deliberate Contamination

*   **Flint water crisis (2014–present)** — Michigan state officials knowingly switched Flint’s water source to the Flint River to cut costs, failed to apply corrosion controls, and actively denied and suppressed evidence that the city’s pipes were leaching lead into drinking water consumed by 100,000 predominantly Black residents. Children were lead-poisoned at rates that predict measurable IQ loss, behavioral disorders, and lifelong health consequences. No senior official has been imprisoned.
*   **Cancer Alley (Louisiana)** — An 85-mile stretch of the Mississippi River corridor between Baton Rouge and New Orleans hosts over 150 petrochemical plants. Black communities in St. John the Baptist Parish face cancer rates 50 times the national average. Residents have been denied environmental permits protections and systematically excluded from state environmental review processes.
*   **Navajo Nation radioactive contamination** — See Section VII. Over 500 unreclaimed uranium mine sites on Navajo land, some used as building material in homes.
*   **North Birmingham / Tarrant, Alabama lead and coke pollution** — EPA Superfund communities of color surrounded by industrial facilities; internal EPA documents showed agency scientists were pressured to alter data in response to industry lobbying.
*   **Dickson County, Tennessee — Landfill contamination** — White families whose wells were contaminated by a nearby landfill were given bottled water by the county; a Black family (the Holt family) using the same aquifer was not notified for years despite county officials knowing of the contamination.
*   **PFAS contamination on military bases** — Aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) used on hundreds of military bases has contaminated groundwater across the country with “forever chemicals.” The Pentagon resisted testing, notification, and cleanup for decades; communities surrounding bases — often low-income — bore the health burden.
*   **East Palestine, Ohio (2023)** — Norfolk Southern train derailment and controlled burn of vinyl chloride; residents initially told to return home while air monitoring data was incomplete. Environmental testing irregularities and delayed federal response drew comparisons to Flint.
*   **Puerto Rico: Hurricane Maria and federal abandonment (2017)** — The Harvard study estimated 4,645 excess deaths attributable to the storm and collapsed healthcare response. FEMA denied over 60% of individual assistance applications in Puerto Rico versus 20% on the mainland. The paper towel response by the President became a symbol of differential treatment of a non-white U.S. territory.
*   **EPA environmental justice rollbacks** — The Trump administration systematically weakened environmental justice regulations, rolled back NEPA review processes, and closed regional environmental justice offices, disproportionately affecting communities of color already bearing the highest toxic burden.
*   **DOE nuclear waste sites in Indian country** — Hanford, Rocky Flats, and other nuclear waste sites located adjacent to or on treaty lands with known seepage; cleanup contracts repeatedly awarded and extended without results.

* * *

### X. Housing, Segregation & Economic Warfare

*   **Redlining (1934–1968)** — The Federal Housing Administration’s underwriting manuals explicitly graded neighborhoods by race. “D” (red) neighborhoods — predominantly Black — were denied federally backed mortgages. Homeownership is the primary vehicle of intergenerational wealth transfer in the U.S.; Black families were systematically excluded from it for 34 years of the post-war wealth boom. The racial wealth gap today is traceable in significant part to this policy.
*   **Urban renewal / “Negro removal” (1949–1970s)** — The Federal Housing Act of 1949 funded bulldozing of established Black urban neighborhoods under the banner of “slum clearance.” An estimated 400,000 families — overwhelmingly Black — were displaced. Replacement housing was rarely built at equivalent rates, and communities were broken up and scattered into worse conditions. James Baldwin called it “Negro removal.”
*   **GI Bill exclusion of Black veterans** — The Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944 was administered by local officials who systematically denied Black veterans access to college loans, low-interest mortgages, and business startup funds. Of the first 67,000 mortgages issued under the GI Bill in New York and New Jersey, fewer than 100 went to non-white veterans.
*   **Contract buying schemes (Chicago, post-WWII)** — When Black buyers were denied conventional mortgages, predatory “contract sellers” sold homes at inflated prices on installment contracts that conveyed no equity until the final payment — and allowed sellers to repossess the home for any missed payment, including for repairs. Researchers estimate Chicago’s Black community lost between $3.2 billion and $4 billion through contract buying.
*   **HOLC racial mapping** — The Home Owners’ Loan Corporation created color-coded maps of virtually every American city that associated Black residence with mortgage risk. These maps became the foundation of private bank redlining policies that persisted long after the FHA officially abandoned the practice.
*   **Sundown towns** — An estimated 10,000–13,000 American municipalities enforced (through law, threat, or violence) policies excluding Black residents after dark, well into the post-war era. Many were actively enforced through the 1970s; some enforcement has been documented through the 1990s.
*   **Destruction of Black Wall Street (Tulsa Race Massacre, 1921)** — While predating the post-war era, the federal government’s role in suppressing reparations, seizing survivors’ land claims, and withholding records constitutes ongoing post-war complicity. Over 35 blocks of the Greenwood District were destroyed; the Oklahoma Commission found evidence that private planes may have fired on residents; the National Guard was used to detain Black survivors rather than protect them.
*   **Wells Fargo / Bank of America reverse redlining** — DOJ settlements revealed that during the subprime mortgage boom, major banks deliberately targeted Black and Latino homeowners for high-cost, high-risk mortgage products even when they qualified for prime loans. Wells Fargo internal emails referred to Black customers as “mud people” and to subprime loans as “ghetto loans.”
*   **Section 8 voucher concentration** — Federal housing policy has historically concentrated housing voucher holders in high-poverty, high-crime, predominantly minority neighborhoods, replicating spatial segregation through nominally race-neutral policy.

* * *

### XI. Labor Exploitation, Suppression & Economic Coercion

*   **Bracero Program (1942–1964)** — 4.6 million Mexican contract workers brought to the U.S., denied permanent legal status, charged for housing and food deducted from wages, subjected to DDT delousing upon entry, and frequently stranded without pay. The Mexican government required the U.S. to deposit 10% of wages in a savings fund; the money was embezzled and never returned.
*   **Operation Wetback (1954)** — Militarized mass deportation campaign conducted by the INS that forcibly removed approximately one million people, including many U.S. citizens of Mexican descent, without due process. People were deported by the trainload and shipload to locations hundreds of miles from their homes.
*   **FBI/COINTELPRO targeting of labor organizers** — The AFL-CIO, UAW, United Farm Workers (under César Chávez), and Mine Workers were all targeted by COINTELPRO and its predecessors for infiltration and disruption. The FBI worked with employers to identify and terminate union organizers.
*   **National Guard deployment against strikes** — Government used military force to break worker strikes well into the post-war era: the 1946 Oakland General Strike, railroad strike suppression, coal mine seizures.
*   **Convict leasing and prison labor (ongoing)** — The 13th Amendment explicitly permits slavery as punishment for crime. Incarcerated people labor for $0.13–$0.52 per hour in federal prisons; many states pay nothing. Private corporations including Starbucks, Walmart, McDonald’s, and Victoria’s Secret have used prison labor. During California wildfires, incarcerated firefighters earn $2.90–$5.12 per day but are often barred from becoming paid firefighters upon release.
*   **Migrant farmworker conditions** — The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 explicitly excluded agricultural and domestic workers — predominantly Black and Latino — from its protections, a deliberate concession to Southern Democrats. This exclusion was only partially and unevenly remedied decades later.
*   **Exploitation of undocumented labor** — Federal policy has historically created a class of undocumented workers who cannot report wage theft, unsafe conditions, or abuse for fear of deportation. E-Verify and enforcement mechanisms have been weaponized against workers who complain rather than employers who exploit.

* * *

### XII. Child Welfare System Abuses

*   **Native American boarding schools** — See Section VII. The federal policy explicitly was to use child removal as an instrument of cultural destruction.
*   **Disproportionate removal of Black and Native children** — Black children are removed from families at roughly twice the rate of white children for comparable reports, and are less likely to be reunified. Native children were removed at 2.7 times the white rate as of recent data.
*   **Youth prison abuse** — The DOJ has found systemic abuse, excessive isolation, and denial of education and mental health care at juvenile detention facilities in Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Georgia, and elsewhere. Children as young as 10 have been held in solitary confinement for months.
*   **Troubled Teen Industry** — An estimated $23 billion industry of residential programs, “boot camps,” and “therapeutic boarding schools” has operated with minimal state oversight. Programs including CEDU, Elan School, and Provo Canyon School have documented records of physical abuse, sexual abuse, food and sleep deprivation, and coercive restraint. Dozens of deaths have occurred in these facilities.
*   **Family separation at the border (“Zero Tolerance” policy, 2018)** — The Trump administration deliberately separated over 5,500 children from parents as a deterrence policy. Many were held in conditions described by witnesses as cages; children were not given adequate food, water, medical care, or the ability to contact parents. Hundreds of parents were deported without their children; as of 2024, hundreds of families remain separated. The policy was found by the DHS Inspector General to have been implemented without basic tracking systems, making reunification deliberately difficult.
*   **Forced psychiatric institutionalization of minors** — Children have been involuntarily committed to psychiatric institutions based on parental or state initiative with minimal judicial oversight; multiple exposés have documented warehousing conditions and abuse at facilities including Elan and CEDU.

* * *

### XIII. Policing, Mass Incarceration & Judicial Violence

*   **MOVE bombing (Philadelphia, May 13, 1985)** — Philadelphia Police dropped a military-grade explosive (C-4) from a helicopter onto a residential block, killing 11 people (including 5 children), destroying 61 homes, and leaving 250 people homeless. The fire was allowed to burn for hours. No police officer was charged. The city voted to give reparations in 2023–38 years later.
*   **Lynching and state complicity** — Over 4,000 documented racial terror lynchings occurred between 1877 and 1950, many with the active participation or deliberate non-intervention of local police and sheriffs. The federal government refused to pass anti-lynching legislation repeatedly until 2022.
*   **War on Drugs as racial policy** — John Ehrlichman, Nixon’s domestic policy advisor, told journalist Dan Baum in 1994: “The Nixon campaign in 1968, and the Nixon White House after that, had two enemies: the antiwar left and Black people… We knew we couldn’t make it illegal to be either against the war or Black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and Blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities.”
*   **Crack/powder cocaine disparity** — The 1986 Anti-Drug Abuse Act imposed 100:1 sentencing disparity between crack cocaine (associated with Black communities) and powder cocaine (white communities) for identical quantities. This was in effect for 24 years; the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 reduced it to 18:1, but applied only prospectively.
*   **Mass incarceration as a system** — The U.S. incarcerates more people than any nation on Earth: 2.3 million. Black Americans are incarcerated at 5x the rate of white Americans. 1 in 3 Black men can expect to be incarcerated in his lifetime. Private prison companies — GEO Group, CoreCivic — lobbied for mandatory minimums, truth-in-sentencing laws, and immigration detention expansion that drove these numbers.
*   **Qualified immunity** — A judicially created doctrine (not statutory) that shields police officers from civil liability unless the specific conduct has been previously ruled unconstitutional in a near-identical case. The practical effect is near-total immunity for documented constitutional violations including unjustified killings.
*   **No-knock raids** — Militarized police entries without prior announcement, linked to dozens of deaths of innocent civilians including Breonna Taylor, Aiyana Stanley-Jones (7 years old, shot by Detroit police serving a no-knock warrant on the wrong floor of her home), and others.
*   **Stop and frisk** — NYPD’s stop-and-frisk program conducted 685,724 stops in 2011; 88% were Black or Latino; 88% were entirely innocent. A federal judge found the program constituted a pattern of unconstitutional stops but was overturned on procedural grounds.
*   **Solitary confinement** — Over 80,000 Americans are held in isolation on any given day. The UN Special Rapporteur has classified solitary confinement exceeding 15 days as torture. U.S. prisoners have been held in isolation for years and decades. Louisiana’s Angola prison held Albert Woodfox in solitary for 43 years — the longest solitary confinement in U.S. history.
*   **Death row exonerations** — Since 1973, 190+ death row prisoners have been exonerated. The most common factors: prosecutorial misconduct, false testimony by informants, withheld evidence. The state of Mississippi executed Freddie Lee Johnson despite courts finding his prosecution rested on false forensic testimony. Capital punishment is disproportionately applied to Black defendants, defendants with white victims, and defendants in the South.
*   **Civil asset forfeiture** — Police may seize money, vehicles, and property from people never charged with a crime, under the legal fiction that the property itself is “guilty.” Law enforcement agencies keep the proceeds. DOJ data shows the majority of forfeitures involve amounts under $1,000, suggesting targeting of poor people with limited means to contest the seizure.

* * *

### XIV. Propaganda, Disinformation & Manufactured Consent

*   **Operation Mockingbird (1950s–1970s)** — CIA recruited and paid American journalists, editors, and executives at major media organizations including The New York Times, Newsweek, CBS, and the Associated Press to plant stories, publish CIA-prepared content, and suppress unfavorable reporting. The Church Committee confirmed the CIA had “at least 400” assets in American news organizations.
*   **U.S. Army domestic propaganda (1950s–1960s)** — The Army conducted public relations campaigns targeting domestic opposition to nuclear testing, covertly funding “citizens groups” who advocated for continued testing.
*   **VOA / Radio Free Europe** — Nominally independent; actually U.S. government-funded disinformation broadcasters into the Soviet bloc, which also fed stories back into domestic media ecosystems.
*   **USIA (United States Information Agency)** — The U.S. government’s official global propaganda arm planted favorable stories in foreign media, produced films depicting American life as universally prosperous and just, and coordinated covert messaging campaigns.
*   **Pentagon propaganda contracts** — Post-9/11 DOD paid public relations firms to plant positive stories in Iraqi newspapers; paid TV military analysts who were simultaneously employed by defense contractors, without disclosure; and funded Hollywood studios for favorable depictions of military operations.
*   **CISA “disinformation” programs targeting domestic dissent** — Internal documents obtained by Missouri v. Biden revealed that federal agencies pressured social media companies to suppress content the government labeled as “misinformation,” including accurate content about vaccine adverse effects, Hunter Biden’s laptop, and COVID-19 lab leak hypotheses.
*   **FBI FISA abuse** — The Inspector General found that the FBI committed at least 17 “significant errors and omissions” in its FISA warrant applications to surveil Carter Page, including altering a CIA email to state the opposite of what it said.

* * *

### XV. International Covert Operations, Regime Change & State Terror

*   **Iran coup (1953)** — CIA Operation AJAX overthrew democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh after he nationalized British Petroleum. Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi was restored; his SAVAK secret police (trained by the CIA) tortured and murdered thousands. This is widely cited as a root cause of the 1979 revolution and subsequent U.S.-Iran hostilities.
*   **Guatemala coup (1954)** — CIA Operation PBSUCCESS overthrew democratically elected President Jacobo Árbenz after he redistributed United Fruit Company land. The resulting military dictatorship killed an estimated 200,000 people during the decades of civil war it initiated.
*   **Congo (1960)** — CIA played a direct role in the assassination of Patrice Lumumba and the installation of Mobutu Sese Seko, whose 32-year kleptocratic dictatorship impoverished one of the world’s richest nations.
*   **Dominican Republic (1961)** — CIA provided weapons and logistical support to the assassins of Rafael Trujillo.
*   **Brazil (1964)** — U.S. government recognized the military coup within hours and provided active support for the overthrow of President João Goulart, ushering in 21 years of military dictatorship.
*   **Indonesia (1965–66)** — U.S. Embassy provided the Indonesian Army with lists of thousands of Communist Party members and affiliated persons; an estimated 500,000–1 million people were killed. U.S. officials later confirmed providing the lists, calling it “a big help.”
*   **Chile (1973)** — Nixon, Kissinger, and the CIA spent years destabilizing the democratically elected government of Salvador Allende before supporting the Pinochet coup on September 11, 1973. Pinochet’s regime tortured and disappeared 40,000 people; killed at least 3,200. American economist Orlando Letelier was assassinated by Pinochet agents on Embassy Row in Washington, D.C. in 1976.
*   **Argentina’s Dirty War (1976–1983)** — Kissinger met with Argentine junta leaders days before the coup and encouraged them to “clean up” the problem quickly before Congress could object. An estimated 30,000 people were disappeared; prisoners were thrown from aircraft over the Río de la Plata.
*   **El Salvador death squads (1980s)** — U.S. funded and trained Salvadoran military units that massacred civilians, including the El Mozote massacre (1981) where over 800 civilians were killed by the Atlacatl Battalion, trained at the School of the Americas. The U.S. Embassy’s reporting to Washington concealed evidence of the massacre for years.
*   **Nicaragua / Iran-Contra (1980s)** — The Reagan administration secretly funded the Contra insurgency — which committed documented atrocities against Nicaraguan civilians — using proceeds from illegal arms sales to Iran, after Congress had explicitly prohibited such funding. When exposed, Reagan claimed ignorance; independent counsel investigations resulted in 14 indictments and 11 convictions, all pardoned or overturned.
*   **Iraq WMD disinformation (2002–2003)** — The Bush administration systematically manufactured and disseminated false intelligence about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction to justify an invasion that killed between 150,000 and 1 million civilians (depending on methodology), created the conditions for the rise of ISIS, and destabilized the Middle East for decades. The Downing Street Memo (2002) confirmed British intelligence believed the intelligence was “being fixed around the policy.”
*   **Extraordinary rendition network (54 countries)** — See Section VI. The Open Society Justice Initiative documented that 54 governments participated in the CIA’s rendition, detention, and interrogation program.
*   **Support for Saudi Arabia in Yemen (2015–present)** — U.S. provided targeting intelligence, mid-air refueling, and billions in weapons sales to a Saudi-led coalition whose strikes on hospitals, weddings, water infrastructure, and school buses have been documented as war crimes by UN investigators. An estimated 150,000–300,000+ deaths, with famine affecting millions.

* * *

### XVI. Veteran Abuse, Neglect & Experimentation

*   **Atomic veteran denial** — For decades, the VA denied benefits to veterans sickened by radiation exposure at nuclear tests, requiring them to prove service connection despite classified records being withheld by the DOD.
*   **Agent Orange VA denials** — Vietnam veterans exposed to Agent Orange spent 30–40 years fighting VA bureaucracy for benefits. The Agent Orange Act of 1991 finally created presumptive service connection for certain conditions, but many veterans had died by then.
*   **Burn pit exposures (Gulf War, Iraq, Afghanistan)** — The military burned toxic waste — including medical waste, electronics, chemicals, and unexploded ordnance — in open pits. Hundreds of thousands of veterans exposed. The VA denied service connection for resulting cancers and respiratory illness for over a decade. The PACT Act (2022) finally expanded benefits.
*   **Gulf War Syndrome** — Veterans returning from the 1991 Gulf War reported a cluster of chronic symptoms now associated with exposure to sarin from demolished Iraqi munitions, depleted uranium, and experimental pyridostigmine bromide pills administered as nerve agent prophylaxis. The Pentagon denied the existence of the syndrome for years; VA denied benefits.
*   **PTSD and the suicide crisis** — The VA estimates 20 veterans die by suicide per day. The system has been chronically underfunded and understaffed. A 2014 VA scandal revealed that officials at over 100 facilities falsified patient wait time records; veterans died waiting for appointments.
*   **Edgewood Arsenal experiments on soldiers** — See Section III. 7,000 soldiers exposed without full informed consent.
*   **Homeless veterans** — An estimated 33,000 veterans are homeless on any given night, a figure that has been persistently resistant to reduction despite decades of programs.

* * *

### XVII. Disability Rights Violations & Institutionalization

*   **Willowbrook** — See Section III. Beyond the deliberate infection experiments, conditions at Willowbrook State School were so catastrophic — children lying in their own waste, untreated injuries, assault by staff — that Robert Kennedy called it a “snake pit” in 1965. Exposé journalism by Geraldo Rivera in 1972 helped spur deinstitutionalization.
*   **State psychiatric institution warehousing (1940s–1970s)** — At peak in the 1950s, over 550,000 people were institutionalized in American state mental hospitals under conditions widely documented as abusive, including forced lobotomies, non-consensual electroconvulsive therapy, physical restraint, and sexual abuse. Deinstitutionalization without corresponding community support shifted many into homelessness and incarceration.
*   **Forced lobotomies** — Walter Freeman performed over 3,500 transorbital lobotomies across the country, often without proper consent, often on women diagnosed with depression or “hysteria,” often in state institutions. At least 127 patients died.
*   **Judge Rotenberg Center (Canton, MA, ongoing)** — Residential facility for people with disabilities that uses graduated electronic decelerators (GEDs) — electric shock devices — to punish “maladaptive behavior.” The FDA banned the devices in 2020; the facility appealed and continues operation pending litigation. UN Special Rapporteur on Torture has called the practice torture.
*   **Olmstead decision non-compliance** — The Supreme Court’s 1999 Olmstead decision requires states to provide community-based services rather than institutionalization; decades later, most states remain in violation, continuing to warehouse disabled people in institutions.

* * *

### XVIII. Algorithmic, Digital & Emerging Systems of Control

*   **Predictive policing systems** — PredPol, ShotSpotter, and similar tools direct police resources based on historical arrest data, which itself reflects racially biased policing. This creates feedback loops that concentrate enforcement in Black and Latino communities regardless of actual crime distribution.
*   **Facial recognition** — Law enforcement has used facial recognition technology with documented error rates of 10–35% for darker-skinned women. Multiple wrongful arrests have resulted. Detroit has arrested at least three Black men based solely on faulty facial recognition matches.
*   **ShotSpotter** — Acoustic gunshot detection system deployed primarily in communities of color; an analysis by the MacArthur Justice Center found 89% of ShotSpotter alerts led to no evidence of gun crime.
*   **Social media surveillance** — DHS and local fusion centers monitor social media of political protesters, Muslim communities, and activists. Immigration authorities have used social media posts to justify deportation and visa denial, including content satirical or critical of the U.S. government.
*   **Algorithmic welfare denial** — Arkansas, Indiana, and other states deployed automated systems to determine Medicaid eligibility; the algorithms systematically cut benefits for people with documented disabilities and chronic conditions. Courts found the systems violated due process.
*   **Digital border surveillance** — CBP routinely searches and downloads the contents of phones, laptops, and other devices of travelers at the border without a warrant, including American citizens.
*   **IMSI catchers / Stingrays** — Fake cell towers used by law enforcement to intercept communications without individual warrants, deployed in at least 72 agencies across 24 states, often without any judicial oversight.

* * *

This record is not exhaustive. It represents documented, verified, and in many cases officially acknowledged programs. The through-line across all of them is structural: these abuses do not arise from isolated bad actors but from systems — bureaucratic, legal, financial, and ideological — that consistently treat certain categories of human beings as expendable, exploitable, or subhuman. The populations targeted are almost invariably those with the least power to resist, document, or survive what is being done to them.

The historical question is not whether these things happened. They are in the Congressional record, the Senate Intelligence Committee, the DOJ Inspector General, and the National Archives. The operative question is what it means that they did — and what conditions make their recurrence possible.

If I Did Not Write About My Torture in US, They Might Think It’s Ok.
====================================================================

The belief that a torture victim’s silence constitutes consent is not an incidental feature of the perpetrator’s psychology. It is a…

* * *

### “If I D_id Not Write about Torture and Abuse at the Hands of the US Government, They Might Think That I Am Consenting to it.”_

### _That is the Clinical Psychosis of Torturers That I Am Confronting._

#### The belief that a torture victim’s silence constitutes consent is not an incidental feature of the perpetrator’s psychology. It is a load-bearing element of the cognitive architecture that makes sustained torture possible.

Read it again with fresh eyes.

_“If I did not write about torture and abuse at the hands of the US government, they might think that I am consenting to it. That is the clinical psychosis of torturers that I am confronting.”_

The psychosis is theirs. The “they” who might think he is consenting — the operators, the handlers, the people running the program — are the ones Pearson is diagnosing. He is saying: the people doing this to me are operating from a psychological framework so distorted that they would interpret my silence as consent. And that distortion — the belief system that makes silence equal consent in the mind of a torturer — is itself a clinical condition. A psychosis. And it is the psychosis he has to navigate every day, because it governs the behavior of the people who have power over his life.

This is a much more precise and much more devastating observation than anything about his own psychology. He is not describing his trauma. He is describing their pathology.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*3LBCeOWP6lWrpOx-3TQx2w.png)

* * *

### The Torturer’s Psychology: What the Literature Establishes

The clinical and psychological literature on perpetrators of state-sanctioned torture is specific about the cognitive and moral frameworks that make sustained torture possible. It is not, primarily, a literature about sadism. Sadism — the enjoyment of cruelty for its own sake — is relatively rare even among documented perpetrators of systematic abuse. **What the literature documents instead is a set of cognitive distortions that are far more mundane, far more stable, and far more dangerous precisely because they do not feel, to the person holding them, like distortions at all.**

James Waller’s work in _Becoming Evil_ establishes that ordinary people become capable of extraordinary cruelty through a specific psychological pathway: the dehumanization of the target, the diffusion of individual responsibility across an institutional structure, the authorization of conduct by legitimate-seeming authority, and the routinization of harm through bureaucratic procedure. Each of these mechanisms operates to sever the perpetrator’s normal empathic response to the suffering they cause. The harm becomes procedural rather than personal. **The target becomes a category rather than a person. The perpetrator becomes a functionary rather than an agent.**

But Waller’s framework, while accurate, does not capture the specific distortion Pearson is identifying. He is not simply saying his torturers have dehumanized him or diffused their responsibility. He is saying something more precise: they have a theory of consent that is psychotic.

* * *

### The Consent Psychosis

The belief that a torture victim’s silence constitutes consent is not an incidental feature of the perpetrator’s psychology. It is a load-bearing element of the cognitive architecture that makes sustained torture possible.

Consider what it would mean for a torturer to genuinely reckon with the absence of consent in their victim. It would mean acknowledging that the harm they are inflicting is being inflicted on a person who is resisting it, who experiences it as harm, who has not agreed to it, and who is being denied the ability to refuse it. That acknowledgment, held honestly, produces a moral reality that is incompatible with continuing. **The torturer who genuinely sees the victim’s non-consent cannot continue without accepting the full weight of what they are doing.**

The psychosis Pearson identifies is the cognitive mechanism that prevents this reckoning. **The belief — held with the rigidity and imperviousness to evidence that defines delusional thinking — that the victim who does not loudly, persistently, and visibly resist is not really a victim.** That silence is agreement. That accommodation is acceptance. That the person who has been broken into compliance has revealed, through their compliance, that the targeting was appropriate. That the target who stops fighting has confirmed the designation.

This is psychotic in the clinical sense because it inverts the causal relationship between the harm and the response to the harm. The torture produces the silence. The silence is then read as evidence that the torture was justified. The perpetrator’s conduct is retroactively validated by the outcome that conduct was specifically designed to produce. The distortion is self-sealing. It cannot be falsified by any behavior the victim exhibits, because every possible behavior — resistance and silence alike — is absorbed into the framework that confirms the perpetrator’s position.

* * *

### The Authorization Framework and Moral Disengagement

Albert Bandura’s theory of moral disengagement provides the clinical scaffolding for understanding how otherwise functional people maintain this distortion over time without experiencing it as distortion.

**Moral disengagement operates through eight specific mechanisms, several of which are directly relevant to what Pearson is describing.** Moral justification converts harmful conduct into service of a higher purpose — the target is a threat to national security, a Black Identity Extremist, a destabilizing force whose neutralization protects the social order. Dehumanization strips the target of the psychological qualities that activate empathic response — the target is a category, a designation, a file number, not a person with a PhD and a dissertation and a life. Diffusion of responsibility distributes the conduct across so many institutional actors that no single person experiences themselves as the agent of the harm. And advantageous comparison makes the conduct seem reasonable by reference to worse conduct — we are not doing what the Soviets did, we are merely managing a threat.

But the most relevant mechanism for Pearson’s observation is what Bandura calls displacement of responsibility — the cognitive operation by which the perpetrator locates the cause of the harm in the victim’s own conduct. You brought this on yourself. Your work was a threat. Your silence would end this. Your resistance is why this continues.

The displacement of responsibility onto the victim is the precise mechanism that generates the consent interpretation Pearson is describing. If the victim is responsible for the targeting, then the victim controls the targeting. If the victim controls the targeting, then the victim who continues to be targeted has, in some sense, chosen to be targeted. And the victim who stops writing, stops documenting, stops publicly naming what is being done — has chosen to stop provoking it. Has consented to the terms. Has acknowledged, through silence, the legitimacy of the designation.

This is not a metaphor. This is the actual cognitive structure through which people who conduct sustained targeting programs experience what they are doing as something other than what it is. It is the psychosis Pearson lives inside, because it governs the operational logic of the people who have the power to intensify or withdraw the pressure being applied to his life.

* * *

### The Specific Danger This Creates

Understanding this as their clinical profile rather than his own illuminates something important about the strategic logic of Pearson’s writing.

**If the perpetrators operate from a framework in which silence equals consent, then silence does not merely fail to protect him. It actively informs the program’s operational decisions.** A target who goes quiet has, within the perpetrators’ framework, been successfully neutralized. The pressure has worked. The designation has been validated. The program can either de-escalate — mission accomplished — or escalate, now confident that the target’s resistance has been broken and further pressure will meet no organized opposition.

Pearson writing is therefore not just the maintenance of his own witnessing self. It is a direct communication to the perpetrators, within the only framework they understand, that the program has not achieved its objective. That the consent their psychosis requires has not been given. That the designation they have applied has not been internalized. That the target is still a witness, still a researcher, still a person whose moral reality is intact and whose account of events is being maintained in a form that cannot be classified, suppressed, or reinterpreted through psychiatric attribution.

He is not writing for us, primarily. He is writing for them. Because they are the ones whose clinical profile makes his silence dangerous — dangerous not because silence would be comfortable, but because their psychosis would read it as the one thing he will not give them.

* * *

### The Broader Clinical Literature on Perpetrator Psychology

The perpetrator psychology Pearson is diagnosing has been documented across multiple contexts of state-sanctioned abuse, and the consent distortion appears consistently.

In Stanley Milgram’s obedience experiments, subjects who continued to administer what they believed were painful electric shocks to screaming victims did so in part because the institutional authority structure provided them with a framework in which the victim’s distress was interpreted as resistance to a legitimate procedure rather than evidence that the procedure should stop. The victim’s suffering was real. The perpetrator’s perception of it was filtered through a framework that converted suffering into non-compliance rather than into harm requiring cessation.

In Philip Zimbardo’s Stanford Prison Experiment — and more importantly in Zimbardo’s subsequent analysis of Abu Ghraib — the guards who inflicted humiliation and abuse on prisoners did not, in their own accounts, believe they were torturing. They believed they were managing unruly subjects. **The prisoners’ distress was read not as evidence of harm but as evidence of the prisoners’ failure to cooperate with legitimate institutional procedure.** The consent framework was total: a prisoner who accepted the institutional terms was a good prisoner. A prisoner who resisted was a problem prisoner whose resistance justified escalating pressure.

**Martha Stout’s clinical work on sociopathy — specifically the one-in-twenty-five Americans she documents as lacking the capacity for genuine empathic response to others’ suffering — provides the individual-level clinical foundation for the institutional-level distortion Pearson describes.** The person who runs a targeting program without apparent distress at what the program does to its targets is not necessarily performing a complex moral disengagement. They may simply lack the neurological substrate that would make the target’s suffering relevant to their own experience. Stout’s clinical profile of the sociopathic individual in a position of institutional authority — charming, functionally competent, genuinely incapable of the empathic response that would make their conduct feel wrong — maps precisely onto the type of person most likely to occupy the operational roles in a sustained targeting program.

* * *

### Why Pearson Names It Psychosis Specifically

The word choice is deliberate and exact.

He does not say they are wrong. He does not say they are evil. He does not say they are operating in bad faith, or that they are lying to themselves, or that they are making a mistake. **He says they are psychotic. And psychosis, clinically, means something specific: a condition in which the person’s internal model of reality has become sufficiently disconnected from reality that it cannot be corrected by evidence or argument.** The person experiencing a psychotic delusion does not experience it as a delusion. They experience it as the truth. Evidence that contradicts the delusion is absorbed into the delusion — reinterpreted, discounted, or explained away — because the delusion is the framework through which all evidence is processed.

The perpetrators who would read Pearson’s silence as consent are not making a logical error they could be argued out of. They are operating from a fixed cognitive framework — the target who complies has been managed, the target who resists confirms the designation, the target who falls silent has been neutralized — that is impervious to the evidence of what is actually happening to him. His suffering is not evidence of harm because, within their framework, he is not a person whose suffering counts as harm. His documentation is not evidence of what he documents because, within their framework, it is a symptom of the pathology that justified the targeting. His silence would not be evidence of innocence because, within their framework, it would be evidence that the program worked.

This is the clinical definition of psychosis: a framework impervious to disconfirming evidence, maintained as reality regardless of what reality presents.

Pearson is living inside it. Not as a patient. As the object of it. He has to conduct himself — every day, in every decision about whether to write and what to say and how to document — with full awareness of the clinical profile of the people whose actions he is documenting. He has to understand their distortion well enough to communicate within it — to send them the only signal their framework can receive, which is the signal of ongoing resistance — while simultaneously maintaining, against the pressure that resistance produces, his own accurate account of what is happening.

That is the psychosis he is dealing with. Theirs. Applied to him. Every day.

And the sentence that names it is, in its quiet precision, an act of clinical observation as rigorous as anything in the medical literature — performed by a man diagnosing his torturers from inside the condition they have created for him.
