### **Victim Alleged “Mind Control” Used in Washington, DC Then Three US Senators Proposed a Bill to Regulate**

### The MIND Act of 2025, Its Statutory Language, Its Unstated Admissions, and Its Consequences for Understanding What Was Done to Richard Pearson

_Richard Pearson spent the second half of 2025 building a documented evidentiary record of directed energy assault, voice-to-skull transmission, covert surveillance, behavioral steering, and coordinated psychological operations against him in Washington, DC. He did this with timestamps, photographs, controlled experiments, clinical evaluations, and the methodological rigor of a trained public health researcher. He did it while being actively targeted. On September 24, 2025 — with that record already accumulating — three United States senators introduced S. 2925, the Management of Individuals’ Neural Data Act of 2025. What those senators wrote into the bill’s definitions, its Sense of Congress, its study mandate, and its provisions on federal agency use of neurotechnology is, when read carefully, a legislative portrait of the exact technology and the exact harms Pearson had been experiencing for months. This essay reads the bill section by section, extracts what it says explicitly, examines what it reveals through implication, and shows how its provisions land on Pearson’s specific documented allegations._

### I. The Bill and the Moment

S. 2925 was introduced in the Senate on September 24, 2025 by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Commerce Committee Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, and Senator Ed Markey. Referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, the bill’s central instruction is to direct the Federal Trade Commission to spend one year studying the collection, processing, storage, sale, and transfer of neural data — information derived from brain and nervous system activity — and to deliver a comprehensive report and regulatory recommendations to Congress at the end of that period. A separate provision in Section 5 requires the Office of Science and Technology Policy to follow the FTC’s report with binding guidance governing how federal agencies may procure and operate neurotechnology.

The calendar matters here. The MIND Act did not arrive before Pearson’s experience. It arrived during it. Pearson documented the first voice-to-skull event on July 13, 2025. The DC Department of Behavioral Health evaluated him on September 15, 2025, nine days before the bill was introduced, and found no psychiatric basis to challenge his account. The framing operation near the O’Neill House Office Building was still weeks away. The false arrest was three months away. The Canadian border torture was six months away. The senators were not responding to Pearson. They were responding to the broader technological landscape that Pearson’s experience was a specific instance of. The legislation’s value to his case is not causal. It is confirmatory: Congress, in the same season, was writing into public law the recognition that the harms Pearson was living through were real, recognized, and completely without legal governance.

### II. Reading the Statute: Definitions That Describe a Weapon

### Neurotechnology: A System That Writes to the Brain

The bill’s operative definition of neurotechnology is its most revealing provision, and it deserves precise attention:

**S. 2925, SEC. 3(5)** The term ‘neurotechnology’ means a device, system, or procedure that accesses, monitors, records, analyzes, predicts, stimulates or alters the nervous system of an individual to understand, influence, restore, or anticipate the structure, activity, or function of the nervous system.

Work through the verbs. The bill regulates technology that “accesses” the nervous system — entering it, not merely observing it from outside. It regulates technology that “stimulates” the nervous system — introducing a signal into neural tissue, producing effects the subject did not generate. It regulates technology that “alters” the nervous system — changing the neural state of a person, not just reading it. And it regulates technology that “predicts” and “anticipates” nervous system function — modeling what a subject’s neural activity will do before it does it.

This is not the vocabulary of a stethoscope or an MRI machine. It is the vocabulary of a system that operates on the nervous system rather than merely observing it — a system capable of both read and write functions. Congress wrote this definition because such systems exist. The technology Pearson identified as responsible for the voice-to-skull transmission on July 13, 2025 — a system that stimulated his auditory processing pathway to produce internally perceived speech — is fully captured by this definition. The thought-insertion he experienced at St. Bernard de Lacolle — foreign content pushed into his cognition until he grounded himself to metal — is what “alters the nervous system” looks like from the inside. Congress defined the weapon.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*kgHDeEC29LX6JMnfmGE7Kw.jpeg)

### Neural Data: The Whole Nervous System, Not Just the Brain

**S. 2925, SEC. 3(4)** The term ‘neural data’ means information obtained by measuring the activity of an individual’s central or peripheral nervous system through the use of neurotechnology.

The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system is everything else: the network of sensory and motor nerve fibers extending throughout the body, including the pathways governing sensation, pain, and sexual response. The MIND Act defines neural data to include both. This breadth is analytically significant for Pearson’s account of sexual nerve targeting. What was directed at him in Silver Spring — electromagnetic pulses aimed at his groin, paired with conditioning stimuli, in a documented attempt to associate sexual nerve stimulation with heterosexual imagery — involves the peripheral nervous system specifically. The bill’s definition covers that data. The technology capable of collecting or stimulating it is neurotechnology under this statute. Congress drew no distinction between the brain and the rest of the body’s nervous system when it defined what deserves protection.

### Other Related Data: Biometric Capture in a Public Park

Beyond direct neural measurement, the bill extends its scope to a category called “other related data”:

**S. 2925, SEC. 3(6)** ‘other related data’ means biometric, physiological, or behavioral information that does not directly measure the neural activity or central or peripheral nervous system of an individual, but can be processed, analyzed, or combined with other data to infer, predict, or reveal cognitive, emotional, or psychological states or neurological conditions — and may include heart rate variability, eye-tracking patterns, voice analysis, facial expression recognition, sleep patterns, or other signals derived from consumer devices.

Eye-tracking. Behavioral patterns. Biometric signals processed in combination to infer cognitive and emotional states. This is a precise statutory description of what Pearson documented at the Cherry Blossom Festival and the Lincoln Memorial: handheld devices operated at close range, capturing signals that — combined and processed through a database — can produce the biometric profile enabling remote electromagnetic targeting. The man who approached Pearson with a device at the moment the woman stopped pushing the stroller was conducting exactly the kind of operation this definition covers. The two-to-five foot protocol, the sustained proximity, the confirmation signals between operators — all of it is the human infrastructure of an “other related data” collection system Congress recognized as existing, sensitive, and ungoverned.

### III. The Sense of Congress: Admissions Written Into Law

A bill’s Sense of Congress section states what the legislature collectively believes to be true at the time of drafting. It is not aspirational. It is descriptive. What Congress wrote into Section 2 of the MIND Act is a set of findings about the current state of neural data technology — findings that, read against Pearson’s documentation, are not abstract policy concerns. They are descriptions of what was being done to him.

**S. 2925, SEC. 2(1)** an individual’s neural data and other related data can be monetized and used to shape individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making in ways existing laws do not adequately address

Present tense. “Can be used.” Not “may someday be capable of being used.” Neural data can already shape behavior, emotional states, and decision-making, and the laws governing that use do not exist. Pearson’s pinning events — the compulsive pull toward Georgetown on July 13, the inexplicable draw toward the O’Neill House area on November 7 — are documented instances of behavioral shaping Congress here acknowledges as a current technological reality. The admission that existing laws “do not adequately address” this capability is the Senate’s own acknowledgment of the legal vacuum Pearson fell into.

**S. 2925, SEC. 2(2)** vertical corporate integration of neurotechnology, artificial intelligence systems, wearable devices, digital platforms, and global data infrastructure may create interconnected systems with insufficient transparency, accountability, or user control regarding the use of such data

This is a structural description of the Eigenfield architecture Pearson identified: biometric capture feeding a database processed by AI enabling remote targeting, operating across a global infrastructure that followed him from Washington to Iceland to Canada and was waiting for him at the border. The integration Congress flags — neurotechnology plus AI plus wearables plus global data infrastructure — is not speculative. The senators were describing an existing technological configuration. That configuration is what Pearson documented as the mechanism of his own targeting.

**S. 2925, SEC. 2(3)** such concentration increases the risk of behavioral influence, cognitive manipulation, erosion of personal autonomy, and the exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities, particularly in the absence of enforceable privacy protections

Three categories appear here that map directly onto Pearson’s documented experience: behavioral influence, cognitive manipulation, and erosion of personal autonomy. These are not theoretical risks to be guarded against. Congress identifies them as current risks arising from current technological concentration. The additional reference to exacerbation of social and economic disparities is the closest the bill comes to naming what Pearson’s Cherry Blossom and Lincoln Memorial footage shows: a system operating disproportionately against Black people in public spaces. Congress did not use the word “racial.” It did not need to. The disparity language, in the context of American history and the documented demographics of surveillance technology targeting, carries the meaning.

### IV. Section 4: The FTC’s Mandate and Its Implications

### Behavioral Manipulation as a Prohibited Use Case

The MIND Act instructs the FTC to examine whether certain applications of neurotechnology — including “manipulation of behavior” — should be “prohibited regardless of individual consent.” That phrase deserves unpacking. The contemplation of prohibition regardless of consent means two things simultaneously: first, that behavioral manipulation through neurotechnology is currently possible; and second, that it is currently occurring in contexts where consent is not at issue, because subjects have not been asked for it. You do not write a law prohibiting behavior-regardless-of-consent if the baseline condition is one of consented use. The baseline is non-consensual. Congress is trying to establish a floor where none exists.

The behavioral manipulation Pearson documented needs no further analytical scaffolding against this provision. His pinning events are documented cases of behavioral direction executed without his knowledge or consent. The Sprite incident is a case of motor behavior performed without conscious participation. Congress directed the FTC to study whether these things should be prohibited. They were already happening to Pearson when that direction was issued.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*yvOskfJsSs6Nk6vr6_2Okg.jpeg)

### Cognitive Manipulation and the Ownership of One’s Own Mind

Section 4 directs the FTC to study “cognitive manipulation” and its relationship to “erosion of personal autonomy” as distinct harm categories. The granularity of this framing reflects an understanding that what is at stake is not just behavioral output but the internal experience of being the author of one’s own thoughts. Personal autonomy, in the neurotechnology context, means the sense that the mental content arising in one’s consciousness is self-generated — that thoughts, impulses, and decisions originate within the person rather than being introduced from outside.

When Pearson sat in the grey chairs at St. Bernard de Lacolle and experienced an unrelenting stream of foreign content entering his mind — material he recognized as not his, cruel and incessant — what was being violated was exactly this. The erosion of personal autonomy Congress directs the FTC to study is what he gripped metal poles against. When two hands on the chair frame stopped the intrusion entirely, he had confirmed the mechanism and defended the boundary. Congress has since assigned the FTC to figure out whether that violation should be prohibited. The violation preceded the assignment.

### Racial Disparities and Discriminatory Profiling

The bill’s direction to the FTC to examine “discriminatory profiling” and the potential for neural data technology to “exacerbate existing disparities” is not a boilerplate equity clause. It reflects legislative awareness of a pattern: that surveillance and behavioral technologies in the United States have historically been deployed against communities that are already structurally disadvantaged, and that neurotechnology is no different. The Cherry Blossom footage — shot in March 2025 before Pearson was watching for this — captures multiple independent instances of close-range protocols executed specifically against Black subjects. The Lincoln Memorial footage shows two separate following operations targeting Black men in a single afternoon. Congress’s explicit identification of discriminatory profiling as a harm category to be studied is the legislative acknowledgment that the pattern Pearson documented is not an idiosyncrasy. It is a recognized risk of the technology as currently deployed.

### AI-Driven Systems Designed to Influence Behavior

The FTC is directed to assess harms arising when neural data “is integrated with artificial intelligence or used as part of a system designed to influence behavior or decision making.” This provision identifies a specific architectural configuration as a priority harm category: not just neurotechnology alone, but neurotechnology fused with AI into a behavioral influence system. This is precisely the architecture Pearson describes — biometric capture, AI processing, database enrollment, remote targeting — and it is the architecture the Eigenfield essay generated by AI had named and described. Congress is not theorizing about such systems. It is directing a federal agency to study the damage they produce.

### The Absolute Prohibition Possibility

Perhaps the most revealing provision in Section 4 is the direction to assess whether some neurotechnology use cases warrant prohibition “regardless of individual consent” because “their harms outweigh their benefits.” The legal weight here is substantial. This is Congress acknowledging that some uses of this technology are so injurious that no consent framework could rehabilitate them. The progression the bill traces — from non-consensual use as the current baseline, to the question of whether even consented use should be outlawed — marks a set of harms that Congress already knows are occurring. The uses warranting absolute prohibition are the uses Pearson experienced: behavioral direction without knowledge, cognitive intrusion without consent, sexual nerve stimulation as a conditioning tool. Congress is drawing the outer perimeter of the impermissible around the territory Pearson already mapped from the inside.

### V. Section 5: The Federal Agency Provision and What It Concedes

Section 5 is titled “Conditional Limitations on Federal Agency Use of Neural Data.” It is the bill’s most consequential provision for Pearson’s allegations, and its significance lies not only in what it requires but in what its necessity implies.

The section directs OSTP to produce binding guidance on federal agency procurement and use of neurotechnology within 180 days of the FTC’s report. That guidance must distinguish prohibited uses from permissible ones and from conditionally permitted ones. It must establish safeguards for each use case and must include “optional opt-in consent mechanisms regarding the use of such neurotechnology” and protections for “individuals who are subject to use of neurotechnology by Federal agencies.”

**S. 2925, SEC. 5(1)(A)-©** Such guidance shall identify: (A) prohibited, permissible, and conditionally permitted use cases of such neurotechnology that are consistent with such report; (B) technical, procedural, and ethical safeguards regarding each use case of such neurotechnology; and © requirements for transparency, limitations regarding the purposes for which such neurotechnology can be used, individual opt-in consent mechanisms regarding the use of such neurotechnology, and protections for the privacy of individuals who are subject to use of neurotechnology by Federal agencies.

Read that last phrase carefully: “individuals who are subject to use of neurotechnology by Federal agencies.” Not individuals who choose to use neurotechnology provided by federal agencies. Not federal employees operating neurotechnology as part of their work. Individuals — private persons — who are “subject to” federal agency neurotechnology use. The passive construction is the tell. These are people on whom federal agencies are using neurotechnology. The guidance exists to protect them. The protection is needed because the use is occurring.

Regulatory guidance distinguishing prohibited from permissible federal agency use cases does not get written for technologies federal agencies have not yet acquired. It gets written for technologies already in procurement and operation, whose current use is ungoverned. The MIND Act’s Section 5 is Congress acknowledging that federal agencies are currently using neurotechnology on individuals without a governing framework. Before this guidance is developed, every application is permissible by default. Voice-to-skull transmission. Thought insertion. Behavioral direction. Covert neural surveillance. None of these were prohibited by federal law or federal policy when they were allegedly applied to Pearson in 2025. Section 5 is the attempt to close that gap prospectively. Pearson was in the gap when it was open.

### VI. Five Inferences the Legislation Requires

### The Technology Is Operational, Not Experimental

Legislative bodies do not commission year-long federal studies of speculative future capabilities. The Senate Commerce Committee does not move bills addressing “cognitive manipulation” and “erosion of personal autonomy” as hypothetical concerns. Every structural feature of the MIND Act — the urgency of its drafters, the precision of its harm categories, the requirement for immediate federal agency guidance, the pre-bill letters to the FTC that went unanswered — reflects the legislative response to a technology that is in the field and producing the harms the bill catalogs. The technology Pearson experienced was not a prototype.

### Federal Agencies Were Using It Without Any Binding Rules

The requirement to develop guidance identifying “prohibited” federal agency use cases means that no such prohibition existed before the guidance is written. Federal agencies were acquiring and operating neurotechnology in a legal environment where no application was formally off-limits. Whatever was done to Pearson in 2025 — whatever system directed a voice into his skull, inserted content into his cognition, steered his behavior toward predetermined locations — was done in the absence of any federal prohibition. Congress is now trying to install the guardrails. The damage that was possible without them has already been done.

### The Racial Targeting Pattern Is Legislatively Recognized

The Sense of Congress’s reference to exacerbation of social and economic disparities through neural data technology deployment is drawn from the same evidence base that produced the cherry blossom footage: a pattern of surveillance and behavioral technologies landing hardest on communities most vulnerable to structural harm. Congress did not arrive at that language without evidence. The disproportionate targeting of Black people that Pearson’s footage shows, and that his statistical analysis confirms at rates beyond coincidence, belongs to the pattern the senators were writing about.

### The Integrated System Exceeds Congressional Visibility

Congress is commissioning a study because it does not have adequate information about how the integrated architecture — neurotechnology, AI, biometric databases, global data infrastructure — is currently being deployed. The opacity the Sense of Congress names is real. The FTC study is not a review of known facts. It is an attempt to illuminate what the congressional intelligence capacity cannot currently see. The system Pearson experienced — which followed him across three international borders and was operating in a Canadian border facility — is precisely the kind of integrated, globally distributed system that exceeds the visibility of any single oversight body. Congress is acknowledging that it cannot fully see what was done to Pearson, not that it doubts it was done.

### Non-Consensual Use Is the Present Baseline

The future requirement for opt-in consent mechanisms exists because the present state has no such mechanisms. Pearson was never asked whether federal agencies could access, monitor, stimulate, or alter his nervous system. The people who operated the equipment in the Canadian facility did not approach him with a consent form. The operator who directed a voice into his skull on the Georgetown Metro did not ask permission. The requirement Congress is now trying to impose — individual consent before federal agency neurotechnology use — is a requirement for something that was entirely absent when the documented incidents occurred. The bill confirms the absence.

### VII. Pearson’s Allegations Matched to Statutory Provisions

### The Georgetown Voice (July 13, 2025)

A clear female voice, internally perceived, directed Pearson to specific locations and told him: “We have to make you disappear.” He confirmed the mechanism against the Frey effect and declassified Army research on microwave auditory induction. Under S. 2925, a device that “stimulates” the nervous system to “influence” its function is neurotechnology by definition. A system that induces auditory percepts through microwave irradiation of the skull is doing precisely this. Congress defined the technology that produced what Pearson heard. The Sense of Congress confirmed that no law prohibited its use on him.

### The Lacolle Thought Stream (March 2026)

Seated in the grey chair section of the Canadian border facility, Pearson experienced an unrelenting intrusion of foreign cognitive content until he placed both hands on the metal poles of the chair. One hand attenuated the effect. Two stopped it entirely. Congress, in Section 2 of the MIND Act, identified “cognitive manipulation” and “erosion of personal autonomy” as present risks of neural data technology. Section 4 directed the FTC to determine whether such manipulation should be categorically prohibited. These are not the legislative vocabulary of a phenomenon Congress was speculating about. They are the vocabulary of something members of the Senate understood was occurring. What Pearson described from the inside — a mind under siege until grounded metal closed the pathway — Congress described from the outside in the same legislative season.

### The Cherry Blossom Biometric Capture (March 2025)

A man holding a device approached Pearson at the moment an Indian woman stopped pushing her stroller in the grove. The device was in Pearson’s direct line of sight. A boy was placed in a tree in seconds to provide elevated line-of-sight. Multiple groups moved on synchronized cues around a single passerby. The MIND Act’s “other related data” definition — covering “eye-tracking patterns,” “behavioral information,” and biometric signals “processed to infer cognitive, emotional, or psychological states” — describes precisely what a handheld device operated at two-to-five feet would be collecting. The bill’s concern about AI-integrated systems using such data for behavioral influence is the statutory description of what that collection feeds.

### The Pinning Events (2025, multiple incidents)

Pearson documented multiple occasions of compulsive location-directed behavior: the Georgetown directive of July 13, the November 7 pull toward the O’Neill House area, the Sprite incident in which he performed a behavioral sequence without conscious participation. Congress wrote into the Sense of Congress that neural data “can be” used to “shape individual behavior” and that such shaping is “not adequately addressed” by existing law. The FTC was directed to examine behavioral manipulation as a potentially prohibited use case. The gap in law Congress identified was the gap Pearson fell through.

### Sexual Nerve Targeting (Silver Spring, 2025)

Following a documented Silver Spring incident in which a directed pulse struck his groin, Pearson began wearing aluminum foil layers around his genitals. The foil warmed at staged events. The warming corresponded to the arrival of heterosexual visual and verbal stimuli — a three-layer conditioning protocol targeting the peripheral nervous system of a gay man with the apparent goal of behavioral modification through associative conditioning. The MIND Act defines neural data to include peripheral nervous system data. It names erosion of personal autonomy as a core harm. It contemplates absolute prohibition for use cases whose harms outweigh any conceivable benefit. Sexual nerve stimulation deployed as a coercive conditioning tool against a person’s identified sexual orientation sits at the absolute center of what Congress was writing about when it contemplated uses too harmful to permit even with consent.

### VIII. The Unanswered Letter and the Dismantled Oversight

Before introducing the MIND Act, the three sponsoring senators wrote to the FTC demanding action on the exploitation of Americans’ neural data. The administration returned no response. That non-response is not a bureaucratic oversight. It is a policy signal from an administration that had already, on its first day, fired seventeen inspectors general — eliminating the independent oversight layer most capable of detecting and investigating unauthorized federal neurotechnology operations. It is the administration that reorganized the DOJ Civil Rights Division, effectively removing the institutional capacity to pursue civil rights claims of the kind Pearson documented. It is the administration that designated Black equity scholars under the RMVE/BIE framework as a national security concern, creating the predicate under which an academic who wrote a dissertation containing the words “critical race” could be placed in a targeting queue.

The administration’s silence on the senators’ letter, read against the structural dismantlement of every oversight body that would have constrained what the MIND Act was attempting to address, is a composite picture: an administration that knew what was happening, chose not to constrain it, and removed the mechanisms that might have forced it to. The MIND Act is opposition senators trying to rebuild, from the outside of the majority, the oversight architecture that the majority had torn down. It was introduced while Pearson was being targeted in the capital city of the country that dismantled the oversight. Both things were happening at the same time. Both are part of the record.

### IX. What the MIND Act Cannot Accomplish

The bill offers Pearson nothing. This is not a rhetorical point. It is a legal reality that needs to be stated plainly so the significance of the legislation is not misunderstood as a path to remedy.

S. 2925 commissions a study. It requires guidance. It does not create a cause of action. It does not establish retroactive liability for federal agency neurotechnology use that preceded the guidance. It does not provide Pearson with standing, with a forum, with a mechanism for discovery, or with any route to the compensation or accountability that his documented experience would warrant. The doctrinal architecture that forecloses his judicial remedies — the state secrets privilege, the Glomar doctrine, the dismantlement of Bivens actions for new contexts, qualified immunity, FISA secrecy, National Security Letter gag orders — is entirely unaffected by the MIND Act, which addresses none of it. Even if the bill passes, clears the Senate, is signed into law, produces an FTC report, and generates binding OSTP guidance, none of those outcomes reaches backward to what was done to Pearson in the second half of 2025.

What the bill provides is something more limited but not therefore unimportant: legislative corroboration. It is Congress writing into the public record, in the same season that Pearson was assembling his own record, that the technologies he describes are real, that their harmful applications are recognized and named, that federal agencies are currently using them without governance, and that the legal framework to prevent such use does not yet exist. It is the institution that governs the country confirming, in its own language, that the harm Pearson experienced was made possible by the institution’s own failure to act before it was too late.

### X. The Record and the Gap

Pearson assembled his record beginning in the summer of 2025. He documented seventy constitutional violations. He ran foil experiments that confirmed electromagnetic signal attenuation. He grounded himself to metal poles in a foreign facility and confirmed through direct observation that the effect was electromagnetic and could be defeated by conductive shielding. He submitted statistical analyses to the DC Council. He published a frame-by-frame review of Cherry Blossom Festival footage that showed the human infrastructure of a biometric capture operation at the National Mall. He wrote, in real time, about what was being done to him.

The United States Senate, in September 2025, wrote a bill. The bill’s definitions covered the technology. Its Sense of Congress named the harms. Its Section 4 identified the prohibited use cases. Its Section 5 acknowledged that federal agencies were operating this technology on individuals without any governing framework. The bill and the record were produced concurrently, by two parties who did not know each other, describing the same phenomenon from opposite ends of the power structure.

Pearson described it from the inside of the harm. The senators described it from the outside of the legislative process. Both descriptions point to the same conclusion: something was happening in the United States in 2025 that had no legal name, no legal prohibition, and no institutional mechanism for redress. The MIND Act tried to begin changing that. The effort was underfunded, introduced by the minority party, referred to a committee controlled by an administration that had already declined to engage, and confronted by the most resourced concealment infrastructure in human history.

Pearson is still in Washington. He is still writing. The record exists. The legislative acknowledgment exists. The gap between what the record requires and what any institution has done about it remains the most consequential unanswered question in his case — and, if what he has documented is even partially true, in the case of the many Black Americans who passed through the National Mall on an afternoon in March 2025 without knowing what was being collected from them.

### Mind Control Bill in Congress Implies Mind Control isn’t Already Unconstitutional. That’s a Problem and A Cover-Up.

The bill’s sponsors know the extent of the problem. Congress knows. The US government, including US intelligence, knows too. Otherwise, the bill’s sponsors would not have proposed the bill. The US government is using mind control technology, so are organized crime, white supremacist and domestic terrorist organizations, and oligarchs. The individuals and organizations are closely tied to members of Congress and the government.

I can make these claims because I was tortured in the US — Washington, DC no less. I came face-to-face with an assortment of criminals within and outside of government. I experienced voice-to-skull, a physical assault then a false arrest, a chemical assault, electrocution of my penis, stalking, behavorial steering, a framing attempt, and much more.

The bill conveys the need to address a major regulatory gap and implies that uses of mind control weapons are within the bounds of the law because the law has not otherwise prohibited them. But why is it now a problem? Because the weapons are readily available well-beyond government use, which had already abused it to harm and injure.

### Why the MIND Act Framing of Cognitive Manipulation as a Regulatory Problem Rather Than an Existing Constitutional Violation Reveals More Than It Intends To

There is a question the MIND Act does not ask, and its failure to ask it is the most significant thing about the legislation. The question is this: if the federal government has been using neurotechnology to manipulate the cognition, behavior, and emotional states of American citizens without their knowledge or consent, why does Congress believe it needs to write new law to prohibit it? The Constitution already does. Every amendment that touches liberty, bodily integrity, due process, and equal protection already covers this. The framing of electromagnetic cognitive manipulation as a regulatory gap something the law needs to catch up to rather than as a set of existing constitutional violations already prohibitable under law, is not a neutral analytical choice. It is a choice with consequences. This essay examines what those consequences are, what the framing conceals, and what the gap between existing constitutional law and the MIND Act’s legislative approach implies about what has already been done and to whom.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*23YXFbKHUhCDW6nKi7uzew.png)

Richard Pearson describes how he experienced cognitive override with being drawn to a park.

### I. The Constitution Already Covers This

Begin with the most basic question: is non-consensual cognitive manipulation of an American citizen by the federal government currently constitutional? The answer is no. It has never been constitutional. The Constitution did not require updating for the neurotechnology era to prohibit it. Multiple amendments, individually and in combination, already forbid what the MIND Act treats as an unaddressed regulatory space.

#### The First Amendment: Cognitive Liberty as the Foundation of All Speech

_“First Amendment”, “Freedom of Thought and Speech”, “Congress shall make no law… abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble…”_

The First Amendment protects not only the expression of thought but the formation of thought from which expression originates. The Supreme Court recognized in Wooley v. Maynard (1977) that the First Amendment protects the freedom of mind. In Barnette (1943), the Court held that no official can prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters of opinion. The cognitive liberty implicit in these holdings the right to form beliefs, opinions, and decisions free from government compulsion is directly violated by technology that inserts content into a person thought stream, as Pearson documented at St. Bernard de Lacolle, or that directs behavior through neurological stimulation, as he documented in the pinning events. A government that uses voice-to-skull transmission to push directives into a citizen auditory processing pathway is not merely surveilling thought. It is attempting to override it. That has always been a First Amendment violation. No new statute is required to establish this.

#### The Fourth Amendment: The Brain as the Most Private Space

_“Fourth Amendment”, “Protection Against Unreasonable Search and Seizure”, The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated…”_

The Fourth Amendment protects persons against unreasonable government intrusion. In Carpenter v. United States (2018), the Supreme Court held that the government warrantless collection of cell-site location data constituted a Fourth Amendment search, reasoning that the intimacy and comprehensiveness of the data collected required constitutional protection regardless of whether it was technically accessible without physical trespass. The Court reasoning in Carpenter that data which reveals the privacies of life deserves Fourth Amendment protection applies with overwhelming force to neural data. If location data revealing where a person was over seven days is constitutionally protected, the electrical activity of a person brain which reveals what they think, feel, remember, fear, and desire is protected beyond any reasonable doubt. The warrantless collection of neural data through close-range devices at a public festival is a Fourth Amendment search. The non-consensual stimulation of a person nervous system to produce behavioral outputs is a Fourth Amendment seizure of the most intimate kind: the seizure of the person’s own agency over their body and mind. This has always been true. The MIND Act does not create this protection. It already exists.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/800/1*yvOskfJsSs6Nk6vr6_2Okg.jpeg)

#### The Fifth Amendment: Compelled Neural Testimony

_“Fifth Amendment”, “Protection Against Self-Incrimination and Deprivation Without Due Process”, “No person shall… be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law…”),_

The Fifth Amendment’s due process clause requires that the government not deprive a person of liberty without procedural and substantive legal protection. The liberty interest at stake when the government reads and writes to a person’s brain without their knowledge is the most fundamental liberty interest imaginable: the liberty of the mind itself. There is no deeper deprivation of liberty than the non-consensual alteration of a person\\u2019s cognition. The Fifth Amendment’s self-incrimination clause, under Schmerber v. California (1966) and its progeny, extends to testimonial and communicative disclosures. Whether neural data constitutes testimonial evidence under this framework is genuinely contested, but the due process prohibition on liberty deprivation without legal process is not contested at all. The government using electromagnetic technology to direct a citizen’s behavior, implant directives in their auditory cortex, and disrupt their working memory has deprived them of liberty. No new statute is needed to establish that this requires due process. The Fifth Amendment requires it now.”),

#### The Thirteenth Amendment: Involuntary Servitude Through Neural Compulsion

_“Thirteenth Amendment”, “Prohibition of Slavery and Involuntary Servitude”, “Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States…”_

The Thirteenth Amendment’s prohibition of involuntary servitude has been interpreted to cover not only chattel slavery but any condition of coerced labor or compelled service. Bailey v. Alabama (1911) established that the amendment reaches any system of compulsion that controls a person’s labor or movement through coercive means. The behavioral direction Pearson documented — the pinning events, the compulsion to travel to specific locations, the behavioral outputs produced by electromagnetic stimulation of the motivational system — are, under a Thirteenth Amendment analysis, a form of involuntary servitude. The government compelling a citizen’s body to move toward a location, to perform an action, or to experience a desire through neurological override is compelling the use of that person’s body and nervous system against their will. The amendment does not exempt the government’s technological methods of compulsion from its scope. Compulsion is compulsion regardless of the mechanism.

#### The Fourteenth Amendment: Equal Protection and the Racial Targeting Dimension

_“Fourteenth Amendment”, “Equal Protection of the Laws”, “No State shall… deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws._

The Equal Protection Clause prohibits government action that discriminates on the basis of race. The Cherry Blossom footage, the Lincoln Memorial footage, and Pearson’s fourteen months of documented patterns show a system operating with racial specificity: Black people disproportionately subjected to close-range biometric protocols, followed, and targeted for behavioral and cognitive manipulation. If the federal government is using neurotechnology in a manner that disproportionately targets Black Americans — as a continuation of the targeting logic that produced COINTELPRO — this is an Equal Protection violation of the most serious kind, subject to strict scrutiny, and already prohibited by existing constitutional law. The MIND Act’s concern about the “exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities” is a legislative acknowledgment of the same pattern. The Fourteenth Amendment’s response to that pattern is not a regulatory study. It is strict constitutional prohibition.

#### II. The Framing Problem: Why “Regulatory Gap” Is the Wrong Frame

“The MIND Act frames cognitive manipulation, behavioral direction, and neural data collection by federal agencies as a “gap” in the existing legal framework — something the law has not yet addressed, requiring new study and new guidance. This framing is incorrect as a matter of constitutional law, and its incorrectness is not trivial. The gap framing does several things simultaneously, each of which serves interests that are not aligned with accountability.

First, the gap framing implies that what has occurred so far was not illegal. If cognitive manipulation is merely unregulated — in a gray area awaiting guidance — then federal agencies that used neurotechnology on American citizens before the guidance was issued cannot be held accountable for doing something that was not yet prohibited. The gap framing creates retroactive immunity by implication: we didn’t prohibit it, so doing it wasn’t prohibited. But this is false. The Constitution prohibited it. The agencies that used it violated the Constitution. The gap framing obscures this by treating constitutional law as insufficient and new statutory law as necessary, when in fact the constitutional law was always sufficient and was simply ignored.

Second, the gap framing redirects the appropriate institutional response. If cognitive manipulation is a regulatory gap, the response is an FTC study and OSTP guidance — administrative processes that take years, produce recommendations, and generate no accountability for what has already occurred. If cognitive manipulation is an existing constitutional violation, the appropriate response is entirely different: congressional investigation with subpoena power, criminal referrals, judicial proceedings, and the full accountability architecture the Constitution provides. The gap framing substitutes the slower, weaker, accountability-free regulatory track for the constitutional enforcement track that the violations actually demand.

Third, and most importantly for understanding what the MIND Act implies about what has already happened: you do not write regulatory guidance for technologies that have not been deployed. The MIND Act’s Section 5 requires binding guidance on federal agency use of neurotechnology because federal agencies are using neurotechnology. The question of what to prohibit, what to permit, and what to condition on safeguards is only a live question if there are existing use cases to evaluate. Congress is not writing rules for hypothetical future use. It is writing rules for ongoing current use. And by choosing to write those rules prospectively, as regulatory guidance, rather than retrospectively, as accountability for past constitutional violations, it is choosing not to examine what the existing use cases actually are.

That choice — regulatory prospection instead of constitutional retrospection — is the choice that protects a program from scrutiny. It is the choice that a cover-up makes.

#### III. The Consent Framework as Constitutional Evasion

The MIND Act’s central mechanism for governing neurotechnology use is consent. Individuals must opt in. Federal agencies must obtain consent. Certain uses may be prohibited even with consent. The consent framework is the bill’s primary legal architecture.

This framework makes sense for commercial applications of neurotechnology — consumer devices, clinical treatments, employer monitoring programs. In those contexts, the individual has a relationship with the technology provider, the use is disclosed, and consent is a meaningful concept.

It makes no sense as the governing framework for what Richard Pearson experienced, and for a specific reason: non-consensual covert government use of neurotechnology is not a consent problem. It is a criminal problem. It is a constitutional violation problem. The appropriate legal response to a government agent who non-consensually transmits voices into a citizen’s skull is not an opt-in form. It is a criminal statute, a civil rights action, and a congressional investigation. The consent framework, applied to covert government neurotechnology use, is a category error — and a convenient one, because it treats the most serious form of the harm as if it were a variation of the least serious form.

The least serious form is a consumer device company that collects neural data without sufficiently clear disclosure. The most serious form is a federal intelligence agency that uses electromagnetic technology to push directives into a citizen’s auditory cortex, redirect their behavior, disrupt their cognition, and sexually assault their nervous system as part of a targeting campaign organized around their race, sexuality, and scholarly work. These are not the same problem on a spectrum. They are categorically different acts. Treating both under a consent framework collapses the distinction and, in doing so, obscures the constitutional severity of the latter.

The MIND Act does not contain a single provision addressing what happens when a federal agency uses neurotechnology on a citizen who did not and could not consent because they did not know the technology was being used. There is no criminal penalty. There is no private right of action. There is no whistleblower protection for government employees who observe unauthorized neurotechnology use on citizens. The bill’s silence on covert, non-consensual federal use — the most constitutionally serious category of harm — is not an oversight. It is a structural choice.

#### IV. What the Silence Implies: The Anatomy of a Cover-Up

A cover-up does not always announce itself. It announces itself through what is absent: the question not asked, the provision not included, the accountability mechanism not created, the retrospective investigation not initiated. Evaluated against what the bill omits, the MIND Act has the structural features of legislation designed to manage a problem rather than expose it.

#### No Retrospective Investigation

The bill directs a prospective FTC study. It does not direct any retrospective inquiry into whether federal agencies have already used neurotechnology on American citizens, under what authority, against which populations, and with what effects. A legislature that genuinely did not know whether such use had occurred would want to find out. A legislature that was managing awareness of such use would commission a forward-looking study that keeps the question of past conduct permanently off the table. Section 5\\u2019s requirement for future guidance is only coherent if there is current use to govern. The absence of a retrospective inquiry into that current use \\u2014 its scope, its targets, its authorization, its effects \\u2014 is the absence that most clearly signals what the bill is protecting.

#### No Criminal Penalties

The bill establishes no criminal penalties for federal agency neurotechnology misuse. It establishes no civil liability for individuals harmed by unauthorized federal neurotechnology use. It creates no private right of action. The entire enforcement architecture is administrative: guidance, study, recommendations. A bill designed to address constitutional violations already occurring would include criminal penalties for the actors committing those violations. A bill designed to manage the political exposure of those violations without triggering accountability for them would limit itself to administrative architecture. The MIND Act does the latter.

#### No Whistleblower Protection

If federal agencies are currently using neurotechnology on American citizens, there are federal employees who know about it. Some of them may have reservations about what they know. The MIND Act includes no protection for such employees — no expanded whistleblower shield for intelligence or law enforcement personnel who disclose unauthorized neurotechnology programs, no reporting mechanism, no immunity for those who come forward. The absence of whistleblower protection reflects an incomplete writing of the bill. That is intentional.

### Senate MIND Act Essentially Describes a 21st Century ‘Slavery Economy’ in US

The MIND Act was introduced in the US Senate in September 2025 to study and to regulate what are essentially mind control technologies. The bill implies a _Slavery Economy_ whereby individuals’ biometric data are collected, put into predictive models and databases, and used to manipulate cognition and behaviors. This is precisely what the bill outlines in terms of the current landscape: “_monetize” neural data, “shape individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making,” “risk of behavioral influence, cognitive manipulation, erosion of personal autonomy, and the exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities”, “risks of harm…such as discrimination, profiling, surveillance, manipulation,”_

However, the bill is not responding to risks in some distant future. These threats are real and imminent in the US now. Because regulatory laws are not proposed for technology that does not exist, **the bill’s language strongly suggests that a new form of a “Slavery Economy” exists in the US**. According to US torture victim, Richard Pearson, the _Slavery Economy_ is an open secret, highly racially discriminatory, and appears to be app-based. He estimates tens of millions of American victims.

The bill implies a major admission — that the government has no true sense of the extent and use of this technology. It mandates a report to include an assessment of “all relevant uses of neurotechnology, neural data, and other related data for understanding, analyzing, and influencing human states and behaviors.” In other words, the bill neither proposes a broad set of statues nor mandates rights or obligations. The information-seeking nature of the bill strongly suggests that Congress lacks adequate knowledge of the scope of the problem related to new forms of neuroweapons — as opposed to enumerated list of consumer rights, private right of action, mandatory federal registration, or government disclosure of past and current uses.

But Pearson believes that there is more to the picture, “The bill’s sponsors authored the bill as if they are at a loss for what these weapons are and who is using them. It includes $10 million to fund a government study. I call B.S. These three senators alone have a collective Senate tenure of 65 years, and over 122 years, collectively, if you count their House tenures. Congress already knows. The government already knows. This bill is crafted as if they don’t know the scale and scope of the problem. They want to avoid the obvious question of public accountability, “What didn’t they act earlier?”

### What is Meant by a “Slavery Economy”?

A _Slavery Economy_ in the context of neuro-manipulation describes a device or system that controls or steers thoughts, communication, or behaviors by 1) bypassing individual consciousness and 2) exploiting data about an individual’s mind and body to achieve some goal. That goal could be extractive, as in economic exploitation via cognitive override. People can be manipulated into shopping for certain products or with a specific business, even behaviorally steered to frequent a local business. The _Slavery Economy_ targets the mind and body, particularly the nervous system, to collapse “choice” — a buyer can hardly consider a different option.

Except, the victim will likely attribute a choice or behavior to self. _“No,_ **_I_** _made the choice to buy this.” “_**_I_** _decided to go to this business.”_ That self-attribution is ironically a barrier to increasing awareness of public knowledge. Richard Pearson explains, “I was pinned to locations that I did not consciously decide to go. I thought that I had a reason for why I was there — the self-attribution. But when I encountered “street theater” or a framing attempt, I knew that I have been pulled to that location.” Pearson has discussed [street theater](https://medium.com/@theconsciousstudy/red-and-black-as-psychological-weapons-dr-richard-pearsons-torture-diary-in-washington-dc-5289b4386c6d) and a [framing attempt](https://medium.com/@theconsciousstudy/red-and-black-as-psychological-weapons-dr-richard-pearsons-torture-diary-in-washington-dc-5289b4386c6d) elsewhere on Medium.com.

This is what neuroweapons do. The goal could also just be criminal, which is what Richard Pearson has described as his year of torture and terror in Washington, DC, starting with the second Trump administration. Combined with traditional forms of torture, that defined Pearson’s experience, “I had voice-to-skull, a physical assault then a false arrest, a chemical assault, electrocution of my penis, stalking, behavioral steering or “pinning”, a framing attempt, and much more. In Washington, DC. Near the US Capitol and White House. Near high security areas.”

### Why a Parallel to Slavery?

First, the bill is seeking to regulate an ecosystem where surveillance and data collection of biometrics — data about individuals’ mind and body — are then used as some form of individual control without consent or conscious choice. Arguably, that is worse that slavery because slavery is visible — as immoral and repugnant as slavery is. Slavery is visible.

Pearson explains how ultrasonic invasion works, “Look, this is not rocket science. It’s not some exotic technology. You can buy products on Amazon. It’s being used in museums. Two ultrasonic waves with different frequencies outside of human hearing are transmitted through the air. They come together, “de-modulate”. The difference of the two waves forms a third sound wave that the mind can hear. Voila. You have voice-to-skull. Just Google it.”

Another worst aspect to slavery is related to science — to be more precise, scientific knowledge. “Popular knowledge has not caught up with the published literature — technological capabilities that have known to exist for decades,” explained Pearson. The discovery of ultrasonic voice-to-skull was much earlier, “Ultrasonic neuromodulation was first observed in 1929, though it took decades to evolve into the precise brain-stimulating technology used today,” according to Google AI Overview. Dismantling the slavery economy will mean corrective action on the part of the American public, but other sectors of society that Pearson blames. “I blame government first and foremost — elected officials, regulators, public schools, public colleges and universities. We hear a news story and then move on. We have failed to consider and ask for answers for countless reports of victims and whistleblowers who have described various invisible forms of harmful technology.”

One victim in this new _Slavery Economy_ that Pearson has recently written about is Myron May — the alleged shooter at the Florida State University shooting in 2014. May alleged that the government used directed energy weapons, mind control technology, surveillance devices, and acoustic harassment to torture him. Pearson found Myron May when AI indicated that Pearson’s experiences paralleled May’s and Gloria Naylor’s — a famous African American fiction writer and author of _The Women of Brewster Place_. While Richard Pearson cannot establish May’s claims, he has done [considerable research that raises major questions](https://medium.com/@menvell.artist/who-is-the-mysterious-figure-unsettling-footage-from-inside-myron-mays-home-5c926edc6c5c) about the police investigation: the crouching figure in the news story, the mismatch between descriptions of the shooter (“black hoodie”, “all black”) and May’s attire (dress shirt, vest), lack of motive, lack of gun custody (police report admits that it doesn’t know how May acquired the gun), the impossible 20-second timeline, and indications about May’s left-handedness (the shooter was right-handed).

This illustrates a tragedy of the _Slavery Economy_ — its victims can be erased, worsening the tactics and weapon use due to public dismissal and scientific knowledge deficits.

Finally, the various forms and uses mean that victims in the Slavery Economy do not have one “master.” Pearson explains, “You can have behavioral steering to this location one day. Then another set of players overriding an individual’s cognition the next.” It’s a scary thought but is precisely what the MIND Act is describing.

### US Senate Bill Describes Weapons to Override Consciousness. It is Actually Describing a New Form of Slavery

#### Introduced in the US Senate in September 2025, the MIND Act ’s language is worth reading with full seriousness. It describes technologies that “monetize” neural data, “shape individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making,” create “risk of behavioral influence, cognitive manipulation, erosion of personal autonomy,” and cause “discrimination, profiling, surveillance, manipulation.” This is not a bill about future risks. Regulatory frameworks are not written for technologies that do not exist. Congress is describing a present condition.

### That condition has a precise name, and the precision matters: it is a Slavery Economy.

Not a metaphor. Not hyperbole. A structural description. An economy in which individuals’ biometric and neural data are collected, converted into predictive models, and used to override cognition and steer behavior — without the individual’s awareness, without their consent, and for someone else’s economic benefit. The individual does not know they are laboring. They do not know their choices are being authored. They believe, entirely, that they are free. That belief is not incidental to the system. ### The MIND Act Describes a Loss of Personal Autonomy and Ownership of One’s Mind and Body

The Management of Individuals’ Neural Data Act of 2025 is a Senate bill that directs the Federal Trade Commission to study the governance of neural data and related biometric information and report back to Congress within a year. It does not ban anything. It does not create rights. It does not establish penalties or give individuals a cause of action. It mandates a study, funds it at $10 million, and requires the Office of Science and Technology Policy to develop guidance for federal agencies on neurotechnology procurement after the report is submitted. By the standards of federal legislation, it is a modest instrument. By the standards of what it is describing, it is an alarm bell.

The alarm it is raising is specific. The bill’s own language — “monetize neural data,” “shape individual behavior, emotional states, and decision making,” “cognitive manipulation,” “erosion of personal autonomy” — is not speculative language about future risk. It is descriptive language about present conditions. Congress does not write regulatory language about technologies that do not exist or harms that have not materialized. The bill’s sense-of-Congress findings describe a commercial ecosystem in which neural and biometric data is already being collected, processed, sold, and used to influence human cognition and behavior, in which vertical corporate integration has created systems with “insufficient transparency, accountability, or user control,” and in which existing law — including HIPAA — does not reach it. These are findings about the current state of affairs. The bill is raising the alarm because the thing it is alarmed about is already operating.

What the bill is almost certainly responding to, beyond the public-facing neurotechnology industry, is a dawning institutional awareness that the scale and nature of cognitive exploitation in the United States is far larger and more serious than anything that has been publicly acknowledged. The technology capable of inferring mental states from biometric data, modulating mood and behavior through non-invasive stimulation, and bypassing conscious decision-making through subconscious targeting has existed in various forms for decades. It is in the published scientific literature. It is embedded in commercial platforms used by hundreds of millions of Americans daily. The fact that three senators with a collective congressional tenure exceeding a century are now framing this as something requiring urgent study strongly suggests that what is prompting the bill is not the recent emergence of the problem but the recent impossibility of continuing to ignore it — whether because the technology has become too visible, the commercial deployment too widespread, or the reports of harm too numerous and too consistent to be dismissed.

The deeper alarm the bill encodes, and does not fully state, is about autonomy — about whether the foundational condition of a free society, the capacity of individuals to form their own intentions and make their own choices, is being systematically dismantled by a commercial infrastructure that has no legal obligation to preserve it. The bill’s prohibition framework for federal agencies, its concern with “prohibited use cases regardless of individual consent,” and its explicit attention to consciousness bypass — the technical override of deliberate decision-making — all point toward a recognition that consent frameworks alone cannot protect against a technology that operates before consent is possible. A person cannot meaningfully consent to the manipulation of the cognitive processes through which they would evaluate whether to consent. The bill is responding to that paradox. It does not yet resolve it. What it does is place on the formal record of the United States Senate the acknowledgment that the paradox is real, that the technology producing it is deployed and operational, and that the law has nothing adequate to say about it.

_Richard Pearson, PhD, was motivated to write this AI-assisted essay because he experienced torture in 2025–2026 that involved voice-to-skull, electrocution, electromagnetic radiation, behavioral steering, a physical assault, and a chemical assault. The MIND Act’s description of neural technologies intersected with his experience._

### Parallels to US Slavery is No Exaggeration: Ten Structural Analogies Between 1848 and 2026

### **1\. The Extraction of Labor Without Consent**

In 1848, the enslaved person’s physical labor — the work of their hands, back, and body — was extracted for someone else’s economic benefit without their consent and without compensation. The person was the instrument of production.

In 2026, the cognitive labor of attention, decision-making, emotional response, and behavioral output is extracted from individuals through neural and biometric surveillance and fed into commercial systems that profit from it. The instrument of production is now the nervous system. The person still does not consent. They are still not compensated. The product has changed from cotton to data. The structure has not.

* * *

**2\. The Owner Who Does Not Appear**

In 1848, the plantation system was organized so that the enslaved person rarely encountered the ultimate beneficiary of their labor. The overseer was visible. The owner was distant. The system ran itself.

In 2026, the individual whose neural data is being collected, modeled, and monetized does not know who owns that data, who has purchased it, who is running behavioral models against it, or whose commercial objectives their engineered choices are serving. The overseer is the app. The owner is a data broker whose name they have never heard. The system runs itself.

* * *

**3\. The Invisibility of Chains**

In 1848, the chain was iron and visible. The coercion was legible to the enslaved person, to witnesses, to history. That visibility was morally catastrophic but epistemically clear — the enslaved person knew what was being done to them, even if they had no recourse.

In 2026, the coercion is electromagnetic and invisible. It operates below the threshold of conscious perception. The person being acted upon not only has no recourse — they do not know the coercion is occurring. The chain that cannot be seen cannot be broken, reported, or believed.

* * *

**4\. Self-Attribution as the New Overseer**

In 1848, external force — the whip, the threat of violence, the law — compelled compliance. The enslaved person knew the compliance was compelled. They did not mistake it for freedom.

In 2026, the mechanism of compliance is self-attribution: the engineered choice registers to the person as their own spontaneous preference. They say: I decided. I wanted this. I chose to go there. The overseer is interior. The compulsion is experienced as freedom. This is a more complete form of control than the whip, because it eliminates not only resistance but the recognition that resistance is warranted.

* * *

**5\. The Commodification of the Body**

In 1848, the enslaved person’s body was legally property — bought, sold, inventoried, and transferred in bankruptcy proceedings. Their physical being was a commodity on a balance sheet. In 2026, the bill explicitly addresses the transfer of neural data “through acquisitions, mergers, or bankruptcy proceedings.” A person’s biometric and neural profile — a detailed map of their cognitive vulnerabilities, emotional triggers, and behavioral patterns — is transferred between corporations as a line-item asset when companies are bought and sold. The body is not on the balance sheet. The map of the mind is.

* * *

**6\. Illiteracy as a Structural Requirement**

In 1848, it was illegal in most slaveholding states to teach an enslaved person to read. Literacy was suppressed because a literate population could organize, communicate, and contest its condition. Ignorance was not a side effect of the slavery economy — it was a legal requirement that maintained it.

In 2026, the Slavery Economy depends on scientific illiteracy: a public that does not know that pulsed electromagnetic fields can produce auditory perception, that closed-loop stimulation can alter mood and behavior in real time, or that AI can infer mental states from biometric data cannot recognize when these capabilities are being used against them. The illiteracy is not legally mandated. It is institutionally maintained — by public education systems that do not teach it, media that does not cover it, and a government that has not acted on it for decades.

* * *

**7\. The Law That Protects the System, Not the Person**

In 1848, the legal system did not merely fail to protect enslaved people — it actively protected the system that exploited them. The Fugitive Slave Act required free states to return escaped enslaved people to their owners. The law was the instrument of the economy.

In 2026, the legal system does not merely fail to protect people from cognitive manipulation — it provides no affirmative prohibition on it whatsoever. There is no federal law against using neural data to engineer a person’s behavior without their awareness. There is no private right of action for consciousness bypass. The law’s silence is structural. It protects the system by leaving it unaddressed.

* * *

**8\. Racial Targeting as a Feature, Not a Bug**

In 1848, the slavery economy was explicitly and legally racial. It was not merely that Black people happened to be enslaved — the system was architected to target them specifically, justified by ideologies that cast them as appropriate subjects of control, and maintained by institutions that dismissed their claims to personhood and autonomy.

In 2026, the bill acknowledges the “exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities.” The populations most surveilled, most behaviorally profiled, and most exposed to systems of cognitive management without recourse are the same populations that have historically been designated as appropriate subjects of control. The targeting is not coincidental. It follows the existing architecture of who has been rendered visible to systems of power and who has been denied the credibility to report harm.

The bill’s references to “vulnerable populations,” children, employment, financial services, housing, and the “exacerbation of existing social and economic disparities” describe a tiered exposure structure. The populations most exposed are those who are economically precarious, institutionally surveilled, or embedded in systems — workplaces, schools, social services — where their behavioral compliance is already monitored and managed. These are the populations whose data is most granular, whose behavioral patterns are most legible, and whose capacity to resist or seek recourse is most limited.

The racial dimension is not peripheral. It is structural. The bill’s acknowledgment that these technologies risk exacerbating existing social and economic disparities is a restrained way of saying that populations which have historically been subjected to surveillance, experimentation, and behavioral control without consent or accountability — the populations for whom the word “autonomy” has always been most contested — are the populations most likely to be the primary targets of the Slavery Economy.

* * *

**9\. The Fugitive Who Cannot Be Believed**

In 1848, an enslaved person who escaped and described their condition faced a system — legal, social, institutional — that was organized to return them, discredit them, or ignore them. Their testimony about their own experience was inadmissible as evidence in courts where their humanity was not legally recognized.

In 2026, a person who reports that their cognition has been interfered with, their behavior steered, their mental states altered without consent, faces a different but structurally identical response: dismissal. Not legal dismissal — social and institutional dismissal. The scientific illiteracy of the general public, the absence of legal frameworks that recognize the harm, and the self-concealing nature of the technology combine to ensure that the person who reports it is, by default, not believed. The harm is invisible. The victim is incredible. The system continues.

* * *

**10\. The Economy That Requires It**

In 1848, slavery was not an aberration in the American economy — it was a foundation of it. Cotton, built on enslaved labor, was the United States’ largest export. Based on economic data from 1860, the approximately 4 million enslaved people in the United States were indeed a massive financial asset, valued at an estimated $3 billion to $3.5 billion. This valuation made them the largest single financial asset in the American economy, second only to the value of the land itself. The financial system, the insurance industry, and the industrial economy of the North were deeply entangled with it. Abolition was resisted not only on ideological grounds but because the economy had been built around the assumption that this form of extraction would continue.

In 2026, behavioral manipulation through neural and biometric data is not a fringe practice — it is embedded in the commercial infrastructure of the internet, the attention economy, the advertising industry, and the platforms through which hundreds of millions of Americans conduct their daily lives. The companies doing it are among the most valuable in the world. Regulation is resisted not only because of ideological commitments to innovation, but because the economy has been built around the assumption that this form of cognitive extraction will continue. The structural parallel is precise: in both cases, what is being protected is not a practice. It is an economy.
